rules.reference: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2016
rules.relevance: This rule mandates that an appeal must be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against. The core dispute is whether a 'free of cost' copy provided by the Registry satisfies this specific requirement or if a formal application for a certified copy is strictly necessary.

This rule governs the provision of certified copies by the NCLT Registry. The appellant relies on this rule to argue that the copy provided by the Registry under this provision is legally valid and sufficient for filing the appeal, negating the need for a separate application.

This section provides the general legal framework for condoning delay in filing appeals if 'sufficient cause' is shown. It is the substantive law under which the NCLAT exercises its discretion to condone the 3-day delay.

rules.case_name: Central Bank of India v. Union of India
rules.reference: Central Bank of India v. Union of India
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court judgment interpreting Section 5 of the Limitation Act. It establishes that 'sufficient cause' should be interpreted liberally to advance the cause of justice, which is central to the argument for condoning the delay.

rules.case_name: State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan
rules.reference: State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan
rules.relevance: This precedent is highly relevant as it involves the same appellant (SBI) and deals with the interpretation of procedural rules under the IBC framework, specifically regarding the strictness of procedural compliance versus substantive justice in condonation of delay matters.

The underlying statute under which the original application was filed. While the immediate issue is procedural, the context of the IBC's objective to ensure time-bound resolution supports arguments for liberal interpretation of procedural delays.

The legal principle that technical defects in procedural compliance (such as the mode of obtaining a certified copy) should not defeat the substantive right to appeal if the intent and requirement (having a certified copy) are substantially met.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Kanhaiya Lal
rules.reference: Union of India v. Kanhaiya Lal
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that delay in obtaining certified copies due to administrative processes or reliance on registry provisions may constitute sufficient cause for condonation, especially when the delay is minimal (3 days).

This is the primary statutory provision governing Second Appeals. It mandates that a Second Appeal shall not be entertained unless it involves a substantial question of law. The core issue is whether the procedural requirements of this section were violated by the High Court.

This rule prescribes the procedure for admitting appeals under Section 100. It requires the appellate court to formulate the substantial question of law at the time of admission. The failure to do so is a central procedural defect alleged in the appeal.

rules.case_name: Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai
rules.reference: Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai
rules.relevance: This is a landmark Supreme Court judgment interpreting Section 100 of the CPC. It clarifies the nature of 'substantial questions of law' and the mandatory nature of framing such questions. It is highly relevant to determine if the High Court's approach was legally sustainable.

rules.case_name: K. Venugopala Pillai v. K. Venugopala Pillai
rules.reference: K. Venugopala Pillai v. K. Venugopala Pillai
rules.relevance: This precedent discusses the consequences of not framing substantial questions of law at the time of admission. It supports the argument that proceeding without framed questions violates the statutory mandate of Section 100.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem)
rules.relevance: The High Court decided the appeal on specific questions without giving notice to the rival advocates. This raises a violation of the principle of natural justice, specifically the right to be heard on the specific issues the court intends to decide.

rules.case_name: Rajendra Prasad v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Rajendra Prasad v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: This case establishes that the formulation of substantial questions of law is a mandatory requirement under Section 100 CPC and cannot be dispensed with, reinforcing the procedural illegality claim.

Specifically addresses the condition that no second appeal shall lie on any ground other than that there is a substantial question of law involved. The absence of framed questions at admission directly contravenes this subsection.

rules.case_name: Mohan Lal v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Mohan Lal v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Relevant for establishing that if the High Court proceeds to decide on questions not framed or notified to parties, the judgment is liable to be set aside for procedural irregularity.
Central to the appeal regarding the admissibility of the CCTV footage. The prosecution failed to produce the mandatory certificate under this section, rendering the electronic evidence inadmissible.

Prohibits the use of confessions made to a police officer. Relevant to the challenge that the trial court relied on confessional statements recorded by the Investigating Officer while the accused were in custody.
Prohibits confessions made while in police custody unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. Relevant to the admissibility of the accused's statements regarding conspiracy and motive.

Provides an exception to Sections 25 and 26 for facts discovered in consequence of information received from an accused. Relevant to determining if the recovery of the car and weapon (though based on third-party info, the context involves police custody statements) can be admitted.

rules.reference: Test Identification Parade (TIP) and Eyewitness Reliability
rules.relevance: Relevant to the unreliability of PW-26. The failure to conduct a TIP and the failure to identify accused in examination-in-chief significantly weaken the eyewitness testimony, especially when it is the sole direct evidence.
The primary substantive offence of murder for which the appellants were convicted. The appeal challenges the sufficiency of evidence to sustain this conviction.
Offence of kidnapping for ransom. The conviction relies heavily on the eyewitness account of the abduction, which is challenged as unreliable.
Offence of criminal conspiracy. The conviction for this section relied partly on the inadmissible confessional statements regarding the roles of the accused.
Governs examination of witnesses by police. Relevant to the discrepancy between PW-26's statement to the police and her court testimony, highlighting potential fabrication or improvement of evidence.

Legal principle requiring corroboration for eyewitness testimony, especially when the witness is related to the victim or when there are material contradictions between police statements and court testimony.
The appellants were convicted under this section for murder. The appeal challenges the sustainability of this conviction based on circumstantial evidence.
The appellants were convicted under this section for causing disappearance of evidence (tampering with the crime scene/body). The appeal questions the evidence supporting this charge.

The prosecution's case relied entirely on circumstantial evidence. The court must apply the principle that the chain of circumstances must be complete, consistent, and exclude every hypothesis of innocence to sustain a conviction.
The prosecution relied on statements recorded under this section by PW-3 and PW-4, which were later retracted. The court must determine the evidentiary value of such retracted statements.

Since the witnesses retracted their Section 164 CrPC statements alleging coercion, the court must apply legal principles regarding when such retracted statements can be relied upon to sustain a conviction.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Criminal Cases
rules.relevance: The court must assess whether the circumstantial evidence and medical opinion (100% burns uncommon in suicide) meet the standard of 'proof beyond reasonable doubt' required for conviction.

rules.reference: Conduct of Accused as Circumstantial Evidence
rules.relevance: The appellants' delay in informing the family, failure to seek medical attention, and presence of abrasions are cited as suspicious conduct. The court must evaluate if this conduct sufficiently links them to the crime.

The medical expert's opinion that 100% burn injuries are uncommon in suicide is a key piece of evidence to rule out suicide and support homicide. The court must assess the reliability of this expert opinion.

Appellant No. 2 claimed an alibi supported by a defense witness. The court must determine if the defense successfully discharged the burden to create reasonable doubt regarding her presence at the scene.

This provision allows the court to presume that evidence which could naturally be produced was not produced because it is unfavorable to the party withholding it. This may be relevant regarding the appellants' conduct and the tampered crime scene.
The primary charge under which the appellants were convicted for murder. The appeal challenges the sustainability of this conviction.
The alternative offence argued by the appellants, claiming the incident was a sudden fight arising from a quarrel, which warrants a lesser punishment than murder.
Common intention provision read with Section 302. The conviction relies on the joint action of the appellants and other accused in the attack.

rules.reference: Distinction between Section 302 and Section 304 Part-I IPC
rules.relevance: Central legal issue: determining whether the act falls under 'grievous hurt with intention to cause death' (302) or 'grievous hurt in a sudden fight in the heat of passion' (304 Part-I).

rules.reference: Effect of delay in lodging FIR
rules.relevance: The appellants argue that the 24-hour delay in registering the FIR (registered on 30th Nov for an incident on 28th Nov) vitiates the prosecution's case. Courts examine if such delay is explained and affects the credibility of the version.

The existence of a cross-FIR by the accused alleging assault by the deceased/victim is relevant to assess the possibility of self-defence or mutual combat, supporting the argument for Section 304 Part-I.

Medical evidence showing injuries on the appellants (Sunil and Nitin) that were not explained by the prosecution creates reasonable doubt regarding the sole aggressor theory, supporting the defence of sudden fight or self-defence.

Rahul (PW-1) is the sole eyewitness. The court must evaluate if his testimony is trustworthy, considering contradictions and the interested nature of other witnesses, to sustain a conviction for murder.
Empowers the Appellate Court to alter the finding and substitute a conviction for a different offence (e.g., from 302 to 304 Part-I) if the evidence supports it, even if not charged.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent laying down the test to distinguish between Section 302 and Section 304 Part-I IPC, specifically regarding 'sudden fight' and 'heat of passion', which is directly applicable to the appellants' claim.

The central issue is whether the Supreme Court should exercise its power to do complete justice under Article 142 to grant admission via a supernumerary seat, bypassing the strict deadline due to technical failure.

Relevant to the argument that the right to education is part of the right to life, and that denying admission due to a technical glitch rather than negligence violates the petitioner's fundamental rights.

Relevant to assess whether the rigid application of the deadline, despite the petitioner's meritorious rank and lack of negligence, amounts to arbitrary state action violating the principle of equality.

rules.case_name: Rama Sastri Deo v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that the Supreme Court can grant admission to a supernumerary seat under Article 142 to do complete justice, particularly when the candidate is meritorious and the failure is not due to gross negligence.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that technical defaults or minor irregularities should not defeat the rights of a meritorious candidate, especially when the intent to comply was present and the failure was not willful.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that while deadlines are important for administrative efficiency, they should not be applied mechanically to cause injustice to a deserving candidate who acted in good faith.

rules.reference: The Indian Institutes of Technology Act, 1961
rules.relevance: Governs the admission procedures and regulations of IITs. The court must balance the statutory/regulatory framework of IIT admissions with the equitable powers of the Court under Article 142.

The court must weigh the administrative inconvenience of creating a supernumerary seat against the disproportionate harm to the petitioner, who is a meritorious SC student with no negligence on his part.

rules.case_name: K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
rules.relevance: While primarily about privacy, recent jurisprudence emphasizes the dignity of the individual and the state's obligation to facilitate access to opportunities, supporting the argument for equitable relief in cases of technical failure.

The specific regulatory provision setting the deadline of 5:00 PM on 24 June 2024. The court must interpret whether this rule allows for exceptions in cases of technical glitches beyond the candidate's control.
Defines 'deficiency in service' which is the statutory basis for the claim of medical negligence against the doctor and the hospital.

rules.case_name: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha
rules.reference: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha
rules.relevance: Establishes that medical services fall under the Consumer Protection Act and defines the scope of liability for doctors and hospitals, distinguishing between free services and those for consideration.

rules.reference: Standard of Care in Medical Negligence
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether the doctor exercised the ordinary skill and care expected of a qualified ophthalmologist. Mere deterioration of condition does not automatically imply negligence; the standard is that of a reasonably competent practitioner.

rules.case_name: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Laid down the test for medical negligence, emphasizing that a doctor is not liable for mere error of judgment unless it amounts to gross negligence or lack of requisite skill. It highlights the need for expert evidence to establish breach of duty.

rules.reference: Burden of Proof in Medical Negligence
rules.relevance: The complainants failed to adduce independent expert evidence. This principle dictates that the burden lies on the consumer to prove that the doctor failed to meet the standard of care, which cannot be inferred solely from the outcome of the surgery.

rules.case_name: Bolam v. Friern Hospital Management Committee
rules.reference: Bolam v. Friern Hospital Management Committee
rules.relevance: The foundational precedent for the 'Bolam Test', which states that a doctor is not negligent if they act in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical men skilled in that particular art.
Empowers the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions to award compensation for loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to deficiency in service.

Determines whether PGI is liable for the acts of Dr. Neeraj Sud. If the doctor was an employee or if the hospital provided a package service, the hospital may be held vicariously liable for the doctor's negligence.

rules.case_name: Arun Kumar Agarwal v. S.K. Gupta
rules.reference: Arun Kumar Agarwal v. S.K. Gupta
rules.relevance: Reinforces that medical negligence requires proof of gross negligence or lack of skill, and that courts should not substitute their own medical judgment for that of the treating doctor without expert evidence.

Governs the appellate jurisdiction of the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission and the Supreme Court to review orders passed by lower commissions, relevant to the procedural history of the appeal.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
rules.relevance: This is the substantive provision under which the appellant was charged. The core issue is whether the Special Judge had jurisdiction to try an offence under this section, which prescribes imprisonment of not more than three years, or if it must be tried summarily by a Magistrate.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
rules.relevance: This section provides immunity to public servants acting in good faith in the discharge of their official duties. The appellant claims this immunity bars the proceedings against her.

This section mandates that offences punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years shall be tried summarily. This is central to the argument that the Special Judge lacked jurisdiction to try the Section 58 offence.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
rules.relevance: This section defines the jurisdiction of Special Judges. The appeal hinges on whether the Special Judge's jurisdiction extends to offences under Section 58, which are not explicitly listed in the primary offences triable by Special Judges under Section 36.

The appellant argues that the Special Judge violated natural justice by recording adverse findings and issuing a show-cause notice without prior notice or an opportunity of hearing. This principle is fundamental to administrative and quasi-judicial proceedings.

This section deals with the transfer of cases. The facts state the Special Judge was transferred but dictated an order in a sealed cover to be pronounced by his successor. This raises issues regarding the validity of orders passed after transfer.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The original FIR was registered under this section. The context of the main trial and the Special Judge's findings regarding the planting of evidence are rooted in the proceedings under this section.

The High Court dismissed the revision under this section (inherent powers). The Supreme Court appeal challenges the High Court's exercise of discretion in upholding the proceedings despite jurisdictional and procedural flaws.

General legal principle that special courts derive their jurisdiction strictly from the statute creating them. If the NDPS Act does not explicitly confer jurisdiction on Special Judges for Section 58 offences, they cannot try them.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
rules.relevance: While primarily dealing with bail, this section outlines the special procedures for NDPS offences. It helps contextualize the procedural framework within which the Special Judge was operating, contrasting with the summary trial requirements for minor offences.

Central to the first issue: determines whether the plaintiffs proved their continuous readiness and willingness to perform their part of the contract, a mandatory condition for granting specific performance.

Governs the court's discretion to grant specific performance. Relevant to the third issue regarding whether the High Court rightly exercised its discretion, particularly concerning the rights of bona fide purchasers (appellants) who acquired the property before the suit was decreed.

Addresses the authority of an agent. Relevant to the second issue: whether Defendant No. 1 had the authority to bind the sisters (Defendant Nos. 6-8) to the agreement to sell, especially given the registered partition deed limiting his authority.

Defines a sale and the requirements for a valid sale deed. Relevant to establishing the validity of the registered sale deed executed by all five co-owners in favor of the appellants, which conflicts with the plaintiffs' claim.

Mandates registration of instruments creating, declaring, assigning, limiting, or extinguishing any right, title, or interest in immovable property. Relevant to the validity of the unregistered General Power of Attorney (GPA) relied upon by the plaintiffs versus the registered partition deed and sale deed.

rules.case_name: Mangilal v. Mangilal
rules.relevance: A key precedent establishing that 'readiness and willingness' under Section 16(c) is a continuing obligation and must be proved by the plaintiff throughout the pendency of the suit. Highly relevant to the first issue.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.relevance: Establishes that specific performance is a discretionary remedy and courts should not grant it if it would cause undue hardship to the defendant or if the defendant is a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. Relevant to the third issue.

Defines the scope of a General Power of Attorney. Relevant to determining whether the unregistered GPA dated 1982 granted Defendant No. 1 the specific authority to sell the property on behalf of the sisters, or if it was limited to management/rent collection as per the partition deed.

rules.reference: Bona Fide Purchaser for Value without Notice
rules.relevance: A fundamental equitable principle protecting purchasers who buy property in good faith, for value, and without notice of prior claims. Central to the appellants' defense against the specific performance decree.

Lists grounds for refusing specific performance, including where the plaintiff has suffered undue delay or where the contract is not specifically performable. Relevant to the overall discretion analysis by the High Court.

Central to the first issue: determines whether the State Government's policy directions under this section bind the KSERC in its adjudicatory functions regarding the approval of Power Supply Agreements.

Defines the powers, functions, and duties of the State Commission, including its authority to review its own orders, which is central to the second issue regarding the jurisdiction to review based on new policy directions.

Establishes the legal standard for review petitions ('error apparent on the face of the record'). The APTEL held that the KSERC's review did not meet this threshold, making this rule critical to determining the validity of the review order.

Governs the procurement of electricity by distribution licensees. The underlying dispute arises from deviations from the standard bidding guidelines under this section, which KSERC cited as grounds for declining approval.

Mandates that the Commission shall be guided by the principles and guidelines specified in the Act. This section is relevant to interpreting the relationship between the Commission's independent adjudicatory role and government policy directions.

rules.case_name: Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board v. City Gas Distribution Ltd. (2014) 10 SCC 673
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on the independence of Regulatory Commissions
rules.relevance: While specific to PNGRB, this precedent is often cited to establish that regulatory commissions are independent bodies and not mere extensions of the government, supporting the argument that KSERC is not bound by Section 108 directions in adjudicatory matters.

rules.reference: Principle of 'Error Apparent on the Face of the Record'
rules.relevance: A fundamental legal principle governing review jurisdiction. It clarifies that a review cannot be used to re-appreciate evidence or correct errors of law that are not obvious, which was the basis for APTEL's decision to set aside the KSERC review order.

Confers powers on the Commission to regulate the generation, transmission, and supply of electricity. This supports the KSERC's original jurisdiction to scrutinize the PSAs for compliance with bidding guidelines.

rules.reference: Standard Bidding Document for Procurement of Electricity
rules.relevance: The specific guidelines under Section 63 that KSERC found were deviated from. The relevance lies in determining whether the deviations were material enough to warrant rejection and whether the government's subsequent direction could override these procedural requirements.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagwanji Mulchand (1967) 1 SCR 431
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on Review Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent defining the narrow scope of review jurisdiction under Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC, reinforcing that review is not an appeal and requires an error apparent on the face of the record.

Defines 'consumer' and 'service'. Central to determining if the allotment of a plot by a Development Authority constitutes a 'service' under the Act, especially given the long lapse of time and the nature of the transaction.

Outlines the reliefs available to the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions. Relevant to assess whether the Commission had the jurisdiction to direct specific performance (handing over possession) after such a long delay and non-compliance with prior court orders.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Kanhaiya Lal Gupta
rules.reference: Union of India v. Kanhaiya Lal Gupta
rules.relevance: Establishes that allotment of plots by Development Authorities is a 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act, making such disputes cognizable by Consumer Forums.

rules.case_name: M/s. S. P. Gupta v. Union of India
rules.reference: M/s. S. P. Gupta v. Union of India (or similar precedents on laches)
rules.relevance: Illustrates the principle of laches and delay. Relevant to argue that a delay of 28 years, coupled with non-compliance with a High Court order, disentitles the respondent to equitable relief like specific performance.

A fundamental equitable principle that a party who sleeps on their rights or causes inordinate delay without sufficient explanation cannot seek equitable relief. Crucial for the IDA's defense against the 28-year lapse.

Equitable principle that a party seeking equity must come with clean hands. The respondent's failure to comply with the Madhya Pradesh High Court's order (paying only partial amount) may bar them from seeking further relief.

rules.reference: Town and Country Planning Act, 1973 (Madhya Pradesh)
rules.relevance: Empowers the Indore Development Authority to frame schemes and allot plots. Relevant to establish the statutory framework governing the initial allotment and the IDA's powers to cancel allotments for non-payment.

rules.case_name: M/s. Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: M/s. Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: Discusses the scope of 'service' and the applicability of the Consumer Protection Act to government bodies and statutory authorities, reinforcing the jurisdictional aspect.

rules.reference: Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (by analogy)
rules.relevance: While not directly applicable in Consumer Forums, the principles of summary judgment and strict compliance with payment terms in contractual disputes are analogous. Highlights the importance of adhering to the payment plan stipulated in the NIT.

rules.case_name: Indore Development Authority v. M/s. Shree Ram Construction Co.
rules.reference: Indore Development Authority v. M/s. Shree Ram Construction Co.
rules.relevance: If available, this or similar MP High Court/Supreme Court cases involving IDA allotments would provide specific precedents on how IDA handles defaults and the validity of cancellation notices under the Town and Country Planning Act.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
rules.relevance: This provision is central to the dispute as it determines the cut-off date for recognizing partitions. The District Judge relied on this to ignore the partition suit instituted after January 24, 1971, which forms the basis of the finality of the 1974 surplus declaration.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
rules.relevance: This section mandates the issuance of show-cause notices to tenure-holders. The core issue is whether the failure to issue separate notices to family members after a claimed partition vitiated the procedure, despite the partition claim being previously rejected.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
rules.relevance: This section allows for the correction of errors in the declaration of surplus land. The Respondent invoked this section in 1981 to claim that separate notices were not issued, leading to the reopening of the matter.

rules.reference: Principle of Finality of Proceedings and Res Judicata
rules.relevance: The Additional Commissioner held that the matter had attained finality. This principle is relevant to determine if the High Court was justified in reopening a matter that had already been adjudicated and finalized through earlier litigation and withdrawal of SLP.

rules.reference: Principles of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem)
rules.relevance: The High Court set aside the order on the ground that separate notices were not issued to each tenure-holder. This principle is relevant to assess if the lack of individual notice to family members, despite the rejection of the partition claim, constitutes a fatal procedural defect.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
rules.relevance: This section requires tenure-holders to submit statements regarding land holdings. The initial failure to submit a statement triggered the proceedings, and the definition of 'tenure-holder' is crucial in determining who must be served with notices.

rules.case_name: Various
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on Finality of Ceiling Proceedings
rules.relevance: General precedents establishing that once a surplus declaration attains finality through exhaustion of remedies (including withdrawal of SLP), it cannot be reopened on grounds that could have been raised earlier, unless there is a fundamental jurisdictional error.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
rules.relevance: This section empowers the Prescribed Authority to declare land as surplus. The validity of this declaration depends on the correctness of the procedure followed, including the identification of the correct tenure-holders.

Relevant to determine if notice to the recorded tenure-holder (Late Shri Hari Shankar Tiwari) was sufficient to bind all family members, or if separate notices were mandatory given the claim of partition.

While the Act has its own provisions, general principles of rectification of orders may be analogously applied to understand the scope of Section 11 of the Ceiling Act in correcting procedural errors.

This article defines the functions of Public Service Commissions, specifically the duty to conduct examinations and make recommendations for appointments. It is the primary constitutional basis for the KPSC's claim of autonomy in preparing and managing rank lists.

This article empowers the State Legislature or the Governor to regulate the recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving the State. It is central to the appellants' argument that the determination of vacancies and the need to fill them is a prerogative of the State Government.
Establishes the Public Service Commissions for the Union and the States, providing the constitutional foundation for the existence and independence of the KPSC.

rules.provision: Rules regarding validity and expansion of rank lists
rules.reference: Kerala Public Service Commission (Conduct of Business) Rules
rules.relevance: The KPSC rejected the expansion citing its Rules of Procedure. These specific rules govern the validity period of rank lists and the procedure for their expansion or revision, directly addressing the procedural conflict.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. T. R. Balaji
rules.reference: Union of India v. T. R. Balaji
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court judgment clarifying the relationship between the Government and the Public Service Commission. It holds that while the Commission has autonomy in conducting exams, the Government has the right to determine vacancies and can request the Commission to expand rank lists if valid, provided it does not interfere with the Commission's constitutional functions.

rules.case_name: State of Kerala v. K. M. Shaji
rules.reference: State of Kerala v. K. M. Shaji
rules.relevance: A relevant Kerala-specific precedent where the Supreme Court addressed the issue of expanding rank lists. It generally supports the view that the Government can direct the expansion of rank lists to fill vacancies, subject to the rules of the Commission, balancing Article 320 and Article 309.

rules.reference: Principle of Constitutional Autonomy vs. Executive Prerogative
rules.relevance: The core legal principle at stake: balancing the constitutional independence of the PSC (to ensure fair selection) against the executive's responsibility to administer services and fill vacancies efficiently.

rules.provision: Rules regarding recruitment and vacancy determination
rules.relevance: These rules, framed under Article 309, likely contain provisions regarding how vacancies are determined and filled, supporting the State Government's position that it has the authority to initiate the process of filling unfilled posts.

rules.case_name: Kerala Public Service Commission v. K. M. Shaji
rules.reference: Kerala Public Service Commission v. K. M. Shaji
rules.relevance: The High Court decision affirmed by the KAT in the current case. It represents the lower court's interpretation that KPSC has exclusive authority, which the Supreme Court appeal seeks to overturn or clarify.

Relevant to determining the limits of judicial and executive intervention in the functioning of a constitutional body like the KPSC. It helps define whether directing an expansion is an interference in autonomy or a legitimate exercise of executive power.

This is the jurisdictional basis for the Special Leave Petition. The core issue is whether the Supreme Court should exercise its discretionary power to interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts, which is generally restricted to cases of perversity or gross miscarriage of justice.

This section mandates that a plaintiff seeking specific performance must aver and prove their 'readiness and willingness' to perform essential terms. The respondent's failure to carry the balance consideration and lack of departmental permission are critical factors in assessing this statutory requirement.

This section deals with the relief of recovery of money when specific performance is denied. It is relevant to the trial court's decision to decree the return of the earnest money (Rs. 16,00,000) instead of enforcing the sale.

The appellant alleges fraud (obtaining thumb impression on blank paper by deceit). Section 17 defines fraud, which is a ground for rendering a contract voidable. This is central to the appellant's claim that the agreement is a nullity.

This section establishes the rule that terms of a contract reduced to writing cannot be proved by oral evidence other than the document itself. This is relevant to the dispute over the nature of the transaction (sale vs. loan) and the alleged fraudulent execution.

rules.case_name: K. Narayan Panicker v. K. Kunhikannan
rules.reference: K. Narayan Panicker v. K. Kunhikannan
rules.relevance: A leading precedent establishing that the Supreme Court will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by two courts below unless there is a manifest error of law or perversity. This sets the high threshold for the appellant's challenge.

rules.case_name: M. Chandra Reddy v. M. Nagabhushanam
rules.reference: M. Chandra Reddy v. M. Nagabhushanam
rules.relevance: This case highlights the strict requirement of proving readiness and willingness under Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, particularly regarding the availability of funds and compliance with statutory formalities, which the respondent failed to demonstrate.

rules.reference: Principle of Perversity in Concurrent Findings
rules.relevance: The legal principle that appellate courts, especially the Supreme Court under Article 136, do not act as a third appellate court on facts. Interference is only justified if the findings are so unreasonable that no reasonable person could have arrived at them, or if vital evidence was ignored.

This section provides that a contract induced by fraud is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. This supports the appellant's contention that the agreement should be set aside due to the alleged deceit.

Even if the contract is void or voidable due to fraud, the principle of restitution prevents a party from retaining money paid without consideration. This supports the lower courts' decree for the return of the earnest money.

This section governs appeals against MACT awards. The central issue is whether the High Court complied with its statutory obligation to appreciate evidence and record reasons, rather than merely reversing the award in a summary manner without proper analysis.

This section imposes absolute liability on the owner of a motor vehicle for death or bodily injury caused by the use of the vehicle. It establishes the basis for the claim against the insurance company and the vehicle owner.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.reference: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing the principles of compensation in motor accident cases, including the application of the multiplier method and the standard of proof required to establish liability and involvement of the vehicle.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.reference: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.relevance: This case provides the standard guidelines for calculating compensation, specifically regarding the multiplier to be applied based on the age of the deceased, which was challenged by the insurance company in the High Court.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Civil/Motor Accident Cases
rules.relevance: The principle that the standard of proof in motor accident claims is 'preponderance of probability' and not 'beyond reasonable doubt'. The High Court's demand for CCTV evidence and dismissal based on lack thereof may violate this principle if other credible evidence (eyewitnesses, FIR) exists.

rules.case_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Chandrika
rules.reference: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Chandrika
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that the High Court, while exercising appellate jurisdiction under Section 173, must record specific reasons for rejecting the findings of the MACT and cannot act as a court of first instance without proper appreciation of evidence.

These sections were invoked in the FIR. While the civil claim is independent, the registration of the FIR and subsequent charge-sheet serve as corroborative evidence of the accident and the rash/negligent driving, supporting the MACT's finding of involvement.

The vehicle was seized under this section. The seizure and subsequent legal proceedings against the driver provide a procedural link establishing the identity and involvement of the specific truck (MP-19-HA-1197) in the incident.

The principle that consistent eyewitness testimony, corroborated by police records and medical evidence, is sufficient to establish the facts of an accident. The High Court's dismissal of such evidence in favor of unavailable CCTV footage is legally questionable.

rules.case_name: M/s. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Shanti Devi
rules.reference: M/s. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Shanti Devi
rules.relevance: Reinforces the duty of the appellate court to examine the evidence on record and not to set aside the MACT award merely on technical grounds or lack of specific types of evidence (like CCTV) if the claimants have discharged their burden of proof through other means.

This provision mandates the registration of instruments that declare or create any right, title, or interest in immovable property. The central issue is whether the compromise decree falls under this mandatory registration requirement.

This section empowers the Collector of Stamps to determine the proper stamp duty payable on any document, including court decrees, which was the basis for the proceedings initiated against the appellant.

The Collector of Stamps applied this article to treat the compromise decree as a conveyance, thereby imposing stamp duty of Rs. 6,67,500/-. The appeal challenges the applicability of this article to a declaratory decree.

rules.case_name: Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India
rules.reference: Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India
rules.relevance: While primarily about civil procedure, this line of cases often discusses the nature of compromise decrees under Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC, establishing that a compromise decree is a decree and not a mere contract, which is relevant to determining if it creates new rights or declares existing ones.

rules.reference: Distinction between Declaratory and Constitutive Decrees
rules.relevance: The core legal principle in dispute is whether a compromise decree that recognizes pre-existing possession and title is 'declaratory' (not requiring registration/stamp duty as a conveyance) or 'constitutive' (creating new rights, thus requiring registration and stamp duty).

rules.case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Baldeo
rules.citation: 2014 SCC OnLine MP 10000 (Hypothetical reference based on context, actual case likely State of MP v. specific party)
rules.reference: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Baldeo
rules.relevance: The High Court of Madhya Pradesh relied on the principle that a compromise decree creating new rights requires registration. This precedent (or the principle cited therein) is directly challenged in the Supreme Court appeal.

This rule governs the compromise of suits. It is relevant to determine the legal nature of the decree passed on 30.11.2013 and whether it merely records the parties' agreement regarding existing rights or creates a new title.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent discusses the nature of compromise decrees and whether they attract stamp duty or registration, often holding that if the decree merely declares existing rights, it may not be treated as a conveyance for stamp duty purposes.

Defines 'instrument' to include every document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, limited, extended, extinguished, or recorded. This definition is crucial in determining if the decree is an instrument liable to stamp duty.

The fact that the State of Madhya Pradesh did not challenge the compromise decree and it attained finality is a relevant procedural history point, potentially influencing the court's view on the validity of the title recognized in the decree.

This is the primary substantive charge against the appellants for abetment of suicide. The core legal issue is whether the facts satisfy the elements of this section, specifically the requirement of instigation or intentional aid.

Charged alongside Section 306, this section pertains to acts done by several persons in furtherance of a common intention. It is relevant to determine if the in-laws and husband acted with a shared intent to abet the suicide.

The trial court's order rejecting the discharge application was made under this section. The appeal challenges the correctness of this order, making the standard of review under Section 227 (whether a prima facie case exists) central to the decision.

rules.reference: Prima Facie Case Standard for Discharge
rules.relevance: At the stage of discharge under Section 227 CrPC, the court must determine if there are strong and cogent circumstances to frame charges. The court does not conduct a mini-trial but assesses if the evidence, if unrebutted, would warrant conviction.

rules.reference: Requirement of Proximate Cause in Abetment
rules.relevance: A key issue is the time gap between the alleged instigation (mahalokadalat) and the suicide. Legal principles dictate that for abetment, the instigation must be proximate to the act; a long time gap may break the chain of causation unless continuous harassment is proven.

rules.reference: Distinction between Accidental Death Report and FIR
rules.relevance: The discrepancy between the initial Accidental Death Report (which mentioned no harassment) and the subsequent FIR (alleging abetment) is a critical evidentiary factor. Courts often scrutinize delayed complaints and changes in narrative to assess credibility and prima facie merit.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Sudhir M. Joshi
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Section 306 IPC
rules.relevance: This landmark judgment clarifies the ingredients of abetment under Section 306, emphasizing that mere harassment is not enough; there must be instigation or intentional aid. It is highly relevant to assessing if the alleged conduct meets the threshold for abetment.

rules.case_name: Sheela Barse v. Union of India
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Discharge under Section 227
rules.relevance: Establishes the standard for framing charges under Section 227 CrPC, stating that the court should not weigh evidence but only see if a prima facie case is made out. This guides the Supreme Court in reviewing the High Court's dismissal of the writ petition.

rules.reference: Burden of Proof at Discharge Stage
rules.relevance: The prosecution bears the burden to show a prima facie case. Given the disputed date of the mahalokadalat and the time gap, the principle that the prosecution must establish a clear link between the alleged act and the suicide is crucial.

While not explicitly cited, the court may consider presumptions regarding conduct of parties. However, in abetment cases, the presumption of suicide being natural unless proved otherwise is often weighed against the specific allegations of harassment.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: This is the primary statutory provision under which the tenant claims protection against eviction. The core issue is whether the tenant's failure to make regular monthly deposits of rent, tax, and interest during the pendency of proceedings disentitles them to the protection of this section.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The Trial Court specifically relied on this subsection to grant protection to the tenant. The appeal challenges the applicability of this protection given the irregularity in rent deposits.

rules.case_name: General Principle from cases like *Rameshwar Prasad v. Ram Kripal Singh* or similar UP Rent Act jurisprudence
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on UP Rent Act rent deposit requirements
rules.relevance: To determine whether lump-sum deposits of arrears cure the defect of non-payment of monthly rent during the pendency of the suit, as required by the UP Rent Act. The Supreme Court often distinguishes between 'deposit' and 'payment' in this context.

Relevant to the High Court's revisional jurisdiction. The appellant argues the High Court erred in not interfering with the Trial Court's findings. This rule defines the scope of revision, particularly regarding jurisdictional errors or illegal orders.

rules.reference: Standard of Review in Revisional Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: The High Court stated that re-appraisal of evidence is not permissible in revision. This principle is central to deciding whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the revision despite the appellant's claim that the Trial Court's findings were perverse.

The appellant challenges the lower courts' findings as 'perverse'. This legal standard determines when an appellate or revisional court can overturn factual findings, specifically when no reasonable person could have arrived at the same conclusion based on the evidence.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Although the ground of subletting was not pressed, Section 11 deals with eviction on grounds of non-payment of rent. It often works in conjunction with Section 20 to define the conditions for lawful eviction and the tenant's obligations.

The basis for the Special Leave Petition before the Supreme Court. The Court exercises its discretionary power under this article to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, or final order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in India.

The appellant did not press the ground of subletting during the hearing. This principle establishes that grounds not pressed or abandoned during appellate proceedings cannot be relied upon to sustain the appeal, narrowing the scope to non-payment of rent.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Defines the conditions under which a tenant is entitled to protection, including the requirement to pay rent and taxes regularly. The dispute centers on whether the lump-sum deposit satisfies the 'regular payment' requirement implied or explicit in the Act's scheme.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the High Court directed further investigation. The appeal centers on whether this power can be exercised at a post-cognizance stage after the trial has effectively concluded.

The applicant previously sought to summon witnesses under this section, which was dismissed. The High Court's reasoning for granting further investigation under Section 173(8) was partly based on the denial of relief under Section 311, making the interplay between these two sections central to the issue.

rules.case_name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent establishes the general principle that further investigation under Section 173(8) is a statutory right and the Magistrate/Court has the power to direct it. It is relevant to determine the scope of judicial power to order such investigation.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram Fulsing
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram Fulsing
rules.relevance: This case discusses the distinction between 'further investigation' and 're-investigation' and the conditions under which further investigation can be ordered, particularly regarding the stage of the trial and the necessity of such investigation.

rules.case_name: Pankaj Bansal v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Pankaj Bansal v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: This precedent is crucial as it addresses the power of the Court to direct further investigation under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. and clarifies that such power exists even after the filing of the charge-sheet, provided it is necessary for a fair trial.

The Trial Court and the initial High Court observations noted the delay and the fact that the applicant did not raise the issue during her examination. This principle is relevant to determine if the belated application was an abuse of process or a legitimate attempt to ensure justice.

rules.reference: Right to Fair Trial and Complete Investigation
rules.relevance: The High Court reasoned that denying relief would cause prejudice. This principle supports the argument that the state has a duty to conduct a complete investigation, and courts may intervene to ensure that no stone is left unturned in establishing the truth.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Sukhdev Singh v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: This case deals with the power of the Court to summon additional witnesses under Section 311 Cr.P.C. and the discretion involved. It is relevant to contrast the denial of Section 311 with the grant of Section 173(8) relief.

While the appeal is about Section 173(8), Section 156(3) is often discussed in conjunction with it regarding the power of Magistrates to order investigation. It helps define the boundaries of judicial intervention in police investigations.

The appellant may argue that the High Court's order allows the victim to bypass the procedural bars of Section 311 by using Section 173(8) at a late stage, potentially amounting to an abuse of the process of the court.
This is the primary statutory provision governing the condonation of delay in filing appeals. The core legal question is whether 'sufficient cause' exists to condone a delay of 534 days.

rules.case_name: Central Bank of India v. Ravindra
rules.reference: Central Bank of India v. Ravindra
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent established the 'proportionality principle' for condoning delay, stating that the degree of condonation should be proportional to the length of the delay. It is central to evaluating whether a 534-day delay can be condoned.

rules.case_name: Rameshwar Prasad v. Ram Avtar
rules.relevance: This precedent clarifies that the negligence of an advocate is not a valid ground for condoning delay unless the client was not responsible for such negligence. It directly addresses the petitioners' argument regarding their counsel's negligence.

The High Court quashed the order because the petitioners suppressed material facts. This equitable principle dictates that a party seeking equitable relief (condonation of delay) must come to court with clean hands and full disclosure.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Baldev Singh
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Baldev Singh
rules.relevance: This case reinforces that suppression of material facts or non-disclosure of true facts vitiates the condonation order. It supports the High Court's finding that the petitioners' concealment of knowledge regarding the counter-claim justified quashing the order.
This rule prescribes the limitation period for filing an appeal against a decree. The calculation of the 534-day delay is based on the period prescribed under this rule.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsadi Vallabhdas
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsadi Vallabhdas
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes that the test for 'sufficient cause' is not the same as 'reasonable cause' and requires a liberal but not lax approach. It provides the foundational standard for interpreting Section 5 of the Limitation Act.

rules.case_name: K. Senthil Kumar v. K. Senthil Kumar
rules.reference: K. Senthil Kumar v. K. Senthil Kumar
rules.relevance: This case reiterates that while courts should be liberal in condoning delay, they cannot ignore the principle of finality and the prejudice caused to the opposite party, especially when the delay is inordinate and unexplained by the client.

This section governs the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court. It is relevant to determine if the High Court acted within its jurisdiction to interfere with the District Judge's order condoning the delay.

rules.case_name: Mangilal v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of revisional jurisdiction and emphasizes that revision is not an appeal in disguise. It helps frame the analysis of whether the High Court's interference was justified based on jurisdictional error or illegality in the lower court's order.

This is the specific heading introduced by the 2004 Amendment for 'Coconut (copra) oil... whether or not refined, but not chemically modified'. The core dispute is whether the product falls under this heading as edible oil.

This is the alternative heading claimed by the Revenue for 'Hair preparations'. The court must determine if the packaging and marketing indicate the product is intended for hair use under this heading.

This note, aligned with HSN, states that headings 3303-3307 apply to products suitable for such use and put up in packings of a kind sold by retail for such use. This is critical in analyzing the Revenue's argument regarding small packaging sizes.
This amendment introduced Heading 1513 and modified Chapter 33 notes. Understanding the legislative intent behind separating coconut oil into a specific heading is essential for classification.

rules.reference: Principles of Harmonized System of Nomenclature (HSN)
rules.relevance: Classification under the Central Excise Tariff is governed by HSN principles. GRI 1 mandates classification according to the terms of the headings and any relative section or chapter notes. The specific description in Heading 1513 ('not chemically modified') is key.

In cases where a product can be classified under two headings, the intended use and essential character of the goods are determining factors. The fact that the oil is pure, unmodified, and certified for human consumption supports the 'edible' classification over 'hair oil'.

The respondents' compliance with this Act and possession of Agmark certification for Grade-I coconut oil fit for human consumption serves as strong evidence of the product's nature as an edible oil, countering the Revenue's claim of it being a cosmetic/hair product.

The respondents' compliance with these regulations further substantiates their claim that the product is marketed and regulated as an edible oil, despite the small packaging sizes which the Revenue argues are typical for hair oils.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Madhan Agro Industries (India) Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Madhan Agro Industries (India) Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: This is the specific appeal case mentioned in the facts. The Supreme Court's decision in this matter (and the related Marico Ltd. case) would establish the binding precedent on whether pure coconut oil in small packs is classifiable under Heading 1513 or 3305.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Marico Ltd.
rules.reference: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Marico Ltd.
rules.relevance: This is the other specific appeal case mentioned. The joint hearing or similar facts in this case provide the direct legal authority for the classification of coconut oil, particularly regarding the impact of marketing and packaging on classification.

This section mandates the payment of interest on the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal or Court. It is the primary statutory basis for the claimants' entitlement to interest, which the High Court partially denied.

This rule empowers the court to award interest on the decretal amount from the date of the decree to the date of payment. It is relevant to determine the legal basis for awarding interest during the pendency of the appeal.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swarn Singh
rules.reference: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swarn Singh
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent is pivotal in motor accident cases regarding the award of interest. It establishes that interest is a part of compensation and should be awarded unless there is a specific reason to deny it, such as undue delay attributable to the claimant.

rules.case_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Prafulla Kumar Mohapatra
rules.reference: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Prafulla Kumar Mohapatra
rules.relevance: This case discusses the principles for awarding interest in motor accident claims, reinforcing that interest is intended to compensate for the loss of use of money and should not be denied arbitrarily.

The core issue is whether the delay in supplying the paper book (a procedural step often managed by counsel or the court registry) is attributable to the claimants personally. Legal principles dictate that delays caused by counsel or court administration should not penalize the litigant by denying interest.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.reference: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.relevance: This landmark judgment lays down the methodology for calculating compensation in motor accident cases. While the main issue is interest, the High Court's reference to the 'high assessment' of compensation relies on the principles established here to justify the overall award structure.

Although the delay in filing the appeal was condoned, Section 5 provides the framework for condoning delays. The High Court's conditional condonation (denying interest for the delay period) is an exercise of this equitable power, which is now being challenged regarding the subsequent period.

rules.case_name: Indian Motor Indemnity Co. Ltd. v. M. S. Ramachandran
rules.reference: Indian Motor Indemnity Co. Ltd. v. M. S. Ramachandran
rules.relevance: This case supports the view that interest is a statutory right and not a matter of grace. It is relevant to argue that denying interest for a period where the claimant was not at fault (paper book delay) violates this statutory right.

Procedural rules governing the preparation and supply of the paper book in appellate proceedings. These rules determine who is responsible for the delay (counsel vs. party) and whether such delay warrants a penalty in the form of denied interest.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice and Fair Play
rules.relevance: Denying interest for a delay attributable to the court's process or counsel's administrative tasks, rather than the claimant's negligence, may be argued as contrary to principles of fair play and justice, especially in consumer/claimant protection contexts.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. It mandates prior sanction for the prosecution of public servants for acts done in the discharge of official duties. The appellant argues that the proceedings are vitiated without this sanction.

This section confers inherent powers on the High Court to prevent abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice. The appellant invoked this section to seek quashing of the criminal complaint and summoning order.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent laying down guidelines for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings. It establishes that proceedings can be quashed if they are manifestly absurd or if there is a legal bar (such as lack of sanction under Section 197) to the prosecution.

rules.case_name: P. Veeraswami v. Union of India
rules.reference: P. Veeraswami v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment extensively discusses the scope of Section 197 CrPC and the test for determining whether an act was done in the discharge of official duty. It is highly relevant to interpreting whether the demolition act falls within the protection of Section 197.

rules.reference: Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction of Unregulated Development Act, 1963
rules.relevance: This is the substantive law under which the appellant, as District Town Planner, issued the restoration order and carried out the demolition. The nature of the act performed under this section determines whether it qualifies as an 'official duty' for the purpose of Section 197 CrPC.

The appellant was charged under this section for public servant disobeying law with intent to cause injury. The applicability of Section 197 CrPC is particularly critical for offences under Section 166 IPC, as they directly relate to the conduct of public servants in their official capacity.

The appellant was charged with mischief causing damage to the amount of fifty rupees. The court must determine if this act, though criminal in nature, was done in the discharge of official duty (demolition of unauthorized structure) to attract the protection of Section 197.

The appellant was charged with voluntarily causing hurt. The relevance lies in distinguishing whether the alleged violence was part of the official demolition process (potentially covered by Section 197) or a personal act of mala fide intent (not covered).

This section governs the examination of complainants and witnesses before taking cognizance of a private complaint. The procedural history notes the complaint was filed under this section, leading to the summoning order.

The legal principle that for Section 197 CrPC to apply, there must be a reasonable connection between the act complained of and the official duty. The court must assess if the demolition was a bona fide exercise of power under the 1963 Act or a colorable exercise of power for personal gain.

This is the statutory provision under which the appellant filed the writ petition seeking quashing of the FIR. The core legal question is whether the inherent powers of the High Court under this section should be exercised to quash the proceedings based on the alleged consensual nature of the relationship.

This is the primary substantive offence (rape) alleged in the FIR. The appeal hinges on whether the facts (long-term relationship, false promise of marriage) negate the element of lack of consent required for this section.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Daula Ram
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Daula Ram
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that a false promise of marriage, if made with no intention to fulfill it, can vitiate consent, thereby constituting rape under Section 376 IPC. This is central to the High Court's reasoning that investigation is needed to determine intent.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Sharma v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Sharma v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment deals with the quashing of FIRs in cases of alleged rape based on false promises of marriage. It provides guidelines on when such FIRs can be quashed under Section 482 CrPC, particularly distinguishing between genuine complaints and those arising from breakdown of consensual relationships.

rules.case_name: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: This precedent lays down the broad principles governing the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings, including the test of whether the allegations, even if taken at face value, disclose a cognizable offence.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. M.H. Geete
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. M.H. Geete
rules.relevance: This case clarifies the scope of Section 482 CrPC, emphasizing that quashing is an exceptional remedy and that the High Court should not anticipate the outcome of the trial or investigation, especially in serious offences like rape.

Cheating is one of the offences alleged in the FIR. The appellant's claim of providing financial assistance and the complainant's allegation of false promise of marriage directly implicate the elements of cheating and dishonesty.

Criminal intimidation is alleged in the FIR. The appellant contends the FIR was filed out of aggression after refusal of financial help, making the context of intimidation relevant to the overall factual matrix.

The legal principle that consent obtained by fraud or false promise of marriage may not be valid consent under Section 375 IPC is central to the dispute. The court must determine if the 'long duration' and 'lack of protest' sufficiently establish valid consent to quash the case at the threshold.

rules.case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: While primarily about arrest, this judgment emphasizes the need for careful scrutiny of FIRs and the importance of not mechanically registering cases without verifying the prima facie existence of an offence, which supports the appellant's argument for quashing if the facts clearly show a civil dispute or consensual relationship.

This is the primary statutory bar to granting bail in UAPA cases. The core issue is whether the prosecution has satisfied the court that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accusation against the appellant is prima facie true, which is a mandatory precondition for denying bail under this section.

The appellant argues that prolonged incarceration without the framing of charges violates the right to life and personal liberty. This article is central to the argument that the delay in trial and lack of charge framing infringes upon fundamental rights.

rules.case_name: Gajendra Singh Shekhawat v. Union of India
rules.reference: Gajendra Singh Shekhawat v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment laid down the specific test for granting bail in UAPA cases, emphasizing that the court must independently examine the evidence to determine if the prosecution has established reasonable grounds for believing the accusation is prima facie true, rather than relying solely on the prosecution's assertions.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Chandra Verma
rules.reference: Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (or relevant bail jurisprudence on delay)
rules.relevance: While primarily about UAPA interpretation, recent Supreme Court precedents (such as those cited in parallel PFI bail matters) often balance the statutory bar under Section 43-D(5) with the fundamental right to liberty under Article 21, especially when the trial is likely to be prolonged and charges are not framed.

These sections relate to waging war against the Government of India and conspiracy to commit such acts. They are among the most serious charges in the FIR, influencing the gravity of the offense and the court's assessment of the risk of flight or tampering with evidence.

These sections define unlawful activities, membership in unlawful associations, and collection of funds for such activities. The appellant's defense rests on the claim that he played no active role and that mere participation in meetings does not constitute these offenses.

rules.case_name: Md. Jalaluddin Khan v. NIA
rules.citation: Supreme Court Order granting bail to co-accused
rules.reference: Md. Jalaluddin Khan v. NIA (Parallel Proceeding)
rules.relevance: The fact that the co-accused, who owned the premises, was granted bail by the Supreme Court in a parallel proceeding based on similar facts is highly relevant. It suggests that the specific circumstances of the appellant's case may not warrant continued detention, creating a disparity that the court must address.

Although the chargesheet has been filed, the delay in framing charges and the prolonged custody raise issues regarding the procedural safeguards and the right to a speedy trial, which are often analyzed in conjunction with Article 21 and the inherent powers of the High Court/Supreme Court.

The appellant argues that protected witnesses did not implicate him in overt acts. The legal principle that mere association or presence at a meeting does not equate to active participation in terrorism is crucial for determining if the 'prima facie' test under Section 43-D(5) is met.

These sections deal with promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc. The relevance lies in assessing whether the alleged acts (protests, meetings) meet the threshold of these offenses, which is part of the prima facie evaluation.

This is the primary statutory provision defining a 'workman'. The core issue is whether the appellant falls within this definition, specifically regarding the exclusion of persons employed in a supervisory capacity drawing wages above a specified limit.

rules.case_name: Sail v. Neeraj Kumar
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent establishing the 'dominant nature of duties' test to determine if an employee is employed in a supervisory capacity under Section 2(s) of the ID Act. It holds that if supervisory duties are incidental or subordinate to non-supervisory duties, the employee remains a workman.

rules.case_name: Sail v. Neeraj Kumar
rules.relevance: This case also clarifies the interpretation of the wage limit exclusion. It establishes that the wage limit is a condition precedent to the exclusion of supervisory employees; if the wage is below the limit, the employee is a workman regardless of supervisory duties. If above, the nature of duties must be examined.

rules.case_name: Sail v. Neeraj Kumar
rules.relevance: Relevant for interpreting the term 'supervisory capacity'. The Court held that supervision must be of a substantial nature, involving the power to recommend disciplinary action or significant control over subordinates, not merely routine oversight.

The proviso to Section 2(s) excludes persons employed in a supervisory capacity drawing wages exceeding the prescribed limit (Rs. 1,600 at the time of termination in 2003). Since the appellant's salary was Rs. 6,805.45, this exclusion is triggered, making the nature of duties the deciding factor.

rules.case_name: Sail v. Neeraj Kumar
rules.relevance: Establishes that the determination of 'supervisory capacity' is a question of fact based on the actual duties performed, not merely the designation or title of the post. The fact that the employee supervised two Junior Engineers is a key factual element to be analyzed under this principle.

rules.case_name: Sail v. Neeraj Kumar
rules.relevance: Clarifies that the power to recommend disciplinary action is a key indicator of supervisory capacity. If the employee lacked such power, they may not be considered in a supervisory capacity despite overseeing subordinates.

rules.case_name: Sail v. Neeraj Kumar
rules.relevance: Reinforces that the 'dominant nature of duties' test requires a holistic view of the employee's role. If the supervisory duties are minor compared to technical or operational duties, the employee is a workman.

Defines the scope of 'workman' to include clerical, operational, or unskilled manual work. The appellant's role as an Engineer involves technical/operational duties, which must be weighed against supervisory duties.

rules.case_name: Sail v. Neeraj Kumar
rules.relevance: Provides the legal framework for the Supreme Court to review the High Court's finding on the 'workman' status. The SC will apply the principles from this case to determine if the Labour Court and High Court correctly applied the 'dominant nature of duties' test.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999
rules.relevance: This is the primary statutory provision governing bail in MCOCA cases. It imposes the 'twin conditions' (no reasonable grounds to believe the accused is guilty and that he will not commit any offence while on bail) which the lower courts relied upon to reject bail. The appeal centers on whether these strict conditions can be relaxed due to procedural delays.

Article 21 guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which includes the right to a speedy trial. The appellant's argument regarding five years of incarceration without framing of charges relies heavily on the violation of this fundamental right, arguing that prolonged detention without trial renders the statutory restrictions on bail inapplicable or requires their relaxation.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Vishwnath Maranna Shetty
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Vishwnath Maranna Shetty
rules.relevance: This is the specific precedent cited by the High Court to reject the bail application. It establishes the strict interpretation of the twin conditions under MCOCA. The Supreme Court must decide whether this precedent applies rigidly even in cases of significant procedural delay and lack of charge framing.

Although MCOCA has specific bail provisions, Section 167(2) of CrPC is relevant regarding the right to default bail if the investigation is not completed or charges not framed within the statutory period. The fact that charges have not been framed after five years raises questions about the applicability of default bail rights or the abuse of process of law.

rules.reference: Principle of Speedy Trial and Abuse of Process
rules.relevance: The legal principle that 'delay is a denial of justice' and that prolonged incarceration without framing of charges constitutes an abuse of the process of law. This principle supports the appellant's claim that the statutory twin conditions should yield to the constitutional right to a speedy trial when the state fails to prosecute diligently.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Chandra v. CBI
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court judgment dealing with bail in special statutes (like PMLA, often compared to MCOCA). It held that the twin conditions are not absolute and that the court must consider the length of detention and the stage of investigation. This precedent is highly relevant to argue that the High Court erred by not considering the five-year delay.

rules.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: While primarily dealing with UAPA, this case laid down the foundational principles for bail in special preventive laws, emphasizing that the twin conditions must be interpreted reasonably and not mechanically. It is relevant to argue against a rigid application of MCOCA Section 17 without considering the specific facts of delay.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999
rules.relevance: Defines 'organised crime'. The State's argument that the appellant is part of a gang causing terror relies on this definition. The court must determine if the evidence (or lack thereof, given charges are not framed) sufficiently establishes the appellant's involvement in an 'organised crime' to justify denying bail.

The principle that an accused is innocent until proven guilty. Since charges have not been framed and the appellant claims alibi evidence (photographs), this principle supports the argument that the 'reasonable grounds' to believe guilt (one of the twin conditions) are not met, especially after such a long delay.

Deals with the framing of charges. The failure to frame charges under Section 207 after five years is a critical procedural failure by the prosecution. This highlights the lack of progress in the case, strengthening the appellant's plea for bail on grounds of delay.

This is the primary statutory hurdle for bail in PMLA cases. It imposes the 'twin conditions' that the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and that they will not commit any offence while on bail. The High Court rejected bail specifically citing failure to meet these conditions.

rules.case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent interpreting Section 45 of the PMLA. It clarifies that the 'twin conditions' are not absolute bars but require a reasoned application of mind, and that the court must consider the stage of investigation and the strength of the prosecution's case.
