rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v. P. Ramachandra Rao
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh v. P. Ramachandra Rao
rules.relevance: This is the leading precedent specifically addressing custodial deaths in Andhra Pradesh. It establishes that the burden of proof shifts to the State to prove that the death was not caused by police excesses and that the plea of self-defence must be scrutinized with extreme caution, especially when the deceased was in custody.

rules.reference: Article 21 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The right to life and personal liberty is the foundational constitutional guarantee violated in custodial deaths. The Supreme Court has held that the State has a strict liability to protect the life of persons in custody, and any death in custody raises a presumption of state responsibility unless rebutted by cogent evidence.

The primary charge against the accused police officials is murder. The appeal concerns whether the evidence at the pre-trial stage is sufficient to sustain a charge of murder or if the plea of self-defence negates the mens rea and actus reus required for this section.

This section defines the exceptions to the right of private defence of the body. It is crucial to determine if the police officials' actions fell within the limits of self-defence or if they exceeded them, thereby attracting criminal liability under Section 302.

The High Court exercised its inherent powers under this section to quash the proceedings. The Supreme Court must review whether this power was exercised judiciously or if it usurped the function of the trial court by deciding factual disputes regarding self-defence at the pre-trial stage.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram Firkhriya
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram Firkhriya
rules.relevance: This precedent lays down the principles for exercising inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC. It establishes that inherent powers should not be used to decide disputed questions of fact, which is the core issue here: whether self-defence is a factual dispute requiring trial.

The accused are charged with causing disappearance of evidence and giving false information to screen the offender. This charge is relevant if the court finds that the 'encounter' was staged, implying an intent to conceal the true cause of death.

This section deals with the liability of members of an unlawful assembly. It is relevant to determine if the police officials acted in concert as an unlawful assembly to commit the murder, which would make each member liable for the act.

A well-settled legal principle in Indian jurisprudence is that when a person dies in police custody, the burden shifts to the State to prove that the death was not due to police excesses. The State cannot rely merely on its own investigation reports to discharge this burden without independent corroboration.

This section provides for common intention. It is relevant to assess whether the police officials shared a common intention to kill the deceased under the guise of self-defence, which is a factual determination typically reserved for trial.

The core issue is the scope of the High Court's jurisdiction under Section 11. The appellant argues the court exceeded its jurisdiction by examining merits rather than just the existence of the arbitration agreement.

rules.case_name: BGS SGPL Ltd. v. NHPC Ltd.
rules.reference: BGS SGPL Ltd. v. NHPC Ltd.
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent establishes the limited scope of judicial intervention under Section 11, distinguishing between 'existence' and 'validity' of an arbitration agreement, and limiting the court's inquiry to prima facie existence.

rules.case_name: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation
rules.reference: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation
rules.relevance: This case clarifies the exceptions where a court can refuse to refer a matter to arbitration (e.g., null and void agreements, non-arbitrable disputes). It is relevant to determine if the High Court's finding of 'manifestly dishonest claim' justified refusing reference.
The respondent initiated CIRP under Section 9. The interplay between the IBC and the Arbitration Act is central, specifically whether a pending arbitration claim can defeat a default under the IBC.

rules.case_name: Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India
rules.reference: Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This precedent holds that the IBC is a special law and that the existence of an arbitration clause does not automatically bar the initiation of insolvency proceedings if a default is established.

rules.case_name: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.reference: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.relevance: Establishes that the NCLT's jurisdiction under the IBC is triggered by the existence of a 'debt' and 'default', and it does not adjudicate the merits of the dispute or defenses raised by the corporate debtor at the admission stage.

Although the application was under Section 11, Section 8 principles regarding the duty of courts to refer parties to arbitration if there is an arbitration agreement are relevant to the standard of review applied by the High Court.

rules.reference: Prima Facie Existence of Arbitration Agreement
rules.relevance: The legal principle that under Section 11, the judicial authority is only required to examine whether a prima facie arbitration agreement exists, and not to delve into the merits of the dispute or the validity of defenses like fraud unless the agreement itself is challenged.

rules.case_name: Board of Control for Cricket in India v. Cochin Smart City Development Ltd.
rules.reference: Board of Control for Cricket in India v. Cochin Smart City Development Ltd.
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that the court's role under Section 11 is limited to examining the existence of an arbitration agreement and should not adjudicate on the merits of the dispute.

Defines 'default' under the IBC. The dispute centers on whether the disputed invoices constitute a 'default' despite the arbitration claim, which is a question of fact for the NCLT, not the High Court in arbitration proceedings.

This article grants the Supreme Court the power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India, which is the basis for the appellant's petition.
The appellant was convicted under this section for murder. The central issue is whether the evidence supports this conviction given the acquittal of co-accused on similar evidentiary grounds.

Although not explicitly listed in the charges in the brief, the context of 'common intention' or joint liability is implied by the presence of co-accused and the High Court's reasoning that 'no one else could have caused the injury.' Precedents regarding the distinction between individual liability and common intention are relevant.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Balram Bapuji Chavan
rules.relevance: This is a leading precedent establishing that the conviction of one accused and acquittal of another is not per se illegal, provided the court records specific reasons for distinguishing between them. It is directly relevant to the issue of whether the High Court's differential treatment was justified.

rules.case_name: Laxman v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: This case discusses the principle that if the testimony of a witness is found unreliable regarding the overt acts of co-accused due to distance or visibility, it casts doubt on the entire prosecution case, including the identification of the main accused, unless there is independent corroboration.

rules.reference: Principle of Corroboration and Reliability of Eyewitness Testimony
rules.relevance: The legal principle that the testimony of a single eyewitness, especially when found unreliable regarding co-accused due to physical constraints (distance), requires careful scrutiny and often corroboration to sustain a conviction for murder.

rules.reference: Principle of Reasoned Decision Making in Differential Convictions
rules.relevance: The principle that when a court acquits some accused and convicts others based on the same witness testimony, it must provide cogent and specific reasons for the distinction. A mere assertion that 'no one else could have done it' without addressing the reliability of the witness's perception may be insufficient.

This section outlines the powers of the Appellate Court (High Court) to alter findings, sentences, or convictions. It is relevant to assess whether the High Court exercised its powers correctly in upholding the conviction while acquitting co-accused.

rules.case_name: Panchu v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: This case highlights the importance of the position of the witness and the possibility of viewing the incident. If the witness was too far to see the co-accused, the credibility of their identification of the main accused is also suspect.

The appellant was also convicted under this section for obscene acts in public. While the murder charge is primary, the consistency of the witness's testimony regarding the initial abuse (Section 294) versus the fatal act (Section 302) is relevant to the overall credibility assessment.

Defines 'mortgage by deposit of title deeds' (equitable mortgage). The central issue is whether the Agreement dated 24.06.2000, involving the handing over of title deeds to secure a debt, satisfies the requirements of this section, specifically the intention to create a security interest.

Defines various types of mortgages. Relevant to distinguish between a simple mortgage, mortgage by conditional sale, and equitable mortgage, and to determine if the transaction was intended as a sale or a security for a loan.

Governs the procedure for setting aside an ex-parte decree or order. The appellant challenged the High Court's dismissal of his application to set aside the First Impugned Order, claiming lack of proper representation/authorization.

Deals with representation of parties, including the validity of Vakalatnamas (power of attorney for advocates). Relevant to the appellant's claim that his counsel was only authorized for condonation of delay and not for the main appeal hearing.

rules.case_name: Karnataka Bank Ltd. v. M. Venugopal
rules.reference: Karnataka Bank Ltd. v. M. Venugopal
rules.relevance: A leading precedent on equitable mortgages. It establishes that the intention to create a mortgage must be clear from the surrounding circumstances and the deposit of title deeds, even if the document does not explicitly state it is a mortgage.

rules.case_name: State Bank of India v. Shyama Devi
rules.reference: State Bank of India v. Shyama Devi
rules.relevance: Clarifies that for a valid equitable mortgage, there must be a deposit of title deeds with the intention to create a security. The court looks at the substance of the transaction rather than just the form.
General principles of contract validity. Relevant to determine if the Agreement dated 24.06.2000 was a valid contract, considering factors like free consent, lawful consideration, and capacity.

Requires the court to ascertain which parties appear and by whom they are represented. Relevant to the procedural dispute regarding whether the appellant was properly represented during the appeal hearing.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem)
rules.relevance: The right to be heard. The appellant's challenge to the ex-parte order relies on the principle that a party cannot be condemned unheard, especially if they were not properly represented or notified.
Deals with the rights of the mortgagee. If the court finds a valid mortgage, this section outlines the remedies available to the appellant, including the right to sue for foreclosure or sale.

The appellant's primary challenge is that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by interfering with concurrent findings of fact. Section 100 CPC strictly limits the High Court's power to grant a Second Appeal only on a 'substantial question of law', prohibiting re-appreciation of evidence unless the findings are perverse or based on no evidence.

This section provides for divorce on the ground of cruelty. The High Court granted divorce based on mental cruelty (false dowry complaint) and desertion. The Supreme Court must determine if the High Court's interpretation of 'cruelty' and 'desertion' involved a substantial question of law or was merely a factual determination.

This section provides for divorce on the ground of desertion. The High Court found the appellant had deserted the respondent for over fifteen years. The relevance lies in whether the finding of 'voluntary desertion' without reasonable cause was a factual finding protected from second appeal or a legal conclusion.

rules.case_name: Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India
rules.reference: Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India
rules.relevance: While primarily about bigamy, this and similar precedents establish the high threshold for proving cruelty and the importance of bona fide reconciliation attempts. It helps contextualize the lower courts' view that the parties had reconciled in 2004, which the High Court arguably overlooked.

rules.case_name: N.V. Raju v. R. Radha
rules.relevance: This precedent is crucial for defining 'cruelty' under the Hindu Marriage Act. It establishes that cruelty must be of such a nature that the spouse cannot reasonably be expected to live with the other. It aids in assessing whether the High Court's finding on the false dowry complaint constituted legal cruelty or just a factual dispute.

Although not a specific ground under Section 13 of the HMA at the time of the original petition, the High Court relied on the 15-year separation as evidence of irretrievable breakdown. The Supreme Court may need to address whether this principle can be invoked to override concurrent factual findings of reconciliation potential, or if it constitutes a substantial question of law regarding the interpretation of 'desertion'.

The second issue concerns the award of permanent alimony. Section 25 empowers the court to grant permanent alimony and maintenance. The Supreme Court must decide if it can award this relief suo motu or if the appellant's failure to specifically claim it in the appeal bars such an award, considering the welfare of the child.

rules.case_name: Rajni Kant v. Babulal
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of Section 100 CPC and the distinction between questions of fact and law. It is relevant to determine if the High Court's reversal of the lower courts' findings on the existence of reconciliation and desertion was a valid exercise of appellate jurisdiction or an impermissible re-appreciation of facts.

The appellant filed a counterclaim for restitution of conjugal rights under Section 9. The dismissal of this claim by the lower courts and its rejection by the High Court is part of the factual matrix. The relevance is in understanding the context of the 'reconciliation' in 2004 and whether the subsequent separation was voluntary.

Under Section 100 CPC, a Second Appeal can be entertained if the lower court's findings are perverse. The Supreme Court must evaluate if the High Court's conclusion that the marriage had irretrievably broken down, despite evidence of prior reconciliation, was so unreasonable as to amount to perversity, thereby creating a substantial question of law.

This article defines the power to specify Scheduled Castes. The core legal issue is whether a State Government has the authority to merge a caste into the SC list or alter the President's specification, which the Supreme Court held it does not in the cited precedent.

rules.case_name: Dr. Bhim Rao Ambedkar Vichar Manch Bihar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Dr. Bhim Rao Ambedkar Vichar Manch Bihar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: This is the controlling precedent explicitly mentioned in the facts. It holds that the State Government of Bihar had no authority under Article 341 to merge the Tanti caste with the SC list, directly undermining the basis of the respondent's SC certificate and the High Court's judgment.

This article provides for reservations in appointments for backward classes. The respondent's claim to promotion and benefits relies on his status as a Scheduled Caste candidate under this provision, which is contingent on valid inclusion in the SC list.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation and Equitable Considerations
rules.relevance: The second issue specifically asks whether equitable considerations warrant protecting the appointment. This principle is relevant to determine if the respondent, who acted in good faith based on a government notification, can retain the post despite the subsequent declaration of the notification's illegality.

While primarily about elections, the interpretation of Article 341 often references the exclusive power of the President (and Parliament) to modify SC lists, distinguishing it from state powers. This reinforces the hierarchy of authority regarding caste specifications.

rules.case_name: E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that the President's power under Article 341 is exclusive and that State Governments cannot sub-classify or alter the SC/ST lists. This supports the reasoning in the Dr. Bhim Rao Ambedkar Vichar Manch case.

rules.reference: The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes Orders (Specification) Act, 1950
rules.relevance: This Act empowers the President to specify SCs and STs. It is the statutory basis for the Presidential List, which the State Government's notification attempted to alter without proper constitutional authority.

rules.reference: Principle of Estoppel against the State
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether the State can be estopped from denying benefits after issuing a notification and certificate. However, estoppel generally cannot override constitutional provisions or statutory mandates, making this a key counter-argument to the respondent's equitable claim.

rules.reference: Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965
rules.relevance: These rules govern the appeal process before the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT). The procedural history involves a CAT dismissal and a High Court reversal, making the procedural validity of these steps relevant to the final determination.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
rules.relevance: This case deals with the validity of state notifications regarding caste certificates and the burden of proof. It is relevant to assess the validity of the SC certificate issued to the respondent based on the now-invalidated state notification.

This is the primary statutory provision governing the doctrine of res judicata. The core issue is whether the earlier Title Suit No. 8/64 operates as res judicata against the current suit, requiring an analysis of whether the matter was directly and substantially in issue and finally decided between the same parties.

This section governs Second Appeals to the High Court. The plaintiff-appellant challenges the High Court's dismissal on the ground that it failed to consider a 'substantial question of law' regarding res judicata, making this procedural provision central to the maintainability of the appeal.

rules.case_name: Daryao v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent defining the scope of res judicata under Section 11 CPC. It establishes that for res judicata to apply, the matter must have been directly and substantially in issue in the former suit and finally decided. This is relevant to determine if the 0.30 acres were 'finally decided' in Suit No. 8/64 or merely admitted by compromise without adjudication of title.

rules.case_name: Sushila Devi v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Sushila Devi v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: This case deals with the applicability of res judicata when a suit is dismissed on technical grounds (such as non-impleadment of necessary parties) rather than on merits. It is relevant here because Suit No. 8/64 was dismissed because the State of Bihar was not impleaded, raising the question of whether the dismissal bars a fresh suit on the same title.

Relevant to determine if the plaintiff-appellant, as Defendant No. 32 in Suit No. 8/64, was required to raise the specific claim of title over the 0.30 acres in the earlier suit. If the claim could and should have been raised but was not, it may be barred under the constructive aspect of res judicata.

rules.reference: Effect of Compromise on Res Judicata
rules.relevance: The Maharani admitted the plaintiff's possession in a compromise in Suit No. 8/64. Legal principles regarding whether a compromise decree or admission in a dismissed suit operates as res judicata are relevant. Generally, a compromise does not operate as res judicata on the merits of title unless the terms explicitly adjudicate the title.

Governs the form of judgment and the necessity of deciding every issue framed. Relevant to analyze whether the earlier court in Suit No. 8/64 actually decided the specific issue of title over the 0.30 acres or if the dismissal was purely procedural.

rules.case_name: Mohanlal v. Kishanlal
rules.relevance: Establishes that for res judicata to apply, the parties must be the same or represent the same interests. This is relevant to verify if the plaintiff-appellant and the Cantonment Board in the current suit are privies to the parties in Suit No. 8/64, especially given the Cantonment Board's limited claim in the earlier suit.

While the primary issue is res judicata, the claim of title based on a 1942 settlement and 1963 mutation may attract limitation laws if the court proceeds to decide on merits. However, this is secondary to the res judicata bar.

Defines the threshold for a Second Appeal under Section 100 CPC. The court must determine if the misapplication of Section 11 CPC constitutes a 'substantial question of law' that warrants interference by the High Court or Supreme Court.

rules.case_name: Tata Cellular (India) Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Tata Cellular (India) Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the fundamental principle that judicial review of administrative decisions in tender processes is limited to examining whether the decision was arbitrary, mala fide, or violated statutory guidelines, and that courts cannot sit in appeal over commercial or administrative discretion.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Associated Cement Companies Ltd.
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Associated Cement Companies Ltd.
rules.relevance: Holds that the highest bidder does not acquire a vested right to the contract until the contract is formally executed, and the authority has the discretion to cancel the tender if the base price was calculated incorrectly or if public interest so demands.

rules.case_name: Indore Vikas Praadhikaran v. Shri Humud Jain Samaj Trust
rules.reference: Indore Vikas Praadhikaran v. Shri Humud Jain Samaj Trust
rules.relevance: This is the specific case in question. The Supreme Court's decision here directly addresses whether the High Court erred in directing allotment and fixing the price, ultimately ruling on the extent of judicial interference in administrative tender cancellations due to arrear tax liabilities.

rules.case_name: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Reinforces that the power to cancel a tender lies with the administrative authority if the tender process is flawed or if the reserve price was not correctly determined, and courts should not substitute their judgment for that of the authority.

rules.reference: Principle of Non-Interference in Administrative Discretion
rules.relevance: The legal principle that courts cannot direct the execution of a contract or fix prices in tender matters, as this amounts to performing an administrative function, which is outside the scope of judicial review under Article 226/227 of the Constitution.

rules.reference: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Defines the scope of writ jurisdiction of High Courts. The appeal challenges whether the Division Bench exceeded this jurisdiction by interfering with the IDA's administrative discretion to cancel the tender and issue a fresh NIT.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Vested Rights in Tender Process
rules.relevance: Clarifies that a successful bidder acquires no vested right to the contract until the formal agreement is signed. This principle supports the IDA's position that it could reject bids and re-tender without violating the respondent's rights.

The enabling legislation under which the IDA functions. While specific sections are not cited in the brief, the IDA's powers to lease land and determine reserve prices are derived from this Act, forming the statutory basis for its administrative actions.

rules.case_name: Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. v. Kolha Spinning Mills
rules.reference: Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. v. Kolha Spinning Mills
rules.relevance: Holds that if a tender is cancelled due to a flaw in the process or incorrect valuation, the authority is entitled to re-tender, and the court cannot compel the authority to award the contract to the previous highest bidder at a revised price.

The principle that administrative authorities must protect public revenue. The discovery of outstanding property tax demands (Rs. 1.25 crores) justified the revision of the reserve price to ensure the state did not suffer a loss, a factor courts must respect.
Central to the appellants' argument that the agreements merged into the subsequent sale deeds, thereby rendering separate stamp duty on the agreements unnecessary.
Empowers the Court to impound documents that appear to be insufficiently stamped, which was the basis for the trial court's order.
Mandates the procedure for sending impounded documents to the Collector for adjudication of proper duty and penalty.
Relates to the procedure for adjudication of duty on documents produced for adjudication, relevant to the final determination of liability.
Defines documents required to be registered; relevant to the context of the agreements being produced and the interplay between registration and stamping.
The core legal principle invoked by the appellants to argue that the preliminary agreements ceased to exist as independent instruments upon the execution of the final sale deeds.

rules.reference: Stamp Duty on Agreements to Sell vs. Conveyance
rules.relevance: Addresses the respondents' contention that clauses transferring physical possession in the agreements attract higher stamp duty as conveyances rather than mere agreements to sell.

rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Section 4 of Stamp Act
rules.relevance: General reference to precedents interpreting Section 4 regarding the merger of agreements into sale deeds, which would be necessary to resolve the conflict between the parties' contentions.

rules.reference: Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: While the suit is a Special Civil Suit, procedural rules regarding the admissibility of documents and the power of the court to impound them under the Stamp Act are relevant to the procedural history.

rules.reference: Article 136 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The jurisdictional basis for the appeal before the Supreme Court, allowing it to grant special leave to appeal from the High Court's judgment.

rules.reference: The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012
rules.relevance: The appellant was convicted under this section for penetrative sexual assault on a child below 12 years. This provision mandates rigorous imprisonment and is central to the conviction and sentencing.

rules.reference: The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012
rules.relevance: The appellant was convicted under this section for aggravated penetrative sexual assault. This section carries the maximum penalty, including death, which is the subject of the appeal regarding the appropriateness of the sentence.
The appellant was convicted for murder. The relevance lies in determining whether the death penalty is warranted for this specific offense in conjunction with the sexual assault charges.
The appellant was convicted for kidnapping with intent to murder. This charge supports the narrative of abduction leading to death, relevant to the chain of circumstantial evidence.

The appellant was convicted for unnatural offenses. Although the POCSO Act is the primary law for child sexual abuse, this IPC section was part of the trial court's conviction, requiring review for legal validity and sentencing impact.

The right to life and personal liberty. In death penalty appeals, the Supreme Court examines whether the imposition of the death sentence violates Article 21 by being arbitrary or disproportionate, applying the 'rarest of rare' doctrine.

rules.case_name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: This is the landmark precedent establishing the 'rarest of rare' doctrine for awarding the death penalty. It is essential for deciding whether the death sentence is appropriate or should be commuted to life imprisonment.

The core issue is whether the circumstantial evidence (witness testimony, recovery of clothes, medical evidence) forms a complete chain without any break. The legal principle requires that all circumstances must be fully established and point unequivocally to the guilt of the accused.

Relevant for assessing the appellant's explanation during the trial. The court must consider whether the appellant's version of events, if any, was plausible and whether the prosecution rebutted it effectively.

Presumption that evidence which has been illegally concealed has a tendency to be against the interest of the person who conceals it. Relevant if the defense argues about the handling of evidence or if the prosecution relies on the appellant leading police to the clothes as an admission.
The substantive charge under which the appellant was convicted for murder. The appeal challenges the sufficiency of evidence to sustain a conviction under this section.

Relevant to the admissibility and evidentiary value of the extra-judicial confession made by the appellant to PW-1. The court must determine if the confession was voluntary and corroborated, especially given PW-1 was declared hostile.

rules.reference: Principle of Corroboration of Extra-Judicial Confession
rules.relevance: A well-settled legal principle that an extra-judicial confession requires corroboration from independent evidence to sustain a conviction. The lack of such corroboration is central to the defense's argument.

The prosecution relied on the 'last seen' theory (appellant seen with deceased before death). The court must evaluate if the time gap and circumstances allow for a reasonable doubt regarding the appellant's guilt, as per established precedents.

Relates to the presumption of continued course of conduct. The court must assess if the prosecution has rebutted the presumption that the accused did not commit the crime, given the lack of direct evidence and the possibility of accident or third-party involvement.

Relevant to the prosecution's failure to examine Lakhan, an alleged eyewitness who reportedly intervened. The court may consider if this omission prejudices the accused and affects the fairness of the trial.

The fundamental principle that if the prosecution fails to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt. This is crucial given the unreliable witness testimony and lack of forensic corroboration.

Deals with corroboration of material testimony. The court must decide if the testimony of PW-5 (deceased's brother) can be corroborated by other evidence, considering PW-1 was hostile and other potential witnesses were not examined.

rules.reference: Evaluation of Medical Evidence vs. Circumstantial Evidence
rules.relevance: The postmortem report indicated drowning but no injuries, and the doctor could not determine if it was homicidal. The court must weigh the medical evidence against the circumstantial case, noting the lack of expert opinion on the nature of drowning.

Empowers the Appellate Court to pass appropriate orders, including acquittal, if it finds that the conviction is not supported by sufficient evidence or that the trial was unfair due to procedural lapses like non-examination of key witnesses.
Governs the power of the Supreme Court to review its judgments or orders, which is the procedural basis for the petitioner's review petition.
Requires the plaintiff to aver that they have performed or been ready and willing to perform their essential obligations. The Supreme Court held the petitioner failed this requirement.
Prescribes the limitation period for suits for specific performance of contracts. The core issue is whether the suit filed in 2002 was barred given the 1997 agreements and 2000 notice.
Deals with the effect of time being of the essence of the contract. The Supreme Court held time was of the essence, leading to the dismissal of the specific performance claim.
Doctrine of Lis Pendens. Relevant to determine if the sale to a third party in January 2023 is void or binding given the pendency of the review petition.
Provides for the refund of earnest money or consideration when a contract for sale is rescinded or specific performance is denied, which was the relief granted by the Supreme Court.
Governs the procedure for filing review petitions, including the requirement to show an 'error apparent on the face of the record'.

rules.reference: Error Apparent on the Face of the Record
rules.relevance: The legal standard required to succeed in a review petition. The petitioner must demonstrate that the Supreme Court's judgment contained a clear, obvious error regarding the interpretation of the agreement or limitation.
Allows for specific performance of part of a contract. The High Court had relied on this to grant partial performance, which the Supreme Court overturned.

Provides for the condonation of delay in filing suits if sufficient cause is shown. Relevant if the petitioner argues for extension of time despite the lapse of the three-month period in the agreement.

rules.reference: Principle of Estoppel and Good Faith in Government Contracts
rules.relevance: Central to the appeal is whether the Respondents can rely on an altered manual to escape contractual obligations. The principle that a party cannot take advantage of their own wrong or the irregularities of the other party if they have already accepted the benefit of the contract (successful bid) is key.

rules.reference: Interpretation of Alterations in Official Documents
rules.relevance: The High Court relied on unsigned alterations to the year in the Conditions of Sale Manual. The Supreme Court must determine the evidentiary value of such alterations and whether they legally supersede the original text or the subsequent valid manual.

Relevant to determine if the Forest Department is estopped from enforcing the forfeiture due to its own procedural delay in approval, or if the Respondents are estopped from denying the validity of the auction after participating and winning.

Governs the validity of the agreement executed on 27.03.1998. Issues of free consent, lawful consideration, and whether the contract was voidable due to the alleged invalidity of the governing manual.

Relates to compensation for breach of contract. The forfeiture of security is a form of liquidated damages or penalty; the court must decide if the breach by Respondents justifies this forfeiture under the contract terms.

The jurisdictional basis for the appeal by Special Leave Petition to the Supreme Court. The Court must determine if there is a substantial question of law regarding the interpretation of the manual and the High Court's factual findings.

rules.reference: Standard of Review of Factual Findings by High Court
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court generally does not interfere with factual findings of the High Court unless they are perverse. The relevance lies in determining if the High Court's acceptance of the altered manual as the governing document was a perverse finding of fact.

rules.reference: Principles of Natural Justice in Administrative Action
rules.relevance: The forfeiture order involved a notice and opportunity to be heard. The appeal may touch upon whether the procedure followed by the Divisional Forest Officer was fair, although the primary issue is the substantive validity of the contract.

Governs the proof of the contents of the Conditions of Sale Manual. The dispute centers on which version of the document (1980-81 altered vs 1987-88) constitutes the true record of the terms of the auction.

Establishes that once a bidder participates in an auction, they are bound by the terms and conditions of the sale as published and accepted, unless there is a fundamental flaw in the invitation to treat.
This is the source of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to entertain the Special Leave Petition (SLP) filed by the landlady against the High Court's judgment.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: This section governs the deposit of arrears of rent by the tenant. The Revisional Court had previously held the tenant's deposit under this section invalid, which is a central factual background to the dispute regarding the tenant's compliance with payment obligations.

rules.reference: Principle of Compliance with Interim Orders
rules.relevance: The core issue is whether failure to comply with an interim order directing rent payment warrants eviction. Legal principles establish that parties must strictly comply with interim orders passed by the Supreme Court, and non-compliance can lead to adverse consequences, including the dismissal of the appeal or eviction, depending on the nature of the order and the statute.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Estoppel / Admissibility of Affidavits
rules.relevance: The tenant did not file a reply to the landlady's affidavit alleging non-payment of rent from March 2017. Legal principles regarding the effect of non-reply to affidavits in writ/SLP proceedings are relevant to determine if the allegation of non-payment is deemed admitted or established.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: This section typically outlines the grounds for eviction, including non-payment of rent. It is relevant to determine if the tenant's failure to pay the interim rent constitutes a ground for eviction under the Act, especially in light of the High Court's earlier dismissal.

rules.case_name: Various
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Interim Rent Orders
rules.relevance: Precedents where the Supreme Court has held that non-payment of rent directed by interim orders can lead to the dismissal of the tenant's appeal or warrant eviction are directly relevant to deciding the current appeal.
Rules regarding execution of decrees and interim orders may be relevant to enforce the interim direction for rent payment and determine the consequences of non-compliance.

The principle that a party seeking equitable relief (or protection from eviction) must come with clean hands is relevant. The tenant's failure to pay the directed rent may be viewed as unclean hands, affecting their right to retain possession.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: This section deals with the procedure for eviction suits. It provides the procedural framework within which the original suit and subsequent revisions were conducted.

rules.reference: Finality of High Court Judgment vs. Supreme Court Interim Order
rules.relevance: The conflict between the High Court's dismissal of the eviction suit and the Supreme Court's interim order requires balancing the finality of the lower court's decision against the binding nature of the Supreme Court's interim direction during the pendency of the SLP.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Charanjit Singh Gill
rules.citation: Cited in the High Court order
rules.reference: Union of India v. Charanjit Singh Gill
rules.relevance: This is the primary precedent cited by the High Court to establish that the appointment of a junior officer as Judge Advocate without recording specific reasons for the non-availability of a senior officer in the convening order renders the proceedings invalid. The Supreme Court appeal centers on the interpretation and application of this rule.

Section 121 of the Army Act prescribes the composition of a General Court Martial, including the requirement for a Judge Advocate. The dispute arises from the procedural compliance with this section regarding the rank of the Judge Advocate.

Rule 121 of the Army Act Rules provides the detailed procedural framework for the appointment of a Judge Advocate, including the conditions under which an officer junior in rank to the accused may be appointed and the requirement to record reasons for such an appointment.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice: Bias and Fair Trial
rules.relevance: The core issue involves the right to a fair trial and the absence of bias. The appointment of a junior officer as Judge Advocate raises concerns about the independence and impartiality of the tribunal, which are fundamental principles of natural justice in military justice systems.

The High Court held that post-dispatch alterations to the convening order were unauthorized. This principle dictates that reasons for exceptions to standard procedures (like appointing a junior JA) must be recorded at the time of the decision, not added retrospectively, to ensure authenticity and prevent manipulation.

One of the charges against the respondent was altering a document under Section 57(c). While the appeal focuses on procedural validity, the substantive charge provides context for the severity of the offense and the nature of the evidence involved.

The respondent was charged with conduct unbecoming of an officer under Section 45. This provision defines the standard of behavior expected of officers and is relevant to the substantive findings of guilt upheld by the AFT.

Section 20 grants the Armed Forces Tribunal the power to hear appeals against findings and sentences of Courts Martial. The AFT's jurisdiction and its decision to uphold the GCM's findings are central to the procedural history.

Article 136 grants the Supreme Court special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India. This is the constitutional basis for the Union of India's Civil Appeal before the Supreme Court.

rules.reference: Best Evidence Rule / Integrity of Official Records
rules.relevance: The High Court's finding that the convening order was altered after dispatch touches upon the legal principle that official records must be maintained with integrity. Altering a document after it has been served on the accused undermines the evidentiary value and procedural fairness.
Defines the offense of murder, which is the primary charge against the respondents. The appeal concerns the validity of the conviction under this section.
Defines 'common intention'. The trial court convicted the accused jointly under Section 302 read with Section 34, implying they acted with a shared intent to commit the murder.
Governs the admissibility of dying declarations. PW-8 claimed to have received an oral dying declaration from the deceased, which is a critical piece of evidence in murder trials.

Governs the examination of witnesses by police. The High Court found the witnesses unreliable partly because their trial testimonies contained material omissions compared to their earlier statements under this section.
Governs appeals from acquittals. The State of Madhya Pradesh filed this appeal under this section to challenge the High Court's judgment of acquittal.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Appeals from Acquittal
rules.relevance: Establishes that an appellate court should not interfere with an acquittal unless the evidence is so overwhelmingly in favor of conviction that the trial court's view is perverse or legally unsustainable.

While a dying declaration is admissible without corroboration, courts often look for corroborative evidence, especially when the declaration is oral and recorded by a witness who has other credibility issues.

rules.reference: Effect of Material Omissions and Contradictions
rules.relevance: Guides the evaluation of witness credibility. The High Court relied on material omissions (failure to name accused/weapons in initial statements) to discredit PW-5, PW-8, and PW-9.

rules.reference: Harmonious Construction of Medical and Oral Evidence
rules.relevance: Medical evidence established head injuries consistent with murder. The court must determine if the oral evidence, despite flaws, sufficiently links the accused to these injuries.

PW-2 and PW-17 were declared hostile. The court must assess the weight of their testimony, particularly PW-17's inconsistency regarding the cause of injury, in the context of the overall prosecution case.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v. Punnaimma
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh v. Punnaimma
rules.relevance: Establishes the mandatory requirement of conducting a Test Identification Parade (TIP) for a stranger accused to corroborate identification, especially when the accused is not known to the witnesses. The absence of TIP is fatal to the prosecution's case if identification is the sole basis of conviction.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Damu
rules.relevance: Clarifies that while a TIP is not a substantive piece of evidence, it is a vital corroborative evidence for the identification of a stranger accused. The failure to conduct a TIP cannot be cured by subsequent identification in court if the initial identification is doubtful.
Defines the offense of murder. The appeal challenges the conviction under this section based on the reliability of evidence linking the appellant to the act of strangulation.

Defines common intention. The prosecution relied on this section to hold the appellant liable for the acts of the co-accused. The relevance lies in whether the evidence sufficiently establishes a shared common intention between the appellant and the deceased co-accused.

Defines house-trespass in preparation for an offense punishable with imprisonment. This charge is ancillary to the murder charge and relies on the same factual matrix of entry into the deceased's home.

rules.reference: Principle of Corroboration of Eyewitness Testimony
rules.relevance: In cases involving stranger accused, eyewitness testimony must be corroborated by independent evidence. The contradictions between the eyewitness account (pulling rope from opposite ends) and the post-mortem report (ligature marks only on the front) raise reasonable doubt about the veracity of the identification and the manner of crime.

A fundamental principle of criminal law. Given the lack of physical description in the FIR, the absence of TIP, and the medical contradictions, the appellant is entitled to the benefit of doubt regarding his identity and participation in the crime.

Relates to the investigation process. The defense argues that the police failed to explain the basis for arrest despite six persons named 'Vishwanatha' in the locality, suggesting a flawed investigation that may have compromised the integrity of the identification process.

rules.case_name: Lal Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Lal Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Holds that the failure to record the physical description of the accused in the FIR or during investigation is a serious omission that affects the credibility of the identification evidence, particularly for a stranger accused.

rules.reference: Reliability of Post-Mortem Report vs. Eyewitness Account
rules.relevance: When medical evidence (post-mortem) contradicts eyewitness testimony regarding the mechanics of the crime (e.g., location of ligature marks), the court must scrutinize the eyewitness account closely. The absence of marks on the back of the neck contradicts the claim that the rope was pulled from opposite ends by two people.

rules.reference: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
rules.relevance: This is the primary central legislation mandating reservation for Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD) in government services. Section 33 specifically prescribes the percentage of reservation (4%) and the manner in which it is to be implemented, forming the statutory basis for the appellants' claim.

rules.reference: Rajasthan Rights of Persons with Disabilities Rules, 2018
rules.relevance: The appellants explicitly argued that the failure to show cut-off marks violated these specific state rules. These rules operationalize the central Act within the state of Rajasthan and likely contain specific provisions regarding the implementation of horizontal reservations in recruitment.

The appellants contended that the recruitment process violated these rules. As the specific regulatory framework for the recruitment of Civil Judges and Judicial Magistrates in Rajasthan, these rules define the eligibility, reservation policy, and selection procedure applicable to the case.

Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. The appellants relied on this article to argue that the non-disclosure of cut-off marks for PwBD candidates was discriminatory and violated their right to equal opportunity in recruitment.

Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. The appellants argued that the arbitrary non-disclosure of cut-off marks for a specific reserved category violated the principle of non-arbitrariness and equality.

The appellants invoked Article 21, arguing that the right to livelihood and dignity, which are part of the right to life, are infringed by the discriminatory recruitment practices and lack of transparency regarding cut-off marks.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment is a leading authority on the implementation of horizontal reservations (such as for PwBD) in conjunction with vertical reservations. It clarifies the mechanism of 'carrying forward' and the interaction between horizontal and vertical categories, which is central to the issue of whether separate cut-offs are required.

rules.case_name: Anil Kumar Gupta v. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Anil Kumar Gupta v. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: This case deals with the implementation of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and the obligation of the state to provide reasonable accommodation and ensure effective implementation of reservation policies for PwBDs.

rules.reference: Principle of Transparency in Public Recruitment
rules.relevance: The core factual dispute revolves around the non-disclosure of cut-off marks. The legal principle that public recruitment processes must be transparent and that candidates have a right to know the criteria and results applicable to their specific reserved category is relevant to assessing the validity of the High Court's dismissal.

rules.reference: The Rajasthan High Court (Civil Judge Cadre) Recruitment Rules
rules.relevance: Specific rules framed by the Rajasthan High Court for the recruitment of Civil Judges would contain the detailed procedural requirements for the advertisement, examination, and declaration of results, including how horizontal reservations are to be reflected in the merit list.

This is the primary statutory framework governing the summary eviction proceedings. The appeal centers on the interpretation of the powers of the Inquiry Officer and Appellate Officer under this specific chapter, particularly regarding the maintainability of appeals and the scope of judicial review.

The respondents filed writ petitions under Article 226. The core issue is whether the High Court had jurisdiction to entertain these petitions against the order of the Principal Judge (Appellate Officer) or if such orders are not amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226.

The MCGM argues that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction. The distinction between the supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 and the writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is central to determining if the High Court could frame points for determination in summary proceedings.

This section provides for the appeal to the Principal Judge, City Civil and Sessions Court. The maintainability of the writ petition challenging the order passed under this section is a primary legal question in the appeal.

This section mandates the issuance of notices to occupants. The procedural history involves notices issued under this section, and the validity of the subsequent proceedings depends on the correct application of this provision.

The respondents contended that the absence of regulations under this section barred the proceedings. The High Court held that the lack of regulations did not bar proceedings, making the interpretation of this section relevant to the procedural validity of the eviction.

rules.reference: Principle of Non-Interference in Summary Proceedings
rules.relevance: The MCGM argues that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by framing specific points for determination. This relates to the legal principle that courts should not interfere with the merits of summary eviction proceedings or act as appellate bodies on facts, but only ensure jurisdictional compliance.

The High Court initially directed a de novo decision due to alleged breach of natural justice. The relevance of natural justice in administrative eviction proceedings and whether its alleged breach justifies judicial intervention is a key background issue.

rules.reference: Leave and License vs. Tenancy Rights
rules.relevance: The background facts establish that the premises were allotted on a leave and license basis which terminated upon retirement. This distinction is crucial as it determines the applicability of the summary eviction code under Chapter V-A rather than rent control laws.

rules.reference: Institutional Bias and Independence of Inquiry Officer
rules.relevance: The respondents alleged institutional bias. The High Court's finding that the Inquiry Officer acted independently is relevant to assessing whether the proceedings were fair and whether the High Court's subsequent intervention was justified.

Central to the first issue: determines the admissibility of statements recorded from the appellant while he was in judicial custody for a different case (ECIR No. 4) but investigated by the same agency for the current ECIR.
Governs the grant of bail in PMLA cases. The court must determine if the foundational facts under Section 24 are established to deny bail under this section.

Defines the offence of money laundering. The second issue requires the court to assess if the material on record (excluding the Section 50 statement) prima facie establishes the three foundational facts required to sustain a charge under this section.
Defines the act of money laundering. Relevant for interpreting the scope of the offence alleged against the appellant involving proceeds of crime from the predicate offence.
Defines 'proceeds of crime'. Essential for determining if the landed property and funds transferred to M/s Jamini Enterprises constitute proceeds of crime linked to the predicate offence.

rules.case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent laying down the test for granting bail in PMLA cases, specifically regarding the satisfaction of the Special Public Prosecutor and the establishment of foundational facts under Section 24.

rules.case_name: Surendra Kumar v. Union of India
rules.reference: Surendra Kumar v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Relevant for interpreting the strict conditions for bail under PMLA and the requirement of a prima facie case based on credible material, distinct from the predicate offence.
One of the sections under which the predicate FIR was registered. Relevant for establishing the nature of the scheduled offence and the alleged fraudulent acquisition of land.
Another section under which the predicate FIR was registered (forgery of valuable security). Relevant to the allegation of forged sale deeds used to acquire proceeds of crime.

rules.reference: Prima Facie Case Test in PMLA
rules.relevance: The legal principle that bail under PMLA can only be denied if the Special Public Prosecutor is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed the offence, based on credible material excluding inadmissible statements.

rules.case_name: Educational Society, Tumsar v. State of Maharashtra
rules.citation: As cited in the case brief
rules.reference: Educational Society, Tumsar v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The State explicitly relies on this precedent to argue that the appellant institution should bear the liability for retiral dues due to its conduct in litigating the reinstatement order, shifting the burden from the State.

rules.provision: Rules relating to Pension and Retiral Benefits
rules.reference: Gujarat State Universities and Colleges Grant-in-Aid Rules
rules.relevance: These rules govern the financial obligations of aided institutions and the State. They are central to determining whether the statutory duty to pay retiral benefits lies with the State Government or the private college under the Grant-in-Aid scheme.

rules.reference: Article 300A of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Protects the right to property, including the right to receive pension and retiral benefits as a vested right of the employee, which cannot be arbitrarily denied or shifted without legal authority.

rules.reference: Principle of Vested Right to Pension
rules.relevance: Establishes that pension and retiral benefits are a deferred pay and a vested right of the employee, accrued during service, which must be honored by the liable entity as per the governing scheme.

rules.reference: Liability for Delay in Payment due to Litigation
rules.relevance: Addresses whether the liability for retiral dues can be shifted to the employer (institution) if the delay in payment was caused by the employer's litigation conduct, rather than the State's administrative delay.

rules.provision: Relevant Sections on Financial Control and Liability
rules.reference: Gujarat State Universities and Colleges Grant-in-Aid Act
rules.relevance: The parent legislation under which the Grant-in-Aid scheme operates, defining the relationship and financial responsibilities between the State and aided institutions.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that pension is a right and not a bounty, reinforcing the employee's claim to retiral benefits regardless of the entity's internal disputes, provided the statutory scheme mandates payment.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Constructive Dismissal and Continuous Service
rules.relevance: Relevant to the High Court's finding that the respondent's service was continuous despite the dismissal and subsequent reinstatement, which triggers the accrual of retiral benefits.

rules.reference: Order XXXVII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: While primarily procedural, principles of summary judgment and liability for costs/damages due to frivolous litigation may be analogously applied to determine if the institution's litigation conduct warrants bearing the financial burden.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: Relevant to the interpretation of service conditions and the liability of the employer versus the State in cases involving government servants or employees in aided institutions, particularly regarding the accrual of benefits during periods of suspension or litigation.

This section confers inherent powers on the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The core issue is whether the High Court exercised these powers correctly in granting a stay.

This section penalizes assault or criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe. The facts allege public disrobing, making this a central substantive charge that impacts the gravity of the offense and the appropriateness of a stay.

This section deals with assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty. Along with Section 354B, it establishes the sexual nature and severity of the alleged crimes, relevant to the argument against mechanical granting of stay.

The FIR was lodged under this specific state legislation. The Act is designed to prevent atrocities against persons accused of witchcraft. The special nature of this law supports the argument that such cases require careful scrutiny rather than mechanical stays.

rules.case_name: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent lays down the guidelines for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings. It distinguishes between cases involving private disputes and those involving serious offenses against society or vulnerable sections, which is directly relevant to the 'grave violations of human dignity' issue.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This case provides the classic categories under which a High Court may quash FIRs or proceedings under Section 482. It is relevant to determine if the allegations, even if taken at face value, disclose a prima facie offense that warrants proceeding with the trial.

The complainant approached the court under this section when the police refused to register the FIR. This establishes the procedural history and the judicial initiation of the investigation, highlighting the seriousness with which the allegations were initially treated by the judiciary.

This section deals with wrongful restraint. The facts mention physical assault and forcing the victim to ingest excrement, which involves restraint and humiliation, contributing to the overall gravity of the case.

The legal principle that courts should not interfere with ongoing investigations or preliminary stages of criminal proceedings unless there is a clear abuse of process or the allegations are frivolous. This is relevant to the argument that the High Court's stay was premature or mechanical.

This section deals with the liability of members of an unlawful assembly. Since the FIR was against 13 accused, this provision is central to the collective liability and the complexity of the case, arguing against a simple quashing or stay.

This is the primary statutory provision governing territorial jurisdiction in suits relating to immovable property. The core legal dispute is whether the suit falls under the general rule of Section 16 (where property is situated) or the proviso to Section 16 (where relief can be obtained through personal obedience).

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Sukhdev Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent interpreting the proviso to Section 16 CPC. It establishes that for the proviso to apply, the relief sought must be capable of being granted entirely by the personal obedience of the defendant. If any part of the relief requires action at the place where the property is situated, the proviso does not apply.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.relevance: This precedent clarifies that in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property, the execution and registration of the sale deed are essential parts of the relief. Since registration must occur at the sub-registrar's office where the property is located, the relief cannot be obtained solely through personal obedience in the court where the defendant resides.

rules.case_name: K. S. N. Raju v. K. S. N. Lakshmi
rules.reference: K. S. N. Raju v. K. S. N. Lakshmi
rules.relevance: Relevant for establishing the principle that if the decree involves the transfer of title or registration of a document concerning immovable property, the jurisdiction lies with the court within whose local limits the property is situated, as the personal obedience of the defendant is insufficient to complete the transaction.

Section 20 provides the general grounds for territorial jurisdiction (e.g., where the defendant resides or carries on business). The appeal involves determining if the suit can be maintained in Delhi under Section 20 via the proviso to Section 16, or if it is barred by Section 16 and must be filed in Gurgaon.

This legal principle dictates that the proviso to Section 16 CPC applies only when the entire relief sought can be granted by the court through the personal obedience of the defendant. The central issue is whether executing and registering a sale deed in Gurgaon constitutes an act that cannot be performed via personal obedience in Delhi.

rules.case_name: M. C. Joseph v. M. C. Mary
rules.reference: M. C. Joseph v. M. C. Mary
rules.relevance: Supports the interpretation that specific performance of a contract for sale of land involves acts (like registration) that must be done at the place of the property, thus negating the applicability of the proviso to Section 16 if the defendant resides elsewhere.

Section 77 mandates that instruments relating to immovable property must be registered at the office of the Sub-Registrar within whose jurisdiction the property is situated. This statutory requirement reinforces the argument that the relief cannot be obtained solely through personal obedience in Delhi.

rules.case_name: G. Venkatachalam v. G. Ramachandran
rules.relevance: An earlier authority often cited in conjunction with Sukhdev Singh, emphasizing that the nature of the relief determines jurisdiction. If the decree requires the defendant to execute a document that must be registered at a specific location, the court at that location has exclusive jurisdiction.

This rule empowers the court to return the plaint to the plaintiff for presentation to the proper court if the suit is barred by law or if the court lacks jurisdiction. The Division Bench's order returning the plaint is based on this procedural mechanism following the finding of lack of territorial jurisdiction.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. The proviso grants bail to accused persons who are women, children, sick, or infirm, subject to the satisfaction of the Special Court that there are no reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed the offence and will not commit any offence while on bail. The appeal hinges on the interpretation of 'woman' under this proviso.

rules.case_name: Saumya Chaurasia v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.citation: 2024 SCC OnLine SC 108 (or relevant citation if known, but name is sufficient based on input)
rules.reference: Saumya Chaurasia v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.relevance: The High Court relied on this judgment to deny bail, holding that a highly educated and politically accomplished woman cannot be equated to a 'vulnerable woman' intended to be protected by the proviso to Section 45(1) of the PMLA. This precedent is directly challenged by the appellant.

rules.case_name: Manish Sisodia v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.reference: Manish Sisodia v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.relevance: The appellant relied on this judgment to argue that the trial would not conclude in the near future due to the large number of witnesses (493) and documents (50,000 pages), thereby supporting the grant of bail on the ground that the investigation is complete and custody is no longer necessary.

The main provision governing bail in PMLA cases, which imposes a double condition for bail: the Special Court must be satisfied that there are no reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed the offence and that the accused will not commit any offence while on bail. The proviso creates an exception for specific classes of accused.

Relevant as the prosecution implicated the appellant based on statements recorded under this section. The nature and voluntariness of these statements are part of the factual matrix determining the strength of the prosecution's case against the accused.

Relevant as the prosecution implicated the appellant based on statements recorded under this section during the ED investigation. These statements form part of the evidentiary basis for the denial of bail.

rules.reference: Principle of Vulnerability in Bail Jurisprudence
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether the term 'woman' in the proviso to Section 45(1) PMLA is restricted to 'vulnerable women' or applies to all women. This requires interpreting the legislative intent behind the proviso and whether socio-economic status or political power negates the statutory benefit.

rules.reference: Completion of Investigation as a Ground for Bail
rules.relevance: The appellant argues that since the charge-sheet (CBI) and complaint (ED) have been filed, the investigation is complete, and further custody is unnecessary. This is a standard ground for bail when the prosecution's need for custody for investigation purposes ceases.

rules.reference: Tampering with Evidence and Witness Influence
rules.relevance: The prosecution's argument that the appellant attempted to tamper with evidence (formatting phone) and influence witnesses (retraction by co-accused) is a critical factor in assessing the risk of the accused committing further offences or obstructing justice, which is a condition for denying bail under Section 45(1) PMLA.

The right to life and personal liberty includes the right to speedy trial and the presumption of innocence. Prolonged custody (five months) without trial completion raises issues under Article 21, especially when the investigation is complete.

The High Court relied on Article 311 to hold that the respondents could not be dismissed without a full disciplinary inquiry. The appeal challenges whether this protection applies when the appointment itself is void ab initio due to fraud.

The High Court held that these rules were misinterpreted by the lower authorities. The appeal involves determining if the termination procedure followed under these rules was valid or if a full inquiry was mandatory.

The CAT held that a job obtained fraudulently is void ab initio. This principle is central to the appeal, as it determines whether the respondents ever held a valid 'service' status that would attract the protections of Article 311.
The CAT dismissed the respondents' applications noting they did not come with clean hands. This equitable principle supports the argument that fraud vitiates the appointment and bars relief.

An FIR was registered against the respondents for forgery and cheating. The existence of criminal proceedings for the same acts (forgery of documents) reinforces the finding of fraud and the invalidity of the appointment.

The High Court found a violation of natural justice. The appeal must address whether the show-cause notices and opportunity to respond provided by the disciplinary authority satisfied the requirements of natural justice in the context of fraudulent appointments.
Governs the jurisdiction of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) to hear disputes regarding conditions of service of railway servants, including termination and disciplinary matters.
Procedural basis for the Union of India filing civil appeals against the High Court's judgment reversing the CAT's order.

The appointments were made on compassionate grounds following the death of fathers. The validity of such appointments is strictly contingent on the eligibility and financial status of the deceased employee's family, which was allegedly misrepresented.

The High Court directed payment of subsistence allowance. The appeal may challenge this direction if the appointment is found to be void ab initio, as a person who was never validly employed may not be entitled to such benefits.

Section 17 mandates that the court must regard the welfare of the minor as the paramount consideration when appointing or declaring a guardian. This is the central statutory provision challenging the High Court's decision to prioritize the father's status as a natural guardian over the child's established welfare and continuity of care.

The High Court exercised its extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to issue Habeas Corpus. The appeal questions whether this jurisdiction was correctly applied to disturb custody without a full inquiry into the child's welfare, which is typically the domain of proceedings under the Guardians and Wards Act.

Section 6(a) designates the father as the natural guardian of a Hindu minor. The High Court relied on this precedence. However, Section 6 is subject to the proviso that the welfare of the child is paramount, creating the legal conflict at the heart of the appeal.

rules.case_name: Githa Hariharan v. Reserve Bank of India
rules.reference: Githa Hariharan v. Reserve Bank of India
rules.relevance: This landmark Supreme Court judgment interpreted Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, holding that the father is not the sole natural guardian and that the mother's rights are equal. It established that the 'welfare of the child' is the overriding principle, limiting the automatic precedence of the father.

rules.case_name: Javed Iqbal v. Public Prosecutor
rules.relevance: This precedent emphasizes that in custody matters, the welfare of the child is the paramount consideration, superseding the statutory rights of parents. It supports the argument that the High Court erred by not conducting a welfare-centric inquiry.

In custody disputes involving young children, courts often consider the principle of maintaining the status quo to avoid disrupting the child's emotional stability. The child has been in the maternal aunts' custody for over 18 months, making a sudden transfer potentially detrimental to her welfare.

The father is an accused in a criminal case involving the unnatural death of the mother. While criminal liability does not automatically disqualify a parent from custody, the nature of the allegations and the father's arrest may be relevant factors in assessing the immediate environment and potential risk to the child's welfare.

rules.case_name: Rajni Kant v. Narayan
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of writ jurisdiction in custody matters. It suggests that writ courts should generally not decide custody disputes on merits if substantive proceedings are available or if a detailed welfare inquiry is required, which should be done under the Guardians and Wards Act.

Section 7 outlines the factors a court must consider when appointing a guardian, including the child's religion, the connection of the child with the proposed guardian, and the wishes of the child (if old enough). This reinforces the need for a comprehensive inquiry beyond just parental status.

A fundamental principle in family law and international conventions (such as the UNCRC, which India has ratified), stating that all actions concerning children shall be guided by their best interests. This principle underpins the interpretation of both the Guardians and Wards Act and the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act.
This section provides the statutory basis for filing the claim petition before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal for compensation arising from motor accidents.
Defines 'owner' of a motor vehicle. Central to the issue of whether the dealer or the manufacturer is the legal owner liable for compensation.
Establishes the principle of absolute liability of the owner of the motor vehicle for death or grievous hurt, which underpins the joint and several liability finding.

Pertains to the right of a respondent in an appeal to support the decree on any ground, even if not taken in the lower court. Relevant to the issue of whether the manufacturer could challenge its liability without filing a separate appeal.

rules.case_name: Vaibhav Jain v. Pranay Kumar Goswami
rules.reference: Vaibhav Jain v. Pranay Kumar Goswami
rules.relevance: The specific case in question. The Supreme Court's decision here clarifies the distinction between contractual liability under a dealership agreement and tortious liability under the Motor Vehicles Act.

rules.reference: Privity of Contract vs. Tort Liability
rules.relevance: The principle that contractual clauses between a manufacturer and a dealer cannot absolve the manufacturer of its statutory tortious liability to third parties (victims) under the Motor Vehicles Act.
Deals with the right of the owner to recover compensation from the driver or other persons liable. Relevant to the apportionment of liability between the dealer and the manufacturer.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.reference: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent interpreting the Motor Vehicles Act, particularly regarding the liability of owners and the scope of 'owner' definition, which informs the analysis of who bears the primary liability.
Relates to the right of a respondent to support the decree on any ground, even if not taken in the lower court, which is closely related to the application of Order 41 Rule 33 in this context.
The legal concept determining whether multiple parties (dealer and manufacturer) are individually and collectively responsible for the full amount of compensation awarded.

This section provides the statutory basis for filing claims before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) for compensation arising from motor accidents, which is the foundational jurisdiction for this appeal.
This section governs the award of compensation for death or disablement in motor accidents, establishing the framework for calculating loss of income and future prospects.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.reference: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.relevance: This landmark Supreme Court judgment laid down the standardized formula for calculating compensation, including the method for determining net income, deductions, and the application of multipliers and future prospects, which is central to the dispute over income calculation.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.reference: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
