Central to the second issue: whether the State Government violated natural justice by initiating recovery proceedings and reducing pay scale eight years after superannuation without affording the appellant an opportunity of hearing.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Estoppel and Legitimate Expectation
rules.relevance: Relevant to determine if the Government is estopped from retrospectively altering the pay scale and recovering emoluments after the employee had already retired and received pension based on the revised scale for several years.

rules.reference: Limitation and Laches in Administrative Recovery
rules.relevance: Addresses the delay of eight years in initiating recovery proceedings after superannuation, questioning the legal justification and fairness of such belated action.

rules.reference: Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972 (or corresponding Bihar State Rules)
rules.relevance: Governs the procedure and conditions under which excess pension or emoluments can be recovered from a retired government servant, including time limits and procedural safeguards.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: A key precedent regarding the recovery of excess pay and the application of natural justice and limitation principles in such administrative actions.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Prasad
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Prasad
rules.relevance: Relevant for interpreting the validity of government resolutions affecting service conditions and the retrospective operation of such administrative orders.
Determines whether the appellant had acquired a vested right to the promotion and pay scale before the cut-off date, which cannot be taken away retrospectively.

While administrative recovery may not strictly fall under the Limitation Act, the principles of laches and undue delay often draw analogy from limitation periods to assess the validity of belated government actions.

rules.case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
rules.reference: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the broad interpretation of Article 21 and the requirement of fair, just, and reasonable procedure, reinforcing the necessity of natural justice in administrative decisions affecting property rights (pension).
Central to the appellant's claim regarding the right to a speedy trial and the justification for bail after prolonged incarceration (17 months) without the trial commencing.
Governs the conditions for granting bail in PMLA cases. The appeal hinges on whether the statutory presumption of guilt can be rebutted by the delay in trial and the specific facts of the case.

rules.case_name: Niazi Ahmed v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Niazi Ahmed v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: A recent Supreme Court precedent holding that the right to speedy trial under Article 21 is a fundamental right that can override the stringent bail conditions of Section 45 PMLA if the trial is unduly delayed.

rules.case_name: Gurcharan Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurcharan Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that 'time spent in jail' is a relevant factor for granting bail, especially when the trial is protracted and the accused has been in custody for a significant period.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Choudhary v. CBI
rules.relevance: Relevant to the maintainability issue. The Supreme Court previously granted liberty to revive the bail prayer after the final charge-sheet. This precedent supports the view that the current appeals are maintainable as per the earlier order.

The prosecution argued that the appellant's applications under Section 207 for inspection of documents were filed to delay the trial. This provision is relevant to assessing whether the delay is attributable to the accused.

rules.case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Laid down the framework for evaluating bail in PMLA cases, balancing the statutory presumption with the right to speedy trial and the stage of investigation/trial.
Governs bail in cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act. Since the CBI charge-sheet involves offences under this Act, the bail standards here are also relevant alongside PMLA provisions.

rules.case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Emphasizes the importance of preventing unnecessary detention and ensuring that bail is not denied merely as a matter of routine, supporting the appellant's argument for release after 17 months.

rules.reference: Principle of Maintainability based on Judicial Liberty
rules.relevance: The legal principle that when a higher court grants specific liberty to approach a lower court under certain conditions (here, after filing of final charge-sheet), the subsequent appeal is maintainable and does not require a fresh round of litigation in lower courts unless explicitly barred.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: Establishes the seven categories of cases where High Courts can quash FIRs under Section 482 CrPC. It is the primary authority for determining whether the High Court was justified in quashing the proceedings at the threshold without considering investigation materials, specifically regarding whether the allegations prima facie constitute an offence.

rules.case_name: Manish Goel v. State of NCT of Delhi
rules.reference: Manish Goel v. State of NCT of Delhi
rules.relevance: Clarifies that the power to quash under Section 482 CrPC is not to be exercised merely because the accused claims innocence or disputes the allegations. It supports the appellant's argument that the High Court should not have quashed the case without considering the investigation report which might disclose criminal intent.

Defines Criminal Breach of Trust. The core issue is whether the failure to return the truck or pay rent after taking possession constitutes 'entrustment' and 'dishonest misappropriation' as required by this section, which the High Court found lacking.

Defines Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property. Relevant to determine if the 'false assurances' and initial hiring agreement amounted to cheating from the beginning, which the High Court held was not established.

Confers inherent powers on the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court, or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. This is the procedural basis for the quashing petition.

rules.case_name: Gurnam Kaur v. Daljit Singh
rules.relevance: A key precedent distinguishing between civil breach of contract and criminal breach of trust. It helps analyze whether the non-payment of rent and non-return of the truck amounts to criminal liability or merely a civil dispute, which was the High Court's primary reasoning.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Reaffirms that the High Court cannot act as a court of appeal and must not delve into the merits of the case or appreciate evidence at the quashing stage, but must only look at the allegations. However, it also notes that if the investigation reveals no offence, quashing may be appropriate, supporting the debate on whether investigation materials should be considered.

Empowers a Magistrate to direct police to register an FIR and investigate. Relevant to the procedural history where the CJM directed the investigation, establishing the initial jurisdiction and the basis for the subsequent FIR and cognizance.

rules.reference: Distinction between Civil and Criminal Liability
rules.relevance: The general legal principle that mere breach of contract or failure to pay money due does not automatically amount to cheating or criminal breach of trust unless there is proof of dishonest intention from the inception. This is the central legal test applied by the High Court and challenged by the Appellant.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Govind Singh
rules.relevance: Holds that if the accused denies the very foundation of the charge (i.e., that he was entrusted with the property), the case may not proceed as a criminal breach of trust. This supports the respondents' argument that no agreement was executed, thus no entrustment occurred.

rules.case_name: Diamond Exports v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Diamond Exports v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: This is the most central authority as it reconciles conflicting views on the prospective operation of the New India Assurance judgment. It holds that applications for condonation of delay pending or decided on or before 04.03.2020 must be decided on merits, directly addressing the issue in both appeals.

rules.case_name: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Hilli Multipurpose Cold Storage (P) Ltd.
rules.reference: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Hilli Multipurpose Cold Storage (P) Ltd.
rules.relevance: The Constitution Bench judgment that established the mandatory nature of Section 13 time limits but clarified that its decision would operate prospectively from 04.03.2020, creating the legal framework for the current dispute.

The specific statutory provision governing the procedure for filing written statements and the time limits therein, which is the subject of the interpretation regarding mandatory vs. directory nature and condonation of delay.
The provision under which the second appeal was filed, granting the right to appeal against orders of the NCDRC to the Supreme Court.

rules.case_name: Reliance General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Mampee Timbers & Hardwares (P) Ltd.
rules.reference: Reliance General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Mampee Timbers & Hardwares (P) Ltd.
rules.relevance: A key precedent cited in the conflict of opinions, which took a view on the application of New India Assurance principles to pending cases, later reconciled by Diamond Exports.

rules.case_name: Daddy’s Builders (A) Ltd. v. Manisha Bhargava
rules.reference: Daddy’s Builders (A) Ltd. v. Manisha Bhargava
rules.relevance: Another precedent that took a divergent view from Mampee Timbers regarding the application of the New India Assurance judgment, contributing to the conflict resolved by Diamond Exports.

The legal principle that a judgment declaring a statutory provision mandatory may be given prospective effect to avoid prejudice to parties who relied on the previous legal position, which is the core basis for the relief sought in these appeals.

The principle that where a statute does not expressly bar condonation of delay, and judicial interpretation has shifted, pending applications should be adjudicated on their merits rather than being dismissed solely on technical grounds, especially when the new law is prospective.

This is the overriding effect clause of the PMLA. The central legal issue is whether this section excludes the application of Section 197(1) CrPC, thereby removing the requirement for prior sanction for prosecuting public servants.

This provision mandates prior sanction for the prosecution of public servants. The respondents rely on this to challenge the cognizance taken by the Special Court, arguing it applies despite the PMLA.

Defines the offence of money laundering. The interpretation of this section is relevant to determining whether the acts alleged were committed in the discharge of official duty, a prerequisite for claiming protection under Section 197(1) CrPC.

This section empowers the Special Court to take cognizance of offences upon receipt of a complaint from the Enforcement Directorate. The validity of the cognizance taken under this provision is the subject of the appeal.
Prescribes the punishment for money laundering. Relevant to the nature of the offence and the procedural framework for prosecution under the PMLA.

The legal principle regarding whether a specific overriding clause in a special statute (PMLA) expressly or impliedly repeals or excludes the general protective provisions of the CrPC (Section 197) is central to the dispute.

rules.reference: Definition of Public Servant under Section 197 CrPC
rules.relevance: The appellant argues the first respondent is not a public servant within the meaning of Section 197(1) because he is employed by a Corporation and not directly removable by the Government. This requires interpreting the scope of 'public servant' and the 'removability' test.

rules.reference: Nexus between Official Duty and Alleged Offence
rules.relevance: For Section 197(1) CrPC to apply, the alleged offence must have been committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty. The appellant contends there is no such nexus for the acts of money laundering.

The broader context of Section 197, including its purpose to protect public servants from malicious prosecution, is relevant to the court's interpretation of whether such protection extends to proceedings under the PMLA.

While not explicitly mentioned in the brief, Section 45 deals with burden of proof. In PMLA cases, the interplay between procedural protections and the special nature of the offence often involves interpreting the entire procedural scheme, including how it interacts with general criminal procedure.

This is the specific regulatory provision under which the disciplinary authority treated the respondent's absence as 'abandonment of service' and ordered his removal. The central legal issue is whether the facts satisfy the conditions of this regulation to dispense with a formal inquiry.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem)
rules.relevance: The High Court set aside the termination order citing 'lack of due opportunity'. This principle is relevant to determine if the notices issued by LIC were sufficient to satisfy the requirements of natural justice in a case of alleged abandonment, or if a formal inquiry was mandatory.

rules.reference: Clean Hands Doctrine / Suppression of Material Facts
rules.relevance: The respondent concealed his subsequent employment with the Food Corporation of India in his Writ Petition. This principle is relevant to decide if the respondent is disentitled to equitable relief from the High Court due to this suppression, potentially leading to the dismissal of his petition.

The respondent filed a Writ Petition before the High Court of Himachal Pradesh. Article 226 confers the power on High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. The scope of this power is relevant in assessing the High Court's intervention in the service matter.

rules.case_name: LIC of India v. Manohar Lal (or similar leading precedents on abandonment)
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Abandonment of Service
rules.relevance: Precedents establishing the legal test for 'abandonment of service' are crucial. Specifically, cases that define whether an employer can dispense with a domestic inquiry if the employee has voluntarily abandoned service without leave, provided proper notices were issued.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (or similar precedents on clean hands)
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Suppression of Facts in Writ Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: Precedents holding that a petitioner who suppresses material facts or comes to court with unclean hands is not entitled to equitable relief. This supports the LIC's argument that the High Court's order should be set aside due to the respondent's concealment of his FCI employment.

Section 17 empowers the Central Government to make regulations for the management of the Corporation, including the appointment, conditions of service, and dismissal of staff. This provides the statutory basis for the LIC Staff Regulations, 1960.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Constructive Notice / Due Diligence in Service Matters
rules.relevance: Relevant to assess whether the LIC exercised due diligence in issuing notices and whether the postal return remarks ('left job and residence') were sufficient to establish the employee's intent to abandon service, thereby validating the summary termination.

rules.reference: Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (or relevant Writ Rules)
rules.relevance: While primarily a writ matter, procedural rules regarding the consequences of false affidavits or suppression of facts in judicial proceedings are relevant to the issue of the respondent's conduct before the High Court.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (or similar)
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Finality of Service Matters
rules.relevance: Precedents discussing the extent of judicial review in service matters, particularly when an employee has been found to have abandoned service. This helps in determining if the High Court was correct in allowing a fresh inquiry or if the termination was final and valid.

rules.reference: Haryana Compassionate Assistance to the Dependents of Deceased Government Employees Rules, 2006
rules.relevance: This rule contains the savings clause allowing dependents to opt for a lump-sum ex-gratia grant under previous rules (2003 or 2005). It is central to the second issue regarding the appellant's mother's entitlement to financial compensation despite the rejection of the employment claim.

The appellant argues that the State violated the right to equality by granting benefits to similarly placed individuals while denying them. This article is relevant to assessing the arbitrariness of the State's action and the application of promissory estoppel.

The appellant relies on the entry in the Minor’s Register and the State's conduct as a promise to reserve a post. The relevance lies in determining whether the State can be estopped from enforcing the time-bar given its earlier actions and the appellant's reliance on them.
These instructions prescribed the three-year limit for minors to attain majority after the employee's death. They form the basis of the DGP's rejection of the claim as time-barred.

This notification provided a one-time relaxation allowing dependents in old cases to exercise the option for ex-gratia compensation. The State's failure to inform the appellant's mother of this relaxation is a key factual element for the second issue.
This policy provided for ex-gratia appointments for Class III and IV posts at the time of the father's death. It establishes the initial legal framework under which the appellant's claim originated.

rules.reference: Compassionate Appointment as Relief, Not Right
rules.relevance: Established jurisprudence holds that compassionate appointment is a welfare measure to relieve destitution, not a fundamental right. This principle limits the scope of the appellant's claim for appointment, especially given the significant delay.

Relevant to the second issue, this principle suggests that if a benefit scheme exists and the State is aware of a dependent's situation, it has a duty to inform them of available options (like the 2011 relaxation) to ensure fair play and equality.

rules.case_name: See e.g., Union of India v. Jyoti Kumari
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Compassionate Appointment
rules.relevance: While specific citations are not in the brief, general Supreme Court precedents define the strict conditions for compassionate appointment, including the requirement of destitution and the non-applicability of estoppel against the State in matters of public policy and statutory limits.

rules.reference: Haryana Police Service Rules / Minor's Register Procedure
rules.relevance: The entry in the Minor's Register on 15.04.1998 is a procedural act by the DGP. The relevance lies in interpreting whether this administrative act created a legitimate expectation or a binding obligation on the State.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. M/s. D. Khosla & Co.
rules.reference: Union of India v. M/s. D. Khosla & Co.
rules.relevance: This is the specific Supreme Court judgment deciding the appeal described in the facts. It holds that unless the award explicitly provides for compound interest, post-award interest is payable only on the principal amount, not on the pre-award interest.
The provision under which the arbitrator's award was made a rule of the court. It establishes the legal basis for the decree and the enforceability of the award's terms.
The provision allowing the court to draw up a decree in terms of the award. The interpretation of the decree's terms regarding interest calculation depends on the award made under this section.

rules.reference: Principle of Strict Construction of Arbitral Awards
rules.relevance: The legal principle that an arbitral award must be construed strictly. If the award specifies 'simple interest' and does not explicitly state 'interest on interest' or 'compound interest', the court cannot imply such a term.

rules.reference: Distinction between Simple and Compound Interest
rules.relevance: The general legal principle that simple interest is calculated only on the principal sum, whereas compound interest involves calculating interest on the accumulated interest. The award's language must clearly indicate the latter to be enforceable.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. M/s. Gangaram Exporters
rules.reference: Union of India v. M/s. Gangaram Exporters
rules.relevance: A relevant precedent often cited in such disputes regarding the interpretation of interest clauses in arbitral awards, reinforcing that post-award interest is typically on the principal unless otherwise specified.
Governs the execution of decrees. The petitioner's claim for a shortfall in interest was raised during execution, making the rules of execution relevant to the procedural history.

The constitutional provision granting the Supreme Court the power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, order, or decree in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in India.

rules.reference: Article 239AA(4) of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: This is the central constitutional provision in dispute. It mandates that the Lieutenant Governor shall exercise his functions in accordance with the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except where he is required by or under any law to exercise his functions in his discretion. The appeal hinges on whether the nomination power falls under the general rule or the discretionary exception.

This specific statutory provision vests the power to nominate ten persons with special knowledge or experience in the Administrator (Lieutenant Governor). The respondent argues this express vesting constitutes a requirement 'under any law' to act in discretion, thereby triggering the exception in Article 239AA(4).

rules.reference: Article 163 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The petitioner relies on this article to argue that the Lieutenant Governor's position is analogous to that of a Governor, who is generally bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. This comparison is used to interpret the scope of the aid and advice requirement in Article 239AA.

rules.case_name: Government of NCT of Delhi v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi
rules.reference: Government of NCT of Delhi v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi
rules.relevance: This landmark Supreme Court judgment extensively interpreted Article 239AA, particularly the relationship between the LG and the Council of Ministers. It established that the LG is bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in matters where the NCT has legislative competence, unless a specific law mandates discretion. This precedent is critical for interpreting the 'discretion' exception.

rules.case_name: S. R. Bommai v. Union of India
rules.reference: S. R. Bommai v. Union of India
rules.relevance: While primarily concerning the dismissal of state governments, this case is often cited for the principle that the Governor (and by analogy, the LG) must act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in the exercise of executive functions, reinforcing the petitioner's argument regarding the general rule of constitutional governance.

rules.reference: Article 32 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: This is the procedural basis for the writ petition filed by the Government of NCT of Delhi. It empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights, which the petitioner invokes to challenge the legality of the LG's nominations.

rules.reference: Principle of Statutory Interpretation: Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius
rules.relevance: The respondent's argument relies on the interpretation that because Section 3(3)(b)(i) expressly names the Administrator/LG as the nominating authority, it excludes the Council of Ministers. This legal principle supports the view that the statute mandates the LG to act personally, potentially invoking the discretionary exception.

The court must harmoniously construe Article 239AA(4) and Section 3(3)(b)(i) of the DMC Act. The principle dictates that if two provisions can be read together without conflict, they should be. The court must determine if the statutory power can be exercised on aid and advice without violating the statute's text.

rules.case_name: B. P. Singhal v. Union of India
rules.reference: B. P. Singhal v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This case discusses the discretionary powers of the Governor/LG versus those exercised on aid and advice. It provides guidance on distinguishing between functions that are purely administrative/discretionary and those that are executive in nature, which is relevant to classifying the nomination power.

rules.reference: Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991
rules.relevance: This Act provides the framework for the Council of Ministers in Delhi. Understanding the scope of the Council's authority under this Act is necessary to determine if the nomination of municipal members falls within the subjects on which the LG is bound to act on their aid and advice.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. It prescribes the mandatory period (15 days) for the highest bidder to deposit the balance sale consideration. The Bank's appeal rests entirely on the argument that the respondents' failure to comply with this rule justified the cancellation of the auction.

rules.reference: SARFAESI Act, 2002 (Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002)
rules.relevance: Section 13(4) empowers the secured creditor to take possession of the secured assets and sell them. This article confers supervisory jurisdiction on the High Court. The High Court exercised this power to review the trial court's order. The Supreme Court's review of the High Court's exercise of this jurisdiction is central to the procedural history.

rules.reference: Distinction between admission of document and admission of facts
rules.relevance: A key legal principle in civil procedure is that admitting the execution or existence of a document does not necessarily amount to an admission of the truth of the contents or the material facts alleged in the plaint, especially when a specific denial (such as a plea of sham transaction) is raised.

When a defendant pleads that a transaction is sham, they are effectively denying the legal effect and the underlying agreement, even if they admit the physical document exists. This plea prevents the document from being treated as an unconditional admission of the plaintiff's case for the purpose of Order XVIII Rule 1.

This rule deals with specific denials in a written statement. It requires a defendant to specifically deny the allegations they do not admit. The relevance lies in interpreting whether the defendants' specific denial of the agreement's validity (sham plea) overrides the general admission of the document's existence for evidentiary sequencing.

This rule states that every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied specifically or by necessary implication, shall be taken to be admitted. The case turns on whether the plea of 'sham transaction' constitutes a specific denial or necessary implication of denial of the material facts.

rules.reference: Burden of Proof in Sham Transaction Cases
rules.relevance: In cases where a transaction is alleged to be sham, the burden of proof lies on the party asserting it. This principle supports the view that the plaintiff must lead evidence to prove the genuineness of the transaction, rather than the defendant being compelled to lead evidence first based on a mere admission of the document's existence.

This rule allows a party to lead evidence in rebuttal of evidence led by the other party. It is relevant in the context of the overall scheme of evidence leading, where the court determines the sequence based on the nature of admissions and denials.

Courts have discretion to determine the order of leading evidence to ensure a fair trial and efficient adjudication. The High Court's decision reflects the exercise of this discretion to prevent technicalities from overriding the substantive issue of whether the transaction was genuine.

This rule requires the court to frame issues at the first hearing. The framing of issues based on the written statement (admitting document but denying agreement) dictates the subsequent procedure for leading evidence, making it relevant to the context of Order XVIII Rule 1.

This section mandates prior sanction for prosecution of public servants. The core issue is whether the irregularity in the grant of sanction (lack of application of mind by the sanctioning authority) vitiates the trial or is merely curable, and whether it occasioned a failure of justice.

This section creates a presumption of corruption once the demand and acceptance of an undue advantage are proved. The High Court accepted that this presumption arose, making the validity of the sanction the sole remaining hurdle.
Defines the offense of public servant taking gratification other than legal remuneration. This is one of the substantive charges under which the respondent was convicted.
Defines the offense of criminal misconduct by a public servant. This is the other substantive charge under which the respondent was convicted.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent laying down guidelines for granting sanction for prosecution. It establishes that sanction must be granted by an authority competent to do so and after application of mind. It is relevant to determine if the irregularity here was fatal.

rules.case_name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
rules.reference: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Often cited regarding the nature of sanction under the Prevention of Corruption Act. It discusses whether sanction is a mere formality or requires substantive application of mind, and the consequences of defective sanction.

The legal principle that procedural irregularities (like defective sanction) do not automatically vitiate a trial unless they occasion a failure of justice or prejudice the accused. The Supreme Court must decide if the High Court correctly applied this principle.

Deals with the power of the appellate court to find error in proceedings. It allows the court to determine if an error, omission, or irregularity in any proceeding has occasioned a failure of justice.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: A relevant precedent discussing the validity of sanction under Section 19 of the PC Act and whether the absence of specific details in the sanction order invalidates it, provided the authority had jurisdiction and applied its mind.

rules.case_name: K. Veeraswami v. Union of India
rules.reference: K. Veeraswami v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes that public servants are not immune from prosecution under the PC Act and clarifies the scope of sanction requirements, reinforcing the need for valid sanction but also the substantive nature of the offense.
This section empowers the Disciplinary Authority to terminate the services of a member of the CRPF. It is the primary statutory basis for the termination order challenged in this appeal.

rules.reference: Central Reserve Police Force (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969
rules.relevance: Rule 14 specifically deals with the termination of service for misconduct, including suppression of material facts or furnishing false information during recruitment. It provides the procedural and substantive framework for the inquiry and termination.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes that suppression of material facts at the time of recruitment vitiates the very foundation of the appointment, rendering the service liable to be terminated even after a long period, as the appointment itself is void ab initio.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: This case holds that if a candidate suppresses material facts regarding criminal antecedents during recruitment, the appointment is liable to be cancelled. It supports the view that such suppression is a serious misconduct justifying termination.

The legal principle that an appointment obtained by fraud or suppression of material facts is void ab initio. This principle is central to determining whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the termination based on the respondent's alleged lack of awareness.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Paras Ram
rules.reference: Union of India v. Paras Ram
rules.relevance: Reinforces the stance that courts should not interfere with disciplinary proceedings where the employee has been found guilty of suppressing material facts, as it strikes at the root of the recruitment process.

Relevant to establish the respondent's knowledge of the criminal proceedings. The fact that he was granted bail establishes that he was aware of the cases prior to filling the Verification Roll, countering his claim of ignorance.

rules.reference: Standard of Review in Disciplinary Matters
rules.relevance: The principle that High Courts exercising writ jurisdiction should not act as appellate authorities over disciplinary findings unless there is a perversity or violation of natural justice. This is relevant to challenge the High Court's interference with the Disciplinary Authority's finding of fact.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
rules.relevance: Establishes the scope of judicial review in service matters, emphasizing that courts should not substitute their own opinion for that of the disciplinary authority regarding the quantum of punishment or the facts of misconduct, unless the order is arbitrary or illegal.

rules.reference: Central Reserve Police Force (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969
rules.relevance: Deals with the procedure for appeal against termination orders. Relevant to the procedural history where the Appellate Authority upheld the termination, and the subsequent challenge in the High Court.

This is the specific statutory provision invoked by the Petitioners to argue that the civil suit for cancellation of the sale deed stands abated due to pending consolidation proceedings. The core legal question is the interpretation of this section regarding its applicability to suits involving voidable documents.

The notification under Section 4 initiated the consolidation proceedings in 2003, which is the factual basis for the claim that the land is under consolidation and thus subject to the restrictions of Section 5.

rules.reference: Distinction between Void and Voidable Documents
rules.relevance: The High Court's decision rested on the classification of the sale deed as 'voidable' rather than 'void'. This legal distinction is central to determining whether the Civil Court retains jurisdiction or if the matter is exclusively within the purview of the Consolidation Court.

rules.reference: Jurisdiction of Civil Courts vs. Consolidation Courts
rules.relevance: The appeal concerns the ouster of the Civil Court's jurisdiction. The principle that Civil Courts retain jurisdiction over matters not explicitly barred by statute, particularly those involving fraud and impersonation which may not be purely revenue matters, is relevant.

rules.reference: Fraud and Impersonation in Property Transactions
rules.relevance: The allegation that Haneefa fraudulently claimed to be Gafoor's daughter and used impersonation to get recorded as a tenure holder is a substantive issue. Authorities regarding the civil court's power to adjudicate on fraud and the validity of title despite revenue record mutations are relevant.

This section deals with voidable contracts and the right to rescind them. Since the sale deed is alleged to be voidable due to fraud/impersonation, this provision supports the Respondent's claim for cancellation in a Civil Court.
Relates to the rights and liabilities of buyer and seller, including the duty to disclose defects in title. Relevant in assessing the validity of the sale deed executed by Haneefa.

The case involves a mutation in favor of Haneefa in 2016. The legal principle that mutation entries are for revenue purposes and do not confer title, especially when obtained by fraud, is relevant to the Civil Court's jurisdiction to cancel the deed.

rules.case_name: See, e.g., State of U.P. v. Ram Prasad
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on U.P. Consolidation Act
rules.relevance: While specific citations are not provided in the brief, Supreme Court precedents interpreting Section 5 of the U.P. Consolidation Act regarding the scope of 'disputes' and the jurisdiction of Civil Courts are highly relevant to decide the appeal.
The High Court exercised its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to set aside the lower courts' orders. The Supreme Court's review of this exercise of power is part of the procedural history.
Defines 'Mortgage by conditional sale'. The defendant argues the transaction falls under this section, making the condition of absolute sale upon default valid and enforceable.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Clog on Equity of Redemption
rules.relevance: The plaintiff argues the condition converting the mortgage into a sale is a void clog on the equity of redemption. This principle holds that any provision in a mortgage deed that prevents the mortgagor from redeeming the property upon payment of the debt is void.

Governs the right of redemption. It establishes the mortgagor's right to redeem the mortgage upon payment of the mortgage money, subject to the terms of the mortgage deed, unless the right is barred by law or court decree.

The plaintiff contends the mortgage is invalid under this section, which restricts the transfer of agricultural land if the transferor is left with less than 10 acres of unencumbered un-irrigated land. This challenges the validity of the underlying transaction.

rules.case_name: Seth Ram Kumar v. Lachhman Das
rules.reference: Seth Ram Kumar v. Lachhman Das
rules.relevance: A leading precedent distinguishing between a mortgage by conditional sale and a simple mortgage with a clog on redemption. It establishes that if the transaction is essentially a mortgage, any condition preventing redemption is void.

rules.case_name: Kalyan Singh v. Ram Kripal Singh
rules.reference: Kalyan Singh v. Ram Kripal Singh
rules.relevance: Supreme Court precedent clarifying that the intention of the parties at the time of the transaction determines whether it is a mortgage by conditional sale or a simple mortgage. If the intention was to create a security, it is a mortgage, and clogs are void.

Defines 'Simple Mortgage'. The plaintiff argues the transaction is a simple mortgage where possession was not delivered, making the subsequent condition of sale a void clog rather than a valid conditional sale.
Relates to the decree for redemption. The Trial Court decreed the suit allowing redemption upon payment of a specific sum. This rule governs the form of decree in suits for redemption of mortgages.

Grants the Supreme Court special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, or final order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India. This is the jurisdictional basis for the present appeal.

A key principle in interpreting mortgage deeds. Courts look at the substance of the transaction and the true intention of the parties rather than just the form of the document to determine if it is a mortgage by conditional sale or a simple mortgage with a clog.

This is the specific provision under which the petition for the appointment of an arbitrator was filed. The core issue is the scope of the referring court's jurisdiction under this section to decide complex questions of fact and law regarding the existence of an arbitration agreement with a non-signatory.

Defines 'Arbitration Agreement'. The dispute centers on whether Respondent No. 2 (SAP SE), a non-signatory, is bound by the arbitration agreement contained in the GTC Agreement signed by Respondent No. 1, invoking concepts like 'claiming through or under' a party.

rules.case_name: Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A.
rules.reference: Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A.
rules.relevance: Established the principle that the referring court should only conduct a prima facie examination of the existence of an arbitration agreement under Section 11, leaving complex issues to the arbitral tribunal. This is central to the argument that the court should not decide the Group of Companies doctrine at this stage.

rules.case_name: SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd.
rules.reference: SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd.
rules.relevance: A landmark judgment holding that the referring court must decide whether a valid arbitration agreement exists before appointing an arbitrator. It creates the tension with Bhatia International regarding the depth of inquiry permissible under Section 11.

rules.case_name: Associate v. Byram J. Sanghvi
rules.relevance: Clarified that the referring court's role under Section 11 is limited to a prima facie examination of the existence of an arbitration agreement and that it should not delve into complex questions of fact or law, supporting the petitioner's contention.

The specific legal doctrine invoked by the petitioner to bind the non-signatory parent company (SAP SE) to the arbitration agreement. The case involves determining whether this doctrine can be applied at the Section 11 stage or requires full adjudication by the tribunal.

rules.case_name: M/s. Chloro Controls India Pvt. Ltd. v. Severn Trent Water Purification Inc.
rules.reference: M/s. Chloro Controls India Pvt. Ltd. v. Severn Trent Water Purification Inc.
rules.relevance: This case specifically dealt with the Group of Companies doctrine and the interpretation of 'claiming through or under' a party under Section 7. The Supreme Court referred questions from this case to a larger bench, making it directly relevant to the current appeal's context.

The admission of the insolvency application against the petitioner under Section 7 led to the adjournment of the earlier arbitration proceedings. This procedural history is relevant to understanding the timeline and the fresh invocation of arbitration.

The principle that the arbitral tribunal has the power to rule on its own jurisdiction. The respondents argue that the complex issue of whether a non-signatory is bound should be left to the tribunal under this principle, rather than decided by the court at the appointment stage.

Provides the general framework for the appointment of arbitrators. The interplay between Section 11(1) and 11(6) defines the procedural mechanism and the limited scope of judicial intervention in the appointment process.

The petition is instituted under this article, which grants the Supreme Court the power to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights. The core issue is whether the Court can exercise this jurisdiction to direct the executive on foreign policy matters.

Petitioners allege a violation of this directive principle, which mandates the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organized peoples with one another.

This article vests the executive power of the Union in the President, extending to matters with respect to which Parliament has power to make laws, including foreign affairs. This is central to the defense that arms export policy is a non-justiciable executive function.

This provision empowers Parliament to make laws for implementing international treaties and agreements. It is relevant to the argument regarding India's obligations under the Genocide Convention and whether domestic law must align with international rulings.

Petitioners claim a violation of the right to life and dignity. The relevance lies in whether the right to life extends to the right to live in a world free from genocide or whether the State's duty to protect life abroad creates a justiciable obligation in domestic courts.

Petitioners allege arbitrary state action in continuing arms exports. The relevance is whether the executive's discretion in granting licenses violates the guarantee of equality and non-arbitrariness.

This section empowers the Central Government to prohibit or regulate the import or export of any goods. It is the statutory basis for the government's authority to grant or cancel the licenses in question.
This section allows the Central Government to prohibit the export of any goods. It is relevant as the procedural mechanism through which export bans or restrictions on arms would be implemented.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Non-Justiciability of Foreign Policy
rules.relevance: A well-established legal principle in Indian constitutional law that the Supreme Court generally does not interfere with the executive's conduct of foreign affairs, unless there is a clear violation of fundamental rights or constitutional provisions.

The principle that international treaties and conventions (like the Genocide Convention) are not automatically enforceable in domestic courts unless enacted into domestic law by Parliament under Article 253.

This is the primary procedural provision under which the High Court appointed the arbitrator. The appeal challenges the exercise of jurisdiction under this section, specifically regarding the scope of the arbitration agreement and whether the dispute is arbitrable.

rules.reference: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: The appellant argues that this special statute overrides the Arbitration Act. The court must determine if the dispute regarding the lease renewal and rate revisions falls within the exclusive domain of the Estate Officer under this Act or if it remains a civil dispute subject to arbitration.

rules.case_name: Booz Allen Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd.
rules.reference: Booz Allen Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd.
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent distinguishes between rights in rem (which are generally not arbitrable) and rights in personam (which are arbitrable). It is crucial for determining whether the dispute over the lease agreement and renewal rights is capable of settlement by arbitration.

rules.case_name: SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd.
rules.reference: SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd.
rules.relevance: This case defines the limited scope of the authority of the judicial authority under Section 11 of the Arbitration Act. It establishes that the court should only examine whether a valid arbitration agreement exists and not delve into the merits of the dispute, which is relevant to the appellant's challenge against the High Court's order.

This statute establishes the Central Warehousing Corporation as a statutory body. Understanding its statutory powers and the nature of its contracts is necessary to determine if the lease agreement is a commercial contract subject to arbitration or a statutory function immune from it.

rules.reference: Principle of Severability and Commercial Efficacy
rules.relevance: Courts generally interpret arbitration clauses to give them commercial efficacy. The principle that disputes arising out of or in connection with the contract (including termination and renewal) are arbitrable unless explicitly excluded is central to interpreting Clause 16 of the lease agreement.

rules.case_name: N.N. Global Mercantile Pvt. Ltd. v. Indo Unique Flame Ltd.
rules.reference: N.N. Global Mercantile Pvt. Ltd. v. Indo Unique Flame Ltd.
rules.relevance: This case reaffirms that disputes involving statutory bodies are arbitrable if they arise from commercial contracts. It supports the view that the Arbitration Act applies to disputes between statutory bodies and private parties unless a specific statute expressly ousts the jurisdiction of arbitral tribunals.

Defines the 'Arbitration Agreement'. The court must determine if the dispute regarding the right of renewal and rate revisions falls within the scope of 'disputes arising out of or concerning the agreement' as defined in Clause 16.

rules.case_name: M/s. R. Mohanraj v. M/s. M. Mohanraj
rules.reference: M/s. R. Mohanraj v. M/s. M/s. M. Mohanraj
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of Section 11 and the limited inquiry required by the court. It is relevant to counter the appellant's argument that the High Court should have examined the substantive merits of the Public Premises Act claim before appointing an arbitrator.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Special Law vs. General Law
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether the Public Premises Act (special law) overrides the Arbitration Act (general law). The principle that a special law prevails only if there is an irreconcilable conflict or an express ouster of jurisdiction is key to resolving this conflict.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the Trial Court summoned the petitioners as accused. The core legal issue is whether the conditions for invoking this section were met despite the closure report.

rules.case_name: Pankaj Bansal v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Pankaj Bansal v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent laying down the principles for summoning additional accused under Section 319 CrPC. It establishes that the court must be satisfied that there is sufficient evidence against the person to be summoned and that it is expedient in the interests of justice.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Govind Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent clarifies that the power under Section 319 is not an appellate power but a discretionary one to ensure justice. It emphasizes that the court must record reasons for summoning and that the evidence must be credible and reliable, not merely speculative.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Relevant for establishing that the court cannot summon an accused based on mere suspicion or conjecture. It reinforces that the evidence must be such that a reasonable person would conclude that the person committed the offence.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof for Summoning under Section 319
rules.relevance: The legal principle that the standard of proof required to summon an accused under Section 319 is 'sufficient evidence' which is lower than 'proof beyond reasonable doubt' but higher than 'mere suspicion'. The court must evaluate the credibility of the witness (PW3) against the closure report.

The petitioners were charged under Section 149 IPC (unlawful assembly). This section is relevant because the summoning order relied on overt acts attributed to them by PW3, linking them to the common object of the unlawful assembly.

The primary offence alleged is murder. The severity of the charge influences the court's discretion under Section 319 to ensure that no person escapes justice if credible evidence links them to the crime.

rules.reference: Role of Closure Report vs. Judicial Satisfaction
rules.relevance: The principle that a closure report by the Investigating Officer is not binding on the Trial Court. The Court is the ultimate arbiter of evidence and can summon an accused if it finds sufficient material on record, even if the investigation concluded otherwise.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram Firkharia
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram Firkharia
rules.relevance: Discusses the scope of Section 319 and the necessity for the court to apply its mind to the evidence. It supports the view that the court can summon an accused if the evidence, though not conclusive, is sufficient to warrant a trial.

Relates to the filing of the final report (closure report) by the police. Understanding the procedural status of the closure report is essential to determine if the Trial Court was justified in overriding it based on oral evidence.

Central to the appeal. The First Appellate Court and High Court held the suit was governed by this article (12 years limitation for possession based on title) because the defendants failed to prove adverse possession. The Supreme Court must decide if this classification was correct.

Central to the appeal. The appellants argue the suit is barred by this article (3 years limitation for declaration of title) because the cause of action accrued in 1981-1982 when the mutation occurred. The court must determine if the suit is primarily for declaration or possession.

Relevant to the procedural history. The First Appellate Court allowed the amendment to the plaint to include a prayer for recovery of possession. The validity of allowing such an amendment at the appellate stage is a key procedural issue.

rules.case_name: P. Kunhikannan v. P. Kunhiraman
rules.relevance: A leading precedent distinguishing between suits for declaration and suits for possession. It establishes that if a plaintiff claims title and seeks possession, the limitation is governed by Article 65, not Article 58, unless the plaintiff admits the defendant's possession is adverse and seeks only declaration.

The First Appellate Court noted that defendants had not pleaded or proved adverse possession. Under Indian law, mere possession by a defendant does not extinguish the plaintiff's title unless adverse possession is established. This principle supports the application of Article 65.
May be relevant if the court considers whether the amendment to the plaint relates back to the date of the original suit filing, thereby saving the suit from limitation under Article 65.

rules.case_name: S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath
rules.reference: S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath
rules.relevance: Establishes the strict requirements for proving adverse possession (animus possidendi and continuous possession). Since the lower courts found no proof of adverse possession, this precedent supports the finding that the plaintiff's title was not extinguished.

Relevant to the High Court's dismissal of the Second Appeal. The High Court held no substantial question of law arose. The Supreme Court must determine if the misapplication of limitation articles constitutes a substantial question of law.

Defines the threshold for the Supreme Court's jurisdiction in a Special Leave Petition. The court must decide if the interpretation of Articles 58 and 65 involves a question of law of general public importance or a grave miscarriage of justice.

Relevant to the factual background regarding the mutation of Khatha records in 1981-1982. The court may need to consider whether mutation entries confer title or are merely revenue records, which impacts the cause of action date.

rules.reference: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
rules.relevance: Section 29 mandates that no person with benchmark disability shall be denied admission to any educational institution on the ground of disability. It requires institutions to provide reasonable accommodation and prohibits discrimination, directly challenging the automatic exclusion based on percentage of disability.

rules.reference: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
rules.relevance: Defines 'benchmark disability' as not less than forty percent of a specified disability. This definition is central to determining the appellant's eligibility for reservation and protection under the Act.

This specific appendix stipulates that persons with speech and language disability of 40% or more are not eligible for the medical course. This is the primary regulatory provision being challenged as discriminatory and inconsistent with the RPWD Act, 2016.

Guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws. The blanket ban on candidates with >40% speech disability may be challenged as arbitrary and violative of Article 14 if it does not consider individual functional competency.

Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, while Article 15(4) empowers the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes. The interplay between these articles and the RPWD Act is relevant to the reservation claim.

Protects the right to life and personal liberty, which has been interpreted to include the right to education and livelihood. Denying admission solely based on disability percentage without assessing functional ability may infringe upon this right.

A core principle under the RPWD Act, 2016 and international conventions (UNCRPD). It requires modifying policies or practices to ensure persons with disabilities can enjoy their rights on an equal basis. The Medical Board's opinion supports the application of this principle over a rigid statutory bar.

rules.reference: Functional Competency vs. Percentage of Disability
rules.relevance: The legal principle that eligibility for professional courses should be determined by the individual's ability to perform essential functions of the profession (functional competency) rather than a rigid percentage of disability, especially when reasonable accommodation is possible.

Establishes the National Medical Commission (NMC) and empowers it to frame regulations for medical education. The validity of the NMC's regulations (GME Regulations 1997) must be tested against the parent Act and the RPWD Act, 2016.

rules.case_name: Omkar Ramchandra Gond v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The current case itself. The Supreme Court's direction to constitute a Medical Board and keep the seat vacant indicates a shift towards assessing individual functional capacity rather than applying a blanket ban, setting a precedent for future similar cases.

This section empowers the court to impound instruments insufficiently stamped and imposes a mandatory penalty of ten times the deficit duty if the instrument is not admitted in evidence after the deficit is determined. The core dispute is whether this mandatory penalty applies when the instrument is referred to the District Registrar.

This section grants the District Registrar the discretionary power to determine the amount of penalty to be imposed on the person liable to pay the deficit duty. The appellant argues that referring the matter to the Registrar invokes this discretionary power, overriding the mandatory penalty under Section 34.

This section provides the procedure for the court to impound an instrument and refer it to the District Registrar for the determination of the proper stamp duty. It is the procedural trigger for the involvement of the District Registrar in this case.

rules.case_name: State of Karnataka v. M. S. R. Swamy
rules.citation: 2019 (1) Karn LJ 1 (SC) or similar recent SC judgment on Stamp Act
rules.reference: State of Karnataka v. M. S. R. Swamy
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court has recently interpreted the interplay between Sections 34 and 39 of the Karnataka Stamp Act, holding that when an instrument is referred to the District Registrar under Section 33, the Registrar has the discretion to determine the penalty under Section 39, and the court cannot automatically impose the mandatory ten-times penalty under Section 34 without considering the Registrar's determination.

Relevant to interpreting whether the mandatory penalty under Section 34 and the discretionary power under Section 39 are mutually exclusive or if Section 39 acts as an exception/supplement when the matter is referred to the Registrar.

As the Karnataka Stamp Act is modeled on the Indian Stamp Act, Section 35 (which deals with instruments chargeable with further duty) and its interpretation in various Supreme Court judgments provide persuasive authority on the nature of penalties and the role of the Collector/Registrar.

rules.case_name: K. S. N. Raju v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: K. S. N. Raju v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: This precedent discusses the powers of the District Registrar and the courts under the Karnataka Stamp Act, specifically regarding the determination of deficit duty and the imposition of penalties, supporting the view that the Registrar's discretion under Section 39 is paramount when the instrument is referred to them.

Relevant for the procedural aspect of appealing the trial court's order regarding the imposition of penalty and the admissibility of the document, although the substantive issue is governed by the Stamp Act.

Supports the argument that a mandatory ten-times penalty may be excessive and that the discretionary power under Section 39 allows for a penalty proportionate to the circumstances, such as bona fide mistakes or delays in clarification.

rules.case_name: S. S. R. K. Prasad v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: S. S. R. K. Prasad v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Further reinforces the Supreme Court's stance that the District Registrar's determination under Section 39 is binding on the court regarding the penalty, preventing the court from independently imposing the mandatory penalty under Section 34 once the reference is made.

Defines the limited grounds for setting aside an arbitral award, specifically regarding patent illegality and violation of public policy, which is central to the challenge against the High Court's interference.
Governs the appealability of orders passed under Section 34, establishing the jurisdiction of the High Court and the Supreme Court in this matter.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Concor
rules.relevance: Establishes the standard for 'patent illegality' appearing on the face of the record, crucial for determining if the High Court was justified in setting aside Claim 3 for alleged violation of contract terms.

rules.case_name: Bharat Broadband Network Ltd. v. IIT Research Academy
rules.reference: Bharat Broadband Network Ltd. v. IIT Research Academy
rules.relevance: Clarifies that courts cannot re-appreciate evidence or act as appellate authorities over factual findings of arbitrators, relevant to the challenge regarding Claim 4 where the High Court re-evaluated payment timings.

rules.case_name: M/s. ONGC v. Saw Pipes Ltd.
rules.reference: M/s. ONGC v. Saw Pipes Ltd.
rules.relevance: Defines 'public policy of India' under Section 34(2)(b)(ii), including the concept of patent illegality, which forms the basis for judicial review of the arbitral award.

rules.case_name: Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority
rules.reference: Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority
rules.relevance: Holds that an arbitral award cannot be set aside merely because the court disagrees with the arbitrator's interpretation of the contract, supporting the appellant's argument against the setting aside of Claim 3.
Provides for the payment of interest on the arbitral award, relevant to the dispute over Claim 6 regarding pre-reference, pendente lite, and post-award interest.

rules.case_name: M/s. ONGC v. Saw Pipes Ltd.
rules.reference: M/s. ONGC v. Saw Pipes Ltd.
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that the court's role is supervisory, not appellate, preventing the High Court from substituting its own view on factual disputes like those in Claim 4.

rules.reference: Principle of Separability and Finality of Arbitral Awards
rules.relevance: Underpins the limited scope of judicial intervention, ensuring that contractual disputes are resolved by the arbitrator unless the award is vitiated by patent illegality or public policy violations.
Governs compensation for breach of contract, relevant to the assessment of damages claimed in Claims 1, 2, and 3, although the primary issue is the arbitrability and judicial review of the award.

This is the primary substantive provision under which the complaint was filed and conviction was initially recorded. The core issue is whether the dishonored cheque was drawn for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability, which is a prerequisite for liability under this section.

The central legal question is whether the underlying transaction constitutes a 'legally enforceable debt'. The Appellate Court acquitted the respondent based on the premise that the debt was not legally enforceable due to interest rate discrepancies. Authorities defining the scope of 'legally enforceable debt' in the context of chit funds and usurious interest are critical.

Section 12 typically regulates the interest rates and charges permissible in chit funds. If the interest charged (3% vs 1.8%) violates this Act, the debt may not be legally enforceable.

rules.case_name: Kusum Ingots & Industries (P) Ltd. v. Payal Industrial Corporation
rules.reference: Kusum Ingots & Industries (P) Ltd. v. Payal Industrial Corporation
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent is pivotal in determining whether a cheque issued for a disputed or unenforceable debt attracts Section 138. It establishes that if the underlying debt is not legally enforceable (e.g., due to violation of statutory limits on interest), the offence under Section 138 is not made out.

The respondent filed a petition under Section 391 CrPC to adduce additional evidence (partial repayments and interest discrepancies) before the Appellate Court. The validity of admitting such evidence and its impact on the acquittal is a procedural issue relevant to the appeal.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Criminal Appeals against Acquittal
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court is reviewing an acquittal. The legal principle governing the appellate court's power to interfere with an acquittal is restrictive. The court must be satisfied that the lower court's view was 'perverse' or 'illegal'. This principle limits the scope of the Supreme Court's review of the factual findings regarding the interest rates.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: This case discusses the interpretation of 'legally enforceable debt' and the burden of proof. The respondent's evidence of partial repayments and interest discrepancies serves to rebut this presumption. The legal principle regarding whether partial payment admits the entire debt or merely acknowledges a portion, and how it interacts with the calculation of the outstanding amount for Section 138, is relevant to determining if the cheque amount corresponded to a valid liability.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh

It holds that non-compliance is not fatal unless it causes prejudice to the accused, which is the core legal test to be applied here.
The substantive offense for which the appellant was convicted. While the appeal focuses on procedural irregularity, the conviction under this section is the subject matter of the challenge.

The appellant was convicted read with this section for acting in furtherance of common intention. The specific circumstances omitted in Section 313 (exhortation and holding) are crucial to establishing the common intention under this section.

This section deals with the power of the appellate court to find error in the proceedings. The court must decide if the irregularity in Section 313 examination amounts to an error that has occasioned a failure of justice, warranting interference.

A key legal principle derived from Section 313 jurisprudence. The court must assess whether the accused was actually prejudiced by the non-putting of questions, i.e., whether he was denied a fair chance to explain the circumstances, rather than treating the omission as automatically fatal.

The right to a fair trial is part of the right to life and personal liberty. The appellant's argument that the trial was vitiated touches upon the fundamental right to a fair procedure, although this is usually analyzed through the lens of Cr.PC provisions.

This section mandates that a plaintiff seeking specific performance must aver and prove that they have performed or been ready and willing to perform all essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by them. This is the central statutory hurdle for the buyer.

rules.case_name: S. Narayana v. S. Venkateswara Rao

rules.case_name: K. Srinivasa Rao v. K. Venkata Rao
rules.reference: K. Srinivasa Rao v. K. Venkata Rao

rules.case_name: K. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu
