rules.reference: Principle of Vicarious Liability in Criminal Law
rules.relevance: The central issue is whether vicarious liability applies to corporate officers in environmental offences. The court must apply the principle that criminal liability is personal and vicarious liability is not presumed unless expressly provided by statute or implied by the nature of the offence.

rules.reference: Requirement of Specific Allegations for Individual Liability
rules.relevance: The complaint failed to name the company or individuals physically present. The court must apply the principle that for individual liability to attach, the complaint must specifically allege personal involvement, active participation, or conscious omission by the accused.

rules.case_name: S. R. Batra v. Taruna Batra
rules.reference: S. R. Batra v. Taruna Batra
rules.relevance: While primarily a civil case, this precedent is often cited in Indian jurisprudence to establish the strict limits of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC, emphasizing that such powers should not be used to interfere with the merits of a case at the threshold unless there is a clear abuse of process or lack of jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent lays down the guidelines for quashing FIRs or complaints under Section 482 CrPC. It is relevant to determine if the complaint against the appellants falls under any of the categories where quashing is appropriate, such as when the allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence.

rules.case_name: Narayan Dutt Aggarwal v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Narayan Dutt Aggarwal v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This precedent is relevant regarding the liability of directors and officers in environmental offences. It discusses the interpretation of 'whoever' in environmental statutes and whether it extends to individuals not directly involved in the physical act, helping decide if the Punjab Land Preservation Act implies such liability.

This section defines 'person' to include any company or association. It is relevant to interpret whether the term 'whoever' in the Punjab Land Preservation Act includes corporate entities and, by extension, their officers, or if it is limited to natural persons committing the act.

rules.reference: Prima Facie Case Test for Issuance of Process
rules.relevance: The court must apply the test of whether the complaint, taken at face value, discloses a prima facie case against the specific individuals named. If the allegations are generic and do not link the appellants to the offence, the issuance of process may be deemed erroneous.

Determines the legal status of the adopted son, specifically whether he is considered the son of the adoptive mother for all purposes and whether the adoption severs his ties with his natural family, thereby establishing his rights as a legal heir.

Defines the order of succession for a female Hindu dying intestate. Since the adoptive mother died during the pendency of the suit, this section determines if the adopted son is the Class I heir entitled to inherit her absolute share.

Defines the essential elements of a valid gift, including the requirement of a transfer made voluntarily and without consideration, and crucially, the necessity of acceptance by or on behalf of the donee.

Defines 'transfer of property by act of parties' and establishes the general principle that an owner is competent to transfer their interest, supporting the High Court's view on the validity of the sale deed if the mother was the absolute owner.

rules.case_name: Smt. Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar
rules.reference: Smt. Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that a gift is incomplete without delivery of possession and acceptance by the donee. This is directly relevant to challenging the validity of the gift deed executed by the adoptive mother.

rules.case_name: V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddy
rules.reference: V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddy
rules.relevance: Clarifies the nature of a widow's estate and her powers of alienation. It helps determine if the property allotted to Defendant No. 1 via the compromise decree was a limited estate or absolute ownership, which dictates her power to sell or gift.

Specifies the conditions for a valid adoption, including the requirement that the person making the adoption must have the capacity to do so. Relevant to verify if the adoptive mother had the legal capacity to adopt the appellant.

Governs the procedure for substitution of parties when a party to a suit dies. Relevant to ensure the legal proceedings continued correctly after the death of Defendant No. 1 and that the appellant was properly substituted or represented.

rules.reference: Principle of Absolute Ownership vs. Limited Estate
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether the compromise decree granted the widow absolute ownership or a limited estate. If absolute, she could alienate the property; if limited, her powers are restricted. This principle underpins the validity of both the sale and gift deeds.

Mandates the registration of instruments of gift and sale deeds. Relevant to establish the formal validity of the documents executed by the adoptive mother, although registration alone does not validate a gift lacking delivery/acceptance.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the High Court purported to act. The central issue is whether this section empowers the High Court to direct a de novo reinvestigation by the CBI while acquitting the accused, or if it is limited to setting aside the conviction and acquitting or directing a new trial.

This section embodies the principle of double jeopardy (autrefois acquit). The appellant argues that the second trial is barred because he was already acquitted. The relevance lies in determining if the High Court's order with a direction for reinvestigation constitutes a final acquittal that triggers the bar under Section 300.

This article guarantees that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. The appellant relies on this to argue that the direction for reinvestigation and subsequent trial violates his fundamental right against double jeopardy.

The appellant filed a petition under this section seeking quashing of the chargesheet. The High Court's dismissal of this petition is the immediate order under appeal, making the scope of inherent powers under Section 482 relevant to the procedural history.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v. P. Ramulu
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh v. P. Ramulu
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent interpreting Section 300 Cr.P.C. and the concept of 'acquittal'. It helps determine whether an acquittal accompanied by a direction for further investigation is a final acquittal that bars subsequent prosecution.

rules.case_name: K. Venugopal v. State of Kerala
rules.reference: K. Venugopal v. State of Kerala
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of the High Court's powers under Section 386 Cr.P.C. and whether it can direct a fresh investigation or a new trial, providing authority on the limits of appellate jurisdiction.

The specific offence of kidnapping for ransom for which the appellant was originally convicted. While the procedural issues are central, the gravity of the offence is relevant to the context of the death sentence and the state's interest in reinvestigation.
The specific offence of murder for which the appellant was originally convicted. Like Section 364A, it defines the substantive crime at the heart of the reinvestigation.

The overarching legal principle that prevents a person from being tried twice for the same offence. The appeal hinges on whether the High Court's order created a situation where the appellant is effectively being prosecuted again for the same facts.

rules.reference: Scope of Inherent Powers of High Court
rules.relevance: The principle that inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. must be exercised sparingly and only to secure the ends of justice or prevent abuse of process. This is relevant to the High Court's decision to dismiss the quashing petition.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: Section 18 explicitly states that the offences under the Act are non-cognizable and non-bailable, and crucially, that no court shall take cognizance of any such offence except upon a complaint in writing made by a public servant or any person who has been given notice in this behalf. More importantly, it implies that these offences are not compoundable, restricting the power of courts to quash proceedings based on private settlement.

The offence of rape under Section 376(2)(N) is a serious non-compoundable offence. The Supreme Court has consistently held that such offences affect society at large and cannot be settled by private compromise, limiting the High Court's inherent powers to quash.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent lays down the guidelines for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC. It establishes that quashing of FIRs or charge sheets is permissible only in exceptional cases, and generally not where the offence is serious and non-compoundable, unless the settlement is genuine and the offence is purely private in nature.

rules.case_name: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: This case clarifies the scope of Section 482 CrPC in light of the Compounding of Offences provisions. It holds that while compoundable offences can be quashed upon settlement, non-compoundable offences (like those under the SC/ST Act and IPC 376) generally cannot be quashed merely on the basis of a settlement, especially if the settlement is not voluntary or genuine.

rules.case_name: Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: This precedent is highly relevant regarding the protection of witnesses, particularly vulnerable ones like illiterate women. It emphasizes that the court must ensure that the witness is not coerced or intimidated into withdrawing complaints or signing settlements, and that the genuineness of such withdrawals must be strictly verified.

This section confers inherent powers on the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the CrPC or to prevent abuse of the process of any court. The appeal centers on whether the High Court correctly exercised these powers to quash proceedings for non-compoundable offences.

Section 80 presumes that documents purporting to be certified copies of public records are genuine. However, in the context of affidavits signed by illiterate persons, the lack of proper attestation or explanation by a witness/notary raises doubts about the voluntariness and understanding of the document, challenging the presumption of regularity.

rules.reference: Principle of Genuineness and Voluntariness in Settlements
rules.relevance: Courts must satisfy themselves that a settlement is voluntary, free from coercion, and entered into with full understanding. For an illiterate victim, the absence of a witness or advocate explaining the contents of the affidavit is a critical defect that undermines the genuineness of the settlement.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: This specific provision prohibits outraging the modesty of a woman belonging to a Scheduled Caste or Tribe. Like other offences under the Act, it is non-compoundable, reinforcing the argument that private settlement cannot extinguish the state's interest in prosecuting such atrocities.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Rajesh Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: While primarily dealing with domestic violence, this judgment reinforces the principle that courts must be cautious in quashing proceedings involving vulnerable victims and must ensure that any settlement is not the result of pressure or coercion, aligning with the appellant's argument about the suspicious nature of the affidavits.
Central to the first issue: determines whether liability to pay customs duty arises when confiscated goods are redeemed after payment of a fine.
Central to the third issue: governs the liability to pay interest on delayed payment of customs duty, which is the core dispute regarding the refund of interest.
Relevant to the second issue: the High Court held that assessment of duty must be done under this section, which inevitably attracts Section 28AB for interest.

rules.case_name: Commr. of Customs (Import) v. Jagdish Cancer and Research Centre
rules.reference: Commr. of Customs (Import) v. Jagdish Cancer and Research Centre
rules.relevance: Explicitly cited in the issues to determine the true and correct ratio regarding the applicability of Section 28 in confiscation proceedings.
The provision under which the goods were proposed to be confiscated for violating the conditions of the exemption notification.
Relevant to the procedural history and the appellant's argument that proceedings were initiated under this section rather than Section 28, affecting the applicability of interest.
The provision under which the appellant applied to the Settlement Commission, whose order regarding the waiver of penalties and refund of interest is being challenged.

rules.reference: Principle of Redemption of Confiscated Goods
rules.relevance: General legal principle governing the relationship between the payment of duty/fine and the right to redeem confiscated goods under the Customs Act.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Kedar Nath Singh
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. Kedar Nath Singh
rules.relevance: Establishes the foundational principle that the registration of a second FIR for the same offence is prohibited if it relates to the same transaction, but permissible if it discloses a distinct offence or transaction.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: Provides the comprehensive guidelines for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash FIRs, including the test for determining whether an FIR is an abuse of process or legally maintainable.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Clarifies that a second FIR is not barred if it discloses a distinct offence or a different transaction, even if it arises from the same general course of conduct, distinguishing between 'same transaction' and 'distinct incidents'.

The procedural provision under which the respondent filed the petition to quash the FIR and which the High Court exercised to allow the petition. The Supreme Court must determine if this power was correctly exercised.
Defines the offence of public servant taking gratification other than legal remuneration, which is the core allegation in both FIRs.
Defines the offence of public servant taking gratification by criminal conspiracy, which is specifically alleged in the second FIR regarding the conspiracy to take bribes for licenses.
Defines the offence of criminal conspiracy, which is charged in the second FIR but not the first, supporting the argument that the second FIR involves distinct legal ingredients.

rules.case_name: Pankaj Bansal v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Pankaj Bansal v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that the existence of a prior FIR does not bar the registration of a subsequent FIR if the subsequent FIR discloses a distinct offence or transaction.
Relates to the requirement of sanction for prosecution. The respondent argued lack of prior sanction; the court must consider if this procedural defect warrants quashing or if it can be cured.

The legal standard applied to determine whether two FIRs relate to the 'same transaction'. The core issue is whether the conspiracy and distinct incidents in the second FIR constitute a separate transaction from the specific bribe demand in the first.

This is the primary statutory provision invoked by the appellants to quash the criminal proceedings. The core issue is whether the Supreme Court exercised its inherent powers under this section correctly to prevent abuse of the process of law.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This is the landmark precedent establishing the categories under which criminal proceedings can be quashed under Section 482 Cr.P.C., specifically regarding allegations that are 'absurd', 'inherently improbable', or 'maliciously instituted'.

rules.case_name: Manohar Lal v. Pragdas Jawaharlal Modi
rules.reference: Manohar Lal v. Pragdas Jawaharlal Modi
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that criminal proceedings cannot be used to settle civil disputes or as a tool for harassment, which is central to the appellants' claim that the FIR was filed to pressure them in the civil suit.

The specific charge of criminal intimidation alleged against the appellants. The relevance lies in determining if the alleged threats were genuine criminal acts or merely aggressive litigation tactics in a civil dispute.

The charge of house-trespass alleged against the appellants. The court must determine if the entry into the property was criminal trespass or an assertion of possession rights in the context of the ongoing civil dispute.

The legal principle that courts have the inherent power to quash proceedings that are an abuse of the process of the court, particularly when criminal cases are instituted with ulterior motives to harass parties in civil litigation.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that where a dispute is essentially civil in nature, criminal proceedings should not be allowed to continue if they are found to be malicious or vexatious, supporting the quashing of the FIR.

Relates to the temporary injunction granted in the civil suit. The existence of a civil remedy and the status of possession under the injunction are relevant to assessing the bona fides of the criminal complaint.

A key test under Section 482 Cr.P.C. where the court examines whether the facts alleged, even if taken at face value, disclose a cognizable offense or are so absurd that no prudent person would believe them.

rules.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Defines the scope of 'inherent powers' under Section 482, emphasizing that these powers are to be used sparingly and only to secure the ends of justice or prevent abuse of the process of the court.

Defines the original jurisdiction of the NGT to hear applications relating to environmental questions, including those arising under the Water Act, Air Act, and Solid Waste Management Rules, which is the basis for the NGT's order being appealed.
Central to the first issue: whether these rules apply retrospectively to a plant authorized under the 2000 Rules. The appellants argue the 2000 Rules apply, while the NGT applied the 2016 Rules.

rules.reference: Municipal Solid Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000
rules.relevance: The regulatory framework under which the Concessionaire obtained authorization in 2015. Relevant to determine if the plant was compliant with the law in force at the time of its establishment.

rules.reference: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
rules.relevance: Relevant to the second issue regarding the requirement of 'Consent to Establish/Operate'. The appellants argue that composite authorization under SWM Rules sufficed, challenging the need for separate consent under this Act.

rules.reference: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
rules.relevance: Relevant to the second issue regarding the requirement of 'Consent to Establish/Operate' for air emissions, parallel to the Water Act argument.
The legal principle cited by the NGT to grant liberty to the MPCB to recover environmental compensation. Relevant to assessing the validity of the compensation order.

The NGT cited violations of the right to a clean environment (derived from Article 21) as a ground for closure. This is the constitutional basis for the environmental rights claimed by the respondents.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966
rules.relevance: Relevant to the third issue concerning the land use. The land was reserved for a GPP in the sanctioned Development Plan. The NGT's order to convert it to a biodiversity park conflicts with this statutory planning instrument.

rules.case_name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
rules.reference: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing the 'Polluter Pays Principle' and the 'Precautionary Principle' in Indian environmental law, which the NGT relied upon for its compensation and closure orders.

A general legal principle relevant to the first issue: whether the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 can be applied to a facility that was legally authorized and operational under the 2000 Rules prior to the 2016 notification.

Defines 'consumer' and 'complaint'. Central to determining whether the respondent trusts, as voluntary associations, had the locus standi to file a representative complaint on behalf of credit card holders.

Empowers the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission to pass orders regarding unfair trade practices. Relevant to the NCDRC's authority to declare high interest rates as an unfair trade practice.

Vests the Reserve Bank of India with the power to regulate interest rates. Central to the appellants' argument that the NCDRC lacked jurisdiction to fix a ceiling on interest rates, as this is the exclusive domain of the RBI.
Relevant to the argument that arbitrary or excessive interest rates charged by banks may violate the right to equality and fair treatment, supporting the claim of unfair trade practice.
The core legal concept under the Consumer Protection Act. The court must determine if charging interest above 30% and capitalizing penal interest constitutes an 'unfair trade practice' under the Act.
Deals with lawful consideration and object. Relevant to the issue of whether the contractual terms regarding interest rates were valid or void as being opposed to public policy or unconscionable.

Governs the procedure for filing complaints by voluntary consumer associations. Relevant to the procedural challenge regarding whether the trusts obtained necessary permission to file a representative complaint.

rules.case_name: M/s. Indian Bank v. Satish Chandra Agarwal
rules.reference: M/s. Indian Bank v. Satish Chandra Agarwal
rules.relevance: A key precedent where the Supreme Court held that the Consumer Forums have jurisdiction to examine banking services and that the RBI's deregulation does not oust the jurisdiction of consumer courts to examine unfair practices.
Empowers the RBI to issue directions to banking companies. Relevant to understanding the scope of RBI's regulatory power versus the adjudicatory power of the NCDRC.
Legal principle determining whether a trust or association can represent individual consumers. Relevant to the first issue framed by the Supreme Court regarding the standing of Awaz and other trusts.

Section 21 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, empowers the arbitrator to grant interest on the amount awarded. The central legal question is whether this statutory power can be excluded by a contractual clause (Clause 22) or if it is mandatory.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. M/s. Gangaram Exporters
rules.reference: Union of India v. M/s. Gangaram Exporters
rules.relevance: This is a landmark Supreme Court precedent holding that the power to award interest under Section 21 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, is not barred by a contractual clause prohibiting interest, as the statutory right to interest is distinct from contractual rights. This directly supports the appellant's challenge.

rules.case_name: M/s. Gangaram Exporters v. Union of India
rules.reference: M/s. Gangaram Exporters v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that an arbitrator has the inherent power to award interest to compensate for the delay in payment, and such power cannot be ousted by a mere contractual stipulation barring interest claims.

Section 30 deals with the setting aside of arbitral awards. The District Judge and High Court relied on this section to set aside the interest component. The relevance lies in determining if the award was 'illegal' or 'in conflict with public policy' due to the contractual bar, or if the lower courts misapplied the law.

rules.reference: Distinction between Contractual Interest and Statutory Interest
rules.relevance: The legal principle that interest awarded by an arbitrator under Section 21 is statutory in nature (compensatory for delay) and not contractual. Therefore, a clause barring 'contractual interest' does not necessarily bar 'statutory interest' awarded by the tribunal.

rules.case_name: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Although primarily dealing with the 1996 Act, this case and related jurisprudence often cite the 1940 Act principles regarding the arbitrator's power to award interest as part of the dispute resolution mechanism, reinforcing that such awards are not easily set aside merely due to contractual bars.

The District Judge awarded 9% simple interest instead of the arbitrator's 15%. Order XX Rule 6 of the CPC governs the rate of interest on decrees. This is relevant to assess the legality of the substitute interest rate awarded by the civil court after setting aside the arbitral award.

Article 136 grants the Supreme Court the power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, or final order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in India. This is the jurisdictional basis for the current appeal.

The principle that denying interest to a contractor when the State retains the benefit of the work for a prolonged period may amount to unjust enrichment. This supports the argument that the arbitrator's award of interest was equitable and legally sound despite Clause 22.

rules.case_name: M/s. R. Rajagopal & Co. v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.reference: M/s. R. Rajagopal & Co. v. State of Tamil Nadu
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of an arbitrator's powers and the interpretation of contractual clauses in the context of arbitration awards, providing context on how courts should interpret bars on interest claims versus the arbitrator's statutory mandate.

rules.reference: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
rules.relevance: This is the primary statutory provision under which the Sub-Divisional Magistrate set aside the Gift Deed. The core legal issue is the interpretation of Section 23(1)(b), specifically whether the condition of maintenance must be explicitly written within the Gift Deed itself or if it can be established through contemporaneous documents like the promissory note.

rules.reference: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
rules.relevance: Section 22 provides the procedural mechanism for a senior citizen to file an application for maintenance or for setting aside a transfer of property. It establishes the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to entertain the Appellant's claim.

rules.reference: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
rules.relevance: Specifically addresses the power to set aside a transfer of property if the transfer was made with the intention of evading the obligation to provide maintenance. The interpretation of 'intention' and the evidence required to prove it is central to the appeal.

As a welfare legislation intended to protect senior citizens, the Act should be interpreted liberally to achieve its beneficial purpose, rather than strictly. This principle supports the argument that contemporaneous documents should be considered to ascertain the true intent of the parties.

rules.reference: Parol Evidence Rule and Contemporaneous Documents
rules.relevance: General principles of contract and property law regarding the admissibility of contemporaneous documents to explain or supplement the terms of a deed. This is relevant to counter the High Court's rejection of the promissory note as evidence of the maintenance condition.

Deals with contingent contracts. The Gift Deed and the promissory note created a contingent obligation where the gift was subject to the condition of maintenance. If the condition fails, the contract (gift) may be voidable.

Defines a 'Gift' and states that a gift may be made of existing or future property. While the Act itself does not explicitly deal with maintenance conditions, the general law of gifts allows for conditions, and the failure of such conditions can lead to revocation.

The right to life includes the right to live with human dignity. For a senior citizen, this includes the right to maintenance and protection from neglect, which is the underlying constitutional mandate for the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act.

The Single Judge observed that the Respondent did not approach the court with clean hands. This equitable principle supports the Appellant's position that the Respondent's failure to maintain the donor and alleged fabrication of documents should preclude him from retaining the property.

Deals with exclusion of oral evidence to contradict written terms. The relevance here is to determine if the promissory note (a contemporaneous written document) can be admitted to explain the terms of the Gift Deed, or if it is barred as collateral contract evidence.

This is the primary statutory provision cited by the Respondent to claim a right to conveyance. The court must interpret whether this section creates an automatic statutory obligation for the Trust to convey the property upon lease expiration, independent of the lease deed's terms.

The Respondent issued a notice under this section in 2006. The relevance lies in determining if this notice preserved any rights or if the failure to file a suit within the subsequent six-month limitation period barred the claim, as argued by the MCGM.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Laches and Inordinate Delay
rules.relevance: Central to the appeal is whether the 61-year delay in filing the writ petition (from 1955 to 2016) and the 10-year delay after the notice (2006 to 2016) disentitle the Respondent to equitable relief. The court must apply principles of laches in writ jurisdiction.

The High Court exercised its writ jurisdiction under Article 226. The Supreme Court must review whether the High Court correctly exercised this discretionary power, particularly considering the alternative remedy of a civil suit and the delay involved.

rules.reference: Interpretation of Lease Deeds and Implied Terms
rules.relevance: Since the lease deed did not contain an express clause for conveyance, the court must determine if such a right can be implied from the scheme approval, the resolution of 1927, or the statutory framework, versus the strict terms of the executed lease.

Although the Limitation Act does not directly apply to writ petitions, the principles of limitation are often read into writ jurisdiction. The 61-year gap suggests the claim is time-barred if viewed as a civil claim for specific performance or declaration.

The MCGM likely argued that the dispute over conveyance is a civil matter requiring a suit for specific performance or declaration, not a writ petition. The court must decide if the High Court was correct in entertaining the writ despite the availability of a civil remedy.

This Act transferred the functions of the Improvement Trust to the Municipal Corporation. The court must examine if the rights and obligations under the 1898 Act were preserved and transferred to the MCGM, making them liable for the conveyance.

The Respondent remained in possession for 51 years after the lease expired without seeking conveyance. The MCGM may argue that the Respondent's conduct estops them from now claiming a right to conveyance, or that they held the property as a tenant at will or licensee.

rules.case_name: e.g., State of Maharashtra v. Chandrabhan Bhai
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Laches in Writ Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: While specific case names are not provided in the brief, the Supreme Court will rely on established precedents holding that writ petitions filed with inordinate and unexplained delay are liable to be dismissed, especially when the delay prejudices the public authority or third parties.

The High Court exercised its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 to dismiss the appellant's petition. The Supreme Court must determine if the High Court correctly applied this provision or if the Family Court's procedural requirement of successive applications warrants intervention.

This section empowers the court to make orders regarding the custody, maintenance, and education of minor children. It is the primary statutory basis for granting interim custody and visitation rights, which is the core subject of the appeal.

In all custody and access matters, the welfare of the child is the paramount consideration. The court must assess whether a structured schedule or successive applications better serves the child's stability and emotional well-being.

rules.case_name: Githa John v. George John
rules.relevance: This landmark Supreme Court judgment emphasizes that custody disputes should be resolved with minimal delay and that the child's right to know both parents is crucial. It supports the argument for a structured, definitive interim schedule rather than ad-hoc applications.

rules.case_name: Siddharth Vishwanath Bhanot v. Bhagyashree Siddharth Bhanot
rules.reference: Siddharth Vishwanath Bhanot v. Bhagyashree Siddharth Bhanot
rules.relevance: This case discusses the importance of maintaining the status quo and the welfare of the child in interim custody matters. It provides guidance on how courts should balance the rights of both parents while ensuring the child's routine is not disrupted.

This rule governs appeals from interlocutory orders. The appellant is challenging the High Court's order regarding interim custody, which falls under the purview of procedural rules for appealing interim decisions.

The appellant's right to maintain a relationship with his daughter is a fundamental aspect of parental rights. The court must consider whether the requirement to file fresh applications each time unduly burdens this right.

rules.case_name: Vijay Karia v. Prysmian Cavi E Sistemi Srl
rules.reference: Vijay Karia v. Prysmian Cavi E Sistemi Srl
rules.relevance: While primarily an arbitration case, it reinforces the principle that courts should avoid unnecessary procedural hurdles that delay justice. This can be analogized to the need for a structured schedule to avoid repetitive litigation.

This section mandates that Family Courts shall endeavor to assist parties in arriving at a settlement. The failure of mediation at the Supreme Court Mediation Centre highlights the need for a judicially imposed structured schedule.

rules.reference: Best Interests of the Child Standard
rules.relevance: This overarching principle requires the court to consider the child's physical, emotional, and educational needs. A structured schedule may be deemed more beneficial than ad-hoc arrangements for the child's stability.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the High Court exercised its inherent powers to direct the transfer of investigation to the CBI. The appeal centers on whether this power was exercised correctly.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent laying down guidelines for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash FIRs or interfere with investigations. It establishes that such powers should be used sparingly and only in exceptional circumstances to prevent abuse of process or secure ends of justice.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This recent Supreme Court judgment restricts the automatic registration of FIRs in certain categories of cases and emphasizes the need for preliminary inquiry. It is relevant to assessing whether the High Court should have directed a CBI investigation at the initial stage without a preliminary inquiry, especially given the civil/business dispute context.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Kunal Singh
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. Kunal Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent specifically addresses the criteria for directing CBI investigations. It holds that mere allegations of bias or lack of trust in local police are insufficient; there must be concrete material showing that the local police are incapable of conducting a fair investigation. This directly counters the complainant's unsubstantiated claims.

rules.case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: While primarily about arrest, this case emphasizes the need to prevent the misuse of criminal process in civil disputes. It supports the appellant's contention that the FIR might be an abuse of process to settle business disputes, similar to the earlier quashed FIR in Himachal Pradesh.

rules.relevance: The principle that a holding company (guarantor) and its subsidiary (principal debtor) are separate legal entities. The resolution plan of one entity cannot automatically extinguish the independent contractual liabilities of the other unless explicitly novated or discharged by the creditor.

Specifically relevant to the clause in the resolution plan stating 'no right of subrogation'. The court must decide if such a contractual exclusion in a resolution plan can override statutory rights under the Contract Act or if it is binding only on the parties to the plan.

rules.case_name: Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This case established the binding nature of resolution plans on all stakeholders. It is relevant to determine if the exclusion of subrogation rights in the ACIL plan is enforceable against the resolution applicant.

Defines 'transfer' in relation to a capital asset, specifically including the extinguishment of any rights in a capital asset. This is the central statutory provision determining whether the reduction in share capital constitutes a taxable event or allows for capital loss.

rules.case_name: Kartikeya V. Sarabhai v. CIT
rules.relevance: A Supreme Court precedent cited in the procedural history. The CIT(A) distinguished the facts from this case, while the ITAT and High Court relied on the principle of extinguishment of rights established or discussed in such contexts to hold that the reduction constituted a transfer.

Governs the computation of capital gains or losses arising from the transfer of a capital asset. Relevant to determine if the loss claimed by the assessee is computable under this section once 'transfer' is established.

Deals with the computation of capital gains, specifically regarding the cost of acquisition and expenditure incurred. Relevant for calculating the actual capital loss if the reduction is deemed a transfer.

Governs the reduction of share capital by a company with the confirmation of the Court. Relevant to establish the legal nature of the transaction (court-ordered reduction) and the extinguishment of rights in the shares.

The core legal principle applied by the ITAT and High Court. The argument is that the reduction in the number of shares, even with unchanged percentage holding, results in the extinguishment of rights in the specific shares surrendered, thereby constituting a 'transfer' under Section 2(47).
Defines 'capital asset'. Relevant to confirm that shares held by the assessee qualify as capital assets, which is a prerequisite for applying Section 2(47) and Section 45.

rules.case_name: CIT v. S. Venkatarama Iyer
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court case interpreting Section 2(47) and the concept of 'transfer' and 'extinguishment of rights'. Often cited in cases involving share capital reduction to determine if a transfer has occurred.

rules.case_name: CIT v. R. Sridharan
rules.relevance: A precedent often cited in the context of share capital reduction and whether it amounts to a transfer. It helps in distinguishing between mere alteration of rights and extinguishment of rights.

Provides exemption for long-term capital gains on transfer of listed shares. While the assessee claimed a loss, this section is relevant contextually to understand the tax treatment of share transfers and the distinction between gains and losses in share capital reductions.

This is the substantive provision under which the appellant was prosecuted for willful failure to file returns of income. The central legal question is determining the exact date the offence under this section is committed (due date vs. actual filing date).

rules.reference: Guidelines for Compounding of Offences under Direct Tax Laws, 2014
rules.relevance: Clause 8 defines the eligibility criteria for compounding, specifically the concept of a 'first offence'. The dispute centers on whether the second offence qualifies as a 'first offence' given the timeline of the show cause notice for the first offence.

This section prescribes the due dates for filing income tax returns. Determining the 'due date' is essential to establish when the offence under Section 276CC is deemed to have been committed according to the appellant's contention.

This section empowers the Central Government to issue guidelines for the compounding of offences. It provides the statutory basis for the 2014 Guidelines and is relevant to the issue of whether the Guidelines are mandatory or directory.

While the prosecution is under 276CC, Section 277 (furnishing false particulars) is often cited in comparative jurisprudence regarding the nature of tax offences and the definition of 'willful failure' or 'voluntary disclosure' in the context of compounding.

The appellant argues that the offence is committed on the day following the due date. This relies on the legal principle that a continuing omission or failure to act constitutes an offence from the moment the duty arises, rather than when the act is eventually performed.

Relevant to interpreting Clause 8 of the 2014 Guidelines. The principle involves determining whether 'voluntary disclosure' requires the return to be filed before any notice is issued, or if the timing of the offence itself is the sole determinant.

The High Court exercised its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to dismiss the petition. This provision is relevant to the procedural history and the standard of review applied by the High Court to the administrative decision of the CCIT.

rules.reference: Mandatory vs. Directory Nature of Administrative Guidelines
rules.relevance: One of the specific issues is whether the 2014 Guidelines are mandatory or directory. This legal principle determines the extent to which the CCIT is bound by the strict interpretation of 'first offence' versus having discretion to compound.

This section allows for the filing of belated returns. The interaction between the right to file a belated return under 139(4) and the penal consequences under 276CC is central to the appellant's argument that the offence date is fixed at the due date, not the belated filing date.

This is the primary source of power invoked by the respondent and the central issue of the appeal. It empowers the Supreme Court to pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, which is being relied upon to grant divorce on grounds of irretrievable breakdown despite statutory limitations.

rules.case_name: Shilpa, S. v. Harish, S.
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent where the Supreme Court granted divorce under Article 142(1) on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage, setting a crucial benchmark for the current appeal regarding the exercise of this extraordinary power.

rules.case_name: Naveen Kohli v. Neelu Kohli
rules.relevance: Establishes the legal principle that the Supreme Court can exercise its powers under Article 142(1) to dissolve a marriage that has irretrievably broken down, even if the statutory conditions under the Hindu Marriage Act are not fully met, provided complete justice requires it.

Relevant as the respondent's previous mutual consent petition was dismissed for non-compliance with the one-year separation requirement. This highlights the statutory hurdle that Article 142(1) is being invoked to bypass.

Governs the award of permanent alimony and maintenance. The Family Court's report recommending Rs. 10 crores or Rs. 2 lakhs per month is based on this provision, making it central to the second issue regarding the quantum of alimony.

rules.case_name: Rajnesh v. Neha
rules.relevance: Provides the comprehensive framework and guidelines for determining the quantum of alimony and maintenance, including the consideration of the parties' net worth, lifestyle, and the standard of living, which is directly applicable to assessing the petitioner's claim.

The provision under which the transfer petition was filed to move proceedings from Bhopal to Pune. While the transfer has occurred, the procedural history under this section is part of the background leading to the current Supreme Court intervention.

The substantive legal ground relied upon by the respondent. The court must determine if the marriage has indeed broken down irretrievably, considering the respondent's categorical refusal to continue the marriage and the failure of mediation.

rules.case_name: Ravi Kishan Das v. Kamla Rani
rules.reference: Ravi Kishan Das v. Kamla Rani
rules.relevance: Relevant for the principle that while Article 142(1) is wide, it must be exercised judiciously and not to override statutory law lightly, but to ensure complete justice, balancing the rights of both parties including financial security for the wife.

The FIRs filed by the petitioner alleging rape, cruelty, and cheating form part of the factual matrix. The existence of these criminal proceedings and the Look Out Circular impacts the assessment of the parties' conduct and the 'complete justice' required under Article 142(1).
Central to the appeal regarding whether the award of the BOOT contract to NTBCL without competitive tenders violated the principle of equality and non-arbitrariness, as held by the High Court.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Industrial Areas Development Act, 1976
rules.relevance: Defines the powers of NOIDA to construct roads and bridges and levy fees, which is crucial to determining if NOIDA had the statutory authority to delegate toll collection rights to NTBCL.

rules.case_name: Tata Cellular v. Union of India
rules.reference: Tata Cellular v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the legal principle that the State is not bound to adopt a particular method of awarding contracts (such as competitive bidding) unless mandated by statute, provided the process is fair, transparent, and non-arbitrary.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Laches and Limitation in Writ Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of maintainability of the Writ Petition filed in 2012 for a project commissioned in 2001, considering the delay and the commercial nature of the dispute.

The High Court declared Articles 13 and 14 of the Concession Agreement bad in law; Article 13 of the Constitution is relevant to determine if the private agreement violates fundamental rights or is void.
Addresses whether NOIDA's delegation of the power to levy fees to a private entity (NTBCL) was excessive or contrary to the enabling statute, a key issue in the appeal.
Relevant to the challenge that Article 14 of the Concession Agreement (formula for returns) is opposed to public policy, particularly in the context of public infrastructure projects.

rules.reference: Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Provides the statutory basis for the CAG's report on the recovery of project costs, which the Supreme Court relied upon to verify NTBCL's financial claims.

rules.case_name: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachor
rules.relevance: While primarily about disqualification, it establishes the scope of judicial review over administrative actions and the balance between contractual rights and constitutional mandates.
Relevant to whether the State/NOIDA can be estopped from challenging the validity of the Concession Agreement after years of operation and reliance by the private party.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. The High Court held that the Civil Court's jurisdiction was barred under this section. The appeal hinges on whether Section 21 bars civil courts from adjudicating suits for declaration of ownership of land claimed to be dedicated to a religious institution, particularly when the land was declared surplus.

Section 13 deals with the determination of surplus land. Since the Collector declared the land as surplus under the Act, the interplay between the surplus determination process and the civil suit for declaration of charitable trust status is relevant to interpreting the scope of Section 21.

The appellants argue that the respondents were precluded from raising the jurisdictional objection in the Second Appeal because it was not pressed in the Trial Court or challenged in the First Appellate Court. This principle addresses whether a party can raise a jurisdictional bar for the first time at a later stage of litigation.

rules.reference: Nature of Jurisdictional Bar under Special Statutes
rules.relevance: Relevant to determining whether the bar under Section 21 is absolute or conditional, and whether it applies to suits for declaration of title based on religious dedication, which may fall outside the specific scope of land reform disputes regarding tenancy or surplus determination.

Relevant to the procedural history. The issue of whether the jurisdictional objection could be raised in the Second Appeal depends on whether it was a ground of appeal available under Order XLIII Rule 1 from the First Appellate Court's judgment.

The core factual dispute is whether the land was dedicated to the Dam Dama Baba Sahib Singh shrine. Legal principles regarding the creation of charitable trusts and the rights of followers to sue for declaration of such trusts are relevant to the merits of the suit if jurisdiction is found to exist.

Specifically addresses the bar on civil courts from entertaining suits relating to matters which are required to be determined by the Collector or other authorities under the Act. The interpretation of 'matters required to be determined' is key.

The Trial Court dismissed the suit on merits (failure to prove dedication) noting the jurisdictional objection was not pressed. The principle of estoppel or res judicata may be relevant to prevent the respondents from raising the jurisdictional bar later, having previously contested the suit on merits.

Article 25 guarantees freedom of religion, including the right to manage religious affairs. This may be relevant in interpreting the scope of civil court jurisdiction in matters concerning religious institutions and their properties.

Although not explicitly raised as a primary issue, the timeline of events (1976 declaration, 1980 trial court dismissal, 2010 High Court order) may involve limitation issues regarding the maintainability of the suit or the appeal, depending on the nature of the declaration sought.
Defines the offense of murder, which is the primary charge against both appellants under which they were convicted by the High Court.
Defines 'common intention'. The central legal issue is whether the husband's omission and presence at the scene establish a shared common intention with the mother-in-law to commit murder.

rules.reference: Reliability and Sufficiency of Dying Declaration
rules.relevance: The conviction of the mother-in-law rests heavily on the dying declaration recorded by the Tehsildar. The court must apply principles regarding the voluntariness, consistency, and medical fitness of the declarant to determine if it is sufficient for conviction without corroboration.

rules.reference: Omission as Actus Reus in Common Intention
rules.relevance: Addresses whether a failure to act (omission to save the wife or take her to the hospital) can constitute participation in a crime under Section 34 IPC, specifically when the accused was present at the scene.
Governs the admissibility of statements made by a person as to the cause of their death. This is the statutory basis for admitting the dying declaration recorded by the Tehsildar.

The FIR included charges under these sections. While the High Court convicted under IPC 302, the background of dowry harassment is relevant to establishing motive and the context of the cruelty leading to death.
Cruelty by husband or relatives of husband. This charge provides the statutory context for the domestic violence alleged to have preceded the fatal incident.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Criminal Cases
rules.relevance: The trial court acquitted the appellants due to lack of proof beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court must review whether the High Court correctly applied this standard in reversing the acquittal based on circumstantial evidence and inference.

Governs the recording of statements in cases of death in custody or police lock-up, but often referenced in context of official recording of dying declarations by Magistrates or authorized officers (like a Tehsildar in certain jurisdictions/circumstances) to ensure procedural regularity.

While not strictly mandatory, courts often look for corroboration in dying declarations, especially in dowry death cases. The relevance lies in assessing if the medical evidence and neighbor testimony sufficiently corroborate the declaration.

rules.case_name: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
rules.reference: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This is the foundational case establishing that the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 applies to all forests irrespective of their classification or ownership, and directing states to identify such lands. The current dispute arises directly from the continuing proceedings of this case.

The definition of 'forest' under this Act is central to the dispute. The issue is whether sacred groves qualify as 'forest land' under this Act, triggering the requirement for prior central approval for non-forest use.

rules.case_name: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
rules.reference: Supreme Court Order dated 03.07.2018 in T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This specific order accepted the Central Empowered Committee's recommendation that sacred groves be classified as 'forest land' regardless of size or density, directly contradicting the earlier Kapoor Committee criteria. It is the binding directive the State is alleged to have failed to implement.

Cited by the Amicus Curiae, this Act recognizes the rights of forest-dwelling communities. It is relevant to the argument that sacred groves are integral to the cultural heritage and livelihood of local communities, supporting their classification as protected forest land.

Cited by the Amicus Curiae, this Act provides for the protection of wildlife and their habitats. Sacred groves often serve as critical biodiversity hotspots, making this Act relevant to the ecological argument for their protection.

This Directive Principle of State Policy directs the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country. It provides the constitutional mandate for the State's obligation to protect sacred groves.

This Fundamental Duty requires every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wild life. It supports the broader legal framework for environmental protection invoked in the appeal.

rules.reference: Principle of Sustainable Development and Precautionary Principle
rules.relevance: These principles, often cited in Indian environmental jurisprudence, support the argument that in cases of potential environmental harm (loss of sacred groves), the burden of proof is on the State to show that development is sustainable, and precautionary measures should be taken.

The applicant alleges that this policy dilutes protections for sacred groves. The court must examine whether this state policy is consistent with the Supreme Court's 2018 order and the Forest Conservation Act, 1980.

Cited by the Amicus Curiae, this international convention underscores the importance of conserving biodiversity. Sacred groves are recognized as important sites for in-situ conservation, supporting the argument for their legal protection.

rules.reference: Jharkhand Superior Judicial Services (Recruitment, Appointment and Condition of Service) Rules, 2001
rules.relevance: These rules govern the specific appointment process in question, stipulating that 65% of posts are filled by promotion based on merit-cum-seniority and passing a suitability test. They define the statutory framework for the appellants' claim.

rules.provision: Suitability Test Criteria (Interview, Service Profile, Judgment Evaluation, Seniority)
rules.reference: Jharkhand Superior Judicial Services (Recruitment, Appointment and Condition of Service) Rules, 2001
rules.relevance: Defines the components of the suitability test and the minimum aggregate of 40 marks required to be treated as 'suitable'. The appellants exceeded this threshold, making the interpretation of 'suitability' vs 'merit ranking' central to the dispute.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent establishing that in promotion matters governed by seniority-cum-fitness, seniority is the primary criterion, and fitness (suitability) is a qualifying condition. Once a candidate is found fit, they cannot be passed over in favor of a junior who is also fit, unless specific rules provide otherwise.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh Sandhu
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that seniority is the main criterion for promotion and that a candidate who is found fit cannot be denied promotion merely because a junior candidate scored higher marks in the selection process, provided the senior has cleared the minimum qualifying marks.

rules.case_name: State of Jharkhand v. Suresh Chandra
rules.relevance: A direct precedent involving the Jharkhand Superior Judicial Services Rules. The Supreme Court interpreted the rules regarding the suitability test and the interplay between seniority and merit marks, holding that clearing the minimum marks makes a candidate eligible for promotion in order of seniority.

Provides the constitutional basis for the appointment of District Judges, stating that appointments shall be made by the Governor in consultation with the High Court. This establishes the High Court's role in the selection process challenged by the appellants.

The appellants likely argue that denying promotion to those who cleared the suitability threshold while promoting juniors with higher marks violates the principle of equality and non-arbitrariness in state action, particularly in the context of seniority-based promotions.

The core legal principle at stake: whether 'fitness' is a binary qualifying condition (pass/fail) or a continuous ranking criterion. If binary, seniority dictates promotion among the fit; if continuous, merit marks dictate promotion. The case hinges on this interpretation.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Baldev Singh
rules.relevance: Discusses the concept of 'seniority' and 'fitness' in promotional contexts, emphasizing that fitness is a prerequisite and seniority is the governing factor for selection among those who are fit.
Procedural rule governing the appealability of orders from the High Court to the Supreme Court, relevant to the maintainability of the Civil Appeal filed by the appellants.
This is the source of the Supreme Court's special leave jurisdiction, under which the appellant filed the appeal challenging the High Court's order.

This section confers inherent powers on the High Court to quash FIRs to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice. The core issue is whether the High Court correctly exercised (or failed to exercise) this power given the vague allegations.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This is the landmark precedent laying down the categories under which an FIR can be quashed under Section 482 CrPC. It is essential to determine if the 'vague allegations' against the appellant fall under the category where allegations, even if taken at face value, do not constitute an offence.

Criminal Breach of Trust. The FIR alleges this offence. The court must determine if the facts alleged against the appellant specifically satisfy the ingredients of this section, particularly regarding the entrustment of property.

Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property. The court must assess if the vague allegations against the appellant amount to cheating or if they are merely civil disputes regarding payment defaults.

Criminal Conspiracy. The appellant is accused of conspiracy. The relevance lies in determining if there is a prima facie case of a 'meeting of minds' between the appellant and others to commit the alleged offences, or if the allegations are too vague to sustain a conspiracy charge.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This precedent emphasizes that criminal proceedings should not be initiated for mere civil disputes or contractual defaults unless there is clear evidence of criminal intent. It supports the argument that payment defaults in a construction chain should not automatically lead to criminal liability for all parties.

The legal principle that at the stage of quashing an FIR, the court must examine whether the allegations, even if taken as true, disclose the commission of a cognizable offence. If the allegations are vague and do not specifically implicate the appellant, no prima facie case is made out.

rules.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: This case defines the scope of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC, stating that these powers are to be used sparingly and only to secure the ends of justice or prevent abuse of the process of the court.

Criminal Intimidation. Included in the FIR. The court must evaluate if the vague allegations against the appellant contain specific threats that constitute criminal intimidation, distinct from the commercial dispute.

rules.case_name: Vijaya Bank Ltd. v. Additional Commissioner of Income Tax
rules.citation: Supreme Court decision relied upon by CIT and High Court
rules.reference: Vijaya Bank Ltd. v. Additional Commissioner of Income Tax
rules.relevance: This is the central precedent cited by the Revenue and the High Court. It held that broken period interest is not deductible. The core legal dispute is whether this precedent, decided under repealed Sections 18-21, applies to the current assessment under Section 37.

The specific provision under which the assessee bank claims the deduction for broken period interest as revenue expenditure. The court must determine if the expenditure is 'wholly and exclusively' for business purposes under this section.

These sections specifically dealt with tax on interest on securities and were in force when the Vijaya Bank precedent was decided. Their repeal is the primary argument used by the Tribunal to distinguish the current case from the precedent.

The procedural provision invoked by the Commissioner of Income Tax to set aside the original assessment orders. The validity of invoking this section based on the application of the Vijaya Bank precedent is part of the procedural history.

Establishes the regulatory context requiring banks to hold government securities. This helps define the nature of the bank's business and the purpose of holding the securities (compliance vs. trading), which influences whether the interest is capital or revenue in nature.

rules.reference: Distinction between Capital and Revenue Expenditure
rules.relevance: The fundamental legal principle governing the appeal. The court must decide if broken period interest is an integral part of the cost of acquisition (capital) or an expense incurred for earning income (revenue).

rules.reference: Nature of Securities as Stock-in-Trade vs. Investment
rules.relevance: The Tribunal's decision hinged on the classification of securities as stock-in-trade. The relevance of this classification to the deductibility of interest under Section 37 versus the repealed sections is a key issue.

rules.reference: RBI Guidelines on Classification of Securities
rules.relevance: The Revenue argues that the treatment differs based on whether securities are Held to Maturity (HTM) or Held for Trading (HFT). These guidelines help determine the intent behind the purchase and the nature of the expenditure.

rules.provision: Repeal of Sections 18-21 of IT Act
rules.relevance: The legislative change that altered the statutory framework for taxing interest on securities. This is the basis for the argument that the legal position has changed since the Vijaya Bank decision.

rules.reference: Principle of Continuity of Legal Position post-Repeal
rules.relevance: The Revenue argues that despite the repeal of specific sections, the underlying principles regarding the nature of broken period interest remain unchanged. The court must decide if the precedent's reasoning survives the statutory repeal.
The primary charge in the case is murder. The Supreme Court must determine if the evidence supports conviction under Section 302 despite the High Court's acquittal.

The prosecution alleged criminal conspiracy against accused not identified as direct perpetrators. Section 120B is central to the second issue regarding conspiracy based on jail meetings and telephone records.
Common intention is a key element in joint liability for murder. The court must assess if the actions of the accused were done in furtherance of a common intention.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Krishna Deo Singh
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Krishna Deo Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes the principle that the testimony of a single reliable eye-witness is sufficient for conviction, and minor discrepancies do not necessarily render testimony unreliable. This is directly relevant to the challenge against the acquittal of A-4 and A-8.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Appeal against Acquittal
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court must apply the principle that an appellate court should not interfere with an acquittal unless the findings of the lower court are perverse or based on no evidence. The court must evaluate if the High Court's reliance on 'unreliability' was justified.
The informant (PW-10) turned hostile. The court must apply principles regarding the admissibility and weight of hostile witness testimony, particularly if corroborated by other evidence.

rules.reference: Testimony of Witnesses with Criminal Antecedents
rules.relevance: PW-25 had prior criminal convictions. The court must consider whether criminal antecedents automatically discredit a witness or if their testimony can be accepted if corroborated and found trustworthy.
Relevant to the procedural aspect of recording statements and the delay in recording Shashi Bhushan Singh's (PW-42) statement, which was challenged by the defense.
The FIR included charges under Section 27 of the Arms Act. Although the primary focus is murder, this statute was part of the original charge sheet and conviction.
Two accused (A-5 and A-7) died during proceedings. The court must apply the legal principle that criminal proceedings abate upon the death of the accused, barring specific exceptions.

This is the substantive offence charged against the appellants. The core legal issue is whether the alleged verbal utterances constitute 'abetment' as defined under this section, requiring proof of instigation or intentional aid.

Defines 'abetment'. To sustain a conviction under Section 306, the prosecution must prove that the appellants abetted the suicide within the meaning of Section 107, which requires instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Sukhdev Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent clarifying that Section 306 IPC is not attracted merely because a person commits suicide after an argument or verbal altercation. It establishes that there must be a proximate link and that the act of abetment must be the immediate cause of the suicide, distinguishing it from mere words spoken in the heat of the moment.

rules.case_name: Pawan Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Pawan Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Relevant for establishing the high threshold of proof required for abetment of suicide. The Court held that the act of abetment must be the immediate cause of the suicide and that the accused must have instigated the deceased with the intention of causing them to commit suicide.

The provision under which the High Court exercised its inherent powers to dismiss the quashing application. The Supreme Court appeal challenges the correctness of this exercise of discretion, requiring an analysis of when inherent powers should be used to quash proceedings at the threshold.

rules.case_name: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Lays down the guidelines for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash criminal proceedings. It establishes that quashing is appropriate only in rare cases where the allegations, even if taken at face value, do not constitute an offence or where continuation of proceedings would be an abuse of the process of law.

The legal principle that for Section 306 IPC to apply, there must be a clear, proximate link between the act of abetment and the suicide. Mere words, even if harsh, spoken in the heat of the moment without the specific intent to drive the person to suicide, do not amount to abetment.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Mohd. Yakub
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Mohd. Yakub
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that at the stage of quashing proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C., the court should not go into the merits of the case or evaluate evidence, but only examine whether the allegations, if accepted as true, disclose the commission of a cognizable offence.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Reinforces the view that Section 306 IPC is a serious offence requiring clear proof of instigation. It cautions against convicting individuals based solely on the fact that a suicide occurred after a dispute, emphasizing the need for evidence of active instigation.

Although the case is at the quashing stage, the relevance of any dying declaration or statement made by the deceased (Tanu) before death is governed by this section. The absence or presence of such evidence is often a key factor in determining if a prima facie case for abetment exists.

Central to the appeal; the High Court held the conversion order illegal partly due to violation of Article 14. The Supreme Court must determine if the lack of a fair, transparent process in converting leasehold to freehold violated the right to equality and non-arbitrariness.

The procedural basis for the School's original Writ Petition. The Supreme Court must assess the scope of the High Court's jurisdiction and whether it correctly exercised its writ powers in quashing the conversion order while leaving the auction question open.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Nazul Land (Vesting, Allotment and Disposal) Act, 1949
rules.relevance: Governs the vesting of Nazul land in the State and the procedures for allotment, lease, and disposal. Relevant to determine if the Special Nazul Officer had the statutory authority to convert the leasehold to freehold in 2001 despite the pending litigation and auction process.

rules.case_name: Tata Cellular v. Union of India
rules.reference: Tata Cellular v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Landmark precedent establishing that government actions involving public funds and resources (like land auctions) must be fair, transparent, and non-arbitrary to satisfy Article 14. Highly relevant to evaluating the legality of the 1995 auction cancellation and the subsequent conversion.

rules.case_name: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India
rules.reference: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India
rules.relevance: Establishes that the State is bound by Article 14 in all its actions, including commercial and contractual dealings. Relevant to argue that the State's decision to cancel the School's bid and favor the lessee's sons must withstand the test of reasonableness and non-arbitrariness.

rules.reference: Principle of Status Quo and Interim Orders
rules.relevance: The High Court had issued an interim order in 1996 maintaining status quo. The conversion in 2001 occurred despite this order. This principle is relevant to determine if the administrative action was taken in contempt of the court's interim direction, rendering it a nullity.

Defines the nature of a lease and the rights of a lessee. Relevant to determine if the alleged lessee had any vested right to demand conversion to freehold or if the leasehold interest was merely a revocable privilege subject to State policy.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Ram Sagar
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Ram Sagar
rules.relevance: Relevant precedent concerning the disposal of Nazul land in Uttar Pradesh and the powers of the State Government to regulate such properties. Helps in interpreting the specific statutory framework under the UP Nazul Land Act.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Laches and Clean Hands
rules.relevance: The School's bid was cancelled in 1995 for procedural default (late purchase of tender). The Supreme Court may consider whether the School is barred from seeking restoration of the bid due to its own delay or procedural non-compliance, despite the State's subsequent illegal conversion.

rules.reference: Order XLVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Governs suits for specific performance or declaration regarding contracts. While the main dispute is in Writ, the underlying civil suit for conversion was dismissed. This rule context helps understand the civil court's rejection of the lessee's claim to freehold title.

Defines 'unfair trade practice'. The central issue is whether the contractual forfeiture of 20% earnest money constitutes an unfair trade practice under this definition, allowing the NCDRC to intervene and modify the penalty.
The procedural provision under which the Appellant filed the appeal against the NCDRC's order. It governs the jurisdiction and scope of the appellate review.

rules.case_name: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. NEPC India Ltd.
rules.reference: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. NEPC India Ltd.
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent distinguishing between 'liquidated damages' and 'penalty'. It establishes that courts can interfere with contractual penalty clauses if they are unconscionable or disproportionate to actual loss, which is directly relevant to the challenge against the 20% forfeiture.

Governs compensation for breach of contract where a sum is named in the contract as penalty. It limits the court's power to award reasonable compensation not exceeding the named amount, serving as the baseline for evaluating the enforceability of the forfeiture clause.

rules.case_name: Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India
rules.reference: Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that consumer forums have the power to modify contractual terms if they are found to be unfair or unreasonable, supporting the NCDRC's authority to reduce the forfeiture from 20% to 10%.
Empowers the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission to issue orders for refund of money paid by the complainant. This is the statutory basis for the NCDRC's direction to refund the balance amount.

rules.reference: Principle of Restitution and Unjust Enrichment
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of interest. Since the cancellation was sought by the buyers due to market conditions (not developer default), the principle of unjust enrichment may limit the developer's right to retain the entire earnest money without accounting for actual losses, and may influence the rate of interest awarded on the refund.

rules.case_name: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Reinforces the interpretation of Section 74 of the Contract Act, emphasizing that the purpose of such clauses is compensation, not punishment. This supports the argument that a flat 20% forfeiture might be excessive if actual losses are lower.
Empowers the Commission to direct the discontinuance of unfair trade practices. If the forfeiture clause is deemed unfair, this section supports the remedial action taken by the NCDRC.

Although the buyers cited market recession, this principle (Section 56 of Contract Act) generally does not apply to mere financial hardship or market fluctuations. Its relevance here is to distinguish why the buyers' claim for cancellation based on price fall is not a statutory frustration, thereby impacting the assessment of who is at fault and whether interest should be awarded.

This is the procedural provision under which the Trial Court and High Court rejected the plaint. The central issue is whether the suit was barred by limitation on the face of the plaint, which is a ground for rejection under this rule.

Article 56 prescribes the limitation period for suits for cancellation of instruments or declaration that they are void or voidable. The respondents argue the suit is time-barred as it was filed 13 years after the deed's execution.

Section 17 deals with the construction of the word 'knowledge' in the Limitation Act. It is crucial for determining when the limitation period begins to run, specifically whether constructive knowledge (presumed from registration) or actual knowledge applies.
