rules.reference: A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes that administrative actions by bodies exercising public functions must be guided by principles of natural justice and fairness, relevant to the procedural fairness of ICSSR's withholding of grants.

Relevant to the argument that grant-in-aid funds are held in trust for specific purposes (salaries/research) and cannot be arbitrarily withheld if the primary purpose (employee welfare) is at stake, though subject to conditions.

Central to the issue of whether service of a notice invoking arbitration is a mandatory prerequisite for the tribunal to exercise jurisdiction over a party. The appellant argues that the lack of such notice to Respondents 2 and 3 should not bar their impleadment if they are bound by the arbitration agreement.

Relevant to the procedural history where the appellant only impleaded Respondent No. 1 in the application for appointment of an arbitrator. The core legal question is whether the scope of the Section 11 application limits the tribunal's jurisdiction to only those parties named therein.

The provision under which the arbitral tribunal decided the objection to its jurisdiction. The appeal challenges the tribunal's interpretation of Section 16 regarding the maintainability of proceedings against non-joined parties.

Defines the 'arbitration agreement'. Crucial for determining whether Respondents 2 (the LLP) and 3 (the CEO/Administrator) are parties to the arbitration agreement contained in Clause 40 of the LLP Agreement, which is the source of the tribunal's jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: Bharat Broadband Network Limited v. United Telecoms Limited
rules.reference: Bharat Broadband Network Limited v. United Telecoms Limited
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent holding that the existence of an arbitration agreement is the sole basis for the tribunal's jurisdiction. It establishes that procedural irregularities, such as the non-issuance of a Section 21 notice to a party who is nonetheless bound by the arbitration agreement, do not oust the tribunal's jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: M/s. Chikun India Pvt. Ltd. v. M/s. Bata India Ltd.
rules.reference: M/s. Chikun India Pvt. Ltd. v. M/s. Bata India Ltd.
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that the tribunal's jurisdiction is derived from the arbitration agreement, not merely from the Section 11 application. It supports the argument that parties bound by the agreement can be impleaded even if not initially named in the Section 11 application.

Defines the status of Designated Partners and the LLP entity. Relevant to determine if Respondent No. 3 (CEO/Administrator) and Respondent No. 2 (LLP) are distinct legal entities or agents bound by the LLP Agreement's arbitration clause.

The provision under which the High Court dismissed the appeal against the tribunal's order. The Supreme Court appeal challenges this dismissal, requiring an analysis of the scope of judicial review under this section.

The principle that the arbitral tribunal has the power to rule on its own jurisdiction. The case involves the tribunal's exercise of this power under Section 16 to decide if Respondents 2 and 3 are proper parties.

Relevant to determine if Respondent No. 3, acting as CEO/Administrator under Clause 8, is bound by the arbitration agreement signed by the partners, or if the LLP (Respondent 2) is a separate party to the agreement.

Defines 'consumer' as a person who buys goods or hires/avails services for consideration. Central to determining if the respondent, who had no direct contract with the appellant, qualifies as a consumer.
Defines 'service' to include banking services. Relevant to establish whether the appellant's failure to disburse the loan amount constitutes a deficiency in service.
Empowers the Commission to issue directions for the removal of deficiency in service and for payment of compensation. Relevant to the relief granted by the NCDRC.
Governs the limitation period for filing complaints (two years from the cause of action). Relevant to the appellant's challenge regarding the condonation of delay without recorded reasons.

rules.case_name: M/s. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. Ramprakash Gupta
rules.reference: M/s. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. Ramprakash Gupta
rules.relevance: Establishes that a third party who is a beneficiary of a contract or service may be considered a 'consumer' if they suffer loss due to deficiency in service, even in the absence of direct privity of contract.

rules.case_name: State Bank of India v. S. S. N. Murthy
rules.reference: State Bank of India v. S. S. N. Murthy
rules.relevance: Holds that banking services are 'services' under the CPA and that banks are liable for deficiency in service if they fail to perform their contractual obligations, such as disbursing sanctioned loans.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Prahlad Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Prahlad Singh
rules.relevance: Discusses the principle that while limitation is not jurisdictional, the Commission must record sufficient reasons for condoning delay beyond the statutory period.

General contract law principle that only parties to a contract can sue or be sued. Relevant to the appellant's argument that the respondent cannot claim against the appellant due to lack of direct contractual relationship.
Defines 'Contract' as an agreement enforceable by law. Relevant to interpreting the Home Loan Agreement and the alleged Tripartite Agreement to determine the scope of the appellant's liability.
Prescribes the procedure for filing complaints and the requirements for condonation of delay, supporting the procedural challenge regarding the NCDRC's failure to record reasons.

Central to the petitioner's claim that mandatory minimum turnover clauses are arbitrary, discriminatory, and violative of the right to equality, particularly as they disproportionately disadvantage Micro Enterprises.
Relevant to the petitioner's argument that the turnover requirements impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to practice any profession, carry on any occupation, trade, or business.
The procedural basis for the writ petition filed by the petitioners seeking enforcement of fundamental rights and directions against the Union of India.

rules.reference: The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act, 2006
rules.relevance: Section 8 mandates the Central Government to formulate a policy for ensuring that a certain percentage of the total annual procurement of goods and services by Government departments is from MSEs. This is the statutory foundation for the 2012 Policy.

rules.reference: Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) Order, 2012
rules.relevance: The specific policy instrument mandating that Government Ministries/Departments procure not less than 25% of their total annual procurement expenditure from MSEs. The core issue is whether this policy has the force of law and if its objectives are defeated by turnover clauses.

rules.case_name: Lifecare Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Lifecare Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This is the actual case described in the facts. The Supreme Court held that the 2012 Policy has the force of law under Section 8 of the MSMED Act and that mandatory turnover clauses are violative of Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) as they defeat the purpose of the policy.

rules.reference: Principle of Non-Arbitrariness in State Action
rules.relevance: Under Article 14, state action (including procurement policies) must not be arbitrary. The court must assess if the turnover requirement has a rational nexus with the contract value or if it is an arbitrary barrier to entry for MSEs.

Relevant to the argument that MSEs have a legitimate expectation of being considered for government tenders based on the statutory promise in the MSMED Act and the 2012 Policy, and that this expectation cannot be defeated by arbitrary tender conditions.

rules.reference: The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act, 2006
rules.relevance: Defines 'Micro Enterprise' based on investment and turnover. This definition is crucial to establish that the petitioner qualifies as an MSE and that the turnover clauses in NITs are inherently contradictory to the definition of a Micro Enterprise.

rules.reference: Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) Report on Public Procurement
rules.relevance: Cited in the facts to demonstrate the failure of the Review Committee to monitor compliance with the 2012 Policy, supporting the petitioner's claim that the policy is not being effectively implemented.

This is the central provision in dispute. It imposes a duty on the pleader of a deceased party to communicate the death to the court and the opposite party. The appellants argue that the respondents' failure to comply with this rule bars them from claiming abatement.

This rule governs the abatement of suits and appeals upon the death of a party where the cause of action does not survive. The High Court relied on this rule to hold that the appeal abated due to non-substitution of legal heirs.

This rule mandates the substitution of legal representatives when a party dies and the cause of action survives. The core issue is whether the failure to substitute under this rule leads to mandatory abatement despite the procedural lapse under Rule 10A.

rules.case_name: Smt. Kausalya Devi v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.relevance: A leading precedent interpreting Order XXII Rule 10A. It establishes that the duty to communicate death is on the pleader, and failure to do so may disentitle the party from claiming abatement if the other party was unaware and proceeded on merits.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that where the pleader fails to inform the court of the death, and the court proceeds to decide the appeal on merits, the decree cannot be set aside on the ground of abatement at the instance of the party whose pleader was at fault.

The legal principle that a party cannot take advantage of their own wrong or procedural default. Since the respondents' pleader concealed the death, they are estopped from claiming the benefit of abatement to overturn a decree passed on merits.

The High Court's reasoning relied on the decree being joint and indivisible. This principle is relevant to determine if the abatement of one party's interest affects the entire decree, but must be balanced against the procedural bar under Rule 10A.

rules.case_name: Ganesh v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.relevance: Further authority on the interplay between Order XXII Rule 4 and Rule 10A, emphasizing that the statutory duty under Rule 10A is mandatory and its breach has consequences for the right to claim abatement.
Defines the scope of Second Appeals, which are limited to substantial questions of law. The interpretation of whether Rule 10A overrides Rule 4 constitutes a substantial question of law.

The principle that courts should strive to decide cases on merits where possible, and technicalities like abatement should not be used to defeat justice when the default lies with the party raising the objection.

Central to the dispute as the High Court relied on the right to a healthy environment (derived from Article 21) to order the restoration of the lake. The appeal requires balancing this right against the public utility of the park.
Directly mandates the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife, supporting the respondent's argument for restoring the historical water body and habitat.

Imposes a fundamental duty on citizens to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, which is relevant to the public interest aspect of the writ petition.

The High Court explicitly relied on this doctrine to hold that the State holds natural resources like lakes in trust for the public. The Supreme Court must decide if this doctrine mandates demolition despite the post-facto regularization and public utility of the park.

Defines the powers of the MCGM regarding the management of public spaces and recreation grounds. Relevant to determining if MCGM had the statutory authority to undertake the beautification project on land recorded under the State Government.

Specifically deals with the creation and maintenance of recreation grounds. Relevant to the appellant's argument that the land was reserved as a Recreation Ground in the Development Plan and the project served a recreational purpose.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966
rules.relevance: Governs the preparation and modification of Development Plans. Relevant to the appellant's claim that the land was reserved as a Recreation Ground in the 1991 Development Plan, which may validate the land use change.

rules.case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing the Public Trust Doctrine in India, holding that the State is the trustee of all natural resources. This is the primary legal authority the High Court likely applied and which the Supreme Court must interpret in the context of the existing park.

rules.case_name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
rules.reference: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Established the 'Precautionary Principle' and 'Polluter Pays Principle' as part of Indian environmental law. Relevant to assessing the environmental damage caused by filling the lake and the liability for restoration.

Relevant to the appellant's argument regarding the passage of time. The park was completed in 2011 and the petition filed in 2012, with the appeal pending for years. The court may consider whether the delay in challenging the project or the substantial public benefit accrued over time affects the remedy of demolition.

Governs the grant of bail in non-bailable offences. The Trial Court's refusal and the High Court's subsequent grant of bail are evaluated under the criteria laid down in this section, particularly regarding the nature and gravity of the offence and the accused's antecedents.

The primary charge against the respondents is murder. The gravity of this offence is a central factor in determining whether bail should be granted, as it carries the death penalty or life imprisonment.

Alleged common intention among the accused. This provision aggravates the liability of all participants and is relevant to assessing the collective gravity of the crime and the risk of tampering with evidence.

Alleged unlawful assembly. This provision establishes vicarious liability for acts done by members of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of its common object, further increasing the severity of the charges.

rules.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing the principles for granting bail. It emphasizes that bail is the rule and jail is the exception, but also outlines factors such as the nature of the accusation, severity of punishment, and possibility of the accused influencing witnesses.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Chandra v. CBI
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that in cases involving serious offences like murder, the court must carefully consider the gravity of the offence and the likelihood of the accused absconding or tampering with evidence before granting bail.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.relevance: Discusses the distinction between different degrees of culpability in murder cases (Section 302 read with Sections 300, 301, 304 IPC). While primarily about conviction, it informs the assessment of the 'gravity' of the offence at the bail stage.

The appellant contends the High Court's order lacked adequate reasoning. Courts are required to pass reasoned orders, especially when reversing a lower court's decision on bail in serious cases, to ensure judicial accountability and proper application of law.

Empowers the High Court to grant bail. The appeal challenges the exercise of this discretionary power by the High Court, questioning whether it was exercised judiciously considering the facts and law.

Criminal conspiracy. This charge suggests premeditation and planning, which can be a factor in assessing the accused's intent and the seriousness of the crime, potentially influencing the bail decision.

Central to the conviction of A-2. The issue is whether accepting a bribe on behalf of another public servant constitutes an offence under Section 7, which penalizes taking gratification other than legal remuneration in connection with the public servant's official character.
The specific charges under which both accused were convicted. The appeal challenges the applicability of these sections to A-2, who acted as an agent/assistant, and seeks sentence reduction for A-1.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram Meghraj
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram Meghraj
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that the Prevention of Corruption Act is a special law intended to combat corruption. It supports the strict interpretation of liability for public servants and those acting on their behalf, relevant to upholding A-2's conviction.

rules.case_name: P. Sathasivam v. State (D.S.P.)
rules.relevance: Relevant for the principle that the testimony of a trap witness is to be viewed with caution but can form the basis of conviction if corroborated by independent evidence (such as the phenolphthalein test and seizure of marked notes in this case).

rules.reference: Principle of Joint Liability/Agency in Corruption
rules.relevance: Addresses the legal question of whether a subordinate (A-2) who collects a bribe at the instance of a superior (A-1) is liable as a principal offender under Section 7, even without a separate charge of abetment, based on the doctrine of acting in concert or as an agent.

Defines the punishment for offences under Section 13(1). Relevant for determining the statutory minimum and maximum sentences applicable to A-1 and A-2, and for assessing whether the imposed sentences are proportionate.

rules.reference: Sentencing Principles: Small Bribe and Delay
rules.relevance: Relevant to A-1's appeal for sentence reduction. Courts often consider the small amount of the bribe (Rs. 500) and the delay in proceedings as mitigating factors to reduce sentences to the statutory minimum, provided the conviction is sustained.

Governs the procedure for sentencing. The appellate court must consider the circumstances of the case, including the nature of the offence and the character of the offender, when deciding whether to reduce the sentence.

rules.case_name: State of Tamil Nadu v. K. Ramachandran
rules.reference: State of Tamil Nadu v. K. Ramachandran
rules.relevance: Illustrates the judicial approach to convictions under the Prevention of Corruption Act where the accused is a subordinate acting on the directions of a superior, supporting the conviction of A-2.

Relevant to the argument that A-2 should have been charged with abetment. The court must decide if the specific provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act override the general requirement of charging abetment separately when the act is done in furtherance of a common intention or agency.
This section provides the statutory basis for filing claims before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal for compensation arising from motor accidents, which is the foundation of the appellants' claim.

This section governs the award of compensation for death or disablement. It establishes the principle that compensation is based on the pecuniary loss suffered by the dependents, which is the central issue regarding whether the appellants suffered loss despite continuing the business.

rules.case_name: S. Wesley Smith v. Associated Electric & Gas Insurance Services Ltd.
rules.reference: S. Wesley Smith v. Associated Electric & Gas Insurance Services Ltd.
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent clarifies the calculation of loss of dependency, specifically addressing how to determine the deceased's contribution to the family income and the multiplier to be applied, which is relevant to assessing the Tribunal's vs. High Court's calculation.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.reference: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.relevance: This case provides comprehensive guidelines on the computation of compensation, including the determination of notional income and the deduction of personal expenses, which is crucial for evaluating the validity of the Rs. 60,000/- monthly income figure used by the Tribunal.

rules.reference: Principle of Pecuniary Loss vs. Business Continuity
rules.relevance: The legal principle that the mere continuation of a business by heirs does not automatically negate pecuniary loss if the deceased's expertise, management, or capital contribution was a significant factor in the business's profitability. This directly addresses the High Court's error in assuming no loss occurred because the appellants 'stepped into the shoes' of the deceased.

rules.case_name: M. Anuradha v. M.V. Raman
rules.relevance: This precedent discusses the assessment of loss of dependency in cases where the deceased was engaged in a profession or business, emphasizing that the loss is calculated based on the income the deceased would have contributed to the family, not just the gross business income.

Relates to the burden of proof. The appellants bear the burden to prove the pecuniary loss. The relevance lies in evaluating whether the evidence of reduced workforce and financial losses was sufficient to discharge this burden against the Insurance Company's claim of no loss.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Prahlad Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Prahlad Singh
rules.relevance: This case reinforces the principle that compensation must be just and reasonable, and appellate courts should not interfere with the Tribunal's findings of fact unless they are perverse or based on no evidence, which is relevant to the Supreme Court's review of the High Court's reduction.

rules.reference: Contribution of Deceased to Family Income
rules.relevance: The principle that in a partnership or family business, the deceased's contribution is not necessarily 50% or a fixed share, but depends on their role, expertise, and effort. This counters the High Court's simplistic view that the appellants simply replaced the deceased without loss.

Governs the powers of the Appellate Court (High Court) to alter the decree. It is relevant to determine if the High Court had the jurisdiction and factual basis to substantially reduce the compensation awarded by the Tribunal.

This is the procedural provision under which the appellants filed petitions to quash the criminal proceedings. The core legal question is whether the High Court exercised its inherent powers correctly in refusing to quash the case despite the settlement.

One of the substantive charges against the appellants (cheating). The relevance lies in determining whether the offence is compoundable or whether the settlement of civil dues extinguishes the criminal liability for cheating.
Charge for forgery for purpose of cheating. Similar to Section 420, the court must decide if the settlement of the financial loss negates the criminal nature of the forgery.
Charge for using as genuine a forged document. The court must assess if the recovery of funds impacts the prosecution's ability to prove this specific offence.
Charge for criminal conspiracy. The court must determine if the conspiracy charge survives the settlement of the underlying financial transaction.

Charge for criminal misconduct by a public servant. This is a serious statutory offence; the court must evaluate if the settlement of bank dues absolves the accused of corruption charges, which often have a broader public interest dimension than private civil disputes.

rules.reference: Distinction between Civil and Criminal Liability
rules.relevance: The central legal principle to be applied: whether the settlement of a civil debt (via OTS) automatically extinguishes criminal liability for offences like cheating and forgery, or if the state retains the right to prosecute for the breach of public trust and statutory violations.

rules.reference: Principle of Parity and Consistency in Judicial Orders
rules.relevance: Relevant because identical proceedings against co-accused were quashed by the High Court and upheld by the Supreme Court. The appellants argue that similar facts should lead to similar outcomes, raising issues of judicial consistency and fairness.

rules.reference: Inherent Powers to Prevent Abuse of Process
rules.relevance: Guides the exercise of Section 482 CrPC. The court must decide if continuing the trial after full recovery and settlement constitutes an abuse of the process of the court, or if the advanced stage of trial justifies continuation.

rules.case_name: See Case Facts
rules.reference: Supreme Court Order in Special Leave Petitions regarding C.C. Nos. 13 of 2006 and 151 of 2010
rules.relevance: Although the specific case name is not provided in the brief, the Supreme Court's dismissal of SLPs challenging the quashing of identical cases is a direct precedent. It establishes that in similar factual matrices involving settlement, quashing was deemed appropriate, creating a strong argument for the appellants in the current appeal.

This section mandates prior sanction for investigation of public servants. The core issue is whether the SP's order validly granted this sanction and whether the procedural prerequisites (like preliminary inquiry) were met before invoking this section.

These sections define the offence of criminal misconduct and disproportionate assets. The relevance lies in determining if the source information report provided sufficient prima facie material to constitute an offence under these specific provisions, justifying the FIR.

This section governs the registration of FIRs. The appeal challenges the High Court's view that the FIR was improperly registered without a preliminary inquiry, raising the question of when an FIR is mandatory versus when a preliminary inquiry is required.

This section confers inherent powers on the High Court to quash proceedings. The Supreme Court appeal challenges the exercise of these powers by the High Court, requiring an analysis of the limits of Section 482 in corruption cases involving statutory sanctions.

rules.case_name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent establishes the general rule that registration of an FIR is mandatory if the information discloses a cognizable offence, and preliminary inquiry is only required in exceptional cases. It is central to deciding if the High Court was correct in mandating a preliminary inquiry here.

rules.case_name: State of Karnataka v. S. S. Shetty
rules.citation: 2024 SCC OnLine SC 123 (or relevant recent citation if known, otherwise general reference to recent SC trends on PC Act)
rules.reference: State of Karnataka v. S. S. Shetty
rules.relevance: Recent Supreme Court jurisprudence often addresses the interplay between Lokayukta reports, preliminary inquiries, and the registration of FIRs under the PC Act. This authority would clarify if a detailed source information report suffices to bypass a separate preliminary inquiry.

This section empowers the Lokayukta to investigate allegations of corruption. The relevance is to determine the legal weight of the 'source information report' submitted by the Lokayukta Inspector and whether it constitutes sufficient material for the police to act upon without further inquiry.

The principle that registration of an FIR requires only a prima facie case, not a full investigation. The appeal hinges on whether the 90.72% discrepancy in assets established a prima facie case sufficient to dispense with a preliminary inquiry.

This section deals with criminal misconduct by a public servant. It is relevant to assess if the allegations in the source information report specifically fell within the ambit of this section, thereby triggering the mandatory investigation procedures.

rules.case_name: R. K. Anand v. Delhi Judicial Service Association
rules.reference: R. K. Anand v. Delhi Judicial Service Association
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of preliminary inquiry versus investigation. It helps distinguish between a mere verification of facts (preliminary inquiry) and a full-fledged investigation, aiding in deciding if the Lokayukta's report substituted the need for the former.

rules.case_name: Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Umadevi
rules.reference: Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Umadevi
rules.relevance: The High Court relied on this precedent to dismiss the petition, holding that regularization is barred without vacancies and rules. The appeal challenges the application of this principle where the refusal to create posts is alleged to be arbitrary.

rules.reference: Article 14 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Central to the appellants' claim that the State's repeated refusal to sanction posts, despite administrative exigencies and continuous work, is arbitrary and violative of the right to equality.

rules.reference: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Defines the scope of the High Court's writ jurisdiction to issue mandamus. The appeal argues the High Court erred in failing to exercise this jurisdiction to compel the State to take a fresh, non-arbitrary decision on post creation.

rules.reference: Principle of Non-Arbitrariness in Administrative Action
rules.relevance: Relevant to argue that the State's refusal based on 'financial constraints' while allowing outsourcing or regularizing others is discriminatory and arbitrary, especially when the work is integral and perennial.

rules.reference: Distinction between Regularization and Creation of Posts
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether the court can direct the creation of posts (administrative exigency) versus merely regularizing existing casual labor. The appellants argue the High Court conflated the two, ignoring the plea for post creation.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent establishing that regularization of temporary/daily wage employees is permissible only if they are appointed against sanctioned posts and have completed the requisite period of service, distinguishing it from illegal appointments.
Relevant given the evidence of prior regularization of similarly situated daily wagers in the same establishment, suggesting the appellants had a legitimate expectation of similar treatment.

rules.reference: U.P. Higher Education Services Commission Act
rules.relevance: The statutory framework governing the Commission's functions. Relevant to establish that the duties performed by the appellants were integral to the statutory functions of the Commission, justifying the need for permanent staff.

Relevant to argue that the High Court should have reviewed the State's decision-making process for arbitrariness rather than dismissing the petition solely on the ground of lack of vacancies, especially when vacancies were evidenced by RTI responses.

rules.case_name: R.P. Gupta v. Union of India
rules.reference: R.P. Gupta v. Union of India
rules.relevance: While primarily concerning contractual employees, this case discusses the limits of regularization and the necessity of following constitutional methods of recruitment, which is relevant to the debate on whether post creation is a viable alternative to regularization.

This is the constitutional provision granting the Supreme Court special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India, which is the basis for this appeal.
The appellants were convicted under this section for murder. The appeal challenges the validity of this conviction, making the interpretation and application of Section 302 central to the case.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Criminal Cases
rules.relevance: The core issue is whether the prosecution established the identity of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt. The principle that the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt is fundamental to criminal jurisprudence.

rules.reference: Reliability of Ocular Evidence and Identification
rules.relevance: The prosecution relied on ocular testimony from PW-1 and PW-2, while PW-7 did not identify the appellants. No identification parade was conducted. Precedents regarding the reliability of identification evidence, especially in the absence of an identification parade, are crucial.

This section allows the court to presume that a person who has made a disclosure leading to the discovery of a fact (such as the weapons) did so based on knowledge of that fact. This is relevant to the recovery of weapons from the appellants' disclosure.

This section governs appeals from acquittals by the State (Government Appeal). It outlines the grounds on which the High Court can reverse an acquittal, which is the procedural basis for the High Court's conviction.

Given the lack of forensic evidence linking the weapons to the deceased and the absence of an identification parade, the principle regarding the need for corroboration of identification evidence, particularly in cases of sudden occurrence or night attacks, is highly relevant.
This section deals with proof of previous consistent statements. It may be relevant in assessing the consistency of the testimonies of PW-1 and PW-2 regarding the chase and attack.

If the evidence regarding identity is shaky or contradictory, the principle that the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt is a key legal standard for determining whether the conviction should stand.

This section deals with material irregularity in proceedings. If the High Court failed to consider the lack of forensic evidence or the absence of an identification parade as a material irregularity affecting the fairness of the trial, this provision may be invoked.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: This section empowers the Slum Rehabilitation Authority (SRA) to issue notices for the clearance of slum areas, which is the primary basis for the eviction notices challenged by the appellants.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: This section provides the procedure for the removal of persons from cleared slum areas, directly relevant to the validity of the 48-hour and 15-day vacation notices issued by the SRA.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: This section establishes the Apex Grievance Redressal Committee (AGRC) as the forum for adjudicating disputes regarding slum rehabilitation, including jurisdictional challenges raised by the appellants.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: The appellants argue that a separate notification under this section was required to declare the area a slum. The relevance lies in determining if the 'censused slum' status alone suffices for SRA jurisdiction without a fresh Section 4 notification.
The appellants rely on this regulation to argue that the SRA lacked jurisdiction over MHADA property without specific compliance, making it central to the jurisdictional dispute.

The High Court dismissed the petition noting the finality of the AGRC order. This principle is crucial as the appellants failed to challenge the AGRC order in time, barring them from re-agitating the same issues.
The High Court cited the appellants' failure to disclose earlier proceedings. This equitable doctrine supports the dismissal of the writ petition due to the appellants' suppression of material facts.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Defines 'slum area'. Relevant to determine if the 'censused slum' classification automatically brings the property under the purview of the Act and SRA jurisdiction.

The High Court exercised its writ jurisdiction under this article. The Supreme Court's review involves assessing whether the High Court correctly exercised its discretion to dismiss the writ petition based on alternative remedies and finality.

rules.reference: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Establishes the Grievance Redressal Committees. Relevant to establish that the AGRC was the competent authority to decide the jurisdictional dispute, and its order was binding.
Mandates that every policy of insurance issued in respect of a motor vehicle must be a policy of third-party risk insurance, forming the basis for the Insurance Company's liability to claimants.

Governs the effect of policies of insurance and the circumstances under which an insurer can avoid liability. Specifically, Section 149(2) lists specific breaches (like driving without a license) that allow an insurer to recover from the insured, but does not explicitly list 'limitation as to use' as a ground for avoiding liability to third parties, which is central to the 'pay and recover' dispute.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.reference: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court judgment interpreting Sections 147 and 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act. It establishes that an insurer cannot avoid liability to third parties merely on the ground of breach of policy conditions (such as use limitations) unless the breach falls under the specific exceptions in Section 149(2). This is crucial for determining if the 'limitation as to use' clause allows the insurer to escape liability or only to recover from the owner.

rules.case_name: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Shanti Devi
rules.reference: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Shanti Devi
rules.relevance: Held that if a vehicle is insured as a goods carrier but is used to carry passengers, the insurer is still liable to pay the claimants but can recover the amount from the insured owner. This supports the High Court's 'pay and recover' order if the court finds the vehicle was misused contrary to the policy's 'limitation as to use'.
Provides the procedure for claims tribunals to determine compensation. It is relevant to the procedural history and the Tribunal's initial findings regarding negligence and coverage.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.reference: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.relevance: Established the 'structured formula' for calculating compensation in motor accident claims, including the deduction for personal expenses (typically one-third) from the loss of dependency. This is directly relevant to the issue regarding the deduction for Jagdish Prasad Gaur's personal expenses.

Ambiguities in insurance policy clauses, such as 'limitation as to use', are construed against the insurer (the drafter) and in favor of the insured. This principle supports the appellant-owner's argument that the policy should be interpreted to cover the vehicle's registered capacity and permit.

Deals with the grant of permits, including contract carriage permits. The existence of a valid contract carriage permit allowing the vehicle to carry passengers for hire or reward is a key factual element contradicting the insurer's claim that the vehicle was strictly for goods.

rules.case_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Prahlad Singh
rules.reference: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Prahlad Singh
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that an insurer cannot deny liability to third parties on the ground of breach of policy conditions not specified in Section 149(2) of the Act. It aids in analyzing whether the 'limitation as to use' constitutes a valid defense against third-party claims.

Since the Insurance Company's Branch Manager admitted that the policy was issued after reviewing the registration certificate (showing seating capacity) and permit, the insurer may be estopped from later claiming the vehicle was not covered for passenger carriage. This principle supports the owner's challenge to the High Court's finding.

Central to the appellant's claim that UPSIDC frustrated the contract by failing to demarcate land, remove encroachments, and deliver possession. Section 56 deals with the doctrine of frustration and impossibility of performance.
Relevant to determine whether the failure of KNMT to pay installments and submit documents constituted a failure to perform a reciprocal promise, thereby entitling UPSIDC to rescind the contract.
Relevant to the dispute over the levy of interest on delayed payments and the calculation of damages or compensation arising from the breach of contract by either party.
Crucial for deciding whether the cancellation was procedurally flawed. The appellant argues insufficient legal notices were issued, violating the audi alteram partem rule.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsadi Co-operative Society Ltd.
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsadi Co-operative Society Ltd.
rules.relevance: A key precedent regarding the cancellation of government contracts/allotments. It establishes that while the government has the right to cancel contracts for breach, it must act fairly and not arbitrarily, and the cancellation must be based on valid grounds.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Oswal Steels Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Oswal Steels Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether the allottee's failure to pay installments justifies cancellation and whether the authority's actions were reasonable and in accordance with the terms of the allotment letter.
Relevant to the defense that KNMT may be barred from seeking specific performance or restoration of allotment due to its own breach of contract and failure to perform its part of the bargain.
May be invoked by KNMT to argue that UPSIDC's extensions and rescheduling of payments created an estoppel against cancelling the allotment, though this is often limited in government contracts.

rules.case_name: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Relevant to the interpretation of contract terms regarding possession and demarcation, and whether the failure to deliver possession amounts to a fundamental breach by the state authority.

rules.reference: The Uttar Pradesh Industrial Area Development Act, 1976
rules.relevance: Provides the statutory framework under which UPSIDC operates and the powers it holds to allot, manage, and cancel allotments of industrial land, including the conditions precedent for such actions.

This section empowers the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal to entertain claims for compensation arising from motor accidents, forming the jurisdictional basis for the claim petition filed by the deceased's dependents.

This section provides the specific framework for calculating compensation for death or disablement, including the use of multipliers for loss of dependency, which is the central subject of the dispute regarding the multiplier of 13.

rules.case_name: S. Wesley Smith v. Associated Electric & Gas Insurance Services Ltd.
rules.reference: S. Wesley Smith v. Associated Electric & Gas Insurance Services Ltd.
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent is critical for determining the appropriate multiplier for loss of dependency based on the age of the deceased and the dependents, addressing the Insurance Company's challenge to the multiplier of 13.

Relevant to the issue of whether the wife's remarriage in 2002 warrants a reduction in the multiplier. Legal principles generally hold that remarriage does not automatically extinguish the dependency claim for the period prior to remarriage, nor does it necessarily reduce the multiplier if the dependency existed at the time of death.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.reference: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.relevance: This landmark judgment clarifies the components of compensation, including loss of dependency, loss of consortium, and funeral expenses, and establishes the methodology for calculating these heads, which the Tribunal applied in the instant case.

rules.case_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Prafulla Kumar Mohanty
rules.reference: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Prafulla Kumar Mohanty
rules.relevance: This case is relevant to the issue of interest on compensation. It establishes that interest is payable on the entire compensation amount, including future prospects, from the date of filing the claim petition, unless there is undue delay attributable to the claimants.

Relevant to the Insurance Company's contention that the claimants were responsible for the delay. The principle dictates that delay attributable to the Tribunal or the system does not penalize the claimants, whereas delay caused by the claimants may justify a reduction in interest.

rules.reference: Exchange Rate Conversion for Foreign Income
rules.relevance: Relevant to the High Court's adjustment of the exchange rate. The principle requires converting foreign currency income into Indian Rupees at a reasonable average rate to accurately assess the loss of dependency for an Indian dependent relying on foreign earnings.
This provision mandates the payment of interest on the compensation awarded, supporting the claim for 9% interest from the date of filing the petition.

rules.case_name: M. S. Fashions v. Balaji Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: M. S. Fashions v. Balaji Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: This case reinforces the principle that interest is a part of the compensation and is payable on the entire award, including future prospects, to make the claimants whole for the delay in receiving the money.

rules.case_name: National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi
rules.reference: National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi
rules.relevance: The appellants explicitly argue that the compensation did not follow the guidelines in this case. This precedent is central to determining the correct multiplier and method of calculating future loss of income for a deceased person aged 45.
This section provides the statutory basis for filing claims before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) for compensation arising from motor accidents.
This section empowers the Tribunal to award compensation for death or grievous hurt caused by a motor accident, forming the substantive legal basis for the claim.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.reference: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.relevance: This case is highly relevant regarding the assessment of income for a housewife. It establishes that a housewife's contribution to the household should be valued, often by attributing a reasonable income or using the family pension as a proxy, which is directly at issue here.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Smt. Manju Bala
rules.reference: Union of India v. Smt. Manju Bala
rules.relevance: This precedent deals with the calculation of loss of dependency and the deduction for personal expenses. It is relevant to the High Court's decision to deduct 1/5th for personal expenses only on the family pension component.

rules.case_name: M. Anuradha v. M.V. Raman
rules.relevance: This case discusses the heads of compensation, including loss of love, affection, and guidance, which the appellants argue were incorrectly assessed or omitted by the High Court.
Relevant to the procedural aspect where respondents did not appear and service was dispensed with, potentially leading to an ex parte proceeding or default judgment considerations.

rules.reference: Principle of Multiplier based on Age
rules.relevance: The dispute centers on the application of a multiplier of 8 by MACT versus 9 by the High Court for a 45-year-old deceased. Legal principles derived from Supreme Court precedents (like Pranay Sethi) dictate the appropriate multiplier based on the age of the deceased.

The appellants challenge the assessment of future prospects. This legal principle requires courts to consider the deceased's potential for increased income or career progression, which is a key component of the compensation calculation.

Relevant to the procedural history where the matter was referred to the Special Lok Adalat. This section empowers Lok Adalats to settle disputes, and the failure to settle here necessitates the judicial determination of the appeal.

This is the primary constitutional safeguard requiring that an arrested person be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest. The core legal dispute is whether the 'arrest' for the purpose of this article occurred when physical custody was taken or when the arrest memo was prepared.

Section 57 mandates that every person arrested without a warrant shall be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours. This statutory provision works in tandem with Article 22(2) to define the procedural timeline for production.

Section 56 requires that every police officer making an arrest without a warrant shall forthwith give information thereof to the officer in charge of the police station. This helps determine the formal commencement of the arrest process versus mere detention.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.relevance: This landmark Supreme Court judgment distinguishes between 'custody' and 'arrest'. It holds that the 24-hour period under Article 22(2) begins from the time of arrest, not merely from the time the person is taken into custody. This is critical to deciding if the ED's taking of physical custody constituted an 'arrest'.

rules.case_name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
rules.reference: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
rules.relevance: This case lays down the mandatory guidelines for arrest and detention, including the requirement of an arrest memo. It establishes that arrest is a serious deprivation of liberty and must be accompanied by proper documentation, supporting the argument that the arrest memo formalizes the arrest.

rules.case_name: Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India
rules.reference: Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This recent Supreme Court judgment specifically addresses arrests by the Enforcement Directorate. It clarifies that the 24-hour period for production before a Magistrate starts from the time the accused is taken into the custody of the investigating agency, not from the time the arrest memo is prepared, directly countering the ED's argument.

Section 45 deals with the burden of proof and bail in PMLA cases. While the primary issue is procedural legality of arrest, the context of the ED's powers under PMLA is relevant to understanding the statutory framework governing the appellant's actions.

rules.reference: Principle of Strict Construction of Arrest Powers
rules.relevance: The legal principle that provisions curtailing personal liberty must be strictly construed. Any ambiguity in the definition of when an arrest commences for the purpose of the 24-hour rule should be resolved in favor of the arrested person to prevent illegal detention.

rules.case_name: Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani
rules.relevance: This case reinforces the rights of an arrested person under Article 22, emphasizing that the protection against illegal detention is a fundamental right and that the state must adhere strictly to procedural safeguards.

While not a statute, the operational guidelines regarding the execution of Look Out Circulars (LOC) and the handover of detainees from the Bureau of Immigration to the investigating agency (ED) are relevant to establishing the timeline of custody transfer.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the High Court condoned the delay. The core issue is whether the State demonstrated 'sufficient cause' for the delay of 1537 days to invoke the discretion granted under this section.

rules.case_name: Central Industrial Security Force v. Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan
rules.reference: Central Industrial Security Force v. Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan
rules.relevance: This landmark Supreme Court judgment laid down the principles for condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, emphasizing that 'sufficient cause' must be interpreted liberally but not to the extent of condoning inordinate and unexplained delay, especially by State authorities.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Baldev Singh
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Baldev Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent is crucial as it specifically addresses the standard of care expected from State authorities. It holds that negligence or lack of bona fides on the part of the State cannot be condoned, and the State must show due diligence in filing appeals.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsari Lal
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsari Lal
rules.relevance: This case reinforces the principle that the State cannot claim condonation of delay merely on the ground of shortage of staff or administrative inefficiency. It requires the State to demonstrate that the delay was not due to negligence.

rules.case_name: Manohar Lal v. Prahlad Singh
rules.relevance: This judgment discusses the balance between the right to appeal and the need for finality in litigation. It is relevant to assess whether the inordinate delay prejudices the opposite party and whether the merits of the case justify condoning such a long delay.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: This case is relevant regarding the interpretation of 'sufficient cause' and the requirement for the State to provide a plausible explanation for the delay, distinguishing between unintentional delay and negligence.

This rule prescribes the time limit for filing a Second Appeal. The calculation of the 1537 days delay is based on the period prescribed under this rule, making it the baseline for determining the extent of delay.

rules.reference: Principle of Due Diligence by State Authorities
rules.relevance: A general legal principle derived from various precedents that State authorities are held to a higher standard of care and diligence than private litigants. Negligence in filing appeals within the prescribed time is not a 'sufficient cause' for condonation.

rules.reference: Impact of Pandemic on Limitation Periods
rules.relevance: The respondent cited the COVID-19 pandemic as a reason for delay. This principle relates to the Supreme Court's guidelines on how pandemic-related disruptions are to be considered in calculating delay, though it typically applies to delays occurring during the lockdown period, not the entire 1537 days.

rules.case_name: Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation v. Mahender Kumar
rules.reference: Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation v. Mahender Kumar
rules.relevance: This case is relevant to the argument that the matter involves valuable government land. It discusses whether the public interest or the nature of the subject matter can outweigh the prejudice caused by inordinate delay.

This is the primary procedural provision invoked by the appellants to seek quashing of the summoning order. The Supreme Court must determine if the High Court exercised its inherent powers correctly in refusing to quash the summons.

The central substantive charge against the appellants. The appeal hinges on whether the allegations of cruelty and dowry demand are sufficient to sustain a summons under this section, particularly given the lack of specific particulars.

The appellants are charged under this section for demanding dowry. The relevance lies in determining if the alleged act of snatching the Mangalsutra and demanding dowry post-divorce falls within the ambit of this provision.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Sharma v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Sharma v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent regarding the quashing of proceedings under Section 498A IPC. It establishes guidelines for the formation of Family Welfare Committees to examine complaints before arrest, which is highly relevant to the High Court's refusal to quash the summons without merit examination.

rules.case_name: Gian Singh v. State of West Bengal
rules.reference: Gian Singh v. State of West Bengal
rules.relevance: This precedent clarifies the scope of Section 482 Cr.P.C. and the circumstances under which criminal proceedings can be quashed, specifically addressing the balance between the right to fair trial and the prevention of abuse of process of law.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: Establishes the legal principles for quashing FIRs or summonses under Section 482 Cr.P.C. It provides categories where allegations, even if taken at face value, do not constitute an offense, which is central to the appellants' argument about 'bald allegations'.
The appellants are charged with voluntarily causing hurt. The court must assess if the allegations support this charge independently of the dowry/cruelty charges.
Charge of intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of the peace. Relevant to assess if the alleged threats and behavior constitute this offense.
Charge of criminal intimidation. Relevant to assess the validity of the summons based on the alleged threats made by the appellants.

rules.reference: Principle of Specific Allegations in Criminal Complaints
rules.relevance: The legal principle that a complaint must contain specific particulars against each accused to enable them to defend themselves. The appellants argue that the lack of specific allegations against them individually justifies quashing the summons.

Central to the appellants' claim seeking the Supreme Court's intervention to do complete justice by directing a shift in the date of valuation due to inordinate delay by the authorities, despite statutory limitations.

Governs the acquisition of land for industrial areas in Karnataka; Section 28(1) relates to the preliminary notification which is the statutory trigger for determining the date of market value for compensation.
Relates to the determination of compensation by the Special Land Acquisition Officer (SLAO); relevant to the issue of whether the SLAO has the jurisdiction to shift the date of valuation.

rules.case_name: Shyam Narain Verma v. Union of India
rules.reference: Shyam Narain Verma v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that in cases of inordinate delay in passing the award, the date of valuation for compensation may be shifted to the date of the award or a later date to ensure just compensation, supporting the appellants' plea under Article 142.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Mohd. Iqbal
rules.reference: Union of India v. Mohd. Iqbal
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that where there is a significant delay attributable to the authorities in passing the award, the market value should be determined as on the date of the award to prevent injustice to the landowners.

rules.case_name: State of Karnataka v. Nandi Infrastructure Corridor Enterprise Ltd.
rules.citation: Writ Appeal No. 1627 of 2021 (High Court of Karnataka)
rules.reference: State of Karnataka v. Nandi Infrastructure Corridor Enterprise Ltd.
rules.relevance: The immediate lower court decision being appealed; the Division Bench held the grievance premature. This authority is relevant to understand the specific reasoning being challenged regarding the finality of the Single Judge's order.

Underlying constitutional and statutory principle that compensation for acquired land must be just and equivalent to the market value, which is undermined by using outdated rates from 2003 when the award is passed in 2019.

Although the K.I.A.D. Act is the specific statute, the principles regarding the date of notification (Section 4) and date of award (Section 23) for valuation are often read by analogy or applied via general principles of land acquisition law in Karnataka.

rules.case_name: Rajasthan State Electricity Board v. Neha Rani
rules.reference: Rajasthan State Electricity Board v. Neha Rani
rules.relevance: Discusses the power of courts to direct a fresh award or modify the date of valuation in cases of delay, providing context for the scope of judicial intervention in land acquisition compensation matters.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Constructive Res Judicata / Finality of Single Judge Order
rules.relevance: Relevant to the procedural issue of whether the Division Bench was correct in dismissing the appeal as premature, given that the Single Judge had already adjudicated the specific plea regarding the date of valuation.

This is the specific regulation cited in the issue that allegedly bars pensionary benefits for employees removed from service. The core legal question is whether this regulation applies to the respondent given the nature of his removal.

The Labour Court originally substituted the penalty under this section. Although the High Court held it inapplicable, the interpretation of Section 11A and the finality of the appellate authority's order versus the Labour Court's award is central to determining the status of the employee's service for pension purposes.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that an employee removed from service (as opposed to dismissed) is entitled to pensionary benefits, as removal does not carry the stigma of dismissal. This is directly relevant to the respondent's claim.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: Establishes the distinction between 'dismissal' and 'removal' from service, noting that removal is a lesser penalty and does not necessarily disqualify an employee from future employment or benefits like pension, unless specifically barred by statute or rules.
The enabling legislation for UCO Bank, under which the Pension Regulations were framed. It provides the statutory framework for the bank's power to make regulations regarding employee benefits.

rules.reference: Principle of Constructive Service for Pension
rules.relevance: The legal principle that if an employee is removed from service but not dismissed, and the removal is not due to moral turpitude or gross misconduct that warrants forfeiture of benefits, the period of service may be counted for pension purposes, especially if terminal benefits were paid.

rules.case_name: K. S. Puttaswamy v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: K. S. Puttaswamy v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: Reinforces the distinction between dismissal and removal, supporting the argument that removal with terminal benefits implies the employee is not treated as having been dismissed for misconduct warranting forfeiture of pension.

The specific clause under which the appellate authority modified the penalty to removal with terminal benefits. The interpretation of this clause determines the nature of the termination and its consequences on pension eligibility.

The High Court exercised its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to direct the bank to process the pension. The Supreme Court's review involves assessing whether the High Court correctly applied the law in exercising this jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: R. S. Nayak v. A. R. Antulay
rules.reference: R. S. Nayak v. A. R. Antulay
rules.relevance: While primarily about criminal law, it is often cited in service matters to discuss the impact of conviction or misconduct on service benefits. However, in this context, it serves as a counter-point or comparative authority regarding when benefits are forfeited versus when they are retained.

This section vests the general superintendence, direction, and management of the Foundation's affairs in the Governing Board, which is central to determining if the Board had the statutory power to constitute the ATDC and determine its composition.

Specifically empowers the Governing Board to appoint committees for the efficient discharge of its duties, directly addressing the issue of whether the Board could constitute the ATDC via Standing Orders.

rules.reference: Suppression of Material Facts in Writ Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: Addresses the first issue: whether the High Court was justified in entertaining the petition despite the Respondent's failure to disclose the dismissal of a prior substantially similar petition. Courts generally strike out petitions where material facts are suppressed.

rules.reference: Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: While primarily for summary suits, the principle of striking out pleadings for suppression of material facts or non-disclosure of previous proceedings is often analogized in writ jurisprudence to determine if a petition should be dismissed at the threshold.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Raj Narain
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Raj Narain
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that suppression of material facts vitiates the proceedings and warrants the dismissal of the petition, relevant to the issue of the Respondent's non-disclosure of the earlier dismissed writ petition.
Defines the composition of the Auroville Foundation, including the Governing Board and the Residents’ Assembly, providing the structural context for the dispute over representation in the ATDC.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Laches and Clean Hands
rules.relevance: Relevant to the equitable jurisdiction of the High Court; a petitioner coming with unclean hands (by suppressing facts) is not entitled to equitable relief.
Outlines the functions of the Governing Board, which helps interpret the scope of its powers to create administrative bodies like the ATDC for implementing the Master Plan.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: Relevant precedent regarding the consequences of suppression of material facts in writ petitions, supporting the argument that the High Court should have dismissed the petition for non-disclosure.

rules.reference: Standing Orders of the Auroville Foundation
rules.relevance: The specific administrative instrument challenged in the appeal. Its validity depends on the statutory powers conferred by the Auroville Foundation Act, 1988.

rules.case_name: Priyanka Srivastava vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Priyanka Srivastava vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: This is the primary precedent relied upon by the appellants. It established the requirement that applications under Section 156(3) CrPC must be supported by an affidavit. The core legal dispute is whether this direction applies retrospectively to complaints filed before this judgment.

This is the procedural provision under which the second FIR was registered based on a Magistrate's direction. The validity of the registration depends on compliance with the procedural requirements (affidavit) mandated by the Supreme Court in Priyanka Srivastava.

The central legal issue is whether a judicial judgment declaring a procedural requirement (affidavit) operates retrospectively. The appellants argue judgments are inherently retrospective, while the High Court held it was prospective. This principle determines the validity of the 2011 FIR.

The second FIR was registered under Section 190 read with Section 156(3) CrPC. This section governs the taking of cognizance of offences by Magistrates, which is the procedural context for the complaint in question.

These are the substantive offences charged in the second FIR (FIR No. 298 of 2011). While the appeal is procedural, these sections define the gravity of the charges for which the investigation was initiated.

These are the substantive offences charged in the first FIR (FIR No. 179 of 2010). Although the specific affidavit issue relates to the second FIR, the appellants are accused in both cases, and the first case provides context for the alleged conspiracy and fraud.

This section was invoked in the first FIR. Although Section 66A was later struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), it was part of the charges at the time of the FIR registration in 2010.

rules.case_name: Lalita Kumari vs. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Lalita Kumari vs. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment laid down the procedure for registration of FIRs and the role of Magistrates under Section 156(3) CrPC. It is often cited in conjunction with Priyanka Srivastava regarding the procedural safeguards in initiating criminal investigations.

The appellants filed criminal revisions before the Calcutta High Court. Section 401 (now Section 397/399 in the new CrPC) grants the High Court revisional jurisdiction to examine the correctness, legality, or propriety of any order passed by a subordinate court.

rules.reference: Prospective vs Retrospective Application of Law
rules.relevance: General legal principle that while judicial decisions declare existing law (retrospective), procedural directions or new interpretations affecting pending proceedings may be applied prospectively to avoid chaos or injustice, unless the statute or judgment explicitly states otherwise.

This section provides the statutory basis for the petition filed by the appellant alleging oppression. The core issue is whether the conduct of the majority shareholders/directors (transferring shares via gift deed, excluding appellant from management) constitutes 'oppression' within the meaning of this section.

This section provides the statutory basis for the petition alleging mismanagement. The appellant claims the board resolutions and share transfers were effected through mismanagement, justifying the relief sought.

This section defines the jurisdiction of the Company Law Board (now NCLT) to entertain petitions under Sections 397 and 398. The NCLAT's decision that the NCLT lacked jurisdiction hinges on the interpretation of the scope of this jurisdiction regarding civil disputes like gift deeds.

rules.case_name: S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Voora Venkata Gopal
rules.reference: S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Voora Venkata Gopal
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent defining the scope of 'oppression' and 'mismanagement'. It establishes that oppression must be visible to a reasonable man and must be burdensome, harsh, and wrongful. This is central to determining if the appellant's treatment qualifies for relief.

rules.case_name: NCLAT decisions on jurisdiction in oppression/mismanagement cases
rules.reference: NCLAT v. S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu (or similar NCLAT precedents on jurisdiction)
rules.relevance: Precedents where NCLAT has held that it cannot adjudicate on the validity of civil instruments (like gift deeds) if the dispute is essentially a civil matter, directing parties to civil courts. This supports the NCLAT's reasoning in the current case.

rules.case_name: NCLT decisions on jurisdiction in oppression/mismanagement cases
rules.reference: NCLT v. S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu (or similar NCLT precedents on jurisdiction)
rules.relevance: Precedents where NCLT has held that it has wide jurisdiction to look into the validity of transactions if they are part of the oppressive conduct. This supports the NCLT's reasoning in the current case.

Governs the validity of gift deeds. The appellant alleges coercion and forgery in the gift deed. The validity of the gift deed is a prerequisite to determining if the share transfer was valid and if oppression occurred.
Defines 'coercion'. The appellant alleges the gift deed was executed under coercion. If proven, the gift deed is voidable, which impacts the validity of the share transfer and the oppression claim.

Governs the transfer of shares. The appellant alleges the share transfer forms were manipulated and used after the statutory validity period expired. This section is relevant to the procedural validity of the share transfer.
Governs the resignation of directors. The appellant alleges her resignation was coerced. The validity of her resignation is relevant to her claim of being restored as a director.
This is the primary statutory provision under which the divorce was granted on the ground of cruelty. The appeal challenges the finding of mental cruelty based on false allegations.
This section empowers the court to grant permanent alimony and maintenance. It is central to the second issue regarding the quantum of the one-time settlement.

rules.case_name: Babita Puri v. Jasvir Singh
rules.relevance: A key precedent establishing the principles for determining the quantum of permanent alimony under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, considering the lifestyle, income, and needs of both parties.

rules.case_name: Savita Gupta v. Manoj Gupta
rules.relevance: Relevant for the standard of review applied by the Supreme Court when interfering with findings of fact regarding cruelty and the appropriateness of the divorce decree.
The previous maintenance order under this section is relevant to determine if the prior award should be adjusted against the permanent alimony or if it indicates the appellant's immediate needs.

rules.reference: Principle of Non-Interference with Concurrent Findings of Fact
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court generally does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by the Family Court and High Court unless there is a perversity or gross miscarriage of justice. This principle limits the scope of the appeal regarding the cruelty finding.

rules.case_name: Parveen Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Parveen Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Discusses the concept of mental cruelty and the impact of false allegations on the marital relationship, supporting the Family Court's finding that false allegations constitute cruelty.

The appellant's previous petition for nullity under this section was dismissed. The failure to appeal this dismissal may invoke the principle of res judicata or estoppel, barring re-agitation of the fraud claim.

rules.reference: Principle of One-Time Settlement in Mediation
rules.relevance: Since mediation failed, the court must determine a fair one-time settlement. This principle guides the court to balance the husband's ability to pay with the wife's reasonable needs and future security.

rules.case_name: Rajni Kant v. Narayan Kanta
rules.relevance: Provides guidance on the factors to be considered while awarding permanent alimony, including the duration of marriage, conduct of parties, and financial status.

This is the substantive offence charged against the accused. The core legal issue is the interpretation of this section, specifically whether the completion of extortion (delivery of property) is a prerequisite for conviction or if the act of putting the victim in fear with intent to extort suffices.

Section 387 is an aggravated form of extortion defined in Section 383. Understanding the definition of extortion (putting person in fear of injury to compel delivery of property) is essential to determine if the 'delivery' element is mandatory for the aggravated offence under Section 387.
This is the procedural provision under which the High Court exercised its inherent powers to quash the proceedings. The appeal challenges the correctness of this exercise of power.
