This fresh notification issued by MoEF&CC reiterates that General Conditions do not apply to Items 8(a) and 8(b). Its validity was upheld by the Supreme Court in Vanashakti, making it the current operative legal framework.

rules.case_name: In Re: Construction of Park at Noida Near Okhla Bird Sanctuary
rules.reference: In Re: Construction of Park at Noida Near Okhla Bird Sanctuary
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court observed in this case that the legislative intent was to exclude Items 8(a) and 8(b) from General Conditions to promote decentralization. This supports the appellants' argument regarding the original intent of the 2006 Notification.

rules.case_name: One Earth One Life v. MoEF
rules.reference: One Earth One Life v. MoEF
rules.relevance: The Kerala High Court quashed the EIA 2014 Notification on procedural grounds (variance between draft and final notification). The NGT relied on this to argue that the 2006 General Conditions were revived. The appellants challenge the legal consequence of this quashing.

Defines the original jurisdiction of the NGT. The appellants argue that the NGT exceeded its jurisdiction by issuing policy directions and interpreting statutory notifications in a manner that created a legal vacuum, rather than adjudicating specific environmental disputes.

This notification explicitly stated that General Conditions do not apply to Items 8(a) and 8(b). Although quashed by the Kerala High Court, its existence and the MoEF&CC's consistent stance (reiterated in 2025) are central to the argument that the exclusion of General Conditions is the intended policy.

rules.reference: Principle of Non-Interference in Policy Matters
rules.relevance: The appellants argue that the NGT lacked jurisdiction to issue policy directions. Courts generally refrain from substituting their judgment for that of the executive in policy matters unless there is a clear violation of law or constitutional rights. This principle supports the challenge to the NGT's order.

This is the primary procedural provision under which the Trial Court dismissed the discharge application. The appeal centers on whether the material on record discloses sufficient grounds to proceed against the accused, which is the test under Section 227.

The appellant specifically challenges the framing of charges for Voyeurism. The court must determine if clicking pictures and recording videos without consent, in the context of a property dispute, meets the statutory definition of voyeurism.

The appellant argues that the allegations do not disclose criminal intimidation. The court must assess if the acts alleged constitute a threat to cause injury to person, reputation, or property as required by this section.

The appellant contends that the obstruction was a bona fide enforcement of rights under a civil injunction. The court must decide if this constitutes 'wrongful restraint' or if it is a lawful act protected by the civil order.

rules.case_name: Sheela Barse v. Union of India
rules.reference: Sheela Barse v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the standard for discharge under Section 227 CrPC: the court must consider whether a prima facie case exists, not whether the accused is guilty. This is central to reviewing the Trial Court's dismissal.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent defining the scope of Section 227 CrPC. It holds that the court should not conduct a mini-trial but should look at whether the evidence, if unrebutted, would warrant conviction.

The legal principle that at the stage of discharge, the court must assume the prosecution's evidence to be true and determine if it discloses a prima facie case. This governs the evaluation of the FIR and chargesheet.

rules.reference: Bona Fide Exercise of Civil Rights
rules.relevance: The principle that acts done in good faith in the exercise of a legal right (such as enforcing a civil injunction) may not constitute criminal offenses like wrongful restraint or intimidation, unless accompanied by criminal intent.

The High Court dismissed the revision petition under this section (inherent powers). The Supreme Court appeal involves reviewing the High Court's exercise of discretion in refusing to quash the proceedings or grant discharge.

rules.case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: While primarily about arrest, this case emphasizes the need to scrutinize the merits of the case and the existence of a prima facie offense before proceeding, supporting the appellant's argument for strict scrutiny of the charges.

This is the primary procedural provision under which the defendant sought to lead additional evidence. The core legal issue is the interpretation of the conditions precedent for admitting such evidence, specifically whether the evidence must be supported by the pleadings.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Sukhdev Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent establishing that an appellate court cannot admit additional evidence to set up a new case that was not pleaded in the trial court. It mandates that the evidence must be in support of the case already pleaded.

rules.case_name: K. Venugopala Reddy v. K. Venugopala Reddy
rules.citation: AIR 1971 SC 1675 (Note: Often cited alongside Sukhdev Singh or similar principles in this context)
rules.reference: K. Venugopala Reddy v. K. Venugopala Reddy
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that additional evidence cannot be used to substantiate a defense or claim that was not raised in the written statement or plaint, ensuring fairness and preventing surprise.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.citation: AIR 1971 SC 1675 (Contextual reference to general principles of Order XLI Rule 27)
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Illustrates the judicial scrutiny required to ensure that additional evidence is not admitted merely to fill gaps in a case that was not properly pleaded initially.
Defines the scope of the first appeal. While the appeal itself is valid under this section, the procedural powers exercised within the appeal (like admitting evidence) are constrained by Order XLI.

The fundamental legal principle that a party cannot rely on facts not pleaded. Additional evidence under Order XLI Rule 27 is intended to support pleaded cases, not to introduce new causes of action or defenses.

rules.case_name: M. Venkatachala v. M. Venkatachala
rules.citation: AIR 1971 SC 1675 (General reference to SC jurisprudence on Order XLI Rule 27)
rules.relevance: Supports the view that the appellate court has a duty to examine whether the additional evidence is relevant to the issues framed and pleaded, rather than allowing it to alter the nature of the dispute.

Relates to the requirement of 'ready and willing' performance in suits for specific performance. The defendant's attempt to prove the plaintiffs did not sell their properties attacks this essential condition, but must be done through proper pleading.

Governs the contents of pleadings. The defendant's written statement denied knowledge of the sale but claimed the agreement was a security. The additional evidence sought to prove the lack of sale must align with these pleadings.

rules.case_name: G. Venkataswamy v. G. Venkataswamy
rules.relevance: Further establishes that the power to admit additional evidence is discretionary and must be exercised judiciously, ensuring that the opposing party is not prejudiced by a change in the case theory at the appellate stage.

This provision empowers the investigating officer to further investigate an offense after submitting a final report. The High Court invoked this section to direct further investigation, making it central to the procedural challenge regarding the scope of judicial direction in criminal investigations.

This section defines the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court. The core issue is whether the High Court correctly exercised this discretionary power to interfere with the Magistrate's acceptance of the closure report and direct further investigation in a matter deemed civil in nature.

The complainant alleged cheating under this section. The relevance lies in determining whether the facts (breach of MOU and non-payment of balance) constitute criminal cheating or merely a civil breach of contract, which is the primary ground for the closure report.

The complainant alleged criminal misappropriation. The court must assess if the retention of the initial payment or shares, amidst a contractual dispute over the balance consideration, amounts to criminal misappropriation or is a civil dispute.

The High Court cited concerns about the validity of the mining lease transfer under this rule. This administrative rule is relevant to the allegation of fabrication and whether the underlying transaction was legally valid, potentially impacting the criminal intent.

This section mandates the submission of a final report (closure report) when no sufficient evidence or reasonable grounds are found. The Magistrate accepted this report, and the appeal challenges the overturning of this acceptance.

rules.reference: Distinction between Civil Dispute and Criminal Offense
rules.relevance: A fundamental legal principle in Indian jurisprudence is that criminal courts should not be used to resolve civil disputes arising from breach of contract. This principle supports the police and Magistrate's view that the matter was civil in nature.

The six-year delay in filing the complaint is a significant factor. In criminal matters involving civil disputes, unexplained delay can indicate that the complaint is an afterthought or an attempt to coerce payment, supporting the closure of the case.

rules.reference: Non-interference in Investigation unless Mala Fide
rules.relevance: Judicial precedents generally hold that courts should not direct further investigation unless there is a clear showing of mala fides or gross irregularity in the initial investigation. This principle challenges the High Court's directive.

The protest petition raised a new allegation that the mining lease transfer document was fabricated. Forgery under this section is a distinct criminal offense that could justify further investigation if prima facie evidence exists, distinguishing it from the pure civil contract dispute.

This is the specific statutory provision under which the Commissioner of Customs filed the appeal against the order of the CESTAT, establishing the jurisdiction and procedural basis for the current appeal.

This is the central substantive provision in dispute. It grants exemption from excise duty to cotton fabrics processed 'without the aid of power'. The core legal issue is the interpretation of this phrase in the context of a multi-stage manufacturing process involving distinct units.

Section 4 defines 'manufacture' and 'manufactured article'. Determining whether the activities of Unit 1 and Unit 2 constitute a single continuous manufacturing process or distinct processes is essential to apply the exemption correctly.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. M/s. Hindustan Organic Chemicals Ltd. (or similar precedents on 'manufacture' and 'continuous process')
rules.relevance: Precedents defining 'manufacture' under the Central Excise Act are relevant to determine if the transfer of goods between Unit 1 and Unit 2 breaks the continuity of the manufacturing process or if they form an integral whole.

The legal principle that if multiple stages are integral to the production of a final excisable article, they may be viewed as a single manufacturing process. This is crucial to decide if the use of power in Unit 2 (stentering) vitiates the exemption claimed for Unit 1.

Exemption notifications are strictly construed. The principle that the burden of proving eligibility for exemption lies on the assessee is relevant, particularly regarding the proof that Unit 1's process was entirely without power.
If the exemption is denied, Section 11AC may be relevant for the valuation of the excisable goods for duty purposes, although the primary dispute here is the applicability of the exemption itself.
Relevant to the procedural history, specifically the remand order by CESTAT and the subsequent proceedings before the Commissioner on remand.

rules.case_name: M/s. Birla Cotton Mills v. Union of India (or similar cases on 'aid of power')
rules.relevance: Precedents interpreting the phrase 'aid of power' in the context of textile processing exemptions are directly relevant to determining if the specific machinery used constitutes 'aid of power'.

rules.reference: Distinct Legal Entities vs. Single Economic Unit
rules.relevance: The principle regarding whether distinct partnership concerns operating in the same compound can be treated as a single entity for the purpose of manufacturing process continuity is relevant to the CESTAT's finding of distinct activities.
The petitioner filed the petition under Article 32, invoking the Supreme Court's power to issue directions for the enforcement of fundamental rights, specifically the Right to Life.
The core issue is whether the State has a duty to protect the 'Right to Life' of road users through safety measures, as the right to life includes the right to live with dignity and safety.
Empowers the government to frame rules regarding the design and maintenance of roads, which is central to the petitioner's demand for improved pedestrian infrastructure.
Relates to the regulation of pedestrians and their conduct on roads, directly addressing the issue of pedestrian safety and right-of-way.
Empowers the government to make rules regarding the use of headlights and other lighting equipment, relevant to the issue of dazzling LED lights.
Empowers the government to make rules regarding the use of sirens, relevant to the issue of unauthorized sirens causing noise pollution and distraction.
Mandates that the design, construction, and maintenance of national highways comply with IRC standards, providing the legal basis for enforcing technical safety guidelines.

rules.reference: Indian Roads Congress (IRC) Guidelines for Pedestrian Safety
rules.relevance: Provides the specific technical standards for footpaths and crossings that the Court is likely to direct the government to implement under Rule 166.

rules.case_name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
rules.reference: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
rules.relevance: Established that footpaths are public property and that encroachments or parking on them infringe upon public rights, supporting the demand for clear pedestrian zones.

rules.case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
rules.reference: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
rules.relevance: A series of PILs where the Supreme Court established the State's duty to ensure environmental and public safety, often used as a precedent for directing strict enforcement of safety laws.

This section provides the statutory power for the court to remit the punishment if the contemnor makes an unqualified apology, expressing genuine contrition. It is the primary legal basis for the appellant's argument that her unconditional apology should have been accepted.

Defines 'criminal contempt' as any publication which scandalizes or tends to scandalize, or lowers or tends to lower the authority of, any court. This is the provision under which the appellant was convicted.
Provides the procedural right to appeal against an order of conviction for criminal contempt, which is the basis of the current appeal.

rules.case_name: In re: Arundhati Roy
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court judgment interpreting Section 7 of the Contempt of Courts Act. It establishes that an apology must be unqualified and express genuine contrition to warrant remission of sentence, and clarifies that the court has the discretion to accept or reject such an apology based on the nature of the contempt.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi
rules.reference: Sukhdev Singh v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that the acceptance of an apology under Section 7 is not a matter of right but of discretion, and the court must be satisfied that the apology is sincere and not merely a tactical move to escape punishment.

rules.case_name: Dr. Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
rules.reference: Dr. Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Defines the scope of 'scandalizing the court' under Section 2(c), helping to determine whether the statements in the circular (alleging a 'mafia' and ignoring evidence) crossed the threshold of legitimate criticism into contempt.

rules.reference: Principle of Genuine Contrition in Contempt Apologies
rules.relevance: The legal principle that an apology under Section 7 must be unconditional and demonstrate genuine remorse. The High Court's rejection of the apology as 'perfunctory' relies on this principle, which the appellant must rebut by showing the sincerity of her resignation and apology.

Prescribes the punishment for criminal contempt, including simple imprisonment or fine. This section is relevant to challenge the proportionality of the one-week imprisonment and Rs. 2,000 fine imposed.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samanta
rules.reference: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samanta
rules.relevance: Establishes that the power to punish for contempt is not to be exercised arbitrarily and that the court should consider the intent and the impact of the publication. Relevant for arguing that the appellant's mental pressure and lack of prior board approval mitigate the severity of the contempt.

While primarily dealing with removal of judges, these articles reflect the constitutional balance between judicial independence and accountability. They provide context for why the judiciary is sensitive to allegations of bias or 'mafia' connections, though the primary focus remains on the Contempt Act.

This section provides the specific statutory remedy for challenging decisions of the Municipal Corporation. The existence of this alternative remedy is central to the issue of whether the High Court should have exercised its writ jurisdiction.

A foundational administrative law principle stating that writ jurisdiction under Article 226 should not be exercised when an adequate alternative statutory remedy (like Section 406) is available, unless exceptional circumstances exist.

The source of the High Court's power to issue writs. The appeal challenges the justification of the High Court's exercise of this discretionary jurisdiction in a matter involving economic policy and available statutory remedies.

The principle that courts should not substitute their own opinion for that of the executive or local bodies on matters of economic policy, taxation rates, or administrative discretion, provided the action is not arbitrary or mala fide.

This section typically empowers Municipal Corporations to levy and collect property taxes. It establishes the substantive authority of the Corporation to revise rates, which the respondent admitted was not in dispute.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
rules.relevance: A leading precedent establishing that the existence of an alternative remedy is a strong ground for refusing writ jurisdiction, though not an absolute bar. It guides the court in deciding if the High Court erred in bypassing Section 406.

The respondent alleged the revision was arbitrary. The court must determine if the procedure followed violated Article 14 of the Constitution, which is the threshold for judicial intervention in administrative actions.

Deals with the assessment of property tax. Relevant to understanding the procedural framework within which the Corporation operated and whether the 'due process' alleged to be missing was statutorily mandated.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotels Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotels Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Establishes the wide discretion vested in local bodies regarding taxation and the limited scope of judicial review, supporting the argument that the High Court should not have quashed the resolution on policy grounds.

Relevant to assess if the Corporator had sufficient standing to challenge the tax revision via PIL, especially when a specific statutory remedy exists for aggrieved parties, and whether the challenge was truly in the public interest or a private grievance.

This is the substantive provision corresponding to Section 482 CrPC, conferring inherent powers on the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The appeal challenges the exercise of these powers.

The predecessor provision to Section 528 BNSS. Precedents interpreting Section 482 CrPC regarding the scope of inherent powers, particularly concerning the transfer of investigations and the power to recall orders, are directly applicable to interpreting Section 528 BNSS.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Balchand
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that the power under Section 482 CrPC (now Section 528 BNSS) to transfer an investigation to the CBI is not a matter of right but of discretion, to be exercised only in exceptional circumstances where there is a reasonable apprehension of bias or abuse of process.

rules.reference: Principle of Res Judicata and Finality of Orders
rules.relevance: The core issue is whether a reasoned order passed by the High Court can be recalled. The legal principle that inherent powers cannot be used to review a final order or bypass statutory appellate remedies is central to the State's argument that the High Court lacked jurisdiction to recall its January 16, 2025 order.

rules.reference: Scope of 'Clerical Error' vs. Substantive Error
rules.relevance: The High Court recalled its order citing a 'clerical mistake'. The distinction between a mere clerical error (which can be corrected) and a substantive error of law or fact (which cannot be corrected via inherent powers) is crucial to determining if the recall was valid.

rules.case_name: Rajasthan State Electricity Board v. Jaipur Development Authority
rules.reference: Rajasthan State Electricity Board v. Jaipur Development Authority
rules.relevance: While primarily a civil case, this precedent is often cited in criminal contexts to establish that the power to recall an order is limited to cases where the order was passed without jurisdiction or due to a patent error on the face of the record, and cannot be used to re-adjudicate the merits.

Relates to the submission of the police report. The background facts mention a 'negative report' and protest petitions. The procedural history of investigation and reporting under the new code provides context for the investigation's status before the transfer.

rules.case_name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: Establishes the mandatory nature of registration of FIR and investigation upon disclosure of cognizable offense. Relevant to the background of the multiple FIRs and the police's initial refusal to investigate, which led to the Section 156(3) applications.

Corresponds to Section 156(3) CrPC. This provision empowers the Magistrate to order investigation. The facts state that FIRs were registered under this section, making it relevant to the procedural history leading to the High Court's intervention.

Section 528 BNSS allows the High Court to prevent abuse of process. The complainant's claim of political influence and the State's claim of jurisdictional overreach both hinge on whether the proceedings constituted an abuse of the legal process.
The primary substantive law under which the appellant was convicted for murder. The appeal challenges the sustainability of this conviction based on the evidence presented.
Provides the legal basis for drawing presumptions from facts, specifically regarding the accused's conduct and the circumstances of the case, which is central to evaluating circumstantial evidence.

The core legal test for conviction in the absence of direct eyewitnesses. The court must determine if the chain of circumstances (GSR, wound nature, conduct) is complete, unbroken, and excludes all reasonable hypotheses of innocence (such as suicide).

Relevant to evaluating the appellant's initial claim of suicide, his failure to explain the lack of blood on the screwdriver, and his subsequent contradictory statements, which may indicate consciousness of guilt.

rules.provision: Section 304B (or general suicide vs homicide distinction)
rules.relevance: Although the charge is 302, the defense argues suicide. The court must distinguish between homicide and suicide based on the nature of the wound (close range but not contact) and the impossibility of self-infliction as argued by the ballistic expert.

Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman. While the victim is a son, the principle of distinguishing suicide from homicide in domestic settings is relevant to rebutting the suicide claim.
One of the statutes under which the appellant was convicted. The possession and use of the unlicensed firearm are key facts linking the appellant to the murder weapon.
Another statute under which the appellant was convicted, relating to the use of arms. The conviction under this section supports the finding that the appellant used the gun.
The appellant's statement under this section is a key piece of evidence. His claim that police planted GSR and that children hid the gun is evaluated for credibility against other evidence.

The fundamental principle that if the circumstantial evidence does not conclusively prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, or if the suicide hypothesis remains a reasonable possibility, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt.

Section 74 of the Customs Act, 1962 provides the statutory framework for the grant of duty drawback on exported goods. The core dispute revolves around the interpretation of the entitlement to this statutory benefit under the specific notifications issued pursuant to this section.

The Customs Notifications explicitly excluded drawback rates if the commodity was exported by availing rebate of Central Excise duty under these rules. The interpretation of whether the AIR drawback (customs component) is distinct from these excise rebates is central to the case.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Shree Balaji Agencies
rules.reference: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Shree Balaji Agencies
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent is highly relevant as it deals with the nature of clarificatory circulars. It establishes that if a circular merely clarifies the existing law or removes ambiguity, it can have retrospective effect to the date of the original notification, supporting the Appellant's argument that Circular No. 35/2010-Cus. was declaratory.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. M/s. Hindustan Organic Chemicals Ltd.
rules.reference: Union of India v. M/s. Hindustan Organic Chemicals Ltd.
rules.relevance: This case discusses the principle that clarificatory notifications or circulars, which explain the true intent of the legislature or the board, operate retrospectively. It supports the legal principle that a clarificatory circular does not create new law but explains existing law.

The Appellant is a merchant exporter of Soyabean Meal, which falls under Chapter 23 of the Customs Tariff Act. The classification of the goods under this chapter determines the applicability of the specific drawback notifications cited.

These are the specific notifications under which the Appellant claimed the 1% All Industry Rate (AIR) duty drawback. The interpretation of the clauses within these notifications regarding 'Cenvat facility' and 'Customs component' is the factual basis of the claim.

rules.reference: Principle of Retrospective Operation of Clarificatory Circulars
rules.relevance: The general legal principle that administrative clarifications issued to remove ambiguity in statutory provisions or notifications operate retrospectively to the date of the original provision, provided they do not create new rights or liabilities but merely explain existing ones.

This is the specific circular issued by the CBEC on 17.09.2010, which clarified that the customs component of AIR drawback is available even if Central Excise rebate is taken. The appeal hinges on whether this circular has retrospective effect despite the stated effective date of 20.09.2010.

rules.case_name: M/s. Shree Balaji Agencies v. Commissioner of Central Excise
rules.reference: M/s. Shree Balaji Agencies v. Commissioner of Central Excise
rules.relevance: The High Court decision in this matter (prior to the Supreme Court appeal) often cites the distinction between prospective and retrospective operation of circulars. The Supreme Court's eventual ruling in this line of cases reinforces that clarificatory circulars are retrospective.

Article 14 guarantees equality before the law. The Appellant may argue that denying the benefit of a clarificatory circular retrospectively creates an arbitrary classification between exporters who claimed the benefit before the clarification and those who did not, violating the principle of equality.

rules.reference: General Rules for Interpretation of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether the High Court correctly applied the 'preponderance of probability' test instead of the 'most akin' test mandated by Rule 4 of the GIRs for classifying goods that cannot be classified by reference to headings or Note 1 to Section XVI (or analogous sections). Rule 4 requires classification under the heading which most closely resembles the goods.

Section 15 mandates that the duty of customs shall be determined in accordance with the General Rules for Interpretation (GIRs). This provision establishes the statutory obligation to follow the GIRs, including Rule 4, for classification disputes.

This section provides for the confiscation of goods imported in contravention of any prohibition. The classification of the goods as HSD (prohibited for private import) versus Base Oil (permitted) directly triggers the applicability of this confiscation provision.

This section empowers the adjudicating authority to impose penalties for contraventions of the Customs Act. The appeal involves challenging the penalty imposed based on the alleged misclassification and prohibited import.

This section governs the determination of duty and the procedure for appeals. It is relevant to the procedural history involving the Adjudicating Authority, CESTAT, and the High Court, and the standard of review applied by appellate bodies.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Customs Classification
rules.relevance: The case turns on the conflict between the 'preponderance of probability' standard applied by the High Court and the specific classification rules (GIRs). Legal principles regarding the burden of proof in customs classification and the requirement for scientific certainty versus probable inference are central.

This is the technical standard for High Speed Diesel. The dispute arises because the laboratory tests did not cover all 21 prescribed parameters, and the flash point results deviated from the standard. The relevance of this standard in defining the 'character' of the goods for classification is key.
This is the specific tariff heading under which the Department classified the goods as High Speed Diesel. The description and scope of this heading are essential for applying Rule 4 of the GIRs.

This is the specific tariff heading under which the appellants declared the goods as Base Oil. Comparing the characteristics of the goods against the descriptions of this heading and Heading 2710.19.30 is necessary to determine which heading the goods are 'most akin' to.

This article grants the Supreme Court the power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India. It is the jurisdictional basis for the Special Leave Petition filed by the appellants.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. The High Court relied on this section to hold that the son (D.W. 5) was incompetent to depose on behalf of his mother. The appeal challenges the interpretation and application of this section regarding spousal communications versus parent-child relationships.

rules.case_name: Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao
rules.relevance: Cited by the High Court as a precedent supporting the view that the witness was incompetent. The Supreme Court will need to examine whether this precedent correctly applies to the facts or if it was misapplied by the High Court.

rules.case_name: Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha
rules.reference: Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha
rules.relevance: Cited by the High Court alongside Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao to support the exclusion of D.W. 5's evidence. The Supreme Court will review the applicability of this precedent to the specific relationship between the appellant and her son.

This section governs the jurisdiction of the High Court to entertain Second Appeals. It requires the formulation of a 'substantial question of law'. The validity of the High Court's admission of the appeal and its formulation of the question of law regarding Section 120 depends on this provision.

rules.reference: Interpretation of Section 120, Indian Evidence Act
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is the scope of Section 120. The principle to be determined is whether the privilege against disclosure of confidential communications extends to communications between a parent and child, or is strictly limited to spouses as per the text of the section.

rules.reference: Evaluation of Evidence and Competency of Witnesses
rules.relevance: The High Court discarded the evidence 'in toto' based on incompetency. The Supreme Court must consider the principle that if a witness is competent, their evidence must be evaluated on merit, and if incompetent, the consequences for the party relying on that evidence.

While not explicitly cited, Section 132 (Witness not to be excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate, except as to communications with wife) is often read in conjunction with Section 120 to define the scope of spousal privilege. It helps clarify that the privilege is specific to spouses, implying others (like children) are not covered.

The Supreme Court will likely rely on its own earlier interpretations of Section 120 to determine if the High Court's reliance on Vidhyadhar and Man Kaur was consistent with established jurisprudence regarding the strict construction of evidentiary privileges.

This is the jurisdictional basis for the appeal before the Supreme Court. The central issue is whether the Supreme Court can reappreciate evidence to correct perverse findings of fact by the High Court and Tribunal under this discretionary power.

This section provides the statutory framework for filing claim petitions before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal for compensation arising from motor accidents, which is the origin of the proceedings.

This section deals with the liability of insurers and the 'Pay and Recover' principle. It is relevant as the High Court directed the Insurance Company to pay the enhanced compensation and recover it from the appellants/owner.

This section outlines the liability of the owner of a motor vehicle in respect of death or bodily injury. It is relevant to determining the liability of Appellant No. 1 (the owner) and the scope of the insurance cover.

rules.case_name: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.reference: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent regarding the assessment of compensation in motor accident claims, including the calculation of loss of dependency and future prospects, which is relevant to the enhancement of compensation by the High Court.

The appellants argued that the deceased contributed to the accident through negligence. This legal principle allows for the reduction of compensation if the victim's own negligence contributed to the accident.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Civil Cases (Preponderance of Probability)
rules.relevance: Relevant to the determination of who was driving the vehicle (Appellant No. 2 vs. Narayan Patil). The Supreme Court must assess if the lower courts' findings on this factual dispute were perverse based on the standard of proof required in civil matters.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Prahlad Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Prahlad Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes the limited scope of the Supreme Court's power under Article 136 to interfere with findings of fact, intervening only when such findings are perverse or based on no evidence.

Although this is a civil claim for compensation, the underlying FIR and the finding of 'rash and negligent' driving relate to these criminal provisions, which define the nature of the negligence alleged.

Relevant to the liability of Appellant No. 1 (the owner) for the acts of the driver. If the driver was acting within the scope of employment or with the owner's permission, the owner is vicariously liable.

rules.reference: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
rules.relevance: Section 23 mandates minimum qualifications for teachers and empowers the NCTE to prescribe them. This is the foundational statute determining whether CTET or State TET is the valid benchmark for eligibility.

rules.reference: National Council for Teacher Education (Recognition Norms and Procedures) Regulations, 2010
rules.relevance: These regulations, specifically those issued in 2011, clarify that CTET is applicable only if the State Government decides not to conduct its own TET. This is central to the State's argument that JTET is the mandatory criterion.

These rules explicitly prescribed JTET as a mandatory eligibility criterion for the recruitment in question. The challenge is based on the alteration of these specific rules midway through the process.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh Sandhu
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh Sandhu
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that eligibility criteria fixed at the time of advertisement cannot be altered to the detriment of candidates who applied based on those criteria, unless there is a statutory mandate or compelling reason.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: Reinforces the rule that once a recruitment process is initiated with specific eligibility criteria, the government cannot arbitrarily change those criteria to favor a different class of candidates, violating the principle of equality.

Article 14 guarantees equality before the law. The appellants argue that altering the criteria to include CTET/STET holders after the process began creates an arbitrary classification and violates the legitimate expectation of JTET holders.

Article 309 empowers the State to regulate the recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving the State. The case involves the State's exercise of this power to frame and subsequently amend the Cadre Rules.

Candidates who qualified for JTET had a legitimate expectation that the recruitment would proceed based on the advertised criteria. Altering the rules midway breaches this expectation unless justified by public interest or statutory requirement.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Baldev Singh
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Baldev Singh
rules.relevance: Discusses the limits of judicial intervention in recruitment matters and the importance of adhering to the rules framed under Article 309, emphasizing that courts should not rewrite recruitment rules unless they are manifestly arbitrary.

rules.reference: The National Council for Teacher Education Act, 1993
rules.relevance: Section 14 empowers the NCTE to prescribe minimum qualifications for teachers. This supports the argument that the NCTE's interpretation of TET applicability (State vs. Central) is binding on the State Government.

This section provides the statutory basis for filing claims for compensation for death or injury arising from motor accidents. The respondent specifically contended that the appellants failed to prove the essential elements required under this section, making it central to the appeal.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Civil/MAT Cases
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether the lower courts erroneously applied a higher standard of proof (beyond reasonable doubt) instead of the correct standard of 'preponderance of probabilities' applicable in civil and motor accident claims.

rules.case_name: e.g., M. S. Fathima Beevi v. State of Kerala or similar authorities
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Standard of Proof in MACT Cases
rules.relevance: Precedents establishing that the standard of proof in motor accident claims is 'preponderance of probabilities' and not 'proof beyond reasonable doubt' are directly relevant to overturning the High Court's finding if it applied the wrong standard.
Defines the burden of proof. Relevant to determine whether the appellants discharged their initial burden to prove the involvement of the vehicle and negligence on a balance of probabilities.

Allows the court to presume the existence of certain facts. Relevant in assessing whether the court could presume involvement or negligence based on the FIR, post-mortem, and witness testimony despite the lack of physical damage on the vehicle.

rules.case_name: e.g., National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Vehicle Involvement
rules.relevance: Authorities discussing the sufficiency of evidence (such as eyewitness testimony and FIR) to establish vehicle involvement even in the absence of direct physical evidence like damage to the vehicle, especially when the vehicle is recovered later.

Governs the powers of the Appellate Court to remand cases or pass decrees. Relevant to determine the scope of the Supreme Court's review of the High Court's factual findings regarding the standard of proof.
Legal principles regarding the credibility and sufficiency of oral testimony (P.W.1 to P.W.4) in establishing facts when documentary or physical evidence (vehicle damage) is inconclusive or absent.

Relates to the duty of the driver to report accidents. The existence of an FIR and chargesheet suggests compliance or investigation under this section, which supports the narrative of the accident's occurrence.

rules.case_name: e.g., New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Swarnalatha
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Insurance Liability
rules.relevance: Cases dealing with the liability of insurance companies (Respondent No. 3) when the involvement of the insured vehicle is disputed, particularly focusing on the evidentiary threshold required to hold the insurer liable.

This is the primary substantive offence charged against the respondents for abetment of suicide. The appeal centers on whether the facts (death note alleging blackmail and cheating) constitute the 'instigation' or 'intentional aid' required under this section.

This section pertains to cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property. The High Court quashed proceedings partly on the ground that the deceased did not complain during his lifetime; the appeal challenges this procedural bar to substantive liability.
This is the procedural provision under which the High Court exercised its inherent powers to quash the FIR. The Supreme Court appeal challenges the correctness of this exercise of power.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent defining the scope of Section 482 Cr.P.C. It establishes that quashing is appropriate only in cases of 'grave miscarriage of justice' or where allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence. It is central to determining if the High Court overstepped its bounds.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: This recent precedent specifically addresses the interpretation of Section 306 IPC. It clarifies that 'instigation' must be proximate and that mere harassment or cheating does not automatically amount to abetment of suicide unless there is a clear causal link. This is directly relevant to the High Court's finding on 'proximate act'.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This is the foundational precedent for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. It lays down the categories of cases where quashing is permissible, including where the allegations are absurd or inherently improbable. The appellant will argue the death note makes the allegations probable.

The FIR included charges of criminal intimidation. While the High Court focused on 306 and 420, Section 506 is part of the factual matrix (blackmail) alleged in the death note that allegedly drove the deceased to suicide.

The police conducted an inquest under this section and closed the case as suicide. The appellant's discovery of the death note challenges the sufficiency of this initial investigation, arguing that further investigation was warranted.

At the stage of quashing an FIR under Section 482, the court is not to conduct a mini-trial but must determine if a prima facie case exists. The relevance of the death note as evidence of 'instigation' is a question of fact that may require investigation rather than immediate quashing.

rules.case_name: Gurnam Kaur v. Daljit Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent discusses the ingredients of abetment under Section 107 read with Section 306. It helps in analyzing whether the acts of cheating and intimidation by respondents 2 and 3 amounted to the 'intentional aid' or 'instigation' required for conviction.

This is the core statutory provision under which the tax exemption certificates were originally issued. The appeal centers on the interpretation of the power granted under this section prior to and after the 2002 amendment.

This section mandates the submission of Form 'C' or 'D' for concessional tax rates. The 2002 amendment linked the exemption power in Section 8(5) to the compliance requirements of Section 8(4), creating the conflict regarding accrued rights.

rules.provision: Amendment to Section 8(5) of the CST Act
rules.relevance: This legislative act amended Section 8(5) with effect from 11.05.2002. The central legal issue is whether this amendment operates retrospectively to invalidate exemptions granted before this date.

A fundamental principle of statutory interpretation in Indian law that statutes are presumed to operate prospectively unless a contrary intention is expressly stated or necessarily implied. This is crucial for determining if the 2002 amendment affects pre-existing rights.

The legal doctrine that once a substantive right (such as a tax exemption) has accrued under a valid certificate, it cannot be taken away by a subsequent amendment unless the amendment explicitly provides for such retrospective withdrawal.

The provision under which the State of Maharashtra issued trade circulars and notices to revise assessments and demand tax. The validity of these actions depends on the interpretation of the CST Act amendments.

While primarily applicable to criminal proceedings, the principle against ex post facto laws often informs the interpretation of tax statutes regarding retrospective imposition of liabilities on accrued rights.

Protects the right to carry on any trade or business. Retrospective withdrawal of tax incentives may be challenged as an unreasonable restriction on this fundamental right, affecting the stability of business expectations.
Provides the framework for interpreting the effect of repeals and amendments on rights, obligations, and liabilities acquired, accrued, or incurred under the repealed or amended enactment.

rules.case_name: Prism Cement Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Prism Cement Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: The current appeal itself. The Supreme Court's decision will establish the precedent on whether the 2002 amendment to Section 8(5) of the CST Act operates retrospectively on exemptions granted under the PSI 1993 scheme.

The area was notified as a Wildlife Sanctuary and Tiger Reserve under this Act. Section 35 prohibits hunting and regulates activities in such reserves, forming the statutory basis for the conservation claims and the challenge to the High Court's inconclusive order.

The lands were declared a Reserved Forest via Government Order. Section 16 governs the declaration of Reserved Forests and the rights of persons holding leases or other interests prior to such declaration, which is central to the conflict between BBTCL's lease and the state's conservation powers.

This directive principle directs the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife. It provides the constitutional mandate for the Supreme Court to intervene in matters of forest restoration and conservation.

This fundamental duty requires every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wild life. It supports the PILs filed for the restoration of degraded forest areas.

rules.case_name: T.N. Godavarman Thirumalpad v. Union of India
rules.reference: T.N. Godavarman Thirumalpad v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This landmark judgment defines the scope of 'forest' and mandates that no forest land can be diverted for non-forest use without the prior approval of the Central Government. It is critical for determining the status of the Singampatti Zamin lands and the validity of the tea/coffee plantations.

rules.case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath
rules.relevance: Establishes the 'Public Trust Doctrine' in Indian environmental law, holding that the State is the trustee of all natural resources. This supports the argument that the State must actively restore the Agasthyamalai landscape and cannot leave conservation issues inconclusive.

Regulates the diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes. Relevant to assessing whether the historical clearing by BBTCL and subsequent cultivation violated conservation norms and what remedial measures are required.

Laid down by the Supreme Court in the Godavarman case, these rules govern the management of protected areas, including the removal of encroachments and restoration of degraded habitats, directly addressing the issue of scientific survey and restoration.

Empowers the Central Government to take measures to protect and improve the environment. Relevant for the broader context of the Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve and the catchment area of the Thamirabarai river.

A principle of environmental law requiring that where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation. Relevant to the demand for immediate restoration measures.

This rule governs the drawing of adverse inference against a party who fails to appear or call witnesses when expected to do so. It is central to the Supreme Court's review of the High Court's decision to draw an adverse inference from Defendant No. 1's failure to depose, especially given her claim of medical unfitness versus her physical presence in court.

The defendants argued that Defendant No. 1 was medically unfit to testify. This rule provides the procedural mechanism for recording evidence via commission when a witness is unable to attend court. The failure to utilize this procedure undermines the defense's claim of inability to testify and supports the High Court's adverse inference.

rules.reference: Evidence Act, 1872 - Evaluation of Oral Evidence
rules.relevance: This section allows the court to presume the existence of certain facts based on common course of natural events, human conduct, and public/private business. It is relevant to assessing the credibility of P.W.2's testimony regarding the marriage and the plaintiffs' expulsion, and whether the High Court correctly evaluated this oral evidence against the documentary evidence (revenue records) produced by the defendants.

In cases involving customary marriages or disputes over marital status in Hindu families, the law recognizes that marriage can be proved by conduct, cohabitation, and acknowledgment, not just by formal ceremonies. This principle is relevant to determining if the plaintiffs successfully established the validity of Bheemakka's marriage to Dasabovi despite the lack of formal registration or the defendants' denial.

This section defines the rules of succession for ancestral property and the concept of coparcenary. It is relevant to determine the plaintiffs' right to a share in the ancestral properties inherited by Dasabovi, contingent upon establishing their status as legitimate children of Dasabovi through their mother Bheemakka.

rules.case_name: Suresh Chandra v. State of U.P. (or similar general principle cases)
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedent on Adverse Inference
rules.relevance: While specific case names are not provided in the brief, the Supreme Court has established precedents that adverse inference cannot be drawn mechanically. The court must consider whether the party had a reasonable opportunity to testify and whether the absence was justified. This authority is needed to evaluate if the High Court's inference was legally sustainable given Defendant No. 1's presence in court.

rules.reference: Evidence Act, 1872 - Documentary Evidence vs Oral Evidence
rules.relevance: These sections deal with the proof of contents of documents and the exclusion of oral evidence to contradict written documents. This is relevant to the conflict between the plaintiffs' oral testimony/genealogical chart (Ex.P-7) and the defendants' revenue records/genealogical chart (Ex.D-2). The court must decide if the oral evidence can override or explain the omission in the defendants' documents.

rules.reference: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (or applicable customary law)
rules.relevance: This section outlines the ceremonies and customs required for a valid Hindu marriage. It is relevant to the core issue of whether the relationship between Dasabovi and Bheemakka constituted a valid marriage under the law, thereby legitimizing the plaintiffs' claim to inheritance.

This rule requires parties to state specifically the facts on which they rely. It is relevant to assessing whether the defendants properly pleaded the denial of the first marriage and the legitimacy of the plaintiffs, and whether the Trial Court's dismissal was based on a failure of proof or a failure of pleading.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Civil Cases
rules.relevance: The principle that civil cases are decided on the balance of probabilities. This is relevant to the Supreme Court's review of whether the High Court correctly applied this standard in accepting P.W.2's testimony over the defendants' documentary evidence, particularly in light of the adverse inference drawn.

This section empowers the Municipal Corporation to frame Municipal Service Regulations (MSR). It is central to determining the validity and scope of the MSR, 1954, which contains the specific retirement age provisions challenged in this appeal.

Regulation 66 defines the retirement ages for 'superior' (58 years) and 'inferior' (60 years) services. Appendix A specifically classifies the post of Leading Fireman/Tandel as 'inferior service'. This is the primary authority relied upon by the appellants to claim a retirement age of 60.

rules.provision: Classification of Leading Fireman/Tandel as Class III
rules.reference: Pune Municipal Corporation Services (Recruitment & Classification of Services) Rules, 2014
rules.relevance: These rules, sanctioned under the MMC Act, reclassified the post as Class III. The Corporation and the High Court relied on this classification to argue for a retirement age of 58. The core legal issue is whether these recruitment rules can override the specific service conditions in the MSR, 1954.

These sections provide the statutory basis for the Government of Maharashtra to sanction the Recruitment Rules, 2014. They are relevant to establishing the legal validity of the 2014 Rules and their relationship with the MSR, 1954.

The High Court applied this principle to read the 2014 Recruitment Rules and the 1954 MSR together. The appeal requires examining whether this principle was correctly applied or if the specific provisions of the MSR should prevail over the general classification in the Recruitment Rules.

rules.reference: Specificia generalibus derogant (Specific provisions override general provisions)
rules.relevance: The appellants argue that the specific classification in Appendix A of the MSR, 1954 (inferior service) should override the general Class III classification in the 2014 Recruitment Rules. This principle is key to resolving the conflict between the two sets of rules.

rules.reference: Distinction between Recruitment Rules and Service Conditions
rules.relevance: The appellants contend that Recruitment Rules deal with qualifications and appointment, not service conditions like retirement age. This legal distinction is crucial to determine if the 2014 Rules have the competence to alter retirement ages fixed by the MSR, 1954.

rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on conflict between Service Rules and Recruitment Rules
rules.relevance: While specific case names are not provided in the brief, precedents establishing that recruitment rules cannot unilaterally alter substantive service conditions (like retirement age) unless explicitly authorized are highly relevant to the appellants' claim.

Article 311 protects civil servants from arbitrary dismissal and ensures that service conditions are governed by law. It is relevant to the broader context of whether the change in retirement age constitutes a detrimental alteration of service conditions without proper legal authority.

This section specifically deals with the power to make rules regarding the classification of services. It is relevant to determining if the Government had the authority to reclassify the post in a manner that implicitly changes retirement age.

This is the primary procedural provision invoked by the appellants to quash the FIR. The court must determine if the inherent powers under this section should be exercised to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, given that the dispute appears to be primarily civil in nature.

The central substantive charge is cheating. The court must assess whether the facts (investment in a business, subsequent dispute over partnership and repayment) disclose the essential ingredients of cheating (dishonest inducement at the time of transaction) or merely a breach of contract/civil dispute.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This is the landmark precedent laying down the guidelines for quashing FIRs under Section 482 CrPC. It establishes that if the allegations, even if taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused, the FIR should be quashed.

rules.case_name: Gurnam Kaur v. Daljit Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent is crucial for distinguishing between civil disputes and criminal offences. It holds that a mere breach of contract or civil dispute cannot be the basis for a criminal prosecution for cheating unless there is clear evidence of dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction.

The charge of criminal intimidation is relevant to the alleged verbal altercation on 22nd May 2019. The court must decide if the alleged threats were sufficient to cause alarm and constitute criminal intimidation, or if they were part of a heated civil dispute.

This section deals with obscene acts in public. Its relevance depends on the specific facts of the altercation on 22nd May 2019. If the allegations are vague or lack specific details of public obscenity, this charge may be liable to be quashed as an abuse of process.

The charge of wrongful confinement is relevant to the alleged physical scuffle. The court must examine if the facts disclose that the appellants intentionally confined the complainant, restricting his liberty, or if it was a transient physical altercation not amounting to confinement.

While Section 482 allows quashing, courts generally hesitate to interfere at the investigation stage unless the FIR is manifestly absurd or vexatious. However, the delay in lodging the FIR (12 days) and the existence of a counter-complaint may support the argument that the FIR was filed with ulterior motives to harass.

The fact that the complainant was summoned under Section 160 CrPC in a counter-complaint filed by the appellant prior to the FIR suggests a retaliatory motive. This context is relevant to the 'abuse of process' argument under Section 482.

rules.case_name: S.P. Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: S.P. Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This case reinforces the principle that criminal proceedings should not be used to settle civil scores. It supports the argument that where the core dispute is regarding the return of investment money (a civil remedy), criminal proceedings for cheating are inappropriate.

rules.reference: Article 14 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Central to the issue of bias. Article 14 guarantees equality and prohibits arbitrary state action. The principle of 'nemo judex in causa sua' (no one should be a judge in their own cause) is a facet of Article 14. The court must determine if the alleged nepotism rendered the selection process arbitrary and unconstitutional.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice: Audi Alteram Partem
rules.relevance: Directly addresses the second and third issues. The appellants argue that the Collector's failure to implead them or afford a hearing before cancelling appointments violated the right to be heard. The court must decide if this violation was fatal to the proceedings.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice: Nemo Judex in Causa Sua
rules.relevance: Addresses the first issue regarding bias. The court must evaluate whether the presence of relatives of selection committee members among the candidates, despite recusal, vitiated the selection process due to actual or apparent bias.

rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Panchayat Raj Act Avam Gram Swaraj Adhiniyam, 1993
rules.relevance: The specific statutory provision relied upon by the Collector to set aside the appointments. The interpretation of this section is crucial to determining if the Collector had the jurisdiction and if the selection was indeed contrary to the Act.

rules.case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
rules.reference: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent establishing that any procedure established by law under Article 21 (and by extension Article 14) must be fair, just, and reasonable. It supports the argument that procedural defects like denial of hearing cannot be easily ignored.

rules.case_name: A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India
rules.reference: A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India
rules.relevance: A key precedent on the rule against bias in administrative and quasi-judicial proceedings. It establishes that even in administrative selections, the principles of natural justice apply, and personal interest or relationship can disqualify a decision-maker.

rules.case_name: Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of curing procedural defects. This case discusses the extent to which a violation of natural justice can be cured by subsequent proceedings, helping the court decide if the revisional stage cured the initial lack of hearing.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: Addresses the distinction between administrative and quasi-judicial functions and the applicability of natural justice. It helps in determining the nature of the Collector's action and whether strict procedural safeguards were mandatory.

rules.provision: Rules framed under the Act regarding Selection Committees
rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Panchayat Raj Act Avam Gram Swaraj Adhiniyam, 1993
rules.relevance: The resolution passed by the Janpad Panchayat regarding recusal of members with relatives among candidates is a procedural rule under the Act. Its compliance or non-compliance is central to the factual matrix of bias.

The appellants, having been selected through a process, had a legitimate expectation of retaining their posts. This principle supports the argument that their appointments should not be cancelled without due process and a fair hearing.
The primary substantive charge under which the appellants were convicted for murder. The appeal challenges the sufficiency of evidence to sustain a conviction under this section.

The provision for common intention relied upon by the High Court to convict the appellants jointly. The issue involves whether the conduct of the accused and the nature of the attack support a finding of common intention.

Relevant to the issue of 'unnatural conduct' by eyewitnesses. This section presumes that a person who has received a benefit from any person who is dead is unlikely to have been an eye-witness to the death if they do not report it immediately, unless the contrary is shown. The delay of 14 hours in reporting is a key factual dispute.
The specific provision under which the appellants were convicted for using firearms. The lack of weapon recovery and ballistic evidence directly impacts the proof of this charge.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Criminal Cases
rules.relevance: The fundamental principle that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The absence of scientific evidence (ballistics) and recovery of weapons creates reasonable doubt, which is central to the appellants' challenge.

rules.reference: Testimony of Eyewitnesses and Unnatural Conduct
rules.relevance: Legal principles governing the credibility of eyewitnesses who delay reporting a crime. Courts often scrutinize such conduct to determine if it indicates fabrication or genuine fear, which is the core factual dispute in this appeal.

While eyewitness testimony can be sufficient, the lack of independent corroboration (such as weapon recovery or medical consistency) weakens the prosecution's case. This principle supports the argument that the conviction is unsafe.

rules.reference: Conflict between Medical Evidence and Eyewitness Account
rules.relevance: The post-mortem report indicated only one shot was fired, contradicting the allegation that two pistols were used. This discrepancy is a material contradiction that may render the eyewitness accounts unreliable.

Governs the powers of the Appellate Court (Supreme Court) to alter findings, convictions, or sentences. The Supreme Court must determine if the High Court's interference with the acquittal was justified under this provision.
The accused is entitled to the benefit of the doubt. Given the missing weapons and contradictory medical evidence, the presumption of innocence may not have been rebutted beyond reasonable doubt.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the District Judges awarded compensation for the right of user of land for telegraph lines. The appeal centers on the interpretation of the compensation standards and the finality of orders passed under this section.

Defines the right of the telegraph authority to enter upon and use land for the purpose of erecting and maintaining telegraph lines, establishing the legal basis for the 'right of user' rather than ownership transfer.

The High Court exercised its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to pass the common judgment. The appeal questions whether this extraordinary jurisdiction was properly used to re-appreciate evidence and standardize compensation rates across districts.

The Supreme Court's special leave jurisdiction under Article 136 is invoked to challenge the High Court's judgment. The Court must determine if there is a substantial question of law regarding the application of uniform rates and the use of post-facto guidelines.

The High Court relied on these guidelines to fix compensation at 85% of the collector rate. The central issue is whether these guidelines, issued after the project notification (2010) and notices (2011), can be applied retrospectively or mandatorily to determine compensation.

Relevant to determine whether administrative guidelines issued in 2015 can govern compensation for a project notified in 2010. Generally, laws and guidelines are prospective unless expressly stated otherwise.

rules.reference: Principle of Territorial Variation in Land Value
rules.relevance: Challenges the High Court's approach of applying a uniform compensation rate based on Sonepat data to lands in Jhajjar, Rohtak, and Bhiwani. Land values vary significantly by district, and uniform application may violate principles of fair compensation.

rules.reference: Scope of Writ Jurisdiction vs. Appellate Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: Addresses the second issue: whether the High Court can re-appreciate evidence under Article 226 when no statutory appeal lies under the Telegraph Act. Writ jurisdiction is generally supervisory, not appellate, and does not typically allow for fresh fact-finding.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent regarding the scope of writ jurisdiction under Article 226. It establishes that writ courts should not act as appellate courts to re-appreciate evidence, which is directly relevant to the challenge against the High Court's re-assessment of compensation.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: Relevant precedent concerning compensation under the Telegraph Act. It discusses the principles for determining 'just and equitable' compensation for the right of user, including the consideration of market value and diminution in value.

This is the primary statutory provision governing the award of interest on decrees. The core dispute is whether the High Court exercised its discretion correctly under this section in awarding 5% simple interest versus the appellants' claim for 15% compound interest.

rules.case_name: Indian Bank v. Satyam Transport Agency
rules.reference: Indian Bank v. Satyam Transport Agency
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent establishing that interest is a compensation for the loss of use of money. It holds that the rate of interest should be commensurate with the commercial rate prevailing at the time, especially in commercial transactions, to prevent unjust enrichment of the defaulting party.

rules.case_name: Suryanarayan v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: Suryanarayan v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: This case is highly relevant as it specifically addresses interest awards against the State. It distinguishes between commercial and non-commercial transactions, holding that while the State is not always liable for commercial rates, in cases involving commercial dealings or where the State acts as a trader, higher interest rates may be warranted to compensate for the time value of money.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. M/s. Hindustan Construction Co.
rules.citation: AIR 1998 SC 1005 (Note: Often cited alongside Suryanarayan or similar principles in later cases like ONGC v. Saw Pipes)
rules.reference: Union of India v. M/s. Hindustan Construction Co.
rules.relevance: Relevant for the principle that the nature of the transaction (commercial vs. sovereign) determines the interest rate. If the transaction is deemed commercial, the State cannot claim immunity from commercial interest rates.

rules.case_name: ONGC v. Saw Pipes Ltd.
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that interest is a form of compensation for the loss of use of money. It reinforces that the rate should reflect the commercial reality and the delay in payment, supporting the appellants' argument that 5% is inadequate for a 50-year delay in a commercial context.

The appellants argue that 5% simple interest does not account for inflation and the time value of money over five decades. This economic principle is central to determining whether the awarded interest constitutes adequate compensation under Section 34 CPC.

rules.reference: Commercial vs. Sovereign Function of the State
rules.relevance: The respondents argue the transaction was a capital infusion to save a loss-making company (sovereign/public welfare function), while appellants argue it was a commercial sale. The classification of the State's role determines the applicable interest rate regime.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Union of India
rules.reference: State of Rajasthan v. Union of India
rules.relevance: While primarily about federalism, this case is relevant background for understanding the State of Rajasthan's role in managing state-owned enterprises like Bikaner Gypsums/Rajasthan State Mines and Minerals, potentially supporting the argument that the transaction had a public policy/sovereign dimension rather than a purely commercial one.

Relevant to the background of the transaction involving the sale of shares in a public limited company (Bikaner Gypsums Ltd.) to the State, establishing the corporate and commercial framework of the deal.

rules.case_name: Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation v. M/s. V. S. R. & Co.
rules.citation: AIR 1998 SC 1005 (Note: Similar principle to Suryanarayan)
rules.reference: Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation v. M/s. V. S. R. & Co.
rules.relevance: Supports the view that statutory corporations or State entities engaged in commercial activities are liable to pay interest at commercial rates when they delay payment for commercial transactions.

rules.reference: Order XX Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: This rule empowers the court to grant any legal or equitable relief to which the plaintiff appears to be entitled, even if not specifically claimed in the plaint. This is the primary statutory basis for the Single Judge's decision to 'mould the relief' in favor of the executor rather than the Trust.

rules.reference: Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Relevant to the determination of whether the Trust was the proper plaintiff. The Single Judge found the Trust had no title to the specific property, implying the suit might have been maintainable only by the rightful owner (the executor/beneficiaries), necessitating the moulding of relief to avoid dismissal on technical grounds.

rules.case_name: S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath
rules.reference: S. P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that courts have the power to mould relief under Order XX Rule 3 CPC to achieve complete justice and prevent multiplicity of proceedings, especially when the plaintiff is not the absolute owner but represents the interest of the true owner.

rules.case_name: K. S. N. Raju v. K. S. N. Lakshmi
rules.reference: K. S. N. Raju v. K. S. N. Lakshmi
rules.relevance: Supports the principle that where a suit is filed by a person who is not the absolute owner but has a sufficient interest, the court can mould the relief to benefit the real owner to avoid further litigation.

Governs the probate of wills. The validity of the wills of Somasundaram Chettiar and Padmini Chandrasekaran, and the authority of the executor (Dr. H.B.N. Shetty) to act on behalf of the estate, are central to determining who holds the title and the right to sue.

Relates to the rights and liabilities of buyer and seller. Relevant in assessing the validity of the 1992 sale deeds executed by Defendant No. 1, who had no title to the property after the court auction sale in favor of Padmini Chandrasekaran.

rules.reference: Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Governs the effect of a sale certificate in execution proceedings. It establishes that the title of the auction purchaser (Padmini Chandrasekaran) relates back to the date of the decree, thereby extinguishing Somasundaram Chettiar's title and rendering his subsequent will and the defendants' subsequent sale deeds void.

rules.reference: Principle of Complete Justice and Avoidance of Multiplicity of Proceedings
rules.relevance: The underlying judicial philosophy justifying the moulding of relief. The court acted to prevent the executor from having to file a fresh suit, thereby saving time and judicial resources, which is a recognized equitable power of civil courts.

Defines the creation of a trust. Relevant to the argument that the Trust was the plaintiff. The court's finding that the Trust had no title to the specific property suggests the bequest did not create a trust over that specific asset in a manner that vested title in the Trust entity for the purpose of this suit.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.relevance: Illustrates the court's discretion to grant relief to the person entitled to it, even if the plaintiff is not the absolute owner, provided the plaintiff has a sufficient interest in the subject matter of the suit.

Central to the maintainability of the writ petition. Article 212(1) bars courts from inquiring into the proceedings of the Legislature. The court must determine if the disciplinary proceedings of the Ethics Committee and the subsequent expulsion fall within this immunity or if they are subject to judicial review for procedural irregularities.

Grants the Legislature the power to make rules with respect to its procedure and the conduct of its business. This provision supports the House's autonomy in conducting disciplinary proceedings through its Ethics Committee, which the petitioner challenged.

Defines the powers, privileges, and immunities of the State Legislature and its members. It is relevant to determine the scope of the House's power to expel a member for disorderly conduct and whether such power is subject to fundamental rights or judicial review.

Empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice. The petitioner specifically invokes this to ask the Court to substitute the expulsion with a lesser penalty, raising the issue of whether the Court can interfere with the quantum of punishment decided by the Legislature.

The procedural basis for the petitioner's writ petition. The Court must decide if the alleged violation of natural justice and proportionality constitutes a violation of fundamental rights (such as Article 14 or 21) that justifies invoking Article 32 despite the bar under Article 212.
