rules.relevance: General legal principle that a party is 'necessary' if no effective decree can be passed without them, and 'proper' if their presence aids in the effective adjudication of the matter. This distinguishes between mandatory and discretionary impleadment.
Section 5 allows for the condonation of delay in filing applications if sufficient cause is shown. This is relevant to the Appellant's delay in seeking impleadment from 2008 to 2018.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. The core legal issue is whether Section 4, which allows for release on probation after due admonition, applies when the sentence imposed is only a fine and not imprisonment.

Section 3 provides the power to release on probation. The appellants seek the benefit of Sections 3 and 4 read together. Understanding the interplay between the power to release (Sec 3) and the conditions of release (Sec 4) is essential.

The appellants specifically invoked Section 12, which empowers the High Court or Court of Session to pass orders under Sections 3, 4, or 5 in any case, even if the trial court did not do so. This is the procedural basis for the Supreme Court's intervention.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Ram Kumar
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Ram Kumar
rules.relevance: This is a landmark precedent often cited regarding the interpretation of the Probation of Offenders Act. It establishes that the Act is remedial and should be interpreted liberally to benefit first-time offenders, supporting the appellants' claim despite the fine-only sentence.

The appellants were convicted under this section for voluntarily causing hurt. The nature of the offense is relevant to determining if the offender is a 'fit person' for probation under the Probation of Offenders Act.
The appellants were convicted under this section for voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons. The severity of the charge influences the court's discretion in granting probation benefits.

The conviction was under Sections 323/324 read with Section 34 (common intention). This establishes the joint liability of the appellants, which is part of the factual matrix for the conviction being appealed.

The Probation of Offenders Act is a welfare legislation intended to prevent first-time offenders from being stigmatized. This principle supports the argument that technicalities regarding the type of sentence (fine vs. imprisonment) should not defeat the legislative intent.

Although the Probation of Offenders Act is the specific statute cited, Section 360 of the CrPC (in force at the time of many such precedents) or its successor provisions regarding alternative sentencing provide the broader procedural context for releasing offenders on probation.

The State argued the appeal was to avoid employment disqualification. The court must balance the statutory benefit of probation against the administrative consequences of conviction for government servants, as highlighted in the facts.

rules.reference: Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: This article provides the constitutional basis for reservation in services. The core issue is whether a candidate who qualified via relaxed standards (under Article 16(4)) can claim a vacancy reserved for General category candidates (unreserved) based on final merit, effectively bypassing the reservation logic.

rules.reference: Article 16(1) of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: This article guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. The appellant argues that treating the SC candidate as 'General' for allocation violates the principle that reservation benefits are distinct from general merit selection.

rules.case_name: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
rules.reference: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This landmark judgment laid down the conditions for reservation in promotions and clarified the distinction between general standards and relaxed standards. It is relevant to determine if 'relaxation' in qualifying marks equates to being selected on 'general standards'.

rules.case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
rules.reference: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Also known as the Mandal Case, this precedent establishes the framework for reservations, including the concept of 'creamy layer' and the distinction between reserved and unreserved vacancies. It supports the view that reserved category candidates are selected against reserved vacancies unless specific rules allow otherwise.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
rules.relevance: This case deals with the concept of 'carry forward' and the distinction between reserved and unreserved vacancies. It is relevant to the argument that a candidate selected under relaxed standards cannot be treated as a general candidate for the purpose of filling unreserved vacancies.
Defines the Scheduled Castes for the purpose of Article 16(4). Relevant to establish the status of Respondent No. 1 as an SC candidate entitled to relaxation.

These rules govern the conduct of the Preliminary Examination, including the provision for relaxation in qualifying marks for SC/ST candidates. The dispute hinges on the interpretation of whether qualifying under these relaxed rules affects the final merit status.

Governs the Main Examination and Interview process. Relevant to establish that the final merit list is based on Main and Interview marks, which is the basis of the High Court's reasoning that Preliminary marks are merely screening.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. G. Kiran
rules.reference: Union of India v. G. Kiran
rules.relevance: This is the actual Supreme Court judgment deciding this specific appeal. The Court held that a candidate who avails relaxation in qualifying marks for the Preliminary Examination is selected under the reserved category quota and cannot be treated as a general candidate for cadre allocation against an unreserved vacancy.

The legal principle that reserved and unreserved vacancies are distinct pools. A candidate selected under the reserved quota (even if they score higher than a general candidate in the final merit) remains within the reserved quota for the purpose of allocation unless explicitly provided otherwise by statute or rule.

rules.case_name: Ansal Crown Heights Flat Buyers Association v. M/s. Ansal Crown Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: Supreme Court Order dated 17th January 2024 in the present matter
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court explicitly held that the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC applies only to the corporate debtor and not to its directors or promoters, and remitted the matter for execution against directors subject to their right to raise objections regarding liability. This is the binding precedent for the current appeal.

Governs the powers of the NCDRC to pass orders and the execution of such orders. The core issue is whether the decree passed against the company can be executed against non-parties (directors) under the procedural framework of the CPA.

Defines the scope of the moratorium. The appeal hinges on the interpretation of whether the moratorium protects directors from execution proceedings when they were not parties to the original decree, as clarified by the Supreme Court.

Governs the execution of decrees against persons other than the judgment-debtor. Since the directors were not parties to the original complaint, the NCDRC must determine if they can be added as judgment-debtors or if the decree is executable against them under principles analogous to CPC.

A fundamental legal principle that a decree is generally executable only against parties to the suit and those claiming under them. The NCDRC's dismissal relied on this, arguing directors were not parties. The appeal challenges this by invoking the Supreme Court's direction to examine liability.

Provides for personal liability of officers in default for fraud or willful default. While not directly cited in the brief, it is the statutory basis often used to pierce the corporate veil and hold directors personally liable for company debts in cases of misconduct, which may be relevant to the 'objections regarding liability' mentioned by the Supreme Court.

rules.case_name: M/s. Ansal Housing Pvt. Ltd. v. Rajesh Aggarwal (or similar NCDRC/SC precedents on promoter liability)
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on piercing the corporate veil in consumer matters
rules.relevance: Precedents establishing that promoters/directors can be held liable for deficiency in service if they are found to be the alter ego of the company or if fraud is established, supporting the appellant's argument for execution against them.
Procedural rules governing how the NCDRC executes its orders, including the process for adding parties or executing against non-parties if permitted by law.

Legal principle allowing courts to disregard corporate personality if the company is a mere facade for the directors. Relevant to determining if directors can be held personally liable for the company's failure to deliver possession.
May be relevant if directors raise objections regarding the limitation period for execution against them, given the timeline of the original complaint and the subsequent execution applications.

Defines the legal concept of a 'contract of guarantee' and the roles of surety, principal debtor, and creditor. This is the primary statutory test to determine if Clause 2.2 of the Deed of Undertaking creates a guarantee liability for ECL.

Establishes the binding nature of the approved resolution plan on all stakeholders, including operational debtors and financial creditors. Relevant to the argument that the debt was extinguished upon implementation of the plan and issuance of the no-due certificate.

Governs the initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) by financial creditors. Relevant to determining if the appellant qualifies as a financial creditor holding a valid financial debt against ESL post-resolution.

rules.case_name: State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan
rules.reference: State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan
rules.relevance: Supreme Court precedent clarifying that a resolution plan approved under the IBC extinguishes all claims against the corporate debtor, and that the 'no due certificate' issued by financial creditors confirms the discharge of dues. Supports the NCLT/NCLAT finding that the debt was extinguished.

rules.case_name: M/s. Electrosteel Castings Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.reference: M/s. Electrosteel Castings Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Directly relevant precedent involving the same parties (ESL/ECL and SREI). The Supreme Court previously examined the nature of the Deed of Undertaking and the validity of the resolution plan, providing authoritative context on whether ECL was a guarantor.

Legal principle distinguishing a contract of guarantee (collateral promise to answer for the debt of another) from a contract of indemnity or an independent undertaking. Clause 2.2's obligation to 'infuse funds' may be construed as an independent covenant rather than a guarantee.

Defines 'financial debt' to include the amount claimed by a financial creditor on account of the transfer of a financial asset or any other transaction having the commercial effect of a borrowing. Relevant to determining if the assigned residual debt qualifies as financial debt.
Defines the liability of the surety, which is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor. Relevant if the court finds that a guarantee exists, to determine the extent of ECL's liability.

rules.case_name: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.reference: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.relevance: Establishes that the approval of a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC is final and binding, and that the corporate debtor is discharged from all liabilities. Reinforces the finality of the resolution process against subsequent claims.
Provides the procedural mechanism for appealing against an order of the NCLAT to the Supreme Court. Relevant as the basis for the current appeal.

This is the central provision in dispute. The Corporation argues it acts as a residuary clause allowing the application of Government rules (specifically the 1982 Pension Rules) to fill gaps in the 1992 Regulations regarding post-superannuation proceedings. The appellant argues it does not confer such jurisdiction without specific adoption.

This rule governs the recovery of dues from pension/retiral benefits. The core legal question is whether Rule 110 of the 1992 Regulations validly incorporates Rule 27 of the 1982 Rules, thereby permitting the Corporation to withhold benefits and recover losses post-superannuation.

Section 13 of the Act empowers the State Government to make regulations for the conduct of business and discipline of employees. This is the enabling legislation that validates the 1992 Regulations and defines the scope of the Corporation's regulatory power.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: A leading Supreme Court precedent holding that departmental proceedings can be initiated against a retired employee if the service rules expressly permit it. It establishes that retirement does not automatically extinguish the right to recover losses or impose penalties if the statutory framework allows it.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Chandrakant
rules.relevance: Relevant for the principle that the power to recover dues from pension/retiral benefits must be explicitly conferred by the relevant service rules or regulations. It supports the appellant's argument that general residuary clauses may not suffice without specific adoption.

The legal principle governing whether a specific set of rules (1982 Pension Rules) can be applied to a different entity (Warehousing Corporation) via a general reference in its own regulations (Rule 110). The court must determine if the incorporation was 'conscious' and specific enough to override the default position.

Although the primary issue is jurisdiction, the facts mention the appellant's non-appearance due to non-supply of documents. Principles of natural justice (Audi Alteram Partem) are relevant to assess if the enquiry was vitiated, though the High Court focused on the jurisdictional aspect.

The High Court directed the appellant to prefer an appeal under the 1992 Regulations. Rule 27 of the 1992 Regulations likely deals with appeals against disciplinary actions. Its applicability depends on whether the initial proceedings were validly instituted.

rules.case_name: Various Supreme Court judgments on Statutory Interpretation
rules.reference: K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Context of Statutory Interpretation)
rules.relevance: General principles of statutory interpretation are relevant to construe Rule 110. The court must decide if 'residuary clause' implies a broad incorporation of all government rules or only those specifically compatible with the Corporation's specific regulatory scheme.

rules.reference: Government of Maharashtra Approval of 1992 Regulations
rules.relevance: The Corporation argues that the State Government's approval of the 1992 Regulations constituted the necessary sanction under Rule 27 of the 1982 Rules. This administrative act is a key factual element in determining if the procedural requirements for recovery were met.

This is the substantive provision in the new criminal procedure code corresponding to Section 438 of the CrPC, governing the grant of anticipatory bail. The appeal concerns the scope and duration of protection under this provision.

rules.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: The landmark precedent laying down the general principles for granting anticipatory bail, including that it should not be granted as a matter of course and must be based on specific facts. It establishes the discretionary nature of the power.

rules.case_name: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: This case specifically addresses the issue of whether anticipatory bail can be restricted to a specific period (e.g., until the filing of the charge sheet). The Supreme Court held that such restrictions are generally impermissible unless justified by exceptional circumstances, as it defeats the purpose of anticipatory bail.

rules.case_name: Emmanuel Remillard de规范 v. State of Kerala
rules.reference: Emmanuel Remillard de规范 v. State of Kerala
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that anticipatory bail is not a right but a discretion, and discusses the conditions under which it can be granted or modified, relevant to the High Court's exercise of discretion in this case.

These are the substantive offences alleged against the appellant (likely corresponding to culpable homicide not amounting to murder and abetment of suicide under the old IPC). The gravity of these offences is a key factor in determining the eligibility for anticipatory bail.

These sections pertain to dowry demand and punishment for dowry death. The involvement of these offences often leads courts to be more cautious in granting anticipatory bail due to the social sensitivity and severity of the crime.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Chandra v. CBI
rules.relevance: Discusses the interplay between anticipatory bail and the investigation process, and the conditions that can be imposed. It is relevant to assess if the High Court's restriction was proportionate to the investigation needs.

rules.reference: Principle of Continuity of Bail Protection
rules.relevance: The legal principle that once anticipatory bail is granted, it should generally continue until the trial is over, unless there are compelling reasons to modify it. Terminating it upon the filing of the charge sheet without a fresh hearing on merits is often viewed as contrary to this principle.

Right to life and personal liberty. Anticipatory bail is seen as a safeguard against arbitrary arrest, ensuring that the liberty of an accused is not infringed without due process, especially when there is no immediate threat of tampering with evidence.

rules.case_name: State of Jharkhand v. Chandra Prakash
rules.reference: State of Jharkhand v. Chandra Prakash
rules.relevance: A recent Supreme Court judgment that reiterates the guidelines for granting anticipatory bail under the new BNSS/CrPC framework, emphasizing that bail is the rule and jail is the exception, and criticizing arbitrary restrictions on bail duration.
This is the specific provision under which the High Court exercised its inherent powers to quash the criminal proceedings. The appeal challenges the correctness of this exercise of power.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This is the landmark precedent laying down the guidelines for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.PC to quash FIRs or criminal proceedings. It establishes that quashing is appropriate only in rare cases, such as when the allegations do not constitute an offense or are frivolous.

rules.reference: Distinction between Civil Dispute and Criminal Offense
rules.relevance: The High Court quashed the proceedings primarily on the ground that the dispute was civil in nature. The appellant must argue that the allegations of forgery and fraud (Sections 465, 468, 471 IPC) constitute distinct criminal offenses that are not merely incidental to a civil dispute.

These sections pertain to forgery and using as genuine a forged document. The relevance lies in determining whether the specific allegations of forgery in the settlement deeds attract criminal liability independent of the civil validity of the deeds.

These sections deal with cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property. The appellant needs to establish that the acts alleged go beyond a mere breach of contract or civil wrong and involve criminal intent (mens rea) required for cheating.

rules.case_name: Gurnam Kaur v. Daljit Singh
rules.relevance: This precedent is relevant to the issue of delay. It holds that delay in filing a complaint is not a ground for quashing criminal proceedings unless the delay is inordinate and unexplained, or if it causes prejudice to the accused. The High Court cited delay as a ground for quashing.

The High Court noted that the civil court had upheld the validity of the deeds. The appellant must argue that a civil decree upholding a deed does not operate as res judicata to bar a criminal prosecution for forgery, as the standards of proof and the nature of the inquiry differ.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of Section 482 and emphasizes that the High Court should not act as a court of appeal over the Magistrate's order of taking cognizance. It supports the argument that the High Court should not have quashed the proceedings at this stage.

This section deals with criminal conspiracy. It is relevant to determine if the alleged joint action by the respondents in executing the forged deeds constitutes a separate criminal conspiracy charge.

rules.reference: Suppression of Facts and Mala Fide
rules.relevance: The High Court held that the appellant suppressed facts. The appellant must address whether the initial ex parte conduct in the civil suit amounts to suppression of facts in the criminal complaint, or if the criminal complaint was filed based on new discoveries or independent evidence of forgery.

This is the primary procedural provision under which the appellant was summoned as an accused. The legal status of an accused added under this section, particularly regarding the presumption of innocence and the stage of trial, is central to the bail determination.

This section governs the grant of bail in non-bailable offences. The High Court's rejection of the appellant's bail application under this section is the specific order being challenged in the Special Leave Petition.

This section governs anticipatory bail. The State's appeal challenges the grant of anticipatory bail to co-accused under this provision, requiring a comparison of the facts and legal standards applied to the appellant versus the co-accused.

rules.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent laying down the general principles for granting anticipatory bail under Section 438 Cr.P.C., including the requirement of special reasons and the gravity of the offence.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Chandra v. CBI
rules.relevance: This precedent is crucial for establishing that an accused summoned under Section 319 Cr.P.C. is entitled to the same bail rights as an accused named in the FIR, and that the court must apply the standard bail tests rather than treating them differently solely based on the mode of impleadment.

The charge of murder is a serious non-bailable offence. The gravity of this charge is a primary factor considered by courts when deciding whether to grant bail, often leading to a stricter scrutiny of the accused's role and likelihood of absconding.

This section deals with unlawful assembly. The application of Section 149 often requires proof of common intention, which is relevant in determining the individual culpability of the appellant versus the co-accused when assessing bail eligibility.

This provision relates to the use of arms in furtherance of an offence. The presence of arms charges typically aggravates the severity of the case, influencing the court's discretion in granting bail.

The legal principle that co-accused in the same case, facing similar charges and circumstances, should generally be treated equally regarding bail. This is relevant to the State's appeal challenging the differential treatment between the appellant (bail rejected) and co-accused (anticipatory bail granted).

Article 21 guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. The Supreme Court has interpreted this to include the right to a speedy trial and the principle that 'bail is the rule, jail is the exception,' which underpins the judicial approach to bail applications.

This is the primary statutory provision governing bail in PMLA cases. It imposes a reverse burden of proof on the accused to show that there are no reasonable grounds for believing they committed the offence and that they will not commit any offence while on bail. The appeal centers on whether the High Court correctly applied the stringent conditions of this section.

The appellant claims a violation of the right to life and personal liberty, specifically the right to a speedy trial, due to prolonged pre-trial incarceration (over 16 months). Article 21 is the constitutional basis for challenging excessive delay in judicial proceedings.

rules.case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment is critical as it clarified that the 'twin conditions' under Section 45 of the PMLA are not absolute and must be read in light of Article 21. It mandates that courts consider the length of incarceration and the stage of investigation/trial when deciding bail, directly supporting the appellant's argument regarding prolonged custody.

rules.case_name: Surendra Kumar v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.reference: Surendra Kumar v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.relevance: This recent Supreme Court judgment further elaborates on the application of Section 45 of the PMLA, emphasizing that the reverse burden of proof cannot be used to deny bail mechanically. It reinforces the principle that if the investigation is complete and the accused has been in custody for a significant period, bail should be granted unless there are specific grounds for denial.

This provision grants the High Court the power to grant bail in cases where the Special Court has rejected the application. It is the procedural vehicle used by the appellant to approach the High Court, and its interpretation in conjunction with PMLA Section 45 is central to the jurisdictional aspect of the appeal.

rules.case_name: Gopal Subramanium v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.reference: Gopal Subramanium v. Directorate of Enforcement
rules.relevance: This judgment discusses the scope of the Special Court's powers and the interpretation of 'reasonable grounds' under Section 45 of the PMLA. It is relevant to assessing whether the High Court correctly evaluated the ED's allegations of witness tampering and dissipation of assets.

A fundamental legal principle derived from Article 21, stating that an accused is entitled to a speedy trial. Prolonged detention without trial is a ground for granting bail, especially when the investigation is complete and the trial is at a preliminary stage (scrutiny of documents).

Defines the offence of money laundering. The relevance lies in the requirement to establish a link between the 'proceeds of crime' and the alleged dissipation of assets. The appellant argues no material link exists between him and the sale documents of Marichika Properties, challenging the predicate offence connection.

rules.case_name: Narayan Keshav Deshmukh v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Narayan Keshav Deshmukh v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that bail is the rule and jail is the exception. While PMLA has stricter norms, this foundational principle supports the argument that bail should not be denied merely on the basis of the gravity of the charge if other factors (like delay and completion of investigation) favor the accused.

The principle that an accused is innocent until proven guilty. The appellant argues that since no cognizance has been taken and the matter is at the scrutiny stage, the allegations of witness tampering and asset dissipation are merely allegations and not proven facts, thus failing to meet the threshold for denying bail under Section 45.
Central to the appeal; the appellant argues the 2015 Act is manifestly arbitrary and violates the guarantee of equality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14.
Central to the appeal; the appellant contends that the Act effects compulsory acquisition and extinguishment of rights in a confiscatory manner, violating the right to property.

rules.reference: Srimati Radhika Sinha Institute and Sachchidanand Sinha Library (Requisition & Management) Act, 2015
rules.relevance: The specific legislation under challenge, which vested rights, title, and interest in the State Government and dissolved the Trust.
The appellant argues the 2015 Act is repugnant to this Act, which governs the creation and administration of private trusts, including the Deed of Trust executed in 1926.

rules.case_name: Unspecified in brief (referenced as Supreme Court holding actions under 1983 ordinances non est)
rules.relevance: Establishes the legal history that previous attempts to acquire the Trust via ordinances were invalid, providing context for the legislative shift to a permanent Act in 2015.
A key constitutional principle under Article 14 used to challenge laws that are irrational, disproportionate, or lack a rational nexus to their objective.

rules.reference: Distinction between Private and Public Trusts
rules.relevance: The High Court upheld the Act by characterizing the Trust as a 'public trust'. This distinction is crucial as the state's power to requisition or manage public trusts differs from its power over private trusts.

rules.reference: Power of State Legislature to Enact Special Laws
rules.relevance: Relevant to determining whether the Bihar State Legislature had the competence to enact a special law overriding general trust laws for the management of a state central library.
Relevant to the Article 300A claim; distinguishes between valid state acquisition for public purpose and invalid confiscatory taking of property without compensation or due process.

rules.provision: Clauses regarding Reversion and Honorary Secretary
rules.relevance: The foundational document establishing the Trust, designating the appellant's family line as trustees and providing for reversion, which the 2015 Act purported to extinguish.

This is the specific regulatory provision cited by the Screening Committee to reject the respondent's candidature based on criminal antecedents. The interpretation of this paragraph regarding the admissibility of candidates with 'benefit of doubt' acquittals is central to the appeal.

rules.case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Narayan Singh
rules.reference: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Narayan Singh
rules.relevance: This is the leading Supreme Court precedent directly addressing the issue of whether an acquittal based on benefit of doubt constitutes an 'honourable acquittal' for the purpose of police recruitment under MP Police Regulations. It establishes that such acquittals do not automatically entitle the candidate to appointment if the charges are serious.

These sections define the serious nature of the offences (kidnapping and rape of a minor) for which the respondent was charged. The gravity of these specific offences is a key factor in determining whether the character verification standards for police personnel were rightly applied.

rules.reference: Distinction between 'Honourable Acquittal' and 'Benefit of Doubt'
rules.relevance: The core legal principle in dispute is whether an acquittal granted solely on the ground of insufficient evidence or benefit of doubt absolves the accused of the stigma of the charge for employment purposes, particularly in sensitive posts like police constable.

Article 309 empowers the State to make regulations for the recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving in the State. This provision validates the existence and authority of the Madhya Pradesh Police Regulations used to reject the candidate.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: A relevant precedent discussing the standards of character and conduct required for police personnel, establishing that the State has a wider discretion in rejecting candidates with criminal antecedents compared to other civil services.

This section deals with the judgment of acquittal. Understanding the procedural context of how the acquittal was recorded (specifically the language used by the trial court) is relevant to the High Court's characterization of the acquittal.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Clean Hands and Character Verification in Police Recruitment
rules.relevance: The principle that police personnel must be of impeccable character. The court must balance the presumption of innocence post-acquittal against the statutory requirement for high moral character in law enforcement roles.

rules.case_name: K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
rules.reference: K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Privacy Judgment context on employment rights)
rules.relevance: While primarily about privacy, this judgment touches upon the right to livelihood and the limits of state interference. However, in this context, it serves as background for the balance between individual rights and state interest in maintaining a disciplined police force.
This section outlines the qualifications and disqualifications for appointment to the police force, providing the statutory backbone for the regulations invoked by the Screening Committee.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. The proviso to Section 245H(1) explicitly states that the Settlement Commission cannot grant immunity from prosecution if criminal proceedings have already been initiated. The High Court relied on this to dismiss the quashing petition, and the appellant challenges its application in light of the subsequent settlement order.

This section empowers the Settlement Commission to pass an order granting immunity from penalty and prosecution. The relevance lies in the Commission's finding of 'full and true disclosure' and 'no suppression of facts,' which the appellant argues should logically preclude continued prosecution despite the procedural bar in Section 245H(1).

This is the specific criminal provision under which the appellant was prosecuted for wilful attempt to evade tax. The appeal concerns whether this prosecution can continue after the Settlement Commission has effectively validated the appellant's disclosure.

rules.case_name: CIT v. K. K. Modi
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent interpreting the scope of Section 245H(1). It established that the Settlement Commission's power to grant immunity from prosecution is subject to the proviso if proceedings are already pending. This case is likely the primary authority the High Court relied upon, and the appellant may seek to distinguish it or argue for its limitation based on the 'abuse of process' doctrine.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Dhanrajgir Dhariemal
rules.reference: Union of India v. Dhanrajgir Dhariemal
rules.relevance: This precedent discusses the relationship between settlement proceedings and criminal prosecution. It is relevant to the argument that once a settlement is reached and facts are disclosed, continuing prosecution may be inconsistent with the spirit of the settlement scheme, although the statutory proviso in 245H(1) creates a specific exception.

This is the procedural provision under which the appellant filed the petition to quash the criminal complaint. The Supreme Court's inherent powers under this section are invoked to prevent abuse of the process of the court or to secure the ends of justice, which is the core of the appellant's argument.

The appellant argues that continuing prosecution after the Settlement Commission has recorded a finding of no suppression of facts constitutes an abuse of process. This legal principle allows courts to quash proceedings that are frivolous, vexatious, or contrary to the ends of justice, even if technically maintainable under a strict reading of the statute.

This section allows an assessee to make an application for settlement. The timing of this application (filed after the complaint but before the final settlement order) is crucial in determining whether the proviso to Section 245H(1) applies and whether the subsequent settlement order can override the earlier initiation of prosecution.

The appellant argues that the prosecution was initiated in violation of binding departmental circulars. While circulars are not statutes, they guide the administration of the Act. If the prosecution was initiated contrary to these guidelines, it may support the argument that the proceedings are irregular or an abuse of process.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment lays down guidelines for quashing FIRs/complaints under Section 482 CrPC. It is relevant to determine whether the facts disclosed in the Settlement Commission order (no suppression) fall under any category where quashing is appropriate to prevent abuse of process.

This is the substantive provision under which the respondent-company claimed the right to retain agricultural land. The core issue is whether the company satisfied the condition of being engaged 'exclusively' in agricultural farming on 01.01.1952.
Section 6 deals with the vesting of estates in the State. The dispute centers on the finality of the vesting order passed under this section in 1971 and whether it could be reviewed.

Section 10 typically empowers the Revenue Officer to determine questions regarding the extent of land retained or vested. The jurisdiction of the Revenue Officer to pass the 1971 order and the subsequent 2008 review order derives from this section.

The central legal question is whether the Revenue Officer had statutory power to review a final order. If the Act does not expressly provide for review, the officer likely lacked jurisdiction, as implied powers of review are generally not recognized in statutory tribunals unless expressly conferred.

rules.case_name: State of West Bengal v. Jai Hind Private Limited
rules.citation: Supreme Court Appeal against High Court Judgment
rules.reference: State of West Bengal v. Jai Hind Private Limited
rules.relevance: This is the current case itself. The Supreme Court's decision will establish the binding precedent on whether a Revenue Officer under the WBEA Act can review a final vesting order after a long lapse of time and after the order has attained finality through dismissal of writ petitions.

The 1971 order became final in 1975 when the writ petition was dismissed for default and restoration was rejected. The principle that final orders cannot be reopened arbitrarily, especially after decades, is central to the State's appeal.

The review was sought in 2008, nearly 37 years after the 1971 order. The principle of laches (undue delay) and statutory limitation periods may bar the review, even if jurisdictional error is alleged.

If the review is considered a fresh application or if the Act is silent on review, the general limitation period for applications to courts/tribunals (3 years under Article 137) would apply, rendering the 2008 application time-barred.

rules.case_name: e.g., State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on Review Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: Precedents establishing that a statutory authority has no inherent power of review unless expressly conferred by the statute. This supports the Tribunal's view that the Revenue Officer lacked jurisdiction.

The 2008 amicable settlement proposal by the company to withdraw litigation in exchange for land retention raises issues of waiver, estoppel, and whether the State can be bound by such an executive settlement to override statutory finality.

The High Court held that the appellant's failure to issue a notice under Section 21 for Disputes 2 to 4 was fatal to the arbitration. This provision defines the commencement of arbitral proceedings and is central to the issue of whether the arbitration was validly initiated for all four disputes.

The Arbitral Tribunal relied on Section 16 (Competence-competence) to determine its own jurisdiction, holding that the arbitration clause was comprehensive. The appeal involves reviewing whether the Tribunal correctly exercised this power to decide on its jurisdiction regarding the scope of disputes.

The District Judge set aside the award under Section 34. The Supreme Court appeal challenges the correctness of this setting aside, particularly regarding the grounds of jurisdictional error and procedural irregularity.

Defines the 'Arbitration Agreement'. The core issue is whether the General Conditions of Contract (GCC) constituted a single arbitration agreement covering all disputes or separate agreements, and whether the respondent's conduct implied a reference of all disputes under this agreement.

The appellant argued that the respondent's conduct (issuing a letter referring only Dispute 1 after the time limit, yet participating in the constitution of the tribunal) indicated an intention to reopen all disputes. The principle of waiver/estoppel is relevant to determine if the respondent is barred from later claiming the tribunal lacked jurisdiction over Disputes 2-4.

Relevant to determining whether the non-issuance of a specific Section 21 notice for Disputes 2-4, when the respondent had already participated in the arbitration process without objection to the scope, constitutes a fatal defect or a curable irregularity.

Relates to the appointment of arbitrators. The respondent appointed its arbitrator in the letter dated 01.10.2004. The scope of this appointment and the subsequent agreement to constitute the tribunal is key to defining the tribunal's mandate.

The appellant filed a Special Leave Petition before the Supreme Court. Article 136 grants the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India.

The principle that arbitration clauses should be interpreted broadly to give effect to the parties' intention to resolve disputes amicably, rather than narrowly to defeat arbitration, is relevant to the Tribunal's finding that the clause was 'comprehensive'.

rules.reference: Kerala State Transport Project General Conditions of Contract (GCC)
rules.relevance: This contractual provision mandated reference to arbitration within 28 days of the Adjudicator's decision. The respondent's failure to adhere to this timeline for Disputes 2-4, followed by its subsequent conduct, is the factual basis for the dispute over jurisdiction and waiver.

rules.reference: State Bank of India Employees’ Pension Fund Rules, 1955
rules.relevance: This is the specific rule under which the appellant claims entitlement to pension, arguing that he completed over 20 years of service. The court must interpret whether 'voluntary abandonment' of service qualifies for benefits under this clause compared to 'voluntary retirement'.

rules.reference: State Bank of India Employees’ Pension Fund Rules, 1955
rules.relevance: The respondent-Bank relies on this rule to deny pension, arguing the appellant did not complete 20 years of qualifying service nor attain the age of 50. The court must determine if the appellant's service period counts as 'qualifying service' despite the abandonment declaration.

The appellant filed the claim petition under this section. The core legal issue is whether the claim for pension involves the computation of a 'money or benefit' due under an existing award or settlement (pre-existing right), which is the jurisdictional limit of Section 33C(2).

rules.reference: Jurisdiction of Labour Court under Section 33C(2) of ID Act
rules.relevance: The Labour Court and High Court dismissed the petition for lack of jurisdiction, holding there was no pre-existing right. The Supreme Court must decide if the dispute over eligibility for pension (factually disputed) falls within the limited jurisdiction of Section 33C(2) or requires a full industrial dispute adjudication.

rules.reference: Distinction between Voluntary Retirement and Voluntary Abandonment of Service
rules.relevance: The Bank declared the appellant 'voluntarily retired' in 2008 but earlier declared services 'voluntarily abandoned' in 1998. The legal consequence of abandonment versus retirement on pension eligibility is central to the appeal.

The appellant claims over 20 years of service. The court must determine if the period of absence without leave and the period after abandonment declaration can be counted towards the 20-year qualifying service required under the Pension Fund Rules.

rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on Section 33C(2) ID Act
rules.relevance: While specific case names are not provided in the brief, the Supreme Court will rely on established precedents defining the scope of Section 33C(2), specifically that it does not adjudicate disputed questions of fact or law regarding the existence of a right, but only computes amounts where the right is established.

Definition of 'retrenchment' or termination. If the abandonment of service is deemed a termination by the employer, it may trigger different statutory protections or interpretations of service continuity compared to voluntary retirement.

The High Court held the appellant could not establish a pre-existing right. The Supreme Court must review whether the appellant's claim was merely for computation of a known right or if it required determining eligibility, which is a disputed fact.

rules.reference: State Bank of India Employees’ Pension Fund Rules, 1955
rules.relevance: Rules governing how periods of unauthorized absence or abandonment affect the continuity of service for pension purposes are relevant to determine if the 20-year threshold was met.

This is the specific procedural rule cited by the High Court. It governs the procedure for dismissal and requires the disciplinary authority to consider the length of service and pension claims. The appeal centers on whether the authority violated this rule by relying on past misconduct not disclosed in the show cause notice.

rules.reference: Principles of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem)
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether the disciplinary authority violated natural justice by considering past misconduct (forfeited service, pending enquiries) that was not disclosed in the show cause notice, thereby denying the respondent a fair opportunity to defend against those specific aggravating factors.

As the respondent was a member of the Punjab Armed Forces, this Act provides the statutory framework for their appointment, discipline, and dismissal, serving as the enabling legislation for the Punjab Police Rules.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsiram
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that while past conduct can be considered for determining the quantum of punishment, it must be disclosed to the delinquent employee to allow them to explain or rebut it, otherwise it violates natural justice.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that in cases of grave misconduct, the disciplinary authority has the discretion to dismiss without necessarily granting leniency based on length of service, provided the procedure is fair.
The broader chapter governing disciplinary proceedings, charges, and punishments for police personnel, providing context to Rule 16.2(1).

The High Court granted consequential service benefits. This principle dictates that if a dismissal is set aside, the employee is entitled to benefits accrued during the period of illegal termination, subject to exceptions like waiver or misconduct during the period of absence.

The High Court denied back wages because the respondent had previously waived them. This principle addresses whether an employee can be estopped from claiming back wages if they had previously accepted a settlement or waiver, or if the absence was unauthorized.

rules.case_name: K. N. Guruswamy v. Union of India
rules.reference: K. N. Guruswamy v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes that the right to back wages is not automatic upon reinstatement; it depends on the conduct of the employee and whether they were genuinely out of employment or received compensation elsewhere.
Procedural rule governing appeals from original decrees. Relevant to the procedural history where the State filed an appeal against the High Court's judgment allowing the second appeal.

This is the primary substantive provision under which the appellant was convicted. The appeal challenges the sufficiency of evidence to sustain a conviction for cruelty by a relative, specifically regarding dowry harassment.

Relevant for assessing the credibility of the testimony of PW-3 (deceased's mother) and PW-2 (deceased's brother). The court must determine if their testimony is reliable and free from enmity or bias, especially given the acquittal of other family members.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Krishna Deo
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Krishna Deo
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent establishing that the testimony of a sole witness (or in this context, the key prosecution witnesses PW-2 and PW-3) can be acted upon if it is found to be reliable, truthful, and trustworthy, despite the lack of corroboration.

rules.case_name: P. Ramachandra Rao v. State of A.P.
rules.reference: P. Ramachandra Rao v. State of A.P.
rules.relevance: Establishes the legal principle that the testimony of a dying declaration or a witness who was present at the scene or closely related to the victim must be scrutinized with care. It guides the court in evaluating whether the testimony of the deceased's parents is sufficient to sustain a conviction under Section 498-A.

rules.case_name: Sushil Kumar Kour v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.reference: Sushil Kumar Kour v. State (NCT of Delhi)
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment is highly relevant as it deals with the distinction between cruelty under Section 498-A and the offense of dowry death under Section 304-B. It emphasizes that mere allegations of dowry harassment without specific instances or proof of demand may not sustain a conviction, especially if the death is not directly linked to such cruelty.

Although the appellant was acquitted of this charge, the facts involve a death within seven years of marriage. The distinction between the evidence required for Section 304-B (dowry death) and Section 498-A (cruelty) is central to the appeal, as the conviction under 498-A stands while 304-B failed.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Criminal Cases
rules.relevance: The principle that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal hinges on whether the testimony of PW-3 and PW-2, in the absence of specific allegations in the initial complaint and with the acquittal of other accused, meets this high standard.

rules.case_name: Ramesh Chandra v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Ramesh Chandra v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: Relevant for the principle that the testimony of a witness who is a relative of the deceased must be viewed with caution and requires corroboration, particularly when the initial complaint did not specifically implicate the appellant with specific acts of cruelty.

Governs the powers of the Appellate Court (Supreme Court) to alter findings, convictions, or sentences. The court will use this provision to determine if it can interfere with the High Court's affirmation of the conviction.

rules.case_name: Bhanwar Singh v. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Bhanwar Singh v. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: Establishes that the testimony of a single witness, even if a relative, can be sufficient for conviction if it is clear, cogent, and reliable. This is relevant to counter the defense argument that the testimony of PW-3 needs corroboration.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Defines the offense of export of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, which is the primary charge against the appellants for allegedly exporting Ephedrine powder to Kenya.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Defines the offense of abetment, conspiracy, and attempt, relevant to the charges against Manoj Jain, Kishorsinh Rathod, and Bharatsinh Kathiya who were not in direct possession of the contraband.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Creates a presumption of possession and knowledge of the nature of the substance. The appeal challenges whether the foundational facts required to invoke this presumption were established for the appellants other than Narendra Kacha.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Creates a presumption of guilt for offenses involving commercial quantities. The court must determine if the prosecution discharged the burden of proving foundational facts to shift the burden of proof to the accused.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
rules.relevance: Governs the recording of confessions by police officers. The appeal argues that Narendra Kacha's statement was not recorded under this section, rendering it inadmissible as a confession and requiring strict scrutiny of its use against co-accused.

Deals with the admissibility of confessions made by co-accused. The court must decide if the statement of Narendra Kacha can be used against the other appellants given the lack of independent corroboration and procedural irregularities.

rules.case_name: State of Gujarat v. Shambhulal Chhaganlal Patel
rules.reference: State of Gujarat v. Shambhulal Chhaganlal Patel
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that the presumption under Section 35 of the NDPS Act is rebuttable and that the prosecution must first establish foundational facts (such as possession and knowledge) before the burden shifts to the accused.

rules.case_name: Laxman v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that a conviction cannot be sustained solely on the basis of a co-accused's statement (Section 30, Evidence Act) without independent corroboration, especially when the statement is not a formal confession under Section 67 of the NDPS Act.

rules.reference: Principle of Corroboration for Co-accused Statements
rules.relevance: The legal principle that a statement by a co-accused is not substantive evidence and requires corroboration by independent evidence to sustain a conviction, particularly when the statement is not recorded under the specific safeguards of Section 67 of the NDPS Act.

The principle that statutory presumptions under the NDPS Act (Sections 35 and 54) are not automatic; the prosecution must prove the basic facts (possession, knowledge, quantity) beyond reasonable doubt before the presumption arises.
The primary substantive charge under which the appellants were convicted for murder. The appeal challenges the sustainability of this conviction.

The provision for 'common intention' relied upon by the prosecution to convict A2, A3, and A4 jointly. The acquittal of the alleged instigator (A1) raises questions about the existence of common intention among the remaining accused.

The provision under which the recovery of the chopper (MO-16) based on the disclosure statements of A3 and A4 was admitted. The reliability of this evidence is challenged due to hostile witnesses regarding the recovery.
The provision placing the burden of proof on the accused to explain the presence of the deceased's body in their house. The High Court relied on this to support the conviction.

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Circumstantial Evidence
rules.relevance: The legal principle that in cases based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of circumstances must be complete, unbroken, and conclusive, excluding every hypothesis of innocence. This is central to the issue of whether the prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

The principle governing the weight and admissibility of extra-judicial confessions, which must be voluntary and corroborated. The appeal challenges the reliance on these confessions given the hostile nature of key witnesses.

rules.reference: Effect of Acquittal of Co-Accused on Common Intention
rules.relevance: The legal principle that the acquittal of one accused (A1) does not automatically lead to the acquittal of others, but the court must examine if the remaining evidence sufficiently establishes common intention among the convicted accused (A2, A3, A4) independent of the acquitted person.

The principle that testimony of witnesses who turn hostile cannot be wholly discarded but must be viewed with caution and requires strong corroboration. This is relevant as key eyewitnesses and recovery witnesses turned hostile.

The procedural provision empowering the Appellate Court (Supreme Court) to alter the finding, enhance or reduce the sentence, or acquit the accused. This is the basis for the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to review the High Court's conviction.

The legal significance of A2's surrender and subsequent confession. While surrender is a mitigating factor, the voluntariness and truthfulness of the confession made to police officials are critical to sustaining the conviction.

This article imposes a constitutional bar on courts interfering in electoral matters relating to Panchayats, except as provided by law. It is central to the issue of whether the High Court could interfere with the election process.

This section provides the statutory remedy for election disputes. The issue specifically questions whether the High Court ignored this available statutory remedy in favor of exercising writ jurisdiction.

This article grants the High Court the power to issue writs. The appeal challenges the justification of the High Court's exercise of this discretionary power in the face of Article 243-O and statutory remedies.

rules.case_name: Jagdish Prasad v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Jagdish Prasad v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court judgment interpreting Article 243-O, holding that courts cannot interfere in the electoral process of Panchayats and that the Election Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over such matters.

The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition citing the availability of an alternative remedy. This principle is relevant to determining if the Division Bench was justified in overriding that dismissal.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Non-Interference in Ongoing Elections
rules.relevance: Courts generally avoid interfering in ongoing election processes to prevent disruption and ensure timely completion of elections, which supports the Supreme Court's stay clarifying that the process continues in accordance with law.

rules.reference: The Representation of the People Act, 1951
rules.relevance: While primarily for parliamentary/assembly elections, the principles regarding the finality of election results and the specific grounds for declaring elections void are often analogized or contrasted with Panchayat election laws to determine the scope of judicial review.

rules.reference: Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Relevant to the procedural aspect of the intra-court appeal filed without impleading the appellant, potentially affecting the maintainability of the appeal before the Division Bench.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsiram
rules.relevance: Establishes the fundamental principle that Industrial Tribunals and Courts cannot re-appreciate evidence or act as appellate authorities in disciplinary matters; their jurisdiction is limited to examining whether the enquiry was conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice and whether the findings are perverse.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Chaudhry Bhagat Ram
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Chaudhry Bhagat Ram
rules.relevance: Reinforces that the Tribunal cannot substitute its own view for that of the Disciplinary Authority regarding the appreciation of evidence, unless the findings are based on no evidence or are manifestly unreasonable.

Defines the scope of reference to Industrial Tribunals. The Tribunal's power is to adjudicate disputes, but judicial precedents interpret this section to mean that the Tribunal cannot re-evaluate the merits of the disciplinary action if the procedure was fair.

rules.case_name: Canara Bank v. N. Govindan
rules.relevance: A binding precedent involving the same employer (Canara Bank) which holds that the Tribunal cannot interfere with the punishment imposed by the Disciplinary Authority merely because it considers the punishment harsh, unless it is shockingly disproportionate or arbitrary.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. T. Ramachandran
rules.reference: Union of India v. T. Ramachandran
rules.relevance: Clarifies that the Tribunal's role is not to re-hear the case but to ensure that the domestic enquiry was conducted fairly and that the conclusions drawn are not perverse.

The primary ground for judicial or tribunalal interference in disciplinary proceedings is a violation of natural justice (e.g., bias, lack of opportunity to defend). The facts state the enquiry was found fair, limiting the scope for interference.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: Holds that the Tribunal cannot interfere with the quantum of punishment unless it is so excessive as to be shocking to the conscience of the court, emphasizing the primacy of the Disciplinary Authority's discretion.

Empowers the appropriate government to refer disputes to adjudication. The interpretation of this section in conjunction with Section 11 limits the Tribunal's power to procedural review rather than substantive re-adjudication.

rules.case_name: Kerala State Electricity Board v. N. Mohan
rules.reference: Kerala State Electricity Board v. N. Mohan
rules.relevance: Reiterates that the Tribunal cannot re-appreciate evidence to arrive at a different conclusion than the Disciplinary Authority, provided the Authority's conclusion is based on some evidence.

While primarily applicable to civil servants, the principles of fair play and natural justice derived from Article 311 are often applied by analogy to bank employees in disciplinary matters to ensure procedural fairness, which was already established in this case.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1975
rules.relevance: This is the specific rule invoked by the Selection and Appointment Committee to carry forward the vacancy and fill it via promotion. The core legal issue is whether this rule applies when a recommended candidate is rejected by the Governor, or if it only applies when the number of successful direct recruits is inherently fewer than the vacancies.

Article 233 prescribes the method of appointment of district judges, requiring consultation with the High Court. It establishes the constitutional framework within which the UP Higher Judicial Service Rules operate, defining the roles of the Governor and the High Court in the appointment process.

Article 309 empowers the State Legislature to make regulations for the recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving the State. This article provides the legislative basis for the Uttar Pradesh Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1975, including Rule 8(2).

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh Sandhu
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes the principle that the Governor's power to appoint is not merely formal but involves satisfaction. It supports the view that the rejection of a candidate by the Governor is a valid exercise of power, creating a vacancy that may be treated differently from a situation where no candidate was selected.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: This case discusses the interpretation of service rules and the concept of 'vacancies'. It is relevant to determining whether a vacancy arises due to the Governor's rejection and whether such a vacancy must be filled from the merit list or can be carried forward/promoted as per specific rules.

rules.reference: Principle of Merit and Seniority in Judicial Appointments
rules.relevance: The appellant claims an automatic right based on merit. This principle argues that once a candidate is recommended by the High Court, they have a legitimate expectation of appointment unless the rules explicitly allow for carry-forward or promotion in such specific scenarios.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1975
rules.relevance: Rule 8 generally governs the method of recruitment (direct vs. promotion). Interpreting the entire rule in context is necessary to understand if the 'carry forward' provision in 8(2) is exhaustive or if general principles of filling vacancies from the merit list apply when a specific candidate is rejected.

rules.case_name: All India Judges' Association v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This case laid down guidelines for the appointment of district judges, emphasizing the importance of the High Court's recommendation and the need for a transparent and fair process. It supports the appellant's argument that the process should follow the merit list unless strictly prohibited.

rules.reference: The Uttar Pradesh Higher Judicial Service (Amendment) Act
rules.relevance: Any amendments to the 1975 Rules or the Act governing them may provide legislative intent regarding the treatment of vacancies arising from Governor's rejection versus insufficient candidates.

The appellant, having been recommended by the High Court, may claim a legitimate expectation of appointment. This principle is relevant to argue that the State cannot arbitrarily bypass the merit list without clear statutory authority.

Central to the issue of whether the High Court's direction to rectify a bid violates the principles of equality, fairness, and non-arbitrariness in public procurement, ensuring that the tender process remains transparent and competitive.

Relevant to the appellant's claim regarding the violation of natural justice due to non-impleadment. The right to a fair hearing (audi alteram partem) is a facet of Article 21, especially when the rights of a successful bidder are affected by a judicial order without their participation.

Addresses the procedural issue of non-impleadment. This rule mandates that all persons whose presence is necessary to enable the court to effectually and completely adjudicate upon and settle all questions involved in the controversy must be made parties.

rules.case_name: Tata Projects Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: Tata Projects Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: A key precedent establishing that the sanctity of the tender process must be maintained and that courts should not interfere to allow rectification of bids after opening unless there is a clear, unambiguous error that does not prejudice other bidders. It supports the argument against allowing post-opening modifications.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Associated Builders & Developers
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Associated Builders & Developers
rules.relevance: Relevant for the principle that the tendering authority has the discretion to reject bids that do not conform to the prescribed format or contain material errors, and that such decisions are subject to judicial review only if they are arbitrary or mala fide.

rules.reference: Principle of Sanctity of Tender Process
rules.relevance: A well-established legal principle in Indian administrative law that once bids are opened, they cannot be altered or rectified to the detriment of other bidders, ensuring level playing field and preventing manipulation.

rules.reference: Audi Alteram Partem (Right to Fair Hearing)
rules.relevance: Directly relevant to the second issue. The appellant (H1 bidder) had a vested interest in the outcome of the writ petition. Excluding them from the proceedings violates the fundamental principle of natural justice that no one should be condemned unheard.

rules.case_name: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Supports the view that gross negligence or inadvertent errors in quoting financial bids, especially when they deviate significantly from the market rate or template, are not rectifiable after bid opening to protect the integrity of the process.

Relevant for interpreting the 'Bill of Quantities' and the specific clauses of the NIB. It aids in determining whether the error was a mere clerical mistake capable of rectification or a substantive error in the bid itself.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. M/s. Rani Builders
rules.reference: Union of India v. M/s. Rani Builders
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that the tendering authority's decision to reject a non-conforming bid is final unless challenged on grounds of illegality or irrationality, and courts should not rewrite the tender document or allow post-facto clarifications that alter the bid's substance.

rules.case_name: State (NCT of Delhi) v. Ajay Kumar Tyagi
rules.reference: State (NCT of Delhi) v. Ajay Kumar Tyagi
rules.relevance: This is the leading Supreme Court precedent holding that exoneration in departmental proceedings does not automatically bar criminal prosecution, as the standards of proof and purposes of the two proceedings are different. The High Court refused to follow this, making it central to the appeal.

rules.case_name: Radheshyam Kejriwal v. State of West Bengal
rules.reference: Radheshyam Kejriwal v. State of West Bengal
rules.relevance: The High Court relied on this case to quash the criminal proceedings, arguing that if an employee is exonerated in disciplinary proceedings (which have a lower standard of proof), criminal proceedings (higher standard) should also be quashed. The Supreme Court appeal challenges this application.

The criminal prosecution was initiated by the Lokayukta under this Act. The scope of the Lokayukta's powers and the nature of proceedings under this Act are relevant to determining if the High Court had jurisdiction to quash them based on departmental outcomes.

The core legal issue rests on the distinction between the 'preponderance of probability' standard in disciplinary proceedings and the 'beyond reasonable doubt' standard in criminal trials. Authorities establishing that these are independent processes are relevant.

rules.reference: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The High Court exercised its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to quash the criminal proceedings. The appeal involves reviewing the propriety of this exercise of extraordinary jurisdiction.
The High Court declared State (NCT of Delhi) v. Ajay Kumar Tyagi to be 'per incuriam'. The Supreme Court must decide if the High Court was correct in disregarding a binding Supreme Court precedent.

Although the prosecution is under the Lokayukta Act, the underlying offence (demanding/accepting bribe) is typically covered under the Prevention of Corruption Act. The principles regarding the independence of criminal prosecution for corruption apply here.

rules.reference: Independence of Disciplinary and Criminal Proceedings
rules.relevance: Legal principle that disciplinary proceedings are for administrative control and removal from service, while criminal proceedings are for punishment. One does not necessarily dictate the outcome of the other.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsamma
rules.relevance: Often cited alongside Radheshyam Kejriwal, this case discusses the relationship between departmental and criminal proceedings, providing context for the High Court's reasoning.

While the High Court used Article 226, the principles governing the quashing of criminal proceedings (inherent powers) under Section 482 CrPC are analogous and often cited to define the limits of judicial interference in ongoing criminal trials.

The High Court granted bail under its writ jurisdiction. The Supreme Court's review of this order involves assessing whether the High Court exercised its extraordinary powers under Article 226 judiciously and in accordance with established legal principles regarding bail.

The High Court relied on the view that the offences were triable by a Magistrate to grant bail. Section 437 governs bail in non-bailable offences triable by a Magistrate. The Supreme Court must determine if this classification was correct given the gravity of the charges (including potential Section 409 IPC) and if the conditions for bail under this section were met.

The State submitted that Section 409 (Criminal Breach of Trust by a public servant, banker, etc.) was added during investigation. This is a serious offence with higher bail thresholds. The relevance lies in determining if the inclusion of this charge alters the triability and the gravity of the offence, thereby affecting the bail decision.

The appellant alleged cheating involving ₹6.5 crores. Section 420 is a core charge in the FIR. The Supreme Court must assess if the High Court adequately considered the magnitude of the fraud and the specific allegations of cheating when granting bail.

The FIR includes charges of forgery of valuable security. The recovery of forged Aadhaar and PAN cards supports this charge. This aggravates the nature of the crime, suggesting a premeditated and sophisticated criminal design, which is relevant to the bail assessment.

rules.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent establishes the general principles of bail, emphasizing that bail is the rule and jail is the exception, but also outlining factors like the nature of evidence, severity of punishment, and possibility of tampering. It provides the framework for reviewing the High Court's discretion.

rules.case_name: Sanjay Chandra v. CBI
rules.relevance: This case is crucial for the issue of 'parity'. It holds that the principle of parity is not an absolute right and cannot be invoked if the accused has distinct aggravating circumstances, such as criminal antecedents or a history of absconding, which differentiate them from co-accused.

The High Court granted bail based on parity with co-accused. The legal principle relevant here is that parity is not a standalone ground for bail if the accused's individual circumstances (like absconding, forged IDs, and other FIRs) make them a flight risk or a threat to the administration of justice.

The respondent absconded for 20 months and used forged identities. The legal principle is that a history of absconding and suppression of material facts (other FIRs) are strong indicators of flight risk and lack of cooperation, which are valid grounds to deny bail regardless of the period of incarceration.

Although the High Court granted bail, the Supreme Court's intervention in a bail matter often involves reviewing the exercise of discretion under Section 439 (Sessions Court/High Court bail) or the writ jurisdiction. The distinction between triability by Magistrate vs. Sessions Court is pivotal here.

The core issue revolves around the right to life with dignity, humane living conditions, and rehabilitation for inmates of Beggars' Homes. Article 21 is the primary constitutional guarantee invoked in the PIL and forms the basis for the State's obligation to provide adequate food, shelter, and medical care.

The appellant approached the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue directions or orders for the enforcement of rights under Part III, which is the procedural basis for the appeal and the Court's monitoring of the implementation of the High Court's order.

The original writ petition was filed in the High Court of Delhi under Article 226. The appeal challenges the High Court's disposal of the implementation application under this article, specifically questioning the propriety of a non-speaking order in a matter involving fundamental rights.

rules.case_name: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
rules.reference: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent established that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to live with human dignity and all that goes along with it, including adequate nutrition, clothing, and shelter. It is directly relevant to the standards of care required in Beggars' Homes.

rules.case_name: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India
rules.reference: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (Asiad Workers Case)
rules.relevance: This case expanded the scope of Article 21 to include the right to live in human dignity and free from exploitation. It is highly relevant to the plight of beggars and the State's duty to ensure their humane treatment and rehabilitation.

rules.reference: Principle of Speaking Orders in Writ Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: The appeal challenges the High Court's summary disposal without a speaking order. Legal principles dictate that courts exercising writ jurisdiction, especially in matters affecting fundamental rights, must pass reasoned orders to ensure accountability and allow for effective appellate review.

The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) is typically responsible for the maintenance of Beggars' Homes and public health infrastructure. Provisions regarding the duties of the MCD in maintaining public institutions and ensuring hygiene are relevant to the allegations of negligence and water contamination.

rules.reference: The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (or relevant Food Safety Laws)
rules.relevance: Given the allegations of cholera outbreak and food quality issues, statutory provisions governing food safety and hygiene in public institutions are relevant to determine the standard of care required and the liability of the authorities for serving contaminated food.

rules.case_name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
rules.reference: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
rules.relevance: This case established the Supreme Court's power to monitor the implementation of its orders and directions in PILs. It supports the Court's extensive monitoring of the Beggars' Home conditions from 2004 to 2025 to ensure compliance with constitutional mandates.

rules.reference: The Delhi State Legal Services Authority Act, 1987
rules.relevance: The Delhi State Legal Services Authority (DSLSA) conducted inspections and submitted reports. The statutory framework empowering LSAs to monitor the implementation of legal aid and welfare schemes for vulnerable groups is relevant to the procedural history and the credibility of the inspection reports.

rules.case_name: S. Nithya v. Union of India
rules.citation: As cited in the case brief
rules.reference: S. Nithya v. Union of India
