rules.relevance: Legal principle that a party who participates in arbitration without raising jurisdictional objections is estopped from raising them later at the challenge stage, unless the defect is fundamental and apparent on the face of the record.
Legal doctrine relevant to the issue of whether L.G. Chaudhary (II) is per incuriam for not considering Lion Engineering, affecting the binding nature of the precedents.
Provision regarding the rules governing the substantive issues; relevant to determining whether the parties' agreement to arbitrate under the 1996 Act excluded the application of the MP Act, 1983.

rules.case_name: Bharat Broadband Network Ltd. v. United Telecoms Ltd.
rules.reference: Bharat Broadband Network Ltd. v. United Telecoms Ltd.
rules.relevance: Supreme Court judgment clarifying the scope of Section 34 and the limited role of courts in reviewing arbitral awards, supporting the principle that jurisdictional pleas not raised earlier are generally barred.

The prosecution case relies entirely on circumstantial evidence. The court must apply the principle that the chain of circumstances must be complete, unbroken, and consistent with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused, excluding every other hypothesis of innocence.

rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on 'Last Seen Theory'
rules.relevance: The prosecution relies on the 'last-seen theory' (PW-5 testifying the appellant was last seen with the victims). Precedents establish that this theory can sustain a conviction only if the time gap between the last sighting and discovery of the body is not so large as to create reasonable doubt about the accused's involvement.

The appellant made extra-judicial confessions leading to the recovery of a sickle, clothes, and a gold chain. Section 27 governs the admissibility of information received from an accused person in police custody leading to the discovery of a fact, which is crucial for corroborating the confession and establishing possession of incriminating articles.

The extra-judicial confessions made by the appellant need corroboration. Section 157 allows previous statements to be used to corroborate the testimony of a witness (or in this context, the consistency of the accused's conduct/confession), ensuring the confession is voluntary and reliable.
The appellant was convicted for murder. The court must determine if the circumstantial evidence sufficiently proves the intention or knowledge required under Section 302 to cause death.

The appellant was convicted for rape. The court must evaluate if the DNA evidence and circumstantial circumstances sufficiently prove sexual intercourse without consent, despite the disputed chain of custody.

rules.reference: Admissibility of DNA Evidence and Chain of Custody
rules.relevance: The appellant challenges the DNA evidence due to procedural lapses in the chain of custody. The court must apply legal principles regarding the reliability of scientific evidence and whether minor procedural irregularities vitiate the evidence or merely affect its weight.

A Test Identification Parade (T.I.P.) was conducted. Section 100 of the CrPC governs the procedure for identification of persons. The court must assess if the T.I.P. was conducted in accordance with statutory requirements to ensure its reliability as corroborative evidence.

The appellant was sentenced to death. The court must apply the 'rarest of rare' doctrine to determine if the aggravating circumstances (murder and rape of two victims) outweigh mitigating circumstances, justifying the extreme penalty.

The appellant was convicted for theft (demanding jewellery). While less central than the murder/rape charges, the recovery of the gold chain links to this charge and supports the motive and sequence of events.

This is the primary statutory provision prescribing the specific enrolment fees (Rs. 600 for general, Rs. 100 for SC/ST) payable to State Bar Councils. The core legal question is whether SBCs can charge fees in excess of this explicit statutory limit.
The petitioner argues that charging arbitrary and varying fees beyond the statutory limit violates the right to equality and protection against arbitrary state action.
The petitioner contends that imposing excessive mandatory fees infringes upon the fundamental right to practice any profession, trade, or business.
This is the procedural basis under which the petitioner filed the writ petition in the Supreme Court for the enforcement of fundamental rights.
Establishes the Bar Council of India and State Bar Councils as the statutory bodies responsible for regulating the legal profession, defining their scope of authority and functions.

Governs the general procedure for enrolment of advocates. The interpretation of this section in conjunction with Section 24(1)(f) determines if 'enrolment' can be conditioned on payment of non-statutory miscellaneous fees.

rules.reference: Principle of Statutory Interpretation: Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius
rules.relevance: Relevant to determining if the specific enumeration of fees in Section 24(1)(f) excludes the power of SBCs to levy other mandatory charges for enrolment.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Colourable Legislation / Ultra Vires
rules.relevance: Relevant to assessing whether the SBCs and BCI, by charging fees beyond the statutory limit, are acting beyond their statutory powers (ultra vires) or attempting to indirectly tax what the statute has expressly limited.

The BCI resolution directing SBCs to charge Rs. 6,000 is a key factual element. Its validity is challenged as it contradicts the explicit fee structure in the Act, raising issues of whether a resolution can override a statute.

rules.case_name: Bar Council of India v. A.K. Balaji
rules.reference: Bar Council of India v. A.K. Balaji
rules.relevance: While primarily concerning eligibility criteria, this precedent establishes the Supreme Court's strict scrutiny of BCI regulations and resolutions against the parent statute (Advocates Act) and the Constitution, reinforcing that statutory bodies cannot act beyond the Act's mandate.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
rules.relevance: This is the primary statutory provision governing the procedure for sampling and preservation of evidence in NDPS cases. The appellant's core contention is that the conviction is vitiated due to non-compliance with this section.

rules.reference: NDPS Rules, 1985 (or relevant Standing Orders in force at the time)
rules.relevance: The appellant specifically alleges violation of Rule 10 regarding the procedure for drawing samples. Although the brief mentions 'NDPS Rules, 2022', the seizure occurred under earlier guidelines (Standing Order No. 1 of 1989), making the procedural rules applicable at the time of seizure critical.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing the distinction between 'mandatory' and 'directory' provisions in the NDPS Act. It holds that non-compliance with Section 52A does not automatically vitiate the trial unless it causes prejudice to the accused or affects the fairness of the trial.

rules.case_name: Laxman v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: This case is highly relevant to the specific issue of 'bunching' or mixing packets. It held that mixing identical packets to draw a composite sample is permissible and does not vitiate the trial, provided the procedure is followed to ensure representative sampling.

rules.case_name: State of Gujarat v. Mohanlal
rules.relevance: Relevant for establishing that minor procedural irregularities in sampling, if they do not prejudice the accused or affect the integrity of the sample, do not warrant acquittal.

The specific procedural guideline in force at the time of the seizure, which prescribed methods for bunching identical packets into lots and drawing representative composite samples. The court must determine if the IO's actions complied with this specific order.

rules.reference: Principle of Prejudice in Procedural Non-Compliance
rules.relevance: The legal principle that procedural lapses in criminal trials, particularly in special statutes like NDPS, must be examined to see if they caused prejudice to the accused. If the sample integrity is maintained and the accused had an opportunity to challenge it, the trial is not vitiated.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Balram
rules.relevance: Supports the view that the mixing of similar packets for the purpose of drawing a sample is a recognized practice to ensure uniformity and does not constitute a fatal irregularity.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The substantive offence under which the appellant was convicted. While the appeal focuses on procedure, the conviction under this section is the subject matter of the challenge.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Manohar Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Manohar Lal
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that the prosecution must prove that the sample drawn was representative and that the procedure adopted did not compromise the identity of the substance.

This is the primary statutory provision under challenge. It mandates specific age limits (23-50 for females, 26-55 for males) for intending couples to obtain an eligibility certificate. The core legal question is whether this provision applies to couples who had already created and frozen embryos before the Act came into force.

This transitional provision grants a ten-month gestation period to existing surrogate mothers. The relevance lies in interpreting its scope: whether it protects only surrogate mothers already pregnant or if it implicitly protects intending couples who had initiated the process (e.g., frozen embryos) prior to the Act's enforcement.

The intending couples likely challenge the age restrictions as arbitrary or unreasonable classification. Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and prohibits arbitrary state action. The court must determine if the age limit is a rational classification based on scientific concerns regarding gamete quality and parenting capability.

The right to form a family and procreate is part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. The couples argue that barring them from using their previously created embryos violates their fundamental right to parenthood, especially given their medical history and prior investment in the process.

A general principle of statutory interpretation is that laws are presumed to operate prospectively unless expressly stated otherwise. The court must decide if the Act's application to couples with frozen embryos constitutes an impermissible retrospective operation affecting vested rights.

The couples claim vested rights because they had completed the medical procedure of creating embryos before the Act came into force. The court must determine if the creation and freezing of embryos constitute a 'vested right' that cannot be extinguished by subsequent legislation.

rules.case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
rules.reference: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This landmark judgment affirmed the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21, including the right to make intimate personal choices regarding reproduction and family planning. It supports the couples' argument that the state's interference in their reproductive choices must be strictly scrutinized.

rules.case_name: X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi
rules.reference: X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi
rules.relevance: This case recognized the right of single women to access ART (Assisted Reproductive Technology) services. While the current case involves couples, this precedent establishes the judiciary's willingness to protect reproductive rights against restrictive statutory interpretations, potentially influencing the interpretation of 'intending couple' and age limits.

Section 6 deals with the effect of repeal and savings. Although the Surrogacy Act is a new enactment, principles from Section 6 regarding the preservation of rights acquired, acts done, or liabilities incurred under previous laws (or common law/medical practice) may be relevant in determining if the couples' prior actions are protected.

The court must harmoniously construct Section 4 (age limits) and Section 53 (transitional provision). If Section 53 is read narrowly to protect only pregnant surrogates, it may create an absurdity where couples who initiated the process are left without remedy. Harmonious construction may lead to a broader interpretation of 'existing cases'.

rules.reference: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
rules.relevance: This is the central statutory provision in dispute. It bars the Central Government from initiating proceedings if the State Government has already initiated proceedings on the same subject matter. The core legal question is whether issuing summons constitutes 'initiation of proceedings' under this clause.

rules.reference: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
rules.relevance: This section empowers the proper officer to issue summons for production of documents or attendance of persons. The appeal hinges on whether the exercise of this power amounts to the 'initiation of proceedings' barred by Section 6(2)(b).

rules.reference: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
rules.relevance: This provision deals with the cross-empowerment of officers of the Central and State Governments. The scope of an 'Order' under this section is relevant to determining the jurisdictional boundaries and the nature of the Central authority's actions.

rules.reference: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
rules.relevance: The State authority initiated proceedings under this section via a show cause notice. This establishes the fact that proceedings had already commenced by the State, triggering the potential bar under Section 6(2)(b).

rules.reference: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
rules.relevance: The Central authority conducted a search under this provision. While the primary dispute is about summons, the search is part of the investigative sequence by the Central authority that the petitioner challenges as ultra vires due to the State's prior initiation.

The legal principle regarding what constitutes the 'initiation of proceedings' versus preliminary inquiry or investigation is central to the case. The High Court distinguished between the two, and the Supreme Court must decide if this distinction holds under the CGST Act.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Res Judicata / Lis Pendens in Tax Proceedings
rules.relevance: The concept of preventing parallel proceedings on the same subject matter by different authorities (Central vs State) is a key legal principle underlying Section 6(2)(b). The interpretation of 'same subject matter' is crucial.
The writ petition was filed under this article in the High Court. The Supreme Court's review of the High Court's exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 is part of the procedural history.

The Special Leave Petition was filed under this article, granting the Supreme Court the power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India.

rules.reference: Jurisdictional Bar in Dual Tax Regimes
rules.relevance: The principle that once one authority (State) has seized jurisdiction over a specific tax liability, the other authority (Central) is barred from acting on the same subject matter to avoid harassment and conflicting orders.

rules.reference: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016
rules.relevance: This is the specific regulation at the heart of the dispute. It prescribes the 90-day timeline for depositing the balance sale consideration and states that failure to do so results in the cancellation of the sale. The central legal question is whether this provision is mandatory or directory.

Section 34 deals with the liquidation process and the powers of the liquidator to sell assets. It provides the statutory framework under which the liquidator conducted the auction and executed the sale deed, establishing the context for the regulations.

This section grants the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) the power to make such orders as it deems just and equitable. The NCLT relied on this inherent power to extend the timeline despite the strict wording of the IBBI Regulations, citing the extraordinary circumstances of the pandemic.

rules.case_name: Sri Lakshmi Hotels Private Limited v. KMC Speciality Hospitals (India) Limited
rules.citation: Civil Appeal No. 5048 of 2021 (or relevant citation from the brief context)
rules.relevance: This is the case itself. The Supreme Court's decision in this matter establishes the precedent that the 90-day timeline in Rule 12 is directory, not mandatory, and that the Adjudicating Authority has the power to extend time in exceptional circumstances like the COVID-19 lockdown to prevent injustice.

rules.reference: Principle of Equity and Good Conscience
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that where a strict application of a procedural rule would lead to manifest injustice, especially when the delay is due to force majeure (lockdown) and the purchaser has acted in good faith (investing in construction), equity should prevail. The substantial performance by the bidder supports this.

The nationwide lockdown imposed by the Government of India constitutes a force majeure event. This legal principle justifies the relaxation of strict timelines as the delay was beyond the control of the auction purchaser, making it unreasonable to enforce the cancellation clause strictly.

Section 35 outlines the role and powers of the liquidator. It supports the liquidator's authority to conduct the auction and execute the sale deed, which was the subject of the challenge. The validity of the liquidator's actions is tied to the interpretation of the regulations under this section.

rules.case_name: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.relevance: While primarily about resolution plans, this precedent emphasizes the commercial reality and the intent of the IBC to maximize value. It supports the view that procedural technicalities should not defeat the substantive goal of the insolvency process, especially when a successful bid has been made and acted upon.

The auction purchaser had deposited the balance amount (albeit late) and had already constructed a hospital on the property. This principle suggests that where the main purpose of the contract (payment and transfer) has been substantially performed, minor procedural delays should not invalidate the transaction.

Section 151 of the CPC deals with the inherent powers of the court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice. Although the IBC is a special law, the NCLT's exercise of inherent powers to extend time is analogous to this principle, ensuring that the court can prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the respondent sought anticipatory bail. The core legal question is whether the phrase 'reason to believe that he may be arrested' in this section is satisfied when the accused is already in custody for a different offense.

rules.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: This is the landmark Supreme Court judgment that laid down the principles governing the grant of anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC. It defines the scope of 'reason to believe' and the conditions for granting such bail, which is essential for interpreting the statute in the context of the current appeal.

rules.case_name: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment reiterates and clarifies the principles of anticipatory bail, emphasizing that it is an exception to the general rule of arrest. It is relevant to determine if the legislative intent behind Section 438 allows for its invocation by a person already in custody for a separate matter.

rules.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Balchand
rules.relevance: Representing the view of the Rajasthan High Court mentioned in the facts, this authority holds that an application for anticipatory bail is not maintainable if the accused is already in custody for another case, as there is no apprehension of arrest for the specific case in question.

rules.case_name: State of Delhi v. Sanjay Kumar
rules.reference: State of Delhi v. Sanjay Kumar
rules.relevance: Representing the view of the Delhi High Court mentioned in the facts, this authority supports the contention that anticipatory bail is not maintainable for an accused already in judicial custody for a different offense, contributing to the divergence of opinion cited in the brief.

rules.case_name: State of Bombay v. Dnyaneshwar
rules.relevance: Representing the view of the Bombay High Court mentioned in the facts, this authority holds that custody in one case does not preclude an accused from seeking anticipatory bail in a different case, supporting the High Court's order being challenged.

These are the specific offenses alleged in CR No. 806 of 2019. The nature and gravity of these offenses (cheating, criminal breach of trust, forgery) are relevant factors for the court to consider on the merits of the anticipatory bail application, as per the principles laid down in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia.

Section 437 deals with bail for non-bailable offenses. It is relevant for comparison, as the distinction between regular bail (Section 437) and anticipatory bail (Section 438) is central to the argument that an accused in custody should seek regular bail rather than anticipatory bail for a new case.

The legal principle that anticipatory bail is a pre-arrest remedy. The court must decide whether 'apprehension of arrest' can logically exist for Case B when the accused is physically detained for Case A, or if the statute protects against the procedural act of arrest in Case B regardless of physical custody in Case A.

Article 21 guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. The interpretation of Section 438 CrPC is often guided by the need to protect personal liberty from arbitrary arrest, which may support the view that an accused should have the opportunity to seek protection from arrest in a new case even if detained in another.

This is the primary statutory provision requiring prior sanction for prosecution of offenses under the UAPA. The core dispute concerns the validity of the sanction granted under this section and whether defects in its grant can be challenged at the appellate stage.

rules.reference: Unlawful Activities (Prevention) (Recommendation & Sanction of Prosecution) Rules, 2008
rules.relevance: The appellant contends that the sanction was invalid due to violation of statutory timelines prescribed in these rules. The court must determine if these timelines are mandatory or directory and if their violation vitiates the sanction.
The appellant claims applicability of the exemption under this section. The court needs to decide if this exemption applies to the appellant at the current advanced stage of the trial.

These sections govern the joinder of charges and joint trials. The appellant argues that the joinder of charges and joint trial with other accused violates these provisions, necessitating a review of the procedural legality of the trial structure.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Natwarlal Damodardas Thakkar (1960) or similar binding precedents on Section 45 UAPA
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on UAPA Sanction
rules.relevance: Precedents are needed to determine the stage at which the validity of a sanction order can be challenged (trial vs. appellate stage) and the standard of review for 'application of mind' by the sanctioning authority.

rules.reference: Principle of Independent Review for Sanction
rules.relevance: The appellant argues that the short duration for recommendation and sanction indicates a lack of independent review. Legal principles regarding the necessity of independent application of mind by the sanctioning authority are relevant here.
The High Court upheld NIA jurisdiction. This section defines the jurisdiction of the NIA to investigate scheduled offenses, which is a foundational element of the case's procedural history.

The appellant initially approached the High Court under this section (inherent powers) to quash the sanction and cognizance. The scope of this power vis-a-vis statutory sanction requirements is relevant context.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Waiver/Estoppel in Criminal Proceedings
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether the objection to the sanction order was waived by not raising it before the Trial Court, given the trial is at an advanced stage.
Defines the offenses related to terrorist acts and funding, which form the substantive basis of the charges against the appellant as an associate of PLFI.

This is the specific statutory provision under which the Assessing Authority levied tax on the value of ink and processing materials. The core legal question is whether these consumables fall within the definition of 'goods' transferred under this section in the context of a works contract.

Defines 'goods'. The appellant argues that lottery tickets are 'actionable claims' and not goods, and that ink/chemicals are consumed, not transferred. The interpretation of this definition is central to determining taxability.

Defines 'sale'. The dispute hinges on whether the transfer of property in the ink and chemicals (which are consumed in the printing process) constitutes a 'sale' or 'transfer of property in goods' liable to tax.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Aristo Printers Pvt. Ltd.
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Aristo Printers Pvt. Ltd.
rules.relevance: This is the specific Supreme Court judgment deciding the appeal. It establishes the precedent that in a works contract for printing, consumables like ink and chemicals are not 'goods' transferred to the principal and thus not taxable under Section 3F(1)(b).

The appellant's argument that lottery tickets are 'actionable claims' rather than 'goods' relies on this legal distinction. If the tickets are actionable claims, the transaction may not attract trade tax on goods.

A key principle in works contract taxation: materials consumed in the process of rendering a service (like ink in printing) do not involve a transfer of property in goods to the client, and therefore are not taxable as sales of goods.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Hindustan Paper Corporation Ltd.
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Hindustan Paper Corporation Ltd.
rules.relevance: A relevant precedent often cited in UP trade tax cases regarding the nature of works contracts and the taxability of materials used in the execution of such contracts, providing context for the Tribunal's initial decision.
Defines 'actionable claim'. Relevant to the appellant's argument that the printed lottery tickets constitute actionable claims rather than tangible goods, potentially exempting them from trade tax.

Rules under the UP Trade Tax Act often provide specific guidelines for valuing works contracts and determining the portion of value attributable to goods versus services. Relevant for assessing the methodology of tax calculation.

Trade tax is a tax on the transfer of property in goods. The central issue is whether the property in the ink and chemicals was transferred to the client or merely consumed by the printer to provide a service.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

rules.case_name: Babulal Parate v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Babulal Parate v. State of Maharashtra

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal

The procedural provision under which the appellant sought anticipatory bail. The interplay between this general provision and the specific bar in Section 18 of the SC/ST Act is the core procedural conflict.

rules.case_name: Rama Bai v. State of Karnataka

rules.case_name: Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra

One of the charges against the appellant. While the SC/ST Act charges are primary, this provision relates to causing disturbance or annoyance, which may be considered in the overall assessment of the appellant's conduct and the nature of the video.

rules.reference: Freedom of Speech and Expression vs. Atrocities

rules.reference: Tamil Nadu Cultivating Tenants’ Protection Act, 1955

rules.case_name: K. Venugopala Pillai v. K. Venugopala Pillai

rules.case_name: M. Venkatachala v. M. Venkatachala

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh

Charges under this section (rioting armed with deadly weapon) were part of the original chargesheet. It supports the finding of an unlawful assembly armed with lethal weapons, which is a prerequisite for applying Section 149.

Governs the recording of First Information Reports (FIR). The appellants argue that the statement of PW-20 was not the FIR because police had prior knowledge. This section defines what constitutes an FIR and its evidentiary value.

Governs the examination of witnesses by police. The appellants contend that PW-20's statement was a subsequent statement under this section rather than an FIR, which affects its weight and admissibility as the primary account of the incident.

rules.reference: Principle of Individual Identification in Unlawful Assembly
rules.relevance: A key legal principle in cases involving Section 149 IPC. Courts must distinguish between active participants in the unlawful assembly and innocent bystanders or mere spectators. The appeal argues this distinction was not made, violating the rule of prudence.

The appellants highlight material inconsistencies in witness testimony and conflicts with medical evidence. This principle requires courts to scrutinize ocular evidence for reliability, especially when there are contradictions or lack of corroboration.

The appellants argue the FIR was ante-dated and tainted. Legal principles regarding the delay in lodging FIR and the possibility of tutelage or coaching are relevant to assessing the credibility of the prosecution's case.

Attempt to murder was one of the charges. While the conviction is for murder, the evidence for attempt to murder (injuries to witnesses) is relevant to establishing the intent and common object of the assembly.

Right to life and fair trial. The appellants' challenge to the conviction based on insufficient evidence and procedural irregularities (FIR issues) touches upon the fundamental right to a fair trial and protection against arbitrary deprivation of liberty.

This is the primary statutory provision at issue. It renders a person ineligible to be an arbitrator if they fall under the Seventh Schedule, specifically addressing the issue of unilateral appointment by one party to the dispute.

The Seventh Schedule lists categories of persons who are ineligible to be arbitrators. The core legal question is whether the Chairman of AAI, acting as the appointing authority for a party to the contract, falls under the category of 'unilateral appointment' prohibited by this schedule.

The proviso allows a party to waive the ineligibility of an arbitrator if there is an 'express agreement in writing'. The appellants' conduct (participation, lack of objection) is being tested against this requirement to determine if waiver occurred.

rules.case_name: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC & Anr. v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
rules.reference: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC & Anr. v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent is central to the interpretation of Section 12(5) and the Seventh Schedule. It held that unilateral appointment of an arbitrator by one party is per se ineligible, establishing the strict standard applied in this appeal.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Concord Biotech Ltd.
rules.reference: Union of India v. Concord Biotech Ltd.
rules.relevance: This case deals with the applicability of the 2015 Amendment Act to pending proceedings and the interpretation of 'express agreement in writing' for waiver of ineligibility, which is directly relevant to the waiver issue raised by the High Court.

The appellants challenged the arbitral awards under this section. The issue of whether an objection to the arbitrator's eligibility can be raised for the first time at this stage is a procedural question governed by the interplay of Section 34 and Section 12.

Section 13 mandates that a challenge to an arbitrator must be made within 15 days of becoming aware of the grounds. The High Court's finding of waiver relies on the appellants' failure to raise objections under this section during the proceedings.

The facts mention that parties jointly applied for extensions of time under this section. This demonstrates active participation in the arbitration process, which the High Court used to argue that the appellants submitted to the jurisdiction and waived their right to challenge eligibility.

The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the appeals under this section, which provides the right to appeal against certain orders passed by the Single Judge. This is the procedural basis for the High Court's decision being appealed to the Supreme Court.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Waiver and Estoppel in Arbitration
rules.relevance: The legal principle that a party cannot take advantage of its own wrong or delay in raising objections. The court must determine if the appellants' conduct (filing claims, seeking extensions) amounts to an estoppel from challenging the arbitrator's appointment later.
The primary substantive charge under which the appellants were convicted for murder. The appeal challenges the sufficiency of evidence to sustain this conviction.

The provision for common intention relied upon to convict the appellants jointly. The acquittal of the third accused (father) raises issues regarding the application of common intention among the remaining accused.
The alternative charge proposed by the appellants. The court must determine if the evidence supports only culpable homicide not amounting to murder due to lack of premeditation.

The appellants challenge the reliability of the sole eye-witness's statement on the ground that it was recorded belatedly (after five days). This provision governs the recording of statements by police.

The trial court recorded the demeanour of the witness Lata Bai under this section. This is relevant to assessing the credibility of the sole eye-witness despite contradictions and hostility of other witnesses.

A central legal issue is whether the conviction can stand on the testimony of a single eye-witness (Lata Bai) who is an interested party (mother of deceased), despite minor discrepancies and belated statement recording.

The appellants argue that the acquittal of their father (Chintaram) on the same evidence necessitates their acquittal. The court must decide if parity is mandatory or if individual culpability can be distinguished.
Several prosecution witnesses turned hostile. The court must apply principles regarding the admissibility and weight of statements of hostile witnesses and whether they vitiate the prosecution case.

rules.reference: Delay in FIR and Statement Recording
rules.relevance: The delay in recording the statement of the sole eye-witness and the timing of the FIR are challenged. The court must evaluate if the delay is satisfactorily explained and affects the core of the prosecution case.

Blood-stained weapons were recovered from the father's room at the instance of the appellants. This corroborative evidence is relevant to linking the appellants to the crime scene and the act of murder.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. Section 2 mandates that no forest land or reserved forest shall be de-reserved or used for non-forest purposes without the prior approval of the Central Government. The core issue is whether the State Government's allotment and permission for non-agricultural use violated this mandatory requirement.

rules.case_name: Nagrik Chetna Manch v. Union of India
rules.reference: Nagrik Chetna Manch v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This is the specific case from which the facts are drawn. The Supreme Court's judgment in this matter directly addresses the validity of the allotment, the application of the Forest (Conservation) Act, the doctrine of public trust, and the status of the land as forest land despite long-term non-use.

One of the key issues is whether the doctrine of public trust applies, rendering the State's action of allotting forest land for private commercial use illegal. This principle holds that certain resources (like forests) are held in trust by the government for the public and cannot be alienated for private gain.

The defense argues that the land ceased to be forest land due to long-term non-use (desuetude). The court must determine if this doctrine applies to statutory reservations under the Forest Act, particularly in light of the Supreme Court's interpretation in the T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad case and the present appeal.

This provision was used to originally notify the land as a Reserved Forest in 1879. It establishes the initial legal status of the land as forest land, which is the foundation for the application of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.

rules.case_name: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
rules.reference: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This landmark judgment defined the scope of 'forest land' under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, holding that the definition is not limited to land recorded as forest in government records but includes all areas defined as forest under any enactment. This precedent is crucial in rejecting the argument that the land lost its forest status due to lack of specific records or non-use.

rules.reference: Bona Fide Purchaser for Value Without Notice
rules.relevance: RRCHS claims protection as a bona fide purchaser. The court must evaluate whether a purchaser can claim this status when the underlying transaction involves a violation of a mandatory statutory prohibition (Section 2 of the FCA, 1980) and involves forged documents, which negates the 'without notice' and 'good faith' elements.

The inquiry by the State CID confirmed that the Gazette Notification of 1944 produced by RRCHS was forged. This implicates provisions related to forgery and using forged documents as genuine, which undermines the legitimacy of RRCHS's title claim and supports the CEC's recommendation for prosecution.

rules.reference: Rules of the Central Empowered Committee (CEC)
rules.relevance: The CEC was constituted by the Supreme Court to monitor the implementation of its orders in environmental matters. The CEC's recommendation to cancel the allotment and restore the land is a critical procedural step and factual finding that the court must consider in deciding the appeal.

Article 21 (Right to Life) has been interpreted to include the right to a healthy environment. The illegal conversion of forest land for commercial housing violates this right, providing a constitutional basis for the court to intervene and protect the forest ecosystem.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the Transfer Petition was filed. The core legal issue is whether the High Court can exercise its power under this section to transfer a case on the ground of lack of territorial jurisdiction or to prevent harassment.

This section defines the offence of dishonour of cheque. The underlying criminal complaint is based on this provision, and the interpretation of where the cause of action arises under this section is central to the jurisdictional dispute.

This provision specifically grants territorial jurisdiction to the court within whose local limits the drawer's bank account is situated or where the cheque is presented for collection. The respondent Bank relies on this to establish jurisdiction in Chandigarh.

rules.case_name: Dashrath Rameshchandra Shewale v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Dashrath Rameshchandra Shewale v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent interpreting Section 142(2)(a) of the NI Act. It clarifies that the place where the cheque is presented for collection is a valid place for filing the complaint, supporting the Bank's argument regarding Chandigarh jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Natwarlal Damodardas Thakkar
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Natwarlal Damodardas Thakkar
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes the principle that the High Court's power to transfer under Section 406 Cr.P.C. is not an appellate remedy for correcting jurisdictional errors but is exercised only when it is 'expedient for the ends of justice'. It addresses the issue of whether lack of jurisdiction alone justifies transfer.

rules.reference: Expediency for the ends of justice
rules.relevance: This is the governing legal principle under Section 406 Cr.P.C. The court must determine if transferring the case serves the ends of justice, balancing the petitioner's claim of harassment and inconvenience against the respondent's claim of valid statutory jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: Kusum Ingots & Steel Works Pvt. Ltd. v. Bank of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Kusum Ingots & Steel Works Pvt. Ltd. v. Bank of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment interprets the phrase 'cause of action' in the context of Section 138 NI Act, holding that the cause of action arises at multiple places, including where the cheque is presented. This supports the Bank's contention that Chandigarh is a valid forum.

This section deals with the place of inquiry and trial in general criminal cases. It is relevant to contrast the general rule of territorial jurisdiction with the specific provisions of the NI Act and to understand the petitioner's argument that the Chandigarh court lacked jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of Section 406 Cr.P.C. and emphasizes that the power of transfer is extraordinary and should be used sparingly, primarily to prevent abuse of process or when there is a real danger of prejudice, rather than for mere convenience.

rules.reference: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
rules.relevance: The petitioner cited parallel proceedings under the SARFAESI Act in Coimbatore. While not the primary basis for the criminal transfer, the existence of these proceedings is relevant to the argument of harassment and the convenience of consolidating related disputes.

This is the primary constitutional provision governing the removal of members of Public Service Commissions. It defines the grounds for removal ('misbehaviour' or 'incapacity') and mandates that the President must refer the question of misbehaviour to the Supreme Court for an opinion before proceeding with removal.
Defines the establishment of Public Service Commissions and sets the context for the tenure and security of tenure of its members, which is the subject of the removal proceedings.

While primarily concerning the Election Commission, the Supreme Court has often drawn parallels between the independence and security of tenure of Constitutional Bodies like the ECI and PSCs. Principles regarding 'misbehaviour' and the high threshold for removal established in ECI cases are frequently cited in PSC removal references.

rules.case_name: S. P. Gupta v. Union of India (Judges' Transfer Case)
rules.relevance: Although concerning judges, this case extensively discusses the concept of 'misbehaviour' and the standard of proof required for removal of constitutional functionaries. It establishes that 'misbehaviour' is not limited to criminal misconduct but includes conduct that renders the person unfit to hold office, yet requires a high degree of certainty.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. T. S. R. Subramanian
rules.relevance: This case deals with the removal of the Chief Election Commissioner. The principles laid down regarding the interpretation of 'misbehaviour', the requirement of specific charges rather than vague allegations, and the protection of the independence of constitutional bodies are directly applicable to the interpretation of Article 317 in the context of the APPSC.

rules.reference: Principle of Individual Responsibility vs. Collective Responsibility
rules.relevance: Central to the issue of whether Ms. Bage can be held liable for institutional failures. The principle asserts that in a collegium or commission structure, members are not vicariously liable for the acts of others unless there is specific evidence of personal connivance, negligence, or failure to perform assigned duties. The work allocation order assigning her to 'Law & Judicial' matters rather than recruitment is key evidence here.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem)
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether the charges are 'too vague'. For a finding of misbehaviour to be sustainable, the charges must be specific, clear, and capable of being defended. Vague charges that do not pinpoint specific acts or omissions attributable to the individual violate the principles of natural justice and fair play in administrative law.

rules.reference: The Arunachal Pradesh Public Service Commission (Conditions of Service) Rules
rules.relevance: These rules, framed under Article 316, define the specific conditions of service, including duties, responsibilities, and potential grounds for disciplinary action or removal specific to the APPSC. They provide the statutory framework for interpreting 'misbehaviour' in the context of the Commission's internal functioning.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of 'misbehaviour' in the context of public servants and constitutional functionaries. It helps in distinguishing between mere administrative lapses or errors of judgment and conduct that amounts to moral turpitude or serious misconduct warranting removal.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Separation of Functions within a Commission
rules.relevance: Relevant to the defense that Ms. Bage was not responsible for the recruitment process. This principle supports the argument that liability for 'misbehaviour' must be tied to the specific functions assigned to a member. If the work allocation order clearly assigned recruitment to another member, holding Ms. Bage liable for leaks in that process would be legally unsustainable without proof of her direct involvement.

These sections define the functions and powers of the Central and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions, including the determination of tariffs and the duty to ensure financial viability of licensees, which is central to the creation and liquidation of regulatory assets.

This specific rule prescribes the conditions for the creation, management, and liquidation of regulatory assets, including caps on new gaps and timelines for liquidation, directly addressing the statutory framework challenged in the appeal.

This section establishes the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) and defines its jurisdiction to hear appeals against orders of Regulatory Commissions, relevant to the challenge against the APTEL's order dated 11.03.2014.

The Supreme Court entertained writ petitions under this article, which guarantees the right to constitutional remedies, allowing the petitioners to approach the Court directly regarding the enforcement of their rights and the regulatory framework.

This provision mandates the Commission to determine tariffs in a manner that promotes competition, efficiency, and economic use of resources, while ensuring financial viability of the electricity supply industry, which is the basis for recognizing regulatory assets.

This section requires the Commission to ensure that the tariffs are such that the licensee is able to recover its costs and earn a reasonable return, which is the fundamental justification for the accumulation of regulatory assets when tariffs are suppressed.

rules.case_name: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Union of India (Current Appeal)
rules.relevance: The current case itself is being heard by the Supreme Court to examine the legal framework governing regulatory assets, making the Court's interpretation in this specific appeal the primary authority for the issues raised.

This section outlines the powers and functions of the APTEL, relevant to determining the extent of the Tribunal's authority to direct the DERC to implement a roadmap for the liquidation of regulatory assets.

rules.reference: Principle of Financial Viability and Prudently Incurred Costs
rules.relevance: This legal principle underpins the concept of regulatory assets, asserting that licensees must be allowed to recover prudently incurred costs to maintain financial health, even if tariffs are temporarily suppressed for public interest.

This section empowers the Commission to regulate the supply of electricity and determine tariffs, establishing the DERC's primary role in the creation and management of the regulatory asset through tariff orders.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the appellant was arrested. The appeal centers on the interpretation of the conditions for arrest, specifically the requirement to record 'reasons to believe' and the necessity of arrest.

rules.case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India
rules.reference: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment is central to the issue as it held that the 'reasons to believe' recorded by the Authorized Officer must be based on tangible material and that the necessity of arrest is a valid ground for judicial review under Section 19(1) of the PMLA.

The appellant was issued notices under this section prior to arrest. The DoE's contention regarding the appellant's failure to appear despite summons under Section 50 is relevant to establishing the 'necessity' of arrest.

rules.reference: Principle of Judicial Review of Arrest under PMLA
rules.relevance: The legal principle that courts can review the satisfaction of the Authorized Officer regarding the 'reasons to believe' and the 'necessity of arrest' to prevent arbitrary deprivation of liberty, as established in recent jurisprudence.

While not the direct basis of arrest, Section 45 deals with the burden of proof in PMLA cases. The context of the predicate offence and the nature of evidence (incriminating vs exculpatory) often intersects with the standards applied during the arrest and remand phase.

These articles protect against arbitrary arrest and detention. The appellant's challenge to the legality of the arrest invokes these fundamental rights, requiring the state to justify the deprivation of personal liberty.

rules.case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Although primarily concerning CrPC, this precedent establishes the general legal principle that arrest is not automatic and that the necessity of arrest must be recorded. This principle is often cited in PMLA cases to argue against mechanical arrests.

Defines 'proceeds of crime'. The DoE's allegation that the appellant used proceeds of crime in election campaigns relies on this definition, which forms the basis of the predicate offence and the subsequent money laundering charge.

rules.reference: Standard of 'Reasons to Believe' vs 'Reasonable Grounds to Suspect'
rules.relevance: The distinction between the standard of proof required for arrest under PMLA (reasons to believe) versus other statutes. The appellant argues the reasons were selective; this principle helps determine if the material cited by the DoE meets the statutory threshold.

While PMLA has its own bail provisions, general CrPC principles regarding the necessity of custody and the conduct of the accused (such as prior cooperation or lack thereof) are often considered by courts when evaluating the 'necessity' of continued detention or the validity of the initial arrest.

rules.provision: General Provisions regarding Governance and Elections
rules.reference: National Sports Development Code of India, 2011
rules.relevance: The primary statutory framework cited by the Delhi High Court and Supreme Court for mandating reforms in sports federations. The entire dispute revolves around the AIFF's compliance with this Code, particularly regarding election processes and governance structures.

Relevant to the challenge regarding the fairness, transparency, and non-arbitrariness of the election processes and the appointment of administrators. The writ petition challenges the working of federations on grounds that may invoke equality and fair procedure.

Relevant to the right of athletes and stakeholders to participate in sports and the impact of FIFA suspension on their livelihoods and opportunities, which the Supreme Court considered when directing expeditious elections.

rules.case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) & Anr. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) & Anr. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: While not explicitly cited in the brief, the principles of autonomy and democratic rights within voluntary associations often draw upon broader constitutional jurisprudence regarding association rights and individual liberties, which underpin the demand for representative governance in the AIFF Constitution.

rules.case_name: BCCI v. Cricket Association of Bihar
rules.reference: BCCI v. Cricket Association of Bihar
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing the judicial review of sports federations' internal affairs when they perform public functions or receive state aid. It sets the boundary for when courts can intervene in the election and governance of sports bodies like AIFF.

Although not yet notified at the time of judgment, its enactment signals the legislative intent to regulate sports governance. The Court's consideration of the draft Constitution must align with the emerging statutory landscape represented by this Act.

The Supreme Court's appointment of a CoA is based on the legal principle that when a sports federation is in a state of administrative vacuum or governance failure, the Court can appoint an interim administrator to ensure continuity and compliance with law, as seen in the appointment of Dr. S.Y. Quraishi and others.

FIFA's suspension of AIFF due to governance issues highlights the necessity for the AIFF Constitution to comply with international sporting standards. The Court's directive to facilitate revocation of suspension implies that the new Constitution must satisfy FIFA's independence and governance criteria.

rules.reference: Principle of Democratic Representation in Voluntary Associations
rules.relevance: Central to the issues regarding the inclusion of players, coaches, and referees in the General Body. The principle dictates that those directly affected by the federation's decisions should have a voice in its governance, supporting the arguments for expanding voting rights.

rules.reference: Separation of Powers and Judicial Restraint in Sports
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether amendments require Supreme Court leave. The Court must balance its supervisory role in ensuring compliance with the NSC 2011 against the principle that it should not micromanage the internal affairs of a sports body once a compliant structure is in place.
Central to the appeal; the petitioners argue that the Madarsa Act is a valid exercise of minority rights to establish and administer educational institutions, which the High Court allegedly violated.
Challenged by the High Court as violated by the Act; the appeal must determine if the classification of Madarsas and the regulatory framework violates the guarantee of equality.
Challenged by the High Court; relevant to determining if the regulation of Madarsa education infringes upon the fundamental right to life and personal liberty, including the right to education.
Challenged by the High Court; relevant to the argument that Madarsa education does not meet the standards of free and compulsory education mandated for children aged 6-14.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Board of Madarsa Education Act, 2004
rules.relevance: The primary legislation under challenge; the appeal seeks to uphold its constitutionality and legislative competence.
Cited by the High Court as conflicting with the Madarsa Act; relevant to the issue of whether the State can grant degrees (Fazil/Kamil) that are not recognized by the UGC.

Defines the concurrent legislative competence of the State regarding 'Education' including technical education, medical education, and universities, excluding institutions declared to be of national importance.

Defines the Union's exclusive competence over 'Coordination and determination of standards in institutions for higher education or research and scientific and technical institutions'; relevant to the conflict with the UGC Act.

Relevant to the issue of whether the entire Madarsa Act must be struck down if provisions regarding higher education degrees are found unconstitutional, or if those specific provisions can be severed.
The foundational constitutional value cited by the High Court to strike down the Act; the appeal must address whether state regulation of religious education violates secularism.
Central to determining whether AWES qualifies as 'State' or an instrumentality of the State, which is a prerequisite for the maintainability of a writ petition under Article 226.
Defines the scope of the High Court's power to issue writs. The appeal challenges whether this power extends to a private, unaided society like AWES.

rules.case_name: Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology
rules.reference: Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology
rules.relevance: Establishes the 'deep and pervasive control' test to determine if a body is an instrumentality of the State under Article 12. Relevant to assess if AWES, despite being a society, falls under Article 12 due to its connection with the Army.

rules.case_name: Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Clarifies the scope of judicial review over private bodies performing public functions. It distinguishes between public law obligations (subject to writ jurisdiction) and private contractual disputes (not subject to writ jurisdiction).

The High Court relied on this doctrine to protect the employees' service conditions. The Supreme Court appeal challenges its applicability in a private employment context where no statutory right exists.

AWES is registered under this Act. This statute defines its legal character as a private society, supporting the argument that it is not a State entity unless specific conditions of Article 12 are met.

rules.case_name: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India
rules.reference: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India
rules.relevance: A foundational case for the 'instrumentality of the State' test under Article 12, providing criteria such as financial aid, functional character, and monopoly status to determine Statehood.

rules.reference: Public Law vs. Private Law Distinction in Service Matters
rules.relevance: Relevant to the second issue: whether service disputes in a private/unaided institution are governed by private contract (civil remedy) or public law (writ remedy), especially when the employer is not a State entity.

rules.case_name: Tata Cellular v. Union of India
rules.reference: Tata Cellular v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Discusses the limits of judicial review in contractual matters and the doctrine of legitimate expectation, holding that legitimate expectation cannot override statutory or contractual rights in private dealings.
The provision under which AWES filed the special leave petition in the Supreme Court, granting the Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment.
The primary charge against the appellants is murder. The court must determine if the evidence supports conviction under this section, which prescribes the punishment for murder.
The appellants were convicted for criminal conspiracy. The court must assess if the prosecution proved a prior agreement between the accused to commit the murder.

A central issue is the admissibility of Call Detail Records (CDRs). The appellants challenge the evidence based on alleged non-compliance with the certificate requirements of this section for electronic records.
The appellants seek to invoke the power of pardon. The court must decide if the appellants are entitled to file petitions for pardon under this article and the procedural implications thereof.
Appellant A-4 was convicted for causing disappearance of evidence. The court must review the sustainability of this conviction alongside the murder charge.

The court must evaluate the testimony of eyewitnesses PW-15 and PW-16. Legal principles regarding the scrutiny of eyewitness accounts, particularly in cases involving motive and potential bias, are relevant.

If ocular evidence is discarded, the conviction must rest on circumstantial evidence (motive, CDRs, recovery). The court must apply the principle that the chain of circumstances must be complete and exclude all hypothesis of innocence.

The recovery of the weapon (M.O.11) and scooter (M.O.12) at the instance of the accused is key evidence. Section 27 governs the admissibility of facts discovered in consequence of information given by an accused person.

rules.case_name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
rules.relevance: This precedent is highly relevant to the issue of admissibility of electronic evidence (CDRs) under Section 65-B of the Indian Evidence Act, establishing that compliance with Section 65-B is a condition precedent for admissibility.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Satish Kumar
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Satish Kumar
rules.relevance: This precedent is relevant to the issue of pardon under Article 161, clarifying that the power of pardon is not a right but a sovereign power, and the procedure for invoking it.

This section mandates the registration of a First Information Report (F.I.R.) for cognizable offences. The core issue is whether the police were justified in not registering an F.I.R. despite complaints alleging murder and atrocities, which are cognizable.

The police conducted an inquiry under this section regarding unnatural deaths. The appeal challenges whether the conclusion of this inquiry (suicide) obviates the need for a formal investigation under Section 154 when specific allegations of foul play exist.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
rules.relevance: The appellants specifically alleged offences under this Act. This provision prescribes punishment for offences committed by non-SC/ST persons against SC/ST persons, making the alleged crimes cognizable and requiring mandatory investigation.

rules.case_name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: This landmark precedent establishes that registration of an F.I.R. is mandatory if the information discloses a cognizable offence, and preliminary inquiry is not permissible to determine whether to register an F.I.R. This directly supports the appellants' claim that the police should have registered the F.I.R.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This case outlines the limited circumstances under which a magistrate or superior officer can stop an investigation. It is relevant to determine if the High Court or Police had the authority to dismiss the complaint without investigation based on lack of corroboration at the initial stage.

rules.case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: While primarily about arrest, this judgment emphasizes the mandatory nature of procedural safeguards in cognizable cases and the duty of police to act on complaints, reinforcing the principle that mechanical closure of cases is impermissible.
The right to life includes the right to a fair and effective investigation into unnatural deaths. The failure to investigate allegations of murder violates the procedural aspect of Article 21.
Allegations of caste-based discrimination implicate the right to equality. Arbitrary refusal to investigate crimes against Scheduled Caste individuals may violate Article 14.
The appellants alleged murder. Section 302 defines the offence of murder, which is a cognizable offence, thereby triggering the mandatory requirement of F.I.R. registration under Section 154 CrPC.
If the deaths were not suicides but abetted suicides due to harassment, this section applies. It is a cognizable offence, further supporting the argument that an F.I.R. was mandatory.
This is the specific provision under which the respondent filed the petition for the appointment of an arbitrator, and which forms the basis of the High Court's order being challenged.

rules.case_name: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act 1899
rules.reference: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act 1899
rules.relevance: Explicitly cited in the issues; this precedent defines the limited scope of judicial scrutiny (prima facie examination) available to the referral court under Section 11, restricting it from deciding complex factual disputes like the validity of a settlement.

Central to the second issue; establishes that the court appointing an arbitrator should only conduct a prima facie review of the existence of an arbitration agreement and not delve into the merits of the dispute or the validity of the settlement voucher.

The core legal concept in dispute. The appellant argues that the discharge voucher constitutes an accord and satisfaction, thereby extinguishing the cause of action and the arbitration agreement, while the respondent claims it was signed under coercion.
Relevant to the respondent's claim that the discharge voucher was signed under 'coercion and undue influence,' which would render the contract voidable under this section.
Relevant to the consequences of a voidable contract being rescinded; if the settlement is found voidable due to coercion, restitution may be claimed, affecting the finality of the settlement.

rules.case_name: BGS SGPL Ltd. v. NHPC Ltd.
rules.reference: BGS SGPL Ltd. v. NHPC Ltd.
rules.relevance: A key Supreme Court precedent clarifying the limited role of the Section 11 authority, reinforcing that complex factual issues regarding the existence or validity of contracts/settlements are for the arbitrator, not the court.

rules.case_name: Sai Krishna Constructions v. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Sai Krishna Constructions v. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: Relevant precedent concerning insurance disputes and the interpretation of discharge vouchers and full and final settlements in the context of arbitration.
Defines the 'Arbitration Agreement.' The dispute hinges on whether the arbitration clause in the original insurance policy survives the alleged full and final settlement.

The principle that an arbitration clause is a separate agreement. Even if the main contract (or settlement) is challenged, the arbitration clause may survive, allowing the arbitrator to decide the validity of the settlement.

This is the central procedural provision in dispute. The issue is whether the second suit for specific performance is barred because the plaintiff could have claimed this relief in the first suit for permanent injunction. The court must determine if the cause of action was the same and if the plaintiff omitted to include the claim for specific performance in the first suit.
The Trial Court rejected the plaint under this provision, holding that the suit was barred by Order II Rule 2. The appellate history revolves around the correctness of this rejection.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Sukhdev Singh
rules.relevance: A leading Supreme Court precedent interpreting Order II Rule 2 CPC. It establishes that the rule applies only when the cause of action is the same and the plaintiff could have claimed the relief in the first suit. It distinguishes between different causes of action arising from different facts or circumstances.

rules.case_name: K. Venugopala Reddy v. K. Venugopala Reddy
rules.reference: K. Venugopala Reddy v. K. Venugopala Reddy
rules.relevance: This precedent clarifies the scope of Order II Rule 2, emphasizing that the rule is not intended to be a trap for the unwary but to prevent multiplicity of proceedings. It helps in determining whether the claim for specific performance was part of the same cause of action as the claim for injunction.

The second suit seeks specific performance of the agreement for sale. Section 10 deals with the grant of specific performance of contracts. The court must consider if the claim for specific performance was available and maintainable at the time of the first suit.

The first suit was for a permanent injunction. Section 38 deals with perpetual injunctions. The distinction between the nature of relief sought in the first suit (protection of possession) and the second suit (enforcement of contract) is crucial for applying Order II Rule 2.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: This case discusses the interpretation of 'cause of action' under Order II Rule 2. It supports the view that if the facts giving rise to the second suit were not in existence or not known at the time of the first suit, the rule may not apply.

Order II Rule 2 is based on the principle of constructive res judicata. The court must apply this principle to determine if the plaintiff is estopped from filing the second suit because they failed to claim all reliefs arising from the same cause of action in the first suit.

rules.case_name: M. Chandra Reddy v. M. Venkata Reddy
rules.reference: M. Chandra Reddy v. M. Venkata Reddy
rules.relevance: This precedent illustrates scenarios where a suit for injunction and a suit for specific performance are considered to arise from different causes of action, particularly when the circumstances change or new facts emerge after the first suit is filed.

The underlying transaction is a sale of immovable property. Section 54 defines sale and the requirements for a valid sale deed. The validity of the agreement for sale and the subsequent sale deed executed by Respondent No. 2 to the Appellant are relevant to the substantive rights being enforced.

This is the primary procedural provision governing the stay of money decrees in appeals. It mandates that the Appellate Court may stay the execution of a money decree only if the appellant deposits the decretal amount or furnishes sufficient security. The core issue is whether the High Court violated this mandatory requirement by granting an unconditional stay.

This provision allows the Appellate Court to dispense with the deposit or security required under Rule 5(1) if it is satisfied that there are special circumstances. The relevance lies in determining whether the High Court properly exercised this discretion or failed to record sufficient reasons for dispensing with security.

rules.case_name: M/s. K. K. Modi v. K. N. Modi
rules.reference: M/s. K. K. Modi v. K. N. Modi
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent establishing the three-fold test for granting stay: (1) Prima facie case, (2) Balance of convenience, and (3) Irreparable injury. This authority is central to evaluating whether the High Court correctly applied the legal standards for granting stay, particularly regarding the balance of convenience and irreparable injury to the decree holder.

rules.case_name: M/s. R. K. Swamy v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: M/s. R. K. Swamy v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: This case emphasizes that the power to grant stay is discretionary and must be exercised judiciously. It supports the argument that unconditional stays without security are exceptional and require strong justification, reinforcing the mandatory nature of Order XLI Rule 5(1) unless specific exceptions are met.

rules.case_name: M/s. Indian Bank v. Satyam Transport Agency
rules.reference: M/s. Indian Bank v. Satyam Transport Agency
rules.relevance: Relevant for the principle that the grant of stay should not defeat the purpose of the decree. It highlights that security is often necessary to protect the decree holder's interest, especially in money decrees, and that dispensing with it requires compelling reasons.

This section provides for the award of damages or accounts of profits in trademark infringement cases. It is relevant to the background of the decree amount and the nature of the relief sought, contextualizing the financial magnitude of the stay application.

The High Court noted prima facie issues regarding service of summons and enhancement of damages without amendment. This legal principle is relevant to assess whether the appellant had a strong prima facie case justifying the relaxation of security requirements under Order XLI Rule 5(3).

A key factor in stay applications. The relevance here is to determine if the balance of convenience favored the defendant (Amazon) enough to warrant an unconditional stay, considering the massive damages awarded and the potential loss to the plaintiffs if the stay is unconditional.

The court must assess if the appellant would suffer irreparable injury if the stay is not granted. In money decrees, injury is often considered compensable by money, making this factor less favorable for unconditional stays unless exceptional circumstances exist.

Although not the primary issue, the High Court's observation about the enhancement of damages without amending the plaint touches upon procedural regularity. This rule governs the rejection of plaints for non-compliance with procedural requirements, supporting the argument that the decree itself may be procedurally flawed.

This is the primary constitutional provision challenged by the appellants. It prohibits a State from imposing restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse that discriminate against goods from other States. The core issue is whether the tax exemption for locally manufactured goods constitutes such discrimination.

Article 301 guarantees freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout the territory of India. The appellants argue that the notification violates this freedom by creating a barrier or disadvantage for goods imported from other States compared to locally manufactured goods.

rules.case_name: Video Electronics Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Video Electronics Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: The Rajasthan High Court relied on this judgment to dismiss the writ petitions. It established the principle that limited-period incentives or exemptions granted to promote local industry or utilize local resources may not violate Article 304(a) if they are not intended to discriminate but to encourage specific economic activities.

This is the statutory provision under which the impugned Notification No. S.O.377 was issued. It empowers the State Government to grant exemptions from tax, forming the legal basis for the challenged notification.

rules.case_name: Atiabari Tea Co. Ltd. vs. State of Assam
rules.reference: Atiabari Tea Co. Ltd. vs. State of Assam
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent interpreting Articles 301 and 304. It distinguishes between taxes that are non-discriminatory (permissible under Article 301) and those that discriminate between local and imported goods (prohibited under Article 304(a)). This helps determine if the exemption creates a discriminatory burden.

rules.case_name: State of Bombay vs. Shri Ram Sugar Mills
rules.reference: State of Bombay vs. Shri Ram Sugar Mills
rules.relevance: This case is crucial for interpreting Article 304(a). It holds that a tax or regulation violates Article 304(a) if it discriminates against goods from other States. The court will examine if the exemption for 'manufactured in Rajasthan' goods effectively discriminates against out-of-state goods.

rules.case_name: Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. vs. State of Rajasthan
rules.reference: Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. vs. State of Rajasthan
rules.relevance: This case elaborates on the scope of Article 304(a) and the concept of discrimination. It helps in analyzing whether the distinction made in the notification (based on place of manufacture) amounts to unconstitutional discrimination against inter-state trade.

rules.reference: Principle of Non-Discrimination in Inter-State Trade
rules.relevance: The general legal principle that State tax laws must not create artificial barriers or preferences that favor local goods over inter-state goods, unless justified by a valid state interest and structured in a non-discriminatory manner (e.g., based on use of local raw materials rather than just place of manufacture).
Section 8 generally deals with exemptions from tax. Understanding the broader context of Section 8 helps in interpreting the specific power exercised under Section 8(3) to issue the notification.

rules.case_name: Tata Iron and Steel Co. Ltd. vs. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Tata Iron and Steel Co. Ltd. vs. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: This case discusses the validity of state taxes and exemptions in the context of industrial promotion. It may provide insights into whether incentives tied to local manufacturing or resource utilization are permissible under the Constitution.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. It mandates that no court shall take cognizance of an offence alleged to have been committed by a public servant while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official functions, except with the previous sanction of the appropriate government. The High Court relied on this to quash proceedings, while the appeal challenges its applicability to acts done in collusion or conspiracy outside official duty.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent defining the scope of Section 482 CrPC. It establishes that inherent powers to quash proceedings should be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases where the allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence or make out a case against the accused.
