It is relevant to determine if the High Court overstepped its jurisdiction by quashing the case at the threshold based on a technical plea of sanction.

rules.case_name: Pankaj Bansal v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Pankaj Bansal v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment clarifies that Section 197 CrPC protection is not available to public servants for acts done in collusion with others to commit a crime, especially when such acts are not in furtherance of official duty. It is directly relevant to the issue of whether police officials conspiring to fabricate an FIR for a false alibi are protected by Section 197.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This case holds that if a public servant acts in collusion with others to commit an offence, the protection of Section 197 CrPC is not available. It supports the argument that the respondents, by conspiring to register a false Excise case to provide an alibi, were not acting in the discharge of official functions.

The respondents were charged with conspiracy to commit murder. Section 120B defines criminal conspiracy. The relevance lies in determining whether the act of conspiring to fabricate evidence/FIRs constitutes an offence distinct from official duty, thereby negating the need for sanction under Section 197 CrPC.

The allegation involves causing disappearance of evidence or giving false information to screen an offender (Ashok Dixit). This section is relevant to the nature of the offence alleged against the police officials, supporting the view that their actions were criminal and not official.

This section confers inherent powers on the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the CrPC or to prevent abuse of the process of any court. The appeal challenges the exercise of this power by the High Court in quashing the proceedings.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi
rules.reference: Sukhdev Singh v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi
rules.relevance: This case discusses the interpretation of 'acting or purporting to act' in the discharge of official functions under Section 197 CrPC. It helps in distinguishing between acts done in the course of duty and acts done in collusion or for personal/malicious motives, which are not protected.

rules.reference: Principle of Collusion and Official Duty
rules.relevance: The legal principle that a public servant is not entitled to the protection of Section 197 CrPC if the act complained of is done in collusion with others to commit a crime or is not in furtherance of official duty. This principle is central to deciding whether the sanction was a mandatory prerequisite in this specific factual matrix.

The underlying offence in the Firozabad case is murder. While the appeal is against the police officials, the context of the murder conviction of Ashok Dixit and the allegation that the Excise case was a false alibi for this murder provides the factual backdrop for the conspiracy charge.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the respondent filed the application for the appointment of an arbitrator. The core legal question is whether a fresh application under this section is maintainable after an unconditional withdrawal of a previous application.

The appellant argues that the fresh arbitration application is barred by the principles of Order 23 Rule 1 CPC, which governs the withdrawal of suits and applications. The court must determine if the unconditional withdrawal of the first Section 11(6) application operates as a bar to a fresh filing.

The High Court relied on Section 14 to exclude the time spent in IBC proceedings. The Supreme Court must decide if proceedings under the IBC constitute 'proceedings in a court lacking jurisdiction' or similar grounds allowing exclusion of time under Section 14.

The respondent seeks condonation of delay in filing the fresh arbitration application. The court must evaluate if the delay is sufficient and if the reasons provided (pursuit of IBC proceedings) constitute 'sufficient cause' under Section 5.

The respondent previously filed an application under Section 9 of the IBC, which was dismissed by the Supreme Court due to a pre-existing dispute. The relevance lies in determining whether the pursuit of this alternative remedy justifies the delay in arbitration or affects the maintainability of the fresh arbitration application.

rules.case_name: M/s HPCL Bio-Fuels Ltd. v. M/s Shahaji Bhanudas Bhad (or similar title based on facts)
rules.citation: As per the case brief, the Supreme Court upheld the NCLAT order noting that CIRP cannot be initiated for disputed debts.
rules.reference: Supreme Court Judgment dismissing the appeal against NCLAT order on IBC application
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes that the debt was disputed and the IBC route was legally untenable. This fact is crucial in assessing whether the respondent's reliance on IBC proceedings was bona fide or dilatory, impacting the condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.

The legal principle that an unconditional withdrawal of an application without liberty to file a fresh one generally bars a subsequent application on the same cause of action, unless specific exceptions apply. This is central to the appellant's argument regarding Order 23 Rule 1 CPC.

While not explicitly mentioned in the brief, Section 12(5) (introduced by the 2015 Amendment) imposes a three-year limitation period for filing applications under Section 11. The calculation of this period and the applicability of exclusion under Section 14 of the Limitation Act are directly linked to this provision.

rules.case_name: Bharat Broadband Network Ltd. v. United Telecoms Ltd. or similar
rules.citation: General reference to SC jurisprudence on limitation in arbitration
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Section 11(6) and Limitation
rules.relevance: Precedents interpreting the interplay between the Arbitration Act and the Limitation Act, specifically regarding what constitutes 'sufficient cause' for condoning delay and whether time spent in other legal proceedings can be excluded.

The principle that a party cannot pursue alternative remedies simultaneously or sequentially to delay the primary dispute resolution mechanism. The court will assess if the respondent's shift from Arbitration to IBC and back to Arbitration was an abuse of process.

Central to the appeal. The prosecution failed to produce a certificate under Section 65-B(4) for the CCTV footage, which is a mandatory condition for the admissibility of electronic evidence. Without this, the CCTV footage linking the appellant to the deceased is inadmissible.

rules.case_name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
rules.reference: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court precedent consolidates the law regarding the mandatory nature of Section 65-B certificates for electronic evidence. It holds that non-compliance renders the electronic evidence inadmissible, directly supporting the appellant's challenge to the CCTV footage.

The primary charge of murder. The appeal questions whether the conviction under this section can be sustained if the key electronic evidence (CCTV) is excluded and the remaining circumstantial evidence is found unreliable.

Charge of rape. The post-mortem report indicated genital injuries, forming the basis for this conviction. The reliability of the chain of evidence linking the appellant to the crime scene is crucial for sustaining this conviction.
Charge of kidnapping. The timeline of the deceased's disappearance and the appellant's last sighting with her are central to this charge, relying heavily on the disputed CCTV and witness testimony.

Since the case relies on circumstantial evidence (CCTV, witness sightings, recovery), the principle that the chain must be complete and unbroken, leading to the exclusive conclusion of the accused's guilt, is critical. Gaps in the chain (e.g., delayed witness statements, inadmissible CCTV) may lead to acquittal.

Relates to the recording of statements by police. The significant delay in recording the statements of PW-20 and PW-21 (two to two and a half months) raises issues regarding the reliability and voluntariness of their testimony, potentially affecting their credibility.

The publication of the appellant's photograph in newspapers prior to the identification parade prejudices the identification process. This legal principle suggests that such identification evidence may be unreliable and should be viewed with caution.

Charge of causing disappearance of evidence. The recovery of the motorcycle and trolley bag based on disclosure statements is linked to this charge. Procedural infirmities in recovery may weaken the prosecution's case on this count.

The testimony of PW-9 regarding an extra-judicial confession is subject to strict scrutiny. Material omissions and contradictions in his testimony compared to his initial statement render this evidence unreliable and insufficient to sustain a conviction on its own.

This section empowers the Electricity Regulatory Commission to investigate complaints or matters relating to the supply of electricity. The core issue is whether an individual petitioner has the standing to invoke this section and whether the Commission has the jurisdiction to investigate the franchisee's performance under this provision.

The petition challenged the franchisee agreement on the grounds that it violated Section 17, which mandates prior approval for the transfer of utility. The relevance lies in determining if the appointment of a franchisee constitutes a 'transfer of utility' requiring such approval.
This section provides the statutory mechanism for appealing orders of the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) to the Supreme Court. It is the procedural basis for the current appeal.

This section outlines the functions of the State Electricity Regulatory Commission, including determining tariffs and ensuring efficient operation. It is relevant to determining the scope of the Commission's jurisdiction over franchisee performance and consumer interests.

This section defines the functions of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, often read with Section 42 for State Commissions, regarding the promotion of competitive mechanisms and efficient operation. It helps define the regulatory scope over distribution licensees and franchisees.

This section deals with the grant of licenses. The interpretation of whether a franchisee agreement falls under the licensing regime or is a separate contractual arrangement is central to the jurisdictional dispute.

The principle determining who has the right to approach the Electricity Regulatory Commission. The case hinges on whether a non-consumer individual can file a petition under Section 128 in the public interest.

The legal principle defining the boundary between contractual disputes (which may be outside ERC jurisdiction) and regulatory matters concerning public interest and consumer protection (which fall within ERC jurisdiction).

This section establishes the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL). The appeal challenges the APTEL's interpretation of its own jurisdiction and the jurisdiction of the UPERC, making the enabling statute relevant.

This section deals with the determination of tariffs. The petition alleged that the input-rate model resulted in undervalued rates and cross-subsidization, making the tariff determination powers of the Commission relevant to the investigation.

These sections prescribe the mandatory procedure for the State to take over possession of surplus land. The core dispute is whether the notices and orders issued under these sections were validly executed and whether actual physical possession was taken before the Repeal Act came into force.

rules.reference: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999
rules.relevance: The Repeal Act extinguished the ULC Act. The critical legal question is whether the acquisition process was 'completed' (i.e., possession taken) before the Repeal Act came into force in Andhra Pradesh on 27.03.2008, thereby saving the vesting from abatement.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v. M/s. A.P. Electrical Equipment Corporation
rules.citation: Supreme Court Special Leave Petition (Current Appeal)
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh v. M/s. A.P. Electrical Equipment Corporation
rules.relevance: This is the specific case at hand. The Supreme Court's decision will determine the validity of the Division Bench's interpretation of possession under the ULC Act vis-a-vis the Repeal Act.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v. M/s. Sree Rama Mills
rules.citation: 2010 (1) ALT 1 (DB) or relevant SC judgment on ULC Repeal
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh v. M/s. Sree Rama Mills
rules.relevance: Precedents involving the ULC Repeal Act in Andhra Pradesh often address the distinction between 'deemed vesting' and 'actual physical possession' required to save an acquisition from the operation of the Repeal Act.

Under the ULC Act, mere issuance of a notice or order is insufficient; the State must demonstrate actual physical entry and control over the land. The appellant argues that the panchnama was fabricated and no actual possession occurred.

The ULC Act is a special statute with strict procedural requirements. The Single Judge held that procedural lapses (discrepancies in dates, lack of signatures) were fatal. The relevance lies in determining if such lapses invalidate the possession claim.

Relevant to the evidentiary value of the panchnama. The appellant challenges the panchnama as fabricated due to lack of signatures and affidavits. The court must decide if the document is admissible and sufficient proof of possession.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v. M/s. K. Venkata Reddy
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh v. M/s. K. Venkata Reddy
rules.relevance: Andhra Pradesh High Court precedents often deal with the validity of panchnamas executed by Enquiry Officers under the ULC Act and whether they constitute sufficient proof of possession in the absence of the landowner.

The writ jurisdiction of the High Court. The appeal challenges the High Court's exercise of this jurisdiction in setting aside the Single Judge's order. The Supreme Court reviews whether the High Court correctly applied the law in its writ proceedings.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Saving of Completed Actions
rules.relevance: General legal principle that if a statutory process is completed before a repealing act comes into force, the rights acquired are saved. The central issue is defining the point of 'completion' (possession vs. notification).

rules.reference: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
rules.relevance: This is the central statutory provision in dispute. The appellant argues that the non-obstante clause in Section 3(1)(b) and the requirement for a 'reasonable and fair provision' at the time of divorce supersede the general maintenance provisions of Section 125 CrPC, thereby barring the respondent from claiming interim maintenance under the CrPC.

This is the secular provision under which the respondent sought interim maintenance. The core legal issue is whether this section remains applicable to divorced Muslim women despite the enactment of the 1986 Act, or if it has been implicitly repealed or overridden for this class of persons.

rules.case_name: Shabana Bano v. Imran Khan
rules.relevance: This is the seminal Supreme Court judgment interpreting the 1986 Act. It held that the 'reasonable and fair provision' under Section 3 of the 1986 Act must extend to the period of iddat and beyond, and that the 1986 Act does not oust the jurisdiction of courts under Section 125 CrPC. This precedent directly supports the respondent's claim and contradicts the appellant's contention.

This provision allows for the modification or cessation of maintenance if the wife remarries or, in the case of a divorced woman, if she receives a 'reasonable and fair provision' under the 1986 Act. The appellant argues that any amount received under the 1986 Act should be considered here to prevent double benefit, rather than barring the initial claim under Section 125.

This is the procedural provision under which the appellant challenged the Family Court's order before the High Court. It confers inherent powers on the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

Article 14 guarantees equality before the law. The respondent's case often relies on the argument that denying a divorced Muslim woman the right to claim maintenance under the secular Section 125 CrPC, while available to women of other faiths, would violate the principle of equality and non-discrimination.

Article 21 protects the right to life and personal liberty, which has been interpreted to include the right to live with human dignity. The right to maintenance is often linked to this article, arguing that a divorced woman's right to sustenance is essential for her dignity and survival.

Although the primary appeal is about maintenance, the background facts mention an FIR under Section 498A (cruelty). This context establishes the breakdown of the marriage and the respondent's status as a neglected wife, which is a prerequisite for claiming maintenance under Section 125 CrPC.

The FIR also included charges under Section 406 (criminal breach of trust), likely regarding stridhan. While not the direct subject of the maintenance appeal, it forms part of the factual matrix demonstrating the deterioration of relations and the respondent's financial distress, supporting the need for interim maintenance.

This legal principle is relevant to resolving the apparent conflict between the 1986 Act and Section 125 CrPC. The court must interpret both statutes in a way that gives effect to both, rather than assuming one repeals the other, unless there is an irreconcilable conflict. This supports the view that Section 125 CrPC can operate alongside the 1986 Act.

Central to the issue of whether the Original Vendees established their continuous readiness and willingness to perform their part of the contract, a mandatory condition for granting specific performance.
Determines whether the Subsequent Purchasers qualify as bona fide purchasers for value without notice of the prior Agreement to Sell, which would bar the decree of specific performance against them.
Addresses the maintainability of the suit for specific performance without a concurrent prayer for declaratory relief regarding the invalidity of the vendor's termination notice.
Governs the rights and liabilities of vendors and vendees, including the vendor's obligation to disclose material defects in title and the effect of prior agreements on subsequent transfers.

Relevant to the doctrine of estoppel and whether the Original Vendors, having sold the property to Subsequent Purchasers, are estopped from denying the title of the Original Vendees or the validity of the ATS.
Addresses the limitation period for filing a suit for specific performance of a contract, particularly concerning when the cause of action accrues in cases of repudiation or termination.

rules.case_name: Mangat Ram v. Prem Chand
rules.relevance: A leading precedent establishing that a suit for specific performance is maintainable even if the contract has been repudiated, provided the plaintiff affirms the contract and seeks specific performance within the limitation period.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.relevance: Relevant to the interpretation of 'readiness and willingness' under Section 16(c) and the burden of proof on the plaintiff to demonstrate continuous ability to perform contractual obligations.
Concerns the requirement of registration for agreements to sell immovable property, which affects the evidentiary value of the unregistered ATS and the notice imputed to the Subsequent Purchasers.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Bona Fide Purchaser for Value without Notice
rules.relevance: A fundamental equitable principle determining whether a subsequent purchaser acquires a better title than the prior equitable interest holder, depending on whether they had actual or constructive notice of the prior agreement.

Central to the appeal. The petitioners argue the termination was punitive and stigmatic, thus attracting the safeguards of Article 311(2) which requires a reasonable opportunity of being heard before dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank.

Establishes the control of subordinate judicial service in a State by the High Court. This provision underpins the High Court's authority to terminate probationary judicial officers, but the scope of this power is subject to constitutional safeguards against arbitrariness.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent distinguishing between termination simpliciter (unsuitability) and punitive dismissal. It establishes that if the termination order contains stigmatic or punitive elements, it attracts Article 311(2) protections.

rules.case_name: State of Orissa v. Khaman Lal Meher
rules.relevance: Relevant for the principle that even in termination simpliciter, the order must not be arbitrary or mala fide. It supports the argument that adverse remarks or complaints used as basis for termination must be substantiated and communicated.

The core legal principle invoked by petitioners. Specifically, the right to be heard (audi alteram partem) and the rule against bias. Relevant because adverse ACR remarks were communicated only after termination, denying the officers a chance to rebut them.

rules.case_name: S. P. Gupta v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Often cited in judicial service matters regarding the standards of conduct and the procedure for termination. It reinforces that termination orders must be based on relevant material and not extraneous considerations.

rules.reference: The All India Services (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1954
rules.relevance: While specific to All India Services, the principles regarding probationary termination and the requirement of a show-cause notice if the termination is based on misconduct or unsuitability linked to specific charges are often applied by analogy to State Judicial Services.

Relevant to Aditi Kumar Sharma's case, where personal hardships and improved performance might have created a legitimate expectation of confirmation, which cannot be defeated by arbitrary or uncommunicated adverse material.

rules.case_name: Madras Bar Association v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Recent precedent dealing with the appointment and service conditions of judicial officers. It emphasizes the need for transparency and fairness in the administrative processes of the High Courts concerning judicial officers.

rules.provision: Rules relating to Probation and Termination
rules.relevance: The specific state rules governing the probation period and the procedure for termination of Civil Judges in Madhya Pradesh. The court must examine if the Administrative Committee followed these specific procedural mandates.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal
rules.reference: Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal
rules.relevance: This is the pivotal precedent cited in the facts. The Supreme Court held that notices issued under the old regime between April 1 and June 30, 2021, should be deemed as show-cause notices under Section 148A(b) of the new regime. This decision forms the factual basis for the subsequent notices issued in 2022 and is central to determining their validity.

This is the specific provision under which the reassessment notices were issued in July-September 2022. The appeal challenges the validity of these notices, making the interpretation of Section 148 under the new regime (post-Finance Act 2021) the primary statutory issue.

Section 148A introduces the new procedural safeguards and the requirement for a show-cause notice (Section 148A(b)) before issuing a notice under Section 148. The validity of the 2022 notices depends on whether the prior 'deemed' notices under Ashish Agarwal satisfied the procedural requirements of Section 148A.

This section prescribes the limitation period for reassessment. The High Courts held the 2022 notices to be time-barred. Determining whether the limitation period was extended by TOLA or reset by the new regime is crucial to deciding if the notices were issued within the permissible time limit.

rules.reference: Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020
rules.relevance: The central issue is whether TOLA applies to actions taken under the new regime after April 1, 2021. The Revenue relies on TOLA to justify the extension of time limits, while the High Courts held that TOLA could not revive the old regime or apply to the new regime's procedural framework.

This Act substituted the old reassessment regime with the new regime effective April 1, 2021. It reduced the general limitation period to three years and introduced Section 148A. The transition from the old to the new regime is the root cause of the legal conflict regarding the validity of the notices.

rules.reference: Principle of Non-Retroactivity and Transitional Provisions
rules.relevance: The case involves the application of a new statutory regime to pending proceedings. The principle that a new law generally applies prospectively unless expressly stated otherwise, and how transitional provisions (like those in the Finance Act 2021) interact with relaxation acts (TOLA), is key to resolving the conflict.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Limitation in Tax Proceedings
rules.relevance: The High Courts quashed the notices as time-barred. The legal principle that tax authorities must act within statutory limitation periods, and the effect of legislative extensions (TOLA) on such periods, is directly relevant to the second issue.

The High Courts also held the notices invalid due to lack of appropriate sanction. Under the new regime, specific approval authorities are required for issuing notices. The relevance of this procedural safeguard is critical to the validity of the 2022 notices.

As the Revenue appealed to the Supreme Court, Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) is the procedural basis for the appeal. While not substantive law, it is the authority under which the Supreme Court exercises jurisdiction to hear this appeal against the High Court orders.

These provisions define 'lottery promotion, marketing or organizing' as a taxable service and impose service tax on the value of such services. The core dispute is whether the distributors' activities fall within this definition.

rules.provision: Article 246 and Schedule VII, Entry 97 of List I and Entry 62 of List II
rules.relevance: The High Court held the Finance Act provisions ultra vires based on the conflict between the Union's power to tax services (Entry 97, List I) and the State's exclusive power to tax betting and gambling (Entry 62, List II). The Supreme Court must resolve this legislative competence issue.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Sikkim Lottery Distributors
rules.citation: Supreme Court Appeal against High Court of Sikkim Order
rules.reference: Union of India v. Sikkim Lottery Distributors
rules.relevance: This is the specific case on appeal. The Supreme Court's decision will determine the validity of the High Court's finding that the relationship was principal-to-principal and that the service tax levy was unconstitutional.

rules.reference: Principle of Agency vs. Principal Relationship
rules.relevance: Determining whether the distributors are agents of the State or independent principals is crucial. If they are agents, the State (as principal) might be the service provider; if they are principals, they may be liable for the service tax on their own promotional activities.
Defines 'service provider' in the context of lottery services. The interpretation of who constitutes the service provider (the State or the distributor) is central to the liability question.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Reliance Communications Ltd.
rules.reference: Union of India v. Reliance Communications Ltd.
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent regarding the interpretation of taxing statutes and the scope of 'service' under the Finance Act, 1994, often cited in service tax disputes involving the definition of taxable activities.

While primarily about trade and commerce, these articles are often invoked in cases involving state monopolies or restrictions on inter-state trade, which may be relevant if the lottery distribution involves inter-state elements or restrictions.

These rules provide the procedural framework for the levy and collection of service tax, including the determination of the value of taxable services, which is relevant to the calculation of the demand.

This constitutional doctrine is used to determine the true nature of a law when it touches upon multiple entries in the Seventh Schedule. It is relevant to decide whether the service tax on lottery promotion is essentially a tax on 'betting and gambling' (State subject) or a tax on 'services' (Union subject).

rules.case_name: State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala
rules.reference: State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala
rules.relevance: A foundational case defining 'betting and gambling' under Entry 62 of List II. It helps distinguish between games of skill and games of chance, and defines the scope of state taxation power over lotteries.
These rules define 'capital goods' and 'inputs'. The core legal question is whether mobile towers and PFBs fall within these definitions to allow CENVAT credit.

This section empowers the Central Government to make rules for the levy and collection of duty of excise, including the grant of CENVAT credit, providing the statutory basis for the CENVAT Credit Rules.

Defines 'immovable property'. The Bombay High Court relied on this to classify towers as immovable, while the appellants argue they remain movable. This definition is crucial for determining if the items are 'goods' under excise law.
Defines 'movable property' as property of every description except immovable property. This is relevant to the argument that towers, being detachable, are movable property and thus 'goods'.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise v. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Commissioner of Central Excise v. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: A key Supreme Court precedent establishing the test for distinguishing between movable and immovable property, focusing on the degree of annexation and the purpose of annexation. This test is directly applicable to determining the nature of mobile towers.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. (regarding prefabricated structures)
rules.relevance: Also relevant for the status of prefabricated buildings (PFBs). The court in this case held that prefabricated structures that can be dismantled and reassembled are movable property, supporting the MSPs' claim for PFBs.

rules.reference: Principle of Degree of Annexation and Purpose of Annexation
rules.relevance: The legal test used to determine if an item attached to land becomes part of the land (immovable) or remains movable. The facts state towers are fixed with nuts and bolts for stability but can be dismantled, making this principle central to the dispute.

Under CENVAT rules, accessories to capital goods are also treated as capital goods. The relevance lies in whether towers and PFBs are essential accessories to the Base Transceiver Stations (BTS) and antennas, which are undisputed capital goods.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Bharti Airtel Ltd. (or similar Delhi HC case)
rules.citation: As per the conflicting decision mentioned in facts
rules.reference: High Court of Delhi decision in the matter of Mobile Service Providers
rules.relevance: The Delhi High Court held that towers and PFBs are movable and qualify as capital goods/inputs. This is one of the conflicting precedents the Supreme Court is resolving.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise v. M/s. Bharti Airtel Ltd. (or similar Bombay HC case)
rules.citation: As per the conflicting decision mentioned in facts
rules.reference: High Court of Bombay decision in the matter of Mobile Service Providers
rules.relevance: The Bombay High Court held that towers and PFBs are immovable property and do not qualify as capital goods/inputs. This is the other conflicting precedent the Supreme Court is resolving.

rules.case_name: Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A.
rules.reference: Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A.
rules.relevance: Established the principle that Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 applies to arbitrations seated outside India unless the parties expressly exclude it. This is the foundational precedent for the petitioner's argument that Indian courts have jurisdiction despite the foreign venue.

rules.case_name: Fiona Trust & Holding Corp v. Privalov
rules.reference: Fiona Trust & Holding Corp v. Privalov
rules.relevance: A key precedent often cited in Indian jurisprudence to distinguish between 'venue' (physical location) and 'seat' (juridical location) of arbitration. It supports the interpretation that 'venue' does not automatically equate to 'seat' unless clearly intended.

Defines the scope of Part I of the Act. The central issue is whether this section applies to the dispute given the foreign seat/venue, determining if the Indian Supreme Court has the power to appoint an arbitrator.

The specific provision under which the petitioner filed the petition for the appointment of an arbitrator. The applicability of this section is contingent on the determination of the seat of arbitration.
Defines the 'seat' of arbitration. The court must interpret Clause 26 of the agreement in light of this section to determine if Dubai is the juridical seat or merely the physical venue.

rules.reference: Distinction between Seat and Venue of Arbitration
rules.relevance: The core legal principle governing the appeal. The court must apply the distinction that the 'seat' determines the supervisory jurisdiction of courts, while 'venue' is merely the physical location of proceedings.

Although the agreement is from 2010, the court may consider the legislative intent behind the 2015 amendment which restricted the application of Part I to arbitrations seated in India, unless the agreement was entered into before the amendment. This affects the temporal application of the law.

rules.case_name: Renusagar Power Co. Ltd. v. General Electric Co.
rules.reference: Renusagar Power Co. Ltd. v. General Electric Co.
rules.relevance: An earlier landmark judgment that laid the groundwork for the application of Part I to foreign-seated arbitrations, often cited alongside Bhatia International to support the petitioner's stance on jurisdiction.

The provision under which the petitioner issued the notice invoking arbitration. Its validity and the subsequent failure of the respondent to appoint an arbitrator trigger the need for court intervention under Section 11.

Interpretation of Clause 27 stating 'non-exclusive jurisdiction of Dubai Courts'. This principle supports the argument that the parties did not intend to oust the jurisdiction of other courts, including Indian courts, thereby allowing the Indian Supreme Court to exercise its powers under Section 11.

Defines 'light motor vehicle' to include transport vehicles with a gross weight not exceeding 7,500 kg, which is the central statutory definition relied upon by claimants to argue that an LMV license covers such transport vehicles.
Mandates that no person shall drive a motor vehicle unless they hold a valid driving license. Insurers argue this requires a license specifically entitling the holder to drive a transport vehicle.

Introduced by the 1994 amendment, this provision creates a separate class for 'Transport Vehicle' licenses. Insurers argue this necessitates a distinct endorsement for all transport vehicles regardless of weight.

Prescribes the conditions for the grant of driving licenses, including specific requirements for transport vehicles such as higher age limits, medical certificates, and training syllabi, which were cited as overlooked in Mukund Dewangan.

rules.case_name: Mukund Dewangan v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.reference: Mukund Dewangan v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
rules.relevance: The primary precedent under review, where a three-judge bench held that an LMV license holder is competent to drive a transport vehicle under 7,500 kg without a separate endorsement. The appeal questions if this was decided per incuriam.

rules.case_name: Bajaj Alliance General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Rambha Devi
rules.reference: Bajaj Alliance General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Rambha Devi
rules.relevance: A subsequent judgment that noted Mukund Dewangan did not consider certain provisions of the MV Act and Rules imposing stricter requirements for transport vehicles, contributing to the conflict requiring a Constitution Bench reference.

The legal principle determining whether a previous judgment can be disregarded because it was decided in ignorance of a relevant statutory provision or binding precedent. This is the core procedural issue regarding the validity of Mukund Dewangan.

Deals with the validity of insurance policies. While not explicitly detailed in the brief, the denial of insurance claims based on license validity inherently invokes the conditions under which an insurer is liable or exempt under the Act.

Details the procedure for obtaining a driving license, including the specific tests and endorsements required for different classes of vehicles, relevant to determining if a separate endorsement is procedurally mandatory.

Establishes that the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India. This article is relevant to the authority of the Mukund Dewangan judgment and the process of overruling it via a Constitution Bench.

The petitioner filed the writ petition under Article 32, invoking the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction to enforce fundamental rights. This is the procedural basis for the appeal and the Court's authority to issue directions.

The petitioner specifically challenges the implementation of Section 16, arguing that Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPOs) are overburdened with multiple responsibilities, thereby hindering effective enforcement of the Act.
The central substantive law governing the prohibition of child marriages in India. The appeal questions the State's failure to effectively enforce this statute despite its enactment.

Article 21 guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which has been interpreted by the Supreme Court to include the right to live with human dignity and the right to health. Child marriage violates these rights, forming the substantive constitutional basis for the petitioner's claim.

This article empowers the State to make special provisions for women and children. It supports the argument that the State has a positive obligation to protect girls from child marriage and provide support systems.

Part of the Directive Principles of State Policy, these articles direct the State to ensure that children are not forced by economic necessity to enter avocations unsuited to their age and to protect the health and strength of workers, children, and tender age of children.

Directs the State to endeavor to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years. This supports the petitioner's argument for awareness programs and education as preventive measures against child marriage.

The case is a PIL challenging systemic failure. The principle that the State has a non-derogable duty to protect vulnerable sections of society and that the Court can issue structural injunctions or guidelines to enforce statutory and constitutional mandates is central to the relief sought.

rules.reference: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
rules.relevance: While the PCMA is the primary law, the JJ Act provides the framework for the care and protection of children in need of care and protection, which is relevant to the petitioner's request for comprehensive support systems for child brides.

The petitioner highlighted discrepancies between reported cases and FIRs. Section 156(3) empowers Magistrates to direct police to register FIRs and investigate, which is a key procedural mechanism for enforcing the PCMA when police fail to act.

This is the primary statutory provision in dispute. It empowers the police to make further investigation and submit a further report, but the central legal issue is whether this power can be exercised independently after a final report has been accepted by the Magistrate, or if it requires the Magistrate's leave.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Ram Sagar Yadav
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Ram Sagar Yadav
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent holding that the power of further investigation under Section 173(8) CrPC is not subject to the leave of the Magistrate. This authority directly supports the High Court's view that the police could initiate further investigation without prior judicial permission.

rules.case_name: Pankaj Bansal v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Pankaj Bansal v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment clarifies the distinction between 'further investigation' under Section 173(8) and 're-investigation'. It establishes that further investigation is a statutory right of the police to gather more evidence, which does not require the Magistrate's permission, whereas re-investigation (to replace the original investigation) does.

rules.case_name: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
rules.reference: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
rules.relevance: While primarily concerning the registration of FIRs, this judgment reinforces the principle that the police have an independent duty to investigate cognizable offences and that judicial interference in the investigative process is limited, supporting the autonomy of the investigating agency under Section 173(8).

This section mandates the submission of the final report to the Magistrate. The interplay between Section 173(2) (submission of final report) and Section 173(8) (further investigation) is crucial to determining if the acceptance of the final report extinguishes the police's power to investigate further.

The substantive offence of gang rape charged against the appellants. The gravity of this offence underscores the necessity for a thorough investigation, including DNA testing as suggested by the High Court, to ensure justice is served.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012
rules.relevance: If the victim is a minor, this section mandates the investigation to be completed within one month and emphasizes the need for sensitive and thorough investigation, including forensic evidence, which supports the High Court's direction for DNA testing.

The right to life and personal liberty includes the right to a fair and effective investigation. The NHRC's involvement and the High Court's direction for DNA testing are grounded in the state's obligation under Article 21 to ensure that serious crimes are not left uninvestigated due to procedural lapses.

The legal principle that the police investigation is an independent function and not subject to the control of the Magistrate at the investigative stage, except for specific statutory checks. This principle underpins the interpretation of Section 173(8) CrPC.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Sukhdev Singh v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This case discusses the scope of judicial review in criminal investigations and the limits of High Court interference, which is relevant to the Appellants' challenge to the High Court's order directing further investigation.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the challenge to the arbitral award is made, specifically regarding whether the award is in conflict with the public policy of India or vitiated by patent illegality.

Central to the issue of whether Enexio's claim was time-barred. The High Court relied on this section to hold that the minutes of the meeting constituted an acknowledgment of debt, thereby extending the limitation period.

rules.case_name: Oxford Shipping Co. Ltd. v. Jindal Agri Products Ltd.
rules.reference: Oxford Shipping Co. Ltd. v. Jindal Agri Products Ltd.
rules.relevance: A key precedent establishing that an acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act must be in writing and signed by the debtor, and that it must unequivocally admit the existence of a subsisting liability. Relevant for analyzing the validity of the April 2018 minutes.

rules.case_name: M/s. R. Viswanathan v. R. Narayana Iyer
rules.reference: M/s. R. Viswanathan v. R. Narayana Iyer
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that an acknowledgment must be an admission of a subsisting liability. Relevant to determine if the meeting minutes acknowledged the specific principal amount claimed by Enexio.

rules.case_name: M/s. Chloro Controls (India) Private Ltd. v. Severn Trent Water Purification Inc.
rules.reference: M/s. Chloro Controls (India) Private Ltd. v. Severn Trent Water Purification Inc.
rules.relevance: The leading Supreme Court judgment on the 'Group of Companies' doctrine. It is directly relevant to the issue of whether Gita Power, a non-signatory holding company, can be held jointly and severally liable under the arbitration agreement signed by OPG.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Concord Biotech Ltd.
rules.reference: Union of India v. Concord Biotech Ltd.
rules.relevance: Clarifies the scope of 'patent illegality' under Section 34(2)(b)(ii) of the Arbitration Act. It holds that an error of law, even if serious, does not amount to patent illegality unless it violates the substantive law of India or the fundamental policy of Indian law. Relevant to the challenge regarding the tribunal's limitation analysis.

Provides that where a provision of the Act states that parties are free to agree, such agreement shall be given effect to. Relevant to the enforceability of the ICC Rules and the arbitration clause in the purchase orders.

rules.case_name: Bharat Broadband Network Ltd. v. United Telecoms Ltd.
rules.reference: Bharat Broadband Network Ltd. v. United Telecoms Ltd.
rules.relevance: Discusses the extent of judicial review in arbitration awards and the concept of 'fundamental policy of Indian law'. Relevant to assessing whether the Single Judge's finding of 'dichotomy' in limitation analysis amounted to a violation of public policy.
Defines the general rule that suits barred by limitation shall be dismissed. Relevant to the tribunal's rejection of the declaratory relief and counterclaims as time-barred.

rules.reference: Principle of Set-off and Counterclaims in Arbitration
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether the tribunal was perverse for rejecting the counterclaims as time-barred while allowing the principal claim, and whether the tribunal should have adjusted the amounts. This touches upon the tribunal's discretion in managing claims and counterclaims within the limitation framework.

This is the primary statutory provision prescribing the limitation period for passing assessment orders following a remand order by the Appellate Tribunal. The core legal dispute centers on whether the time taken for proceedings under Section 144C is included within this limitation period.

This section governs the mechanism for resolution of disputes by the Dispute Resolution Panel (DRP) for eligible assessees. The appeal hinges on whether the procedural timelines under this section are independent of the limitation period under Section 153(3) or subsumed within it.

rules.reference: Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020
rules.relevance: This Act extended the limitation period under Section 153(3) to 30.09.2021. It is relevant to determine the exact deadline by which the Assessing Officer was required to pass the order, and whether the Draft Assessment Order passed on 28.09.2021 was within time.

rules.case_name: Shelf Drilling Ron Tappmeyer Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer
rules.relevance: This is the impugned judgment where the High Court held that the time period for proceedings under Section 144C is subsumed within the limitation period of Section 153(3). The Supreme Court appeal directly challenges this interpretation.

rules.reference: Principle of Statutory Interpretation regarding Limitation
rules.relevance: The general legal principle that limitation periods are strictly construed, and that time spent on mandatory statutory procedures (like DRP proceedings) may or may not be excluded depending on the specific wording of the statute. The court must decide if Section 153(3) explicitly or implicitly excludes DRP time.

This section deals with the general limitation for passing assessment orders after a remand. Comparing the language of Section 153(1) with Section 153(3) may help determine if the legislature intended different treatment for DRP cases versus regular remand cases.

The argument that Section 144C creates a distinct procedural framework for eligible assessees, and thus its timelines should operate independently of the general limitation provisions applicable to non-eligible assessees or regular remands.

rules.case_name: Various
rules.reference: Supreme Court Precedents on Limitation in Tax Matters
rules.relevance: General precedents establishing how courts interpret 'time taken for proceedings' in the context of limitation periods under the Income Tax Act, particularly whether administrative delays or mandatory appellate processes are excluded from the limitation clock.

Mentioned in the facts as the initial notice issued. While less central to the limitation issue, it establishes the procedural history and the start of the assessment process, providing context for the timeline calculations.

Rules governing the procedure before the Dispute Resolution Panel may define the specific timelines for filing objections and passing recommendations, which are relevant to calculating the total time consumed under Section 144C.

This article guarantees minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions. It is the primary constitutional shield relied upon by minority institutions to argue that the RTE Act and TET mandates are ultra vires as they interfere with their administrative autonomy.

This article provides the fundamental right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14. It serves as the constitutional basis for the RTE Act and the State's argument for enforcing minimum teacher qualifications like TET to ensure quality education.

rules.case_name: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India
rules.reference: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The Constitution Bench held that the RTE Act is ultra vires the Constitution insofar as it applies to minority educational institutions. This is the central precedent cited by the Madras High Court to exempt minority schools from TET requirements and is the subject of the appeal regarding whether it needs reconsideration.

rules.reference: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
rules.relevance: Section 23 empowers the Central Government to prescribe minimum qualifications for teachers. This is the statutory basis for the NCTE's mandate of TET as a minimum qualification, which is challenged in its applicability to minority institutions and in-service teachers.

rules.reference: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (Amendment) Act, 2017
rules.relevance: This amendment introduced a specific timeline requiring in-service teachers appointed before 31st March 2015 to acquire minimum qualifications (including TET) within four years. It is directly relevant to the claims of individual teachers seeking promotion without TET.

rules.case_name: Ahmedabad St. Xavier’s College Society v. State of Gujarat
rules.reference: Ahmedabad St. Xavier’s College Society v. State of Gujarat
rules.relevance: Cited by the Bombay High Court to support the view that reasonable regulations regarding teacher qualifications do not violate Article 30(1). It establishes the balance between minority rights and state regulatory power over educational standards.

rules.reference: National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) Regulations
rules.relevance: These notifications mandated TET as a minimum qualification for teacher recruitment. Their validity and applicability to minority institutions and in-service teachers are the core regulatory instruments under challenge in these appeals.

The court must apply this principle to reconcile the apparent conflict between Article 21A (Right to Education/Quality) and Article 30(1) (Minority Rights), determining whether TET mandates can be read as reasonable regulations that do not destroy the minority character of institutions.

Relevant to the issue of whether the Constitution Bench decision in Pramati requires reconsideration by a larger bench. The court must determine if there are sufficient grounds to depart from or overrule the existing precedent.

A key legal distinction under Article 30(1). The court must decide if TET is a 'reasonable regulation' concerning educational standards (permissible) or an intrusion into the 'administration' of the institution (impermissible for minorities).

The central provision under dispute; it grants minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions. The appeal seeks to determine the criteria for qualifying as a 'minority educational institution' under this article.

rules.case_name: S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India
rules.reference: S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The primary precedent being challenged. It held that AMU was not a minority institution because it was established by statute (AMU Act, 1920) rather than by the Muslim minority community.
The statute that incorporated AMU, dissolving the MAO College. The interpretation of this Act is crucial to determining whether the University was 'established' by the minority or by the State.

rules.case_name: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
rules.reference: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
rules.relevance: An eleven-Judge Bench decision that framed questions regarding the indicia for treating an institution as a minority educational institution, leaving the specific application to a regular bench.

rules.case_name: Anjuman-e-Rahmaniya v. District Inspector of Schools
rules.reference: Anjuman-e-Rahmaniya v. District Inspector of Schools
rules.relevance: A two-Judge Bench decision that doubted the correctness of Azeez Basha and referred the matter to a larger bench, initiating the re-examination of minority status criteria.

rules.reference: National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions Act
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether legislative amendments and the establishment of a regulatory commission affect the criteria for qualifying as a minority educational institution.

rules.case_name: Prof. Yashpal v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.reference: Prof. Yashpal v. State of Chhattisgarh
rules.relevance: Cited in the issues to determine its bearing on the criteria for qualifying as a minority educational institution, particularly regarding the definition of 'establishment'.
Relevant to the issue of whether registration as a society under this Act causes an institution to lose its minority status.
Often read in conjunction with Article 30(1) to understand the scope of minority rights in education and non-discrimination in admission.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Essential Ingredients of Minority Institution
rules.relevance: The legal principle under scrutiny: whether 'establishment' and 'administration' must both be by the minority, and whether state participation or statutory incorporation negates minority character.

rules.case_name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
rules.reference: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This is the foundational precedent establishing the 'Polluter Pays Principle' and 'Precautionary Principle' in Indian environmental law. It directed the constitution of the LoEA and established that liability for environmental damage is not limited to the period of pollution but continues until the damage is reversed.

rules.reference: Article 21 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The right to a wholesome environment is an integral part of the right to life under Article 21. This provision underpins the court's power to enforce environmental protection and compensation for victims of pollution.

rules.reference: Article 48A of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: This directive principle imposes a duty on the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife, supporting the State's obligation to enforce the LoEA's orders.

rules.reference: Article 51A(g) of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: This fundamental duty requires every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures. It supports the argument that polluters have a continuing duty to reverse damage.

rules.reference: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
rules.relevance: Sections 7 and 16 empower the State Pollution Control Board to issue directions to industries to stop or prevent pollution. Section 24 deals with the duty of occupiers to prevent escape of poisonous substances. These sections form the statutory basis for regulating tannery effluents.

Section 3 empowers the Central Government to take measures to protect and improve the environment, including laying down standards for effluents. Section 5 requires persons handling hazardous substances to take all necessary measures to prevent accidents. This Act provides the overarching framework for the LoEA's authority.

A core legal principle affirmed in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum, stating that the polluter is liable for the cost of remedying pollution and compensating victims. It establishes that this liability is not a one-time payment but continues until the ecological damage is fully reversed.

This principle requires that where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation. It supports the enforcement of strict compliance and continuous monitoring.

rules.reference: Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (as applied to LoEA proceedings)
rules.relevance: The LoEA proceedings are often treated as summary proceedings akin to Order XXXVII CPC for the recovery of compensation. This procedural framework supports the binding nature of the LoEA awards and the limited scope for challenging them on merits once passed.

rules.case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
rules.reference: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case)
rules.relevance: This case established the principle of absolute liability for hazardous industries and the concept of 'fundamental right to compensation' for victims. It reinforces the argument that compensation for environmental damage is a continuing obligation until the harm is remedied.

This provision mandates the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor if the Resolution Plan is not implemented within the time specified in the plan or as extended by the Adjudicating Authority. It is central to the issue of whether the SRA's failure to infuse cash and pay dues warrants liquidation.

Section 31 deals with the approval of the Resolution Plan by the Adjudicating Authority. The dispute arises from the interpretation of the approved plan's terms, specifically regarding the payment structure and the role of the Performance Bank Guarantee.

Section 30 outlines the requirements for a Resolution Plan, including the payment of operational debts and the manner of implementation. The SRA's failure to pay Provident Fund and Gratuity dues violates the statutory hierarchy and implementation requirements under this section.

rules.case_name: Swiss Ribbons Private Limited v. Union of India
rules.reference: Swiss Ribbons Private Limited v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment upholds the constitutionality of the IBC and emphasizes that the Resolution Plan approved by the CoC and NCLT is binding on all stakeholders. It supports the argument that deviations from the approved plan (like adjusting PBG against cash consideration) are impermissible without proper legal basis.

rules.case_name: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.reference: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.relevance: This precedent establishes that the implementation of the Resolution Plan is a critical phase of the CIRP. It highlights that the NCLT has the power to monitor implementation and that failure to implement can lead to liquidation, supporting the appellants' claim for liquidation due to non-compliance.

rules.reference: Privity of Contract and Terms of RFRP
rules.relevance: The Request for Resolution Plans (RFRP) explicitly stated that the PBG shall not be set-off against the consideration. As the Resolution Plan is a contract between the SRA and the CoC, general principles of contract law dictate that the specific terms of the RFRP and the approved Plan must be strictly adhered to, making the adjustment of PBG impermissible.

While the case is at the implementation stage, Section 7 initiated the CIRP. The objective of the IBC, as interpreted in various precedents, is to maximize the value of assets and ensure timely resolution. Indefinite extensions for implementation defeat this objective.

rules.case_name: Committee of Creditors of Essel Pinnacle Infrastructures Limited v. Wecon Engineers Limited
rules.reference: Committee of Creditors of Essel Pinnacle Infrastructures Limited v. Wecon Engineers Limited
rules.relevance: This case discusses the binding nature of the Resolution Plan and the limited scope of judicial review. It reinforces that once a plan is approved, it must be implemented as per its terms, and deviations (such as altering payment modes) are not permissible unless explicitly allowed by the plan or law.

Section 53 prescribes the waterfall order of distribution of assets. The SRA's failure to pay statutory dues (Provident Fund and Gratuity) which rank high in the waterfall order, indicates a fundamental breach of the statutory framework governing the resolution process.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Frustration of Purpose / Timely Implementation
rules.relevance: The IBC is designed for time-bound resolution. Granting indefinite extensions for implementation, especially when the SRA fails to meet core financial obligations, frustrates the purpose of the Code. This principle supports the argument that the NCLAT's order allowing adjustment and extensions was contrary to the spirit of the IBC.

Central to the case as it abolishes 'Untouchability' and forbids its practice in any form. The petitioner argues that caste-based segregation and assignment of menial labour (like manual scavenging) to marginalized castes constitutes a violation of this article.
Prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Relevant to challenge the classification of prisoners and allocation of labour based on caste.

Guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which includes the right to live with human dignity. The Court must determine if caste-based discrimination and degrading labour violate the dignity of prisoners.
Prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour. Relevant to the claim that assigning menial or 'degrading' labour to specific castes amounts to forced labour or exploitation.
Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of laws. Relevant to challenge the arbitrary classification of prisoners based on caste or 'habitual offender' status without reasonable nexus.

rules.reference: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955
rules.relevance: Enacts penalties for the preclusion of certain civil rights, including those arising from the practice of 'untouchability'. Relevant to the legal consequences of caste-based discrimination in prisons.

rules.reference: The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013
rules.relevance: Prohibits manual scavenging and employment of manual scavengers. Highly relevant as the petitioner alleges that prison manuals assign manual scavenging duties to marginalized castes.
The Union of India relies on this manual to argue that caste-based discrimination is prohibited. The Court must examine its adequacy in addressing caste-based division of labour and segregation.

rules.reference: Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act, 2023
rules.relevance: Cited by the Union of India as a legislative framework prohibiting discrimination. The Court must assess if this model act sufficiently addresses the targeting of Denotified Tribes and caste-based issues.
Defines 'Prisons' as a State subject. Relevant to the procedural and jurisdictional argument regarding the Union's role versus State responsibility in framing prison manuals.

Central to the appeal; protects the right to property by stating that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. The appellants argue that resumption without due process or compensation violates this article.

rules.reference: The Andhra Pradesh (Record of Rights in Land and Pattadar Pass Books) Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Relevant to the evidentiary value of the Pattadar Passbook held by the appellants. Section 11 typically provides that entries in the record of rights are prima facie evidence of the rights recorded therein, creating a presumption of ownership that the State must rebut.

rules.reference: Burden of Proof regarding Government Assigned Land
rules.relevance: Addresses the issue of whether the State discharged the burden of proving the land was assigned with non-alienation conditions. The principle holds that the burden lies on the State to prove the existence of such conditions and that the burden is not lightly discharged against a person holding a valid title deed and possession.

Relevant to the appellants' title derived from the 1970 sale deed. It governs the rights and liabilities of buyers and sellers, supporting the validity of the title acquired through a registered sale deed from a court auction purchaser.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Due Process of Law in Property Deprivation
rules.relevance: Relevant to the procedural flaw in resumption. Even if the State has the power to resume land, it must follow a valid 'authority of law' which includes fair procedure, notice, and opportunity to be heard, as implied by Article 300-A and Article 14.

Procedural relevance. The appellants issued a statutory notice under Section 80 before instituting the suit. This demonstrates compliance with procedural requirements for suing the Government, validating the maintainability of the suit for declaration and possession.

rules.reference: Presumption of Ownership from Long-standing Possession
rules.relevance: Supports the appellants' claim. Long-standing possession coupled with payment of land revenue and holding of a Pattadar Passbook creates a strong presumption of title, which the State failed to effectively rebut with specific evidence of non-alienation conditions.

Addresses the issue of resumption without compensation. While Article 300-A does not explicitly mandate compensation, judicial precedents often hold that deprivation of property without compensation, especially when the owner has a valid title, may be arbitrary and violative of Article 14 and 300-A.

Relevant to the suit for declaration of title. Section 34 allows any person having a beneficial interest in immovable property to institute a suit for declaration of their right, which is the primary relief sought by the appellants.

Relevant to the root of the appellants' title. The land was sold in a court auction in 1970. The principle that a court auction sale extinguishes prior encumbrances and vests title in the purchaser is central to establishing the appellants' valid title against the State's claim of prior assignment conditions.

Central to the first issue regarding fraudulent or wrongful trading. The appeal concerns whether recoveries from Section 66 applications should accrue to the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) or the creditors, and whether the NCLAT was justified in interfering with the CoC's commercial wisdom on this specific clause.

Governs the approval of the Resolution Plan by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT). Relevant to determining the scope of the NCLT's and NCLAT's power to interfere with the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) regarding the distribution of assets and Section 66 recoveries.

The overriding provision of the IBC. Crucial for the second issue regarding whether the IBC overrides the RBI Act and NHB Act, thereby validating the Resolution Plan's distribution mechanism despite it not providing for full repayment of Fixed Deposits.

Empowers the RBI to supersede the Board of Directors of a housing finance company. Relevant to the third issue concerning the status of erstwhile promoters/directors after supersession and their subsequent rights during the CIRP.

Regulates housing finance companies and their deposits. Relevant to the challenge by Fixed Deposit Holders claiming that the Resolution Plan violated statutory protections under the NHB Act, which the NCLAT dismissed in favor of the IBC's overriding effect.

Defines the functions of the Committee of Creditors (CoC). Relevant to the first issue regarding the extent of the CoC's commercial wisdom in structuring the Resolution Plan, including clauses related to Section 66 recoveries.

Deals with the management of the affairs of the Corporate Debtor by the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) or Resolution Professional (RP). Relevant to the third issue regarding the exclusion of erstwhile promoters from management and CoC meetings after the Board's supersession.

rules.case_name: Swiss Ribbons (P) Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Swiss Ribbons (P) Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent upholding the constitutional validity of the IBC and emphasizing the primacy of the CoC's commercial wisdom. Likely relevant to the Supreme Court's review of the NCLAT's interference with the CoC's decision on Section 66 recoveries.

rules.case_name: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.reference: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
rules.relevance: Establishes that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is not subject to judicial review unless there is a violation of the IBC or manifest arbitrariness. Directly relevant to the first issue regarding the NCLAT's setting aside of the SRA's clause on Section 66 recoveries.

Specific provision under the IBC allowing the RBI to initiate CIRP against housing finance companies. Relevant to the procedural history and the initial trigger for the insolvency process, establishing the context for the supersession of the Board.

This article empowers the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, including Scheduled Castes, which is the primary source of power for reservation policies and the subject of the sub-classification debate.

This article allows the State to make provisions for reservation in matters of promotion or appointment for any class of citizens which is not adequately represented in the services under the State, directly relevant to the Punjab and Haryana service reservation schemes.

The core issue involves whether the 'deeming fiction' in Article 341, which specifies that only the President can specify Scheduled Castes, creates a homogeneous class that prohibits further sub-classification by States.

The challenge to sub-classification often rests on the argument that it violates the guarantee of equality before law and equal protection of laws, requiring an analysis of whether such classification is reasonable and non-arbitrary.

The Supreme Court noted inconsistencies with Article 338, which establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Castes to safeguard their interests, implying a recognition of diverse needs within the SC community that may support sub-classification.

rules.case_name: E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: This is the specific precedent relied upon by the High Court to strike down the sub-classification. The Constitution Bench is tasked with reviewing the correctness of this judgment, which held that sub-classification of SCs is impermissible.

rules.case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
rules.reference: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court noted inconsistencies between Chinnaiah and this landmark judgment. Indra Sawhney established the framework for reservations and the concept of 'creamy layer' for OBCs, raising questions about whether similar logic applies to SCs.

rules.reference: Punjab Scheduled Castes and Backward Classes (Reservation in Services) Act, 2006
rules.relevance: This is the specific state legislation challenged in the appeal, which provided for 25% reservation for SCs with a further sub-classification favoring Balmikis and Mazhabi Sikhs.
This statute is cited as another example of state-level sub-classification of Scheduled Castes (allocating 16% to Arunthathiyars), reinforcing the factual context of the constitutional question.

rules.reference: Principle of Sub-classification within Backward Classes
rules.relevance: The legal principle regarding whether a class identified as 'backward' can be further sub-classified to ensure equitable distribution of benefits among the most disadvantaged sections within that class, distinguishing between homogeneity and heterogeneity of the class.
Central to the appeal; defines the procedure for re-assessment of duty and the issuance of show cause notices, which is the subject of the jurisdictional dispute regarding DRI officers.

The specific legislative provision enacted retrospectively to validate actions taken under the Customs Act, including show cause notices issued by DRI officers, which is challenged for constitutional validity.
The respondents challenge Section 97 of the Finance Act, 2022, as manifestly arbitrary and violative of the right to equality under Article 14.
Defines 'proper officer'. The Department argues that Notification No. 44/2011 assigned functions of 'proper officer' to DRI officers under this definition read with Section 5.

Deals with assessment of duty. The Canon India judgment relied on the principle that only officers with assessment powers under Section 17 could act as proper officers under Section 28, a point contested by the Department citing amendments by the Finance Act, 2011.
Pertains to the entrustment of functions. The Canon India judgment held that DRI officers required entrustment under Section 6 to act as proper officers, which the Department contends was overlooked.

The Department contends that the Canon India judgment suffered from an error apparent on the face of the record by failing to consider this notification, which assigned functions of 'proper officer' to DRI officers.

rules.case_name: M/s Canon India Private Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (2021)
rules.reference: M/s Canon India Private Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs
rules.relevance: The judgment under review. It held that DRI officers lacked jurisdiction to issue show cause notices under Section 28, relying on the Sayed Ali precedent.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Customs v. Sayed Ali (2011)
rules.reference: Commissioner of Customs v. Sayed Ali
rules.relevance: The precedent relied upon in Canon India to hold that only officers assigned functions of assessment under Section 17 could act as 'proper officers' under Section 28.
Introduced by the Validation Act, 2011. Its constitutional validity is a key issue, with conflicting High Court judgments (Mangali Impex vs. Sunil Gupta) cited in the background.

The core procedural mechanism invoked by the appellant to challenge the Tribunal's jurisdiction to implead non-signatories. The issue is whether the Tribunal correctly exercised its power under Section 16 to reject the counter-claim against non-signatories or if it overstepped by impleading them.

The appellant contends that no notice of invocation was issued to it under Section 21. This provision governs the commencement of arbitral proceedings and is central to the argument that the appellant was never properly brought into the arbitration.

This section provides the limited scope for appealing an arbitral tribunal's order on a preliminary point of jurisdiction. The High Court's dismissal under this section is the specific order being challenged in the Supreme Court.

The substantive legal doctrine relied upon by SPCPL to bind the non-signatories (ABPL and AISPL). The appeal hinges on whether the facts satisfy the requirements of this doctrine (common will, direct involvement, etc.) to extend the arbitration agreement to non-signatories.

rules.case_name: Chloro Controls Private Limited v. Severn Trent Water Purification Private Limited
rules.reference: Chloro Controls Private Limited v. Severn Trent Water Purification Private Limited
rules.relevance: A landmark Supreme Court precedent that recognized the 'Group of Companies Doctrine' in Indian arbitration law. It sets out the criteria for impleading non-signatories, which is directly relevant to assessing the validity of the Tribunal's and High Court's application of this doctrine.

The appellant argues it was not impleaded at the Section 11 referral stage. This section deals with the appointment of arbitrators and the determination of the existence of an arbitration agreement, raising the issue of whether jurisdictional challenges regarding non-signatories must be resolved at this stage.

The principle that an arbitral tribunal has the authority to rule on its own jurisdiction. The appellant challenges the extent of this power, specifically whether it allows the Tribunal to implead a new party on its own accord without prior consent or invocation.

Defines the 'Arbitration Agreement'. The dispute centers on whether the agreement in the Works Contract extends to ABPL and AISPL, who are not signatories, thereby questioning the very existence of an arbitration agreement binding them.

rules.case_name: Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A.
rules.reference: Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A.
