rules.relevance: While primarily about the applicability of Part I of the Act, this case and subsequent jurisprudence often discuss the scope of arbitration agreements and the autonomy of the arbitral tribunal, providing background context for jurisdictional limits.

The general common law principle that only parties to a contract can sue or be sued on it. The appellant relies on this to argue that as a non-signatory, it cannot be bound by the arbitration clause, absent specific exceptions like the Group of Companies Doctrine.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Sanjeev V. Deshpande
rules.reference: Union of India v. Sanjeev V. Deshpande
rules.relevance: This is the central precedent relied upon by the appellant (DRI). It holds that dealing in any psychotropic substance listed in the Schedule to the NDPS Act constitutes an offence under Section 8(c) if regulatory conditions are not met, effectively overruling the earlier view that Schedule I of the Rules was a prerequisite for Section 8 applicability.

rules.case_name: State of Uttaranchal v. Rajesh Kumar Gupta
rules.reference: State of Uttaranchal v. Rajesh Kumar Gupta
rules.relevance: This is the precedent relied upon by the High Court and Special Judges to dismiss the DRI's case. It held that Section 8 of the NDPS Act does not apply to substances not listed in Schedule I of the NDPS Rules. The appeal challenges the continued validity of this decision in light of Sanjeev V. Deshpande.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The specific provision under which the respondents were charged. The core legal issue is whether this section applies to psychotropic substances listed in the Act's Schedule but not in Schedule I of the Rules.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The provision under which Respondent No. 1 was charged in Criminal Appeal No. 1319 of 2013 for illegal possession. The applicability of this section depends on the interpretation of Section 8 and the scheduling of Buprenorphine Hydrochloride.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
rules.relevance: The provision under which respondents were charged for contravention of provisions of the Act or rules made thereunder. The validity of these charges hinges on whether the lack of Schedule I listing negates the offence.

rules.reference: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Rules, 1985
rules.relevance: The specific schedule referenced in the conflicting precedents. The dispute centers on whether the absence of Buprenorphine Hydrochloride from this schedule exempts it from the penal provisions of the NDPS Act.

The procedural provision under which the respondents sought alteration of charges. The appeal raises the issue of whether an accused can seek discharge or deletion of an offence from a charge already framed under Section 228.
The provision under which the Special Judges framed the charges. The third issue in the appeal concerns the procedural propriety of challenging a charge once it has been framed under this section.

The alternative statute under which the Special Judges proposed to try the case. The relevance lies in determining whether the matter falls exclusively under the NDPS Act or concurrently/alternatively under the D&C Act.

rules.reference: Prospective vs. Retrospective Operation of Judicial Decisions
rules.relevance: A key legal principle at issue: whether the Supreme Court's decision in Sanjeev V. Deshpande, which overruled Rajesh Kumar Gupta, operates with prospective effect only, thereby potentially saving the earlier convictions or proceedings based on the old law.
Creates the statutory presumption that a cheque is drawn for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt. The central issue is whether the accused rebutted this presumption.
Defines the offence of dishonour of cheque. Relevant for the procedural requirement of issuing a statutory notice and the accused's failure to reply to it.
Presumes that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration. The Trial Court relied on this presumption alongside Section 139.
Grants the Supreme Court special leave to appeal. Relevant to the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to hear the appeal against the High Court's revisional order.
Governs the High Court's revisional jurisdiction. The issue is whether the High Court was justified in interfering with concurrent findings of fact in the absence of perversity.

rules.case_name: Kusum Ingots & Steel (P) Ltd. v. Payal Industrial Corporation
rules.reference: Kusum Ingots & Steel (P) Ltd. v. Payal Industrial Corporation
rules.relevance: Holds that the presumption under Section 139 is rebuttable only by cogent and credible evidence. Mere denial or vague assertions are insufficient.

rules.case_name: Dalbir Singh v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Dalbir Singh v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: Clarifies that the accused must lead evidence to rebut the presumption under Section 139. The accused's failure to lead evidence regarding financial capacity is critical.
Establishes that appellate or revisional courts should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts unless the findings are perverse or based on no evidence.
Once the presumption under Section 139 arises, the burden shifts to the accused to rebut it. The accused's failure to file documents or examine witnesses supports the presumption.
Defines the burden of proof. Relevant to determining who bears the burden to prove the existence of the debt and the accused's burden to rebut the statutory presumption.

Central to the issue of arbitrator independence and impartiality. The provision renders a person ineligible to be an arbitrator if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to their independence or impartiality. The conflict in precedents (TRF/Perkins vs. CORE) hinges on whether a party with such ineligibility can still nominate an arbitrator.

Mandates that parties shall be treated with equality and each party shall be given a full opportunity of presenting his case. The appeal specifically questions whether this principle of equal treatment applies at the stage of appointment of arbitrators, challenging unilateral appointment clauses.

Guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws. The appeal examines whether unilateral appointment clauses in public-private contracts, where a government entity appoints the sole or majority of arbitrators, violate this constitutional guarantee.

rules.case_name: TRF Ltd v. Energo Engineering Projects Ltd.
rules.reference: TRF Ltd v. Energo Engineering Projects Ltd.
rules.relevance: A key precedent holding that a person ineligible to be an arbitrator under Section 12(5) cannot nominate a sole arbitrator, applying the maxim 'qui facit per alium facit per se'. This view conflicts with CORE and is central to the reference.

rules.case_name: Central Organisation for Railway Electrification v. ECI-SPIC-SMO-MCML (JV) A Joint Venture Company (CORE)
rules.reference: Central Organisation for Railway Electrification v. ECI-SPIC-SMO-MCML (JV) A Joint Venture Company (CORE)
rules.relevance: A conflicting precedent that upheld an appointment process where one party curated a panel and the other selected from it, arguing that the selection process counterbalanced the initial power. The correctness of this judgment is explicitly under review in the current reference.

rules.case_name: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
rules.reference: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
rules.relevance: Reinforced the TRF Ltd position, holding that an ineligible party cannot nominate an arbitrator. It is one of the conflicting decisions prompting the Constitution Bench reference.

rules.case_name: Voestalpine Schienen GmbH v. Delhi Metro Rail Corporation Ltd.
rules.reference: Voestalpine Schienen GmbH v. Delhi Metro Rail Corporation Ltd.
rules.relevance: Upheld a panel curated by DMRC but directed it to be broad-based. It represents an earlier judicial approach to panel curation clauses that differs from the strict ineligibility stance in TRF/Perkins, contributing to the legal uncertainty.

rules.reference: Qui facit per alium facit per se
rules.relevance: The legal maxim meaning 'he who acts through another acts himself'. This principle is the basis for the argument in TRF and Perkins that a party lacking independence/impartiality cannot cure that defect by nominating an arbitrator on their behalf.
Deals with the appointment of arbitrators. The validity of the appointment mechanisms (unilateral or panel-based) directly impacts the jurisdiction and procedure under this section.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tantia Constructions Limited
rules.citation: (2020) 1 SCC 71 (Note: Often cited alongside CORE or as a subsequent development)
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tantia Constructions Limited
rules.relevance: A three-Judge Bench that prima facie disagreed with the CORE judgment and requested a larger Bench to examine its correctness, directly leading to the current Constitution Bench reference.

rules.reference: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 8
rules.relevance: This is the primary source of State legislative competence regarding 'intoxicating liquors'. The central issue is whether this entry grants exclusive power over all forms of alcohol or only potable alcohol, and whether it is ousted by Union powers.

rules.reference: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 52
rules.relevance: This entry grants Parliament power over industries declared expedient for Union control. It is the basis for the argument that Parliament can regulate alcohol industries, potentially overriding State powers under Entry 8.

rules.reference: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 33
rules.relevance: This concurrent entry covers trade and commerce in products of industries under Entry 52. The case involves determining if Parliament has occupied this field, thereby restricting State legislation on trade and commerce in alcohol.

The IDRA is the specific law enacted under Entry 52. Section 18G empowers the Central Government to regulate supply and distribution. The amendment to Item 26 excluding 'potable alcohol' is crucial to determining the current scope of Union vs. State power.

rules.case_name: Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd. v. State of U.P. (1990) 1 SCC 109
rules.reference: Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd. v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: This is the leading precedent ('Synthetics (7J)') that held 'intoxicating liquor' is limited to potable alcohol and that industrial alcohol falls under Union control via IDRA. The current appeal questions the correctness of this judgment.

rules.case_name: Bihar Distillery v. Union of India (1997) 2 SCC 727
rules.reference: Bihar Distillery v. Union of India
rules.relevance: This judgment expressed doubts about the correctness of Synthetics (7J), particularly regarding the interpretation of Entry 8 and the impact of IDRA on State powers, leading to the reference to the nine-Judge Bench.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. v. Lalta Prasad Vaish (2007) 13 SCC 463
rules.reference: State of U.P. v. Lalta Prasad Vaish
rules.relevance: Another judgment expressing doubts about Synthetics (7J), contributing to the legal uncertainty that necessitated the Constitution Bench reference to resolve the conflict between Entries 8, 52, and 33.

rules.reference: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 24
rules.relevance: This entry grants States power over industries subject to Entries 7 and 52 of List I. It is relevant to determining the residual power of States over alcohol industries if they are not fully occupied by the Union under Entry 52.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Pith and Substance / Harmonious Construction
rules.relevance: General constitutional principles for resolving conflicts between entries in different lists of the Seventh Schedule. The court must determine the true nature of the legislation and whether entries can be read harmoniously or if one overrides the other.

Relevant to assess if State laws regulating alcohol are merely a colourable attempt to legislate on matters reserved for the Union under Entry 52 and the IDRA, or if they genuinely fall within Entry 8.

rules.reference: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 97
rules.relevance: Central to the appellants' argument that DTH services constitute 'broadcasting' or 'services' exclusively taxable by the Central Government, thereby excluding State legislative competence.

rules.reference: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 62
rules.relevance: The basis for State Governments' claim to levy entertainment tax on DTH services, arguing that the 'entertainment' aspect of the service falls within their legislative domain.

The core legal doctrine invoked by respondents to argue that both Central Service Tax and State Entertainment Tax can coexist on DTH services by taxing different aspects (service vs. entertainment) of the same transaction.

Relevant to the Kerala High Court's finding that the exemption for cable operators with fewer than 7,500 connections under the Kerala Tax on Luxuries Act, 1976, was discriminatory and violative of the right to equality.

rules.provision: Provision regarding exemption for cable operators with <7,500 connections
rules.relevance: The specific state enactment challenged for being discriminatory under Article 14, forming the subject matter of the appeal from the Kerala High Court.

rules.provision: Amendments introducing tax on DTH services
rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Entertainment and Betting Tax Act, 1979
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of whether amendments introducing DTH taxation can be applied retrospectively, as held by the Allahabad High Court.

rules.provision: Provisions regarding commencement and retrospective application
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of validity of retrospective taxation and the method of bringing the Act into force, as upheld by the Jharkhand High Court.

rules.case_name: State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries Ltd.
rules.reference: Supreme Court precedents on Aspect Theory (e.g., State of W.B. v. Kesoram Industries)
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent establishing the Aspect Theory, which is central to resolving the conflict between Central and State taxing powers on DTH services.

rules.reference: Principle of Retrospective Legislation in Tax Laws
rules.relevance: Relevant to determining whether the State legislatures can validly enact clarificatory amendments with retrospective effect to tax DTH services for periods prior to the amendment.
Governs the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, providing the framework for analyzing the conflict between Entry 97 of List I and Entry 62 of List II.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the challenge to the arbitral award was made. The core legal issue is whether the power to 'set aside' an award under this section implicitly includes the power to 'modify' it, given that the 1996 Act removed the explicit modification power present in the 1940 Act.

The Supreme Court considered whether its plenary power to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice under Article 142 allows it to modify an arbitral award, even if the Arbitration Act does not explicitly grant such power to lower courts.

rules.case_name: Project Director NHAI v. M. Hakeem
rules.reference: Project Director NHAI v. M. Hakeem
rules.relevance: This is the leading precedent cited in the reference that held courts do not have the power to modify arbitral awards under the 1996 Act. The current appeal seeks to clarify or distinguish this holding due to conflicting judicial opinions.

Section 31 deals with the form and content of the arbitral award. It is relevant to the issue of whether courts can correct computational or clerical errors, as the Act provides specific mechanisms for such corrections within the award process itself.

Although Section 33 (Power to correct award) was omitted by the 2015 Amendment, it was part of the original 1996 Act and is relevant to the historical context of the dispute and the interpretation of the legislature's intent regarding modification versus correction.

This section deals with appeals against orders under Section 34. The reference questions whether the appellate court has the power to modify the award when hearing an appeal against a setting aside order.

rules.reference: UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration
rules.relevance: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, is modeled on the UNCITRAL Model Law. The Model Law does not provide for the modification of awards, only their setting aside. This international framework is crucial for interpreting the restrictive nature of Section 34.

The 1940 Act explicitly granted courts the power to modify awards. The contrast between the 1940 Act and the 1996 Act is central to the argument that the legislature intentionally removed the power to modify, thereby limiting courts to setting aside awards.

Both judges in the reference acknowledged that if an award is severable, the court may set aside the invalid portion while upholding the rest. This principle is relevant to determining the extent of judicial intervention in modifying the operative parts of an award.

rules.reference: Correction of Clerical and Computational Errors
rules.relevance: A narrow exception recognized by both opinions is the power to correct obvious clerical, typographical, or computational errors. This distinguishes between substantive modification (generally prohibited) and technical correction (permissible).

This is the primary statutory provision under which the suit was instituted. The core legal issue is whether a society registered under the Societies Registration Act falls within the definition of 'charitable or religious trust' or 'endowment' contemplated by this section.

The society in question is registered under this Act. The interpretation of the Act's nature and the legal status of societies registered under it is central to determining if they can be equated to trusts for the purpose of Section 92 CPC.

rules.case_name: Operation ASHA v. Dr. Shelly Batra
rules.reference: Operation ASHA v. Dr. Shelly Batra
rules.relevance: This is the specific case on appeal. The Supreme Court's decision in this matter will definitively settle the question of whether a society under the 1860 Act can be treated as a trust for Section 92 CPC purposes, overturning or affirming the High Court's view.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: A key precedent often cited in this context, holding that a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 is not a 'trust' within the meaning of Section 92 CPC, as it is a distinct legal entity governed by its own statute.

The High Court relied on the concept of 'constructive trust' to bring the society within the ambit of Section 92. The Supreme Court must evaluate whether this equitable doctrine can be stretched to cover statutory societies, or if it is limited to traditional trust relationships.

Defines the legal concept of a 'trust'. Comparing the definition here with the structure of a society under the 1860 Act is essential to determine if the society's MoA and AoA create a trust relationship.

rules.case_name: Gobind Dayal v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gobind Dayal v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: An older precedent that has been discussed in the context of whether societies can be treated as trusts. It provides historical context on the judicial interpretation of Section 92 CPC regarding non-trust entities.

rules.reference: Statutory Interpretation: Specific vs. General Law
rules.relevance: The principle that a specific statute (Societies Registration Act, 1860) governs the entity, and general provisions (like Section 92 CPC regarding trusts) should not be applied unless the specific statute explicitly allows or the entity fits the strict definition.

Section 91 deals with suits for direction regarding public charities. While Section 92 is the specific provision for trusts, Section 91 is often read in conjunction to understand the scope of judicial intervention in charitable matters, distinguishing between public charities and private trusts/societies.

rules.case_name: K. S. N. Raju v. K. S. N. Venkateswara Rao
rules.reference: K. S. N. Raju v. K. S. N. Venkateswara Rao
rules.relevance: Discusses the nature of charitable trusts and the requirements for invoking Section 92. It helps in analyzing whether the 'charitable' objective of the society is sufficient to override the structural difference between a society and a trust.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: This is the primary substantive provision under which the accused was charged. The central issue is whether 'possession' or 'viewing' falls within the scope of 'producing', 'directing', 'organizing', 'permitting', 'facilitating', 'participating in', or 'offering' child pornography as defined in this section.

This section penalizes publishing or transmitting child pornography in electronic form. The High Court quashed proceedings partly on the ground that mere possession without transmission does not violate this section. The Supreme Court must determine if the High Court's interpretation aligns with the legislative intent.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: This section creates a statutory presumption of culpable mental state for offences under the POCSO Act. The appellants argue that the High Court failed to consider this presumption, which shifts the burden of proof regarding intent to the accused.

This provision grants the High Court inherent powers to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court, or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The scope of these powers in quashing FIRs at a preliminary stage is a key procedural issue.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
rules.relevance: This is the landmark precedent laying down the guidelines for the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. It establishes that quashing is appropriate only in rare cases where the allegations, even if taken at face value, do not constitute an offence.

rules.case_name: G. Vijay Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: G. Vijay Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: This Supreme Court judgment clarifies that the High Court should not decide disputed questions of fact or law at the stage of quashing proceedings under Section 482, but should only examine if the allegations disclose a prima facie offence.

rules.reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
rules.relevance: This section defines 'child pornography'. The interpretation of this definition is crucial to determine if the material found on the accused's phone (including files depicting underage boys) falls within the statutory definition, thereby triggering the applicability of Section 15.

rules.reference: Principle of Statutory Interpretation regarding 'Possession' vs 'Transmission'
rules.relevance: The case hinges on the legal distinction between passive possession/viewing and active transmission/publishing. The court must interpret whether the legislature intended to criminalize mere possession under the specific wording of Section 15 POCSO and Section 67B IT Act, or if such an omission implies it was not intended to be an offence.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: While primarily concerning Section 498A IPC, this judgment reinforces the principle that inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. cannot be used to decide complex questions of law or fact that require trial. It supports the argument that the High Court may have overstepped by interpreting substantive criminal law provisions in a quashing petition.

Although the charges are under POCSO and IT Act, Section 292 IPC deals with sale, etc., of obscene books, etc. It provides context for the general legal framework regarding obscenity and possession, helping to distinguish the specific, stricter liability imposed by special statutes like POCSO.

This is the central provision in dispute. It empowers the Court to extend the time for making the arbitral award. The key legal question is whether this power can be exercised or an application entertained after the award has already been passed, which determines the maintainability of the appellant's application.

This section establishes the statutory time limit of twelve months for making the award from the completion of pleadings. It defines the period within which the arbitrator must act, the expiry of which triggered the need for extension and the subsequent challenge.

This section provides the grounds for setting aside an arbitral award. The respondent challenged the award under this section, arguing that the award was invalid because it was passed after the mandate expired. The appeal requires determining if the procedural defect of late award is a valid ground for setting aside under Section 34.

This provision allows parties to extend the arbitrator's mandate by mutual consent. The facts indicate the parties exercised this right, extending the mandate to 20.02.2024. This is relevant to establish the timeline and the fact that the award was passed after even this extended period had lapsed.

This section states that the arbitral award shall be final and binding on the parties and persons claiming under them. It underscores the finality of the award, which is weighed against the procedural irregularity of the delay in passing it.

rules.reference: Principle of Curability of Procedural Defects
rules.relevance: This legal principle suggests that minor procedural irregularities, such as delay in passing an award, may be curable if they do not affect the merits of the case or cause prejudice to the parties. This is relevant to the argument that the award should not be set aside merely for delay if the extension application was filed.

Since the parties had previously agreed to extend the mandate and engaged in settlement discussions, this principle may be relevant to argue that the respondent cannot now take advantage of the delay to set aside the award, especially if they contributed to the delay.

This section deals with the rules applicable to the substance of the dispute and the making of the award. It is relevant to ensure that the award was made in accordance with the agreement of the parties and the law, independent of the timing issue.
This section governs the form and content of the arbitral award. It is relevant to confirm that the award passed on 11.05.2024 met the formal requirements, even if passed late.

General principles of statutory interpretation regarding whether time limits in arbitration statutes are mandatory or directory, and whether courts have inherent powers to condone delay in the interest of justice, are relevant to deciding the appeal.
